Now, the *Śrītattvanidhi*.
Therein, first is the *Mahāśaktidevatālakṣaṇanidhi*. May there be auspiciousness!
May there be no obstacles.
Salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas.
Salutations to the illustrious Caṇḍikā.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, and has four arms.
One should meditate upon the one with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles. || 1 ||
At the time of bestowing prosperity, she has the luster of fresh coral; at the time of bestowing knowledge, she is as white as the autumnal moon.
I take refuge in the Mother, the progenitor of the three worlds, who possesses the hue of a sapphire and was born from a lotus, for the sake of conquering the host of enemies.
Victory to you, O Goddess Cāmuṇḍā; victory to you, the remover of the suffering of living beings!
Victory to you, O omnipresent Goddess! O Bhadrakālī, salutations to you! || 3 ||
The illustrious goddess Cāmuṇḍikā, through the auspicious glance of her sidelong look.
Of the Nigamas, Āgamas, Tantras, and even the words of the Purāṇas.
The term *dharmaśāstra* applies even to jokes and incidental remarks.
Having truly extracted the essence of mantra, astrology, and the arts.
And for each of the deities headed by Cāmuṇḍā, separately.
Of their own forms, weapons, colors, ornaments, vehicles, and marks. || 3 ||
And after that, the various classifications of garments designated by the names of flowers.
And the characteristics of the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, Īśa, Brahmā, and Śakra.
The distinctions between the times of the Yugas and the qualities and defects arising from time, as well as the sequences of other topics to be discussed, will be explained here in this context. (5)
By King Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign lord of the city of Mahīśūra.
In the auspicious treatise named Śrītattvanidhi, which consists of nine nidhis.
They are being elucidated according to my understanding for the benefit of the world of conceptual proliferation.
This sequence, however, is to be understood in relation to the procedures that are about to be described. || 7 ||
The characteristics of the great powers (mahāśakti), such as Cāmuṇḍā and others, are in the first treasure (nidhi).
In the second [chapter], the characteristics of the various forms of Viṣṇu have been declared.
In the third [chapter], the characteristics of the forms of Śiva, Śaiva, and so forth, are taught.
In the fourth [chapter], there is the description of the forms of the gods, such as Brahmā and Śakra.
In the fifth [chapter], there is the description of the planets, constellations, time, and so forth.
In the sixth [chapter], the characteristics of Harikṣetra, Śāligrāma, and so forth, have been declared.
In the seventh [chapter], however, there is the description of the sacred fields of Śiva, the Śiva-liṅgas, and so forth.
The characteristics of the Nigamas, Āgamas, Tantras, and so forth were proclaimed in the eighth [chapter].
And in the ninth [chapter], the wonders beginning with the enumeration of the scripts have been declared.
Through the knowledge of these nine treasures, the nine treasures become easily attainable.
1. Now, the meditation on Śrī Cāmuṇḍeśvarī (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda) is proclaimed: Caṇḍī is golden-hued and possesses a most beautiful form.
She is armed with a bow, stands in the prime of youth, is wrathful, and is considered to be standing upright. || 1 ||
She had a slender waist, large eyes, and beautiful, full breasts.
She has one face, beautiful necks, and is endowed with twenty arms.
Tridents, swords, spears, discuses, arrows, conchs, and thunderbolts as well.
And [he holds] the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and a small knife (churikā) with his right hands. || 3 ||
Always auspicious, she bears [the world] through the sequential application of the upward and other directions.
A serpent, a noose, likewise a shield, an axe, a goad, and a bow.
Bearing a bell, a banner, a mace, and a mirror, she is able to assume any form at will.
Then that buffalo fell with its head severed and its skull shattered.
A man arose from its neck, enraged, with hands raised in terror.
His eyebrows, beard, and eyes were red, like those of a goat pierced by a spear.
But while being devoured by the lion, he was bound tightly by the neck with a noose.
She stands with her left foot treading upon a lion and her right foot in the ālīḍha posture, trampling a demon.
This Caṇḍī, with her uplifted weapon, is the destroyer of all enemies; she is golden-hued. 1.
2. Now, the meditation on Rājarājeśvarī (from the Ṣoḍaśīkalpa): [One should meditate upon her] who dwells on the left lap of Śiva, possessing the pride and beauty of ten million [goddesses].
[She who possesses] the splendor of many tens of millions of moons and tens of millions of suns risen at one time.
Her radiance reddens the circles of many millions of cosmic eggs.
Resembling the hibiscus flower, we meditate upon her who is of the nature of the *japā* [flower]. || 2 ||
Resembling the interior of saffron and as red as a pomegranate flower.
She possesses the radiance of ten million rising suns, has three eyes, and is resplendent with the young moon as her crown.
Her hands shine with a noose, a goad, a bow, and five arrows.
He possessed the luster of the tip of an unswerving lightning flash and was clothed in tawny garments.
Her thighs, hips, and the circles of her breasts were perfectly symmetrical and well-rounded.
The millions of hollows within it were fashioned like moons drenched in nectar.
(3) She whose forehead is adorned with a tilaka, whose eyes are like the earth, and whose glances are like lotuses;
she whose eyes are filled with compassion flowing forth from the channels of her sidelong glances. (6)
Adorned with jeweled earrings shaped like the orbs of the sun and moon.
She is adorned with a nose-ornament that has the appearance of the planet Venus.
Her row of teeth creates the illusion of a dense cluster of pomegranate seeds.
She whose own voice brings forth the excellence of qualities that cause the sound of the lute to seem dull.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by the scent of camphor betel rolls.
The radiance of her cheek-plates, which dispels the pride of the jewel-mirror.
Her lotus-face was serene, and her eyes were filled with gentle smiles.
Her neck, resembling a conch shell, was radiant with a jeweled auspicious thread.
Whose four creeper-like arms have become a support for the wish-fulfilling vine.
Her sprout-like fingers were radiant with clusters of jewel rings.
Her breasts were like golden mountains, radiant with streams of bright pearl necklaces.
Her waist was bent by the weight of her breasts, and her belly was beautiful with its three folds.
Her hips were encircled by a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels.
Her shanks, thighs, and lower legs were well-rounded, her ankles were hidden, and she had curly locks of hair.
Her lotus feet are beautiful and charming, with anklets and jeweled ornaments jingling.
Adorned with necklaces, bracelets, crowns, armlets, and bangles made of jewels.
She possessed a neck like a conch shell, was endowed with a beautiful nose, had lips like the bimba fruit, and a face like the moon.
She was enriched with every kind of elegant attire and adorned with all manner of ornaments.
Fragrant with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk.
To her whose lotus-feet are rubbed by the moon-jewels of [the gods'] crowns during the act of worship.
Seated upon a throne of five corpses, she is the embodiment of the five *praṇavas*; her complexion is the color of vermilion. (1)
3. Now, the meditation on Mahākālī (from the Caṇḍīkalpa):

[One should meditate upon her] holding in her hands a sword, a discus, a mace, arrows, a bludgeon, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, a severed head, and a conch; she has three eyes and is adorned with ornaments on all her limbs.

He praised Mahākālikā—who possesses the luster of a blue gem and whose feet are served by ten elephants—when Hari had fallen asleep, so that she might slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha; she who is blue in color. 1.
4. Now, the meditation on Mahālakṣmī (from the Caṇḍīkalpa):
[She holds] a rosary, an axe, a spear, and a thunderbolt; a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, a javelin, a sword, a shield, a lotus, a bell, and a vessel of wine.

I worship here Mahālakṣmī, who sits upon a lotus, possesses the luster of coral, and holds a trident, a noose, and the Sudarśana discus in her hands, as she tramples upon an elephant. (1) [Her complexion is the color of coral. (1)
5. Now, the meditation on Mahāsarasvatī (from the Caṇḍīkalpa):
She holds a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her lotus-like hands; she possesses a luster equal to the cool-rayed moon shining at the end of the dark clouds.

I worship Sarasvatī, who emerged from the body of Gaurī, who is the support of the three worlds, the Great One (Mahāpūrvā), and the destroyer of the Daityas such as Śumbha; she is white in color. 1. 1.
Now, according to the method of the *Lalitopākhyāna*, the meditation on the deities residing within the Śrīcakra begins:
6. Meditation on the deities who bestow the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā* and others:
*Aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *garimā*, and likewise *laghimā*.
Attainment, the power of irresistible will, lordship, and sovereignty—these are the eight prosperities.
Liberation, accomplishment, and the accomplishment of all things—these are declared to be the ten accomplishments (siddhis).
These goddesses have four arms and resemble the hibiscus flower in hue.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the skull-cup, the trident, and the perfected collyrium.
They are filled with compassion and are resorted to by perfected yogis. [The color is] red. 10.
7. Now, the visualization of the eight Mātṛkās together with Mahālakṣmī:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī;
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh.
Mahālakṣmī and Aṣṭamī have two arms and red complexions.
She wears red garments and carries both a skull-cup and a blue lotus. || 2 ||
Alternatively, some explain meditation in another manner.
They possess forms resembling those of Brahmā and others, and they bear weapons resembling those of Brahmā and others.
They are proclaimed as those who bear the supreme insignia of Brahmā and the other deities. [Their] color is red. 8.
8. Now, the visualization of the ten deities of the mudrās, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī:
[They are visualized] with hands possessing the luster of lotuses, engaged in the formation of mudrās.
Resembling the pomegranate flower, they were enchanting in their yellow garments. || 1 ||
Four-armed, with two pairs of hands holding shields and small swords.
Listen to their names, as their eyes are restless with intoxication. || 2 ||
She who agitates all, and likewise she who causes all to flee.
The mudrā that attracts all, and likewise the one that subjugates all. || 3 ||
The sixty-first is the Sarvonmādinī Mudrā, and the sixty-second is the Sarvamahāṅkuśā.
The Sarvakhecarī mudrā and likewise the supreme Sarvabījā. || 4 ||
The ninth is Sarvayoni, and likewise Sarvatrikhaṇḍikā.
Thus have been described these ten mudrās and their presiding deities. [The color is] red. 10.
9. Now, the meditation on the Guptayoginīs:
Kāmākarṣiṇikā, and likewise Buddhyākarṣiṇikākalā.
She is the attractor of the ego, the digit that attracts everything.
The digit of Karṣiṇī is eternally formless and attracts through touch.
And Rasākarṣiṇikā, as well as the digit (kalā) Gandhākarṣiṇikā.
She who attracts the mind, she who is eternally steadfast, and she who possesses the art of drawing [all] to herself.
Smṛtyākarṣiṇikā is the eternal one; she is the digit (kalā) that draws [everything] toward herself. || 3 ||
The eternal Bījākarṣiṇikā is the self, the digit (kalā) that attracts.
The eternal Amṛtākarṣiṇī, the supreme one who draws forth the body.
These are the sixteen Nityās, who are powers (śaktis) whose forms are the Kalās.
Resembling coral trees, their faces were graced with gentle smiles.
They have four arms and three eyes, and are radiant with crowns adorned by the crescent moon.
Holding a bow and arrow, a shield and sword, they possess divine splendors; [the sixteenth is] red in color.
10. Now follows the meditation on the most secret Yoginīs: Anaṅgakusumā and the second is Anaṅgamekhalā.
Together with Anaṅgamadanā, who was afflicted by the passion of Anaṅga. || 1 ||
Anaṅgararekhā, Anaṅgavegā, and Anaṅgāṅkuśā as well.
The goddesses Anaṅgamālinī and Parācetanā [attained] the splendor of their recitation. || 2 ||
The bow is the arrow, the arrows are flowers, and the flower-arrow is the *kamu* or blue lotus.
They bear a majestic stride like that of a great elephant, graced by her graceful command. [8] She is red in color.
11. Now, the meditation on the Yoginīs of the Saṃpradāya: those headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī are joined with that which is called the Saṃpradāya.
Their hair was fashioned into braids, and they were radiant with vermilion tilakas. || 1 ||
And they are of an extremely intense nature, with a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
The bow of fire, the arrow of fire, and likewise the sword in the form of fire.
Their bodies were ablaze, bearing the fire-wheel known as the *phalaka* (shield).
Highly incensed against the lord of the Asuras, they [uttered] the mantra originating from the ashes of Kāma.
These very powers of command belong to Lalitā, who possesses great majesty.
She who agitates all beings and likewise she who causes all to flee.
The power that attracts all things, as well as that which pertains to every day.
The power that deludes all, and likewise the one that paralyzes all.
The power Sarvajṛmbhiṇikā, as well as Sarvavaśaṅkarī.
Sarvarañjinikā is the Power, and likewise Sarvonmādinikā.
The power that accomplishes all aims and fulfills all prosperity.
She is the power consisting of all mantras, the destroyer of all dualities.
Thus indeed have the names of the traditions been told; [he is] red in color. 14.
12. Now, the meditation on the Kulottīrṇa Yoginīs:
they resemble crystal and hold an axe as well as a noose.
Holding maces, bells, and jewels, their forms were ablaze with light.
Enraged against the enemy of the gods, their faces were contorted with frowns.
O Pot-born one, listen now to the names of these as well.
The goddess who bestows all accomplishments, as well as the one who bestows all prosperity.
The goddess Sarvapriyaṃkarī, the maker of all auspiciousness. || 3 ||
The goddess who bestows all desires and destroys all suffering.
She is the pacifier of all death and the warder-off of all obstacles. || 4 ||
Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī, the bestower of all auspicious fortune.
These ten goddesses, whose intentions were fulfilled by Udayā, have been described. [The tenth is] Śvetavarṇa.
13. Now, the meditation on the Nigarbha Yoginīs: ten [deities] renowned by the name Nigarbha-yoginī are proclaimed.
She is omniscient, omnipotent, and the bestower of all sovereignty. || 1 ||
The Goddess who consists of all-knowledge, the destroyer of all diseases.
She is the support of all, her very nature being such, and likewise the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists entirely of universal bliss and is the very embodiment of all protection.
The goddesses, possessing a luster equal to that of white pearls, were released because they had granted every desired boon.
These should be known as four-armed, holding a vajra, a śakti, and a tomara.
And they are bearing wheels, intent on the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura; their color is white.
14. Now follows the meditation on the Secret Yoginīs;
indeed, these Vāgīśvarīs are well-known by the name "Secret Yoginīs."
Resembling the blossoms of the red Aśoka tree, they hold arrows and bows in their hands. || 1 ||
Their entire bodies were covered by armor, and they were adorned with lutes and books.
Vaśinī, Kāmeśī, Modinī, and likewise Vimalā. || 2 ||
Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśī, and likewise Kaulinī.
These eight goddesses are remembered as the causes for the destruction of the Daityas. [The eighth is] red in color.
15. Now, the meditation on the most secret Yoginīs:
they are the three who reside in the three seats (pīṭhas), endowed with eight arms.
A bow, an arrow, a water-skin, a vessel, a citron, and a sword. || 1 ||
A shield, a serpent-noose, and a bell of great sound.
Bearing [the marks of] madness from their sloughing-off, they possess secrets more ancient than the most ancient.
Kāmeśī, Kāmeśī, Bhagamālinī, and likewise the supreme [Parā].
These three are remembered as being possessed by the demon Bhaṇḍa and filled with wrath.
Lalitā is equal in majesty to Lalitāsamatējasa.
These, however, are proclaimed as the eternal inner circle (antaraṅga) of the Goddess Śrī. [The color] is the hue of vermilion (siṃdūra). 3. 4.

16. Now follows the visualization (dhyāna) of the deities of the Nityaklinnā group, according to the manner of the Lalitopākhyāna, together with Tripurasundarī, the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī), for all sixteen [deities].
They had the appearance of goddesses and carried the weapons of goddesses.
They exist in every age for the benefit of the worlds. || 1 ||
The meditation on these very [deities] is now commenced according to the method taught in the Śarabha-tantra.
(Although [the meditation] for Bheruṇḍā is not mentioned in the Śarabha-tantra, it has been written in the Jñānārṇava, in the section on the liberation through the Candrajñāna-vidyā.
17. Now, the meditation on Kāmeśī.
A noose, a bow of sugarcane, a vessel filled with honey, a great goad, and an excellent flower-arrow.
I perpetually worship Kāmeśvarī, who is red in hue, three-eyed, and who holds [her attributes] with her hands. Her color is red. 1.
18. Now, the meditation on Bhagamālā:
she holds in her six arms a white lotus, a red lotus, a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and a flowery arrow.
I worship in my heart that Mother Bhagamālinī, whose limbs are exceedingly beautiful and as radiant as the *baṃdhūka* flower; she is red in color. 1. Red in color. 1.
19. Now, regarding the meditation on Nityaklinna:

[one should meditate on her] resembling the rising rays of the sun, three-eyed, adorned with a crescent moon as a head-ornament, and her limbs decorated with ornaments such as girdles and shining jewels.
I meditate daily in my mind upon Nityaklinnā, who holds in her arms a noose, a supreme goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and a drinking vessel; she is red in color. (1) [She is] red in color. (1)
20. Now, the meditation on Bheruṇḍā (from the *Jñānārṇava*, in the *Candrajñānavidyā*):

She is as white as a pearl, a kunda flower, or the moon; she wears a crown made of jewels and is adorned with jeweled earrings; she holds a rosary and flowers in her hands, while her other two hands grant the gesture of fearlessness; she has the crescent moon upon her crest and possesses three eyes.

Seated upon a lotus, her slender waist bending under the weight of her breasts adorned with garlands of *guñjā* berries, she is endowed with various ornaments, while her golden pedestal is illuminated by the jewels from the crowns of the gods. || 1 ||

With my mind, I meditate upon Bheruṇḍā, the presiding deity of the desires of her devotees, who bestows supreme bliss, who possesses a beautiful form and a lovely face, whose hair is disheveled, and who is the mother of the three worlds. Her complexion is white. (1)
21. Now, the meditation on Vahnivāsinī:
She holds in her left hands a lotus, a conch, a sugarcane bow, and a moon; and in her right hands, she holds a white water-lily, a golden horn, a flower-arrowed bow, and a mātuliṅga fruit.

I worship daily in the lotus of my heart the eternal Goddess, who has the luster of molten gold, wears a jeweled crown, possesses eight hands and three eyes, and dwells in fire. (1) Her complexion is like that of gold. (1)
22. Now, the meditation on Mahāvajreśvarī:
She is seated upon a lotus pedestal shimmering with nine jewels, situated on a boat in a red ocean; she holds a noose, a bow made of sugarcane, a goad, and the fruit of a pomegranate.
I meditate upon that Vajreśī, who is red in color, who gazes with devotion through her three eyes, and who is being praised by hosts of gods and sages—O Bhavānī! (1) Her color is red. (1)
23. Now, the meditation on Śivadūtī:
she holds a jewel-vessel in her lower left hand and a mace above it, while with her right hands she holds a lotus, an axe, a great sword above that, and a goad.

I worship the eternal messenger who possesses the luster of the midday sun, whose ornaments shine with fresh jewels, who has eight hands and three eyes, and who is praised by hosts of gods and sages. (1) Her complexion is pale-red. (1)
24. Now, for the swift meditation:

[one should visualize] the young girl who has three eyes, whose ornaments are fashioned by the *nāgas*, whose body is adorned with a string of *guñjā* berries, and who holds in her hands the noose, the goad, the gesture of protection, and the gesture of boon-granting.

I meditate daily upon the beautiful one, yellow-hued, dwelling amidst young sprouts, radiant with a crest-ornament of peacock feathers, seated upon a throne surrounded by hosts of bears and lions. (1) Her color is yellow. (1)
25. Now, the meditation on Kulasundarī:
She has three eyes, is as reddish as the rising sun, wears the crescent moon upon her crest, possesses lips fragrant with wine and exceedingly tender, and is playful and beautifully smiling.

I meditate upon that young maiden who bestows complete perfection, who holds a garland, a book, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her arms, and who wears ornaments upon all her limbs. Her complexion is reddish-orange. 1.

26. Now, for the daily meditation: [one should contemplate her] possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun, with six left hands holding a noose, a rosary, a bow, a shield, a trident, and the desired [object], and with a face like the essence of nectar.

I worship the eternal Bhavānī, who is radiant with rubies and ornaments, possessing three eyes, and holding in her right hands a goad, a book, and a flower, and in her left hands a sword, a skull, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is red in color. (1)
27. Now, the meditation on Nīlapatākā:

She has a blue luster and wears a crimson garment; she is three-eyed and five-faced, with a beautiful smile. In her left hands, she holds a noose, a banner, a lotus, and a bow shining [with splendor], while holding a sword in her right.

I take refuge in her who stands upon a lotus, who holds in her arms a spear, a goad, a sword, a trident, a great arrow, and the gesture of fearlessness; she whose breasts are adorned with jewels and pearls, and who has a blue banner—she who is blue in color. 1. Blue in color. 1.
28. Now, the meditation on Vijayā:

[One should meditate upon her] holding in her hands the conch, the discus, the noose, the goad, as well as a great shield, a sword, a bow, an arrow, a white lotus flower, and thereafter a citron fruit.

I constantly meditate upon the Goddess who has the color of the rising morning sun, who is the conqueror of the three worlds, who possesses five faces and three eyes, who is adorned with yellow garments, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. [Her] complexion is red. 1.
29. Now, for the visualization of Sarvamaṅgalā:
she has a golden complexion, eyes filled with compassion, and is radiant with rubies as ornaments; she stands upon a lotus endowed with thirty-two, sixteen, and eight petals, and is smiling gently.

I meditate upon the glorious Maṅgalā, the supreme bestower of wealth to her devotees, who holds a lotus in her left hand and, with her right, the excellent fruit of the *ātulaṅga* tree that grants fearlessness. She is golden-hued. 1. 1.
30. Now, the meditation on Jvālāmālinī:

She possesses six faces with a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an aeon, and is endowed with twelve arms; in her left hands, she holds a noose, a shield, a lotus, an excellent arrow, a trident, and a boon-granting gesture.

I take refuge in her who is known as Jvālāmālinī, who is adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments, and who, being skillful, bears an elephant-goad, a sword, a spear, excellent arrows, a bow, and the gesture of fearlessness, while blazing with garlands of fire; she is red in color. 1. 1.
31. Now, the meditation on Mitrā:
She possesses the splendor of a face adorned with the crescent moon and the luster of the rising sun, and she holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I meditate upon Citrāmbikā in my heart—she who wears variegated silken garments, whose limbs are adorned with the nine precious gems, and who possesses three eyes. [Her] complexion is red. 1.

32. Now, the meditation on Tripurasundarī: She should be visualized as having the color of vermilion, like Rājarājeśvarī, with a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows in her hands. || 1 ||
33. Now, the meditation on the six-limbed goddesses:
the goddess of the heart, the goddess of the head, and likewise the goddess of the crest-lock;
The goddess of armor, the goddess of vision, and the goddess of weapons—these six are devoted to the Lord. || 1 ||
Their bodies were filled with nectar-like beauty, and they held their weapons with focused attention.
And the seat of the surrounding dots, with blazing forms revolving [therein]. [The color is] red. 6.
34. Now, the meditation on the goddess Yoganidrā (from the Pāñcarātra-Padmasaṃhitā):
Nidrā, however, is seated upon a bed, gentle and lotus-eyed.
And she is known to have two arms, holding a noose and a vessel, and is dark-complexioned. [1] Her complexion is dark. [1]
35. Now, the meditation on eighteen-armed Bhadrakālī (from the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
The eighteen-armed Bhadrakālī should be visualized as captivating.
Standing in the ālīḍha posture, she is seated upon a chariot drawn by four lions. || 1 ||
He always holds a rosary, a trident, a sword, and a shield.
The arrow and the bow are to be fashioned, and likewise the conch and the lotus.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should likewise be prepared, as well as a divine water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
And when the power of punishment must be exercised, [one should employ] the black antelope skin and the sacrificial fire.
The excellent [mantra] of Hastā and Bhadrakālī shall bring about peace.
In one place alone, O highly fortunate one, she shall become a bearer of a jewel-vessel; [her] color is blue.
Now, the meditation on the Goddesses of the seven seats, beginning with Mūlādhāra (from the Ṣoḍhākalpa):
Next, the meditation on Śākinī residing in the Mūlādhāra seat:

In the lotus situated at the Mūlādhāra, which possesses eight petals, one should meditate upon her who has five faces and three eyes, who is golden-hued, seated upon a corpse, and holding a goad, a lotus, a book, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā).

One should meditate upon that Śākinī, who is beautiful, whose mind is attached to mung-bean rice, who is delighted by the intoxication of wine, and who carries with her staff-like arms various lovely gestures such as the boon-granting mudrā. She is golden-hued. 1. 1.
37. Now, the meditation on Kākinī residing at the seat of Svādhiṣṭhāna:

One should contemplate her seated upon the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, which shines with sixty-four petals; she has four faces and three eyes, possesses a yellow luster, and holds in her hands a trident, a rosary, a skull-cup, and the gesture of granting fearlessness, while bearing the *antastha* and *ūṣman* groups of consonants.

One should meditate upon that goddess who is established in the fat-element (medodhātu), who binds [the world] with the intoxication of impurity, who is encircled by the power of the betel-nut tree (pūga), who is attached to curds, and who bestows desired fruits; she is yellow in color. 1. 1.
38. Now, the meditation on Lākinī at the Maṇipūraka seat:

[one should meditate upon] the most formidable Śakti, black in color, with three faces and three eyes shining, holding a thunderbolt, a staff, and the gesture of fearlessness in her arms, [seated] upon a lotus with eight petals at the navel.

One should meditate upon that Lākinī, who is surrounded by Ḍāmārī and the others, who causes fear to the ignorant masses, who is seated upon a seat of flesh-elements, whose mind is attached to molasses and food, and who bestows all happiness—she who is dark-complexioned. 1. She is black in color. 1.
39. Now, the meditation on Rākiṇī residing on the Anāhata seat:

she is seated upon a solar petal in the heart-lotus, dark-complexioned, possessing two faces and gleaming fangs, three-eyed, and holding in her arms a ṭaṅka, a trident, a skull-cup, and a ḍamaru drum.

One should meditate upon that Rākinī, who stands upon a red [lotus], surrounded by Kālarātri and others, arisen from pure passion, venerable to the illustrious Vīrendra, and the bestower of desired fruits. She is dark blue in color. (1) 1.
40. Now, the meditation on the Ḍākinī residing in the Viśuddha-pīṭha:
In the lotus of the throat-cavity, which is pure and possesses eight petals, she is red in color and three-eyed; she holds a glorious khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a trident, and a great human skin.

I bow to the fierce Ḍākinī Vīracaṇḍā, who is endowed with a single face, who strikes fear into common folk, who is intent upon milk-rice offerings, whose skin-clad body is surrounded by floods of blood, and whose complexion is red. (1) (The color is red. (1)
41. Now, the meditation on Hākinī residing at the seat of command (ājñāpīṭha):

In the two-petaled lotus of the bindu between the eyebrows, she is white in color and holds in her lotus-like hands the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), a drum (ḍamaruka), a pure rosary, and a skull-cup.

One should meditate upon that Hākinī, who has six faces, is seated upon a lotus, is beautiful with three eyes, possesses a gait like that of a swan and other graces, is intent on yellow food, and is praised by all the gods. [Her] color is white. 1.1.1.
42. Now, the meditation on Yākinī residing at the Jālandhara-pīṭha:

One should meditate upon that Bhairavī Yākinī, who is the collective totality of all colors, whose hands shine with all weapons, and who resides within a lotus situated in the space of the severed head (muṇḍavyoma) and possesses every petal.

One should meditate upon that Yākinī, who possesses all faces beginning with 'Ra', who bestows all happiness, whose nature is identical to all elements, whose mind is unattached to all objects of desire, and who delights in the supreme Śiva. (1) [Her] complexion is variegated. (1)
Now, the meditation on the deities of the Seven Mothers (*saptamātṛkā*) [as described] in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda* (43):
therein, the meditation on Brāhmī—
therein, Brāhmī has four faces and six arms, and she is seated upon a swan (*haṃsa*).
She was endowed with tawny-colored ornaments and wore a deer skin as an upper garment.
He holds the sacrificial thread, the staff, and the wooden ladle in his three right hands in successive order.
In her left [hand], she holds a book and a water-pot, and displays the gesture of granting fearlessness. Her complexion is yellow. 1. 2.
44. Now, the meditation on Māheśvarī:
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, has five faces, and three eyes.
She is white in complexion, has ten arms, and is adorned with the crescent moon.
A sword, a vajra, a trident, and an axe, as well as the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
She holds a noose, a bell, a serpent, and a goad in her hands; her complexion is white.
45. Now, the meditation on Kaumārī:
Kaumārī has six faces, is pale-red in color, and possesses excellent conduct.
She has arms as radiant as the sun, she stands upon a peacock, she is the bestower of boons, and she holds a spear.
She bears a banner, a staff, a vessel, and an arrow in her right hands.
In the left hands, he holds a bow, a bell, a lotus, and likewise a cock.
She holds an axe and, beneath that, displays the gesture of granting fearlessness; her complexion is pale red (pāṭala). 1–2.
46. Now, the meditation on Vaiṣṇavī:
Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned like a Tārkṣya bird, has six arms, and wears a garland of lotuses.
In her right hand she holds the boon-granting gesture and a lotus flower.
She has a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and her arms are resplendent; she is blue in color.
47. Now, the meditation on Vārāhī: Vārāhī is black in color, mounted upon a buffalo, and has a large belly.
Bestowing boons, she holds a staff and a sword in her right hands.
In her left hands she holds a pestle, a skull-cup, and the gesture of fearlessness; she has eight arms and rests upon a sow-faced being; her color is black. (1)
48. Now, the meditation on Aiṃdrī:
Aiṃdrī has a thousand eyes, is gentle, possesses a golden luster, and is seated upon an elephant.
The goddess Varadāsūtriṇī holds a vajra aloft in her right hand. || 1 ||
In the left [hand] is a lotus-bowl, and in the hand below that is the gesture of fearlessness; he is golden-colored. (1)
49. Now, the meditation on Cāmuṇḍā: Cāmuṇḍā stands upon a corpse; she is black, deformed, and indeed adorned with ornaments.
Daṃṣṭrālākṣī, Kṣīṇadehā, Gartākṣī, and Kāmarūpiṇī. || 1 ||
With arms reaching to his knees and a slender waist, he holds a mace, a discus, and a chowrie.
She holds a goad and a sword in her right and left [hands], respectively.
She holds a shield, a noose, a bow, a staff, and also an axe; she is black in color. 1.
14) 50. Now, the meditation on Caṇḍikā (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
Caṇḍikā is white in color, she has the form of Śiva, and she rides upon a lion.
She has matted hair and a rounded form, possesses three eyes, bestows boons, and holds a trident. || 1 ||
She holds a small knife in her right hand, and is endowed with a noose, a vessel, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is white in color. (1)
Now, the meditation on the nine Durgās (according to the Śaiva Āgama) [where all are dark-complexioned]:
51. Therein, the meditation on Śailaputrī Durgā: "O Goddess, for the sake of obtaining the desires of the gods, [I meditate upon you] who have the crescent moon as your crest-ornament..."
Mounted upon a bull, bearing a trident, the illustrious daughter of the mountain.
52. Then [he meditated on] Durgā as a female religious student (brahmacāriṇī), holding a rosary and a water-pot in her lotus-like hands.
O Goddess, supreme one, be gracious toward me, who am a celibate student.
53. Now, the meditation on Caṇḍakhaṇḍadurgā:
She is mounted upon the most excellent of birds and accompanied by her fierce-tempered warrior consort, Arbhaṭī.
May she who is renowned as Caṇḍakhaṇḍā extend her grace toward me.
54. Now, the meditation on Skandadurgā: She is eternally seated upon a lion-throne, with her two hands adorned with lotuses.
May the illustrious goddess, the mother of Skanda, always bestow auspiciousness.
55. Now, the visualization of Kūṣmāṇḍadurgā: [she holds] a jar completely filled with liquor and likewise drenched in blood.
May the Kūṣmāṇḍas, holding [these] with their lotus-like hands, bestow auspiciousness upon me. || 1 || 1 ||
56. Now follows the meditation on Kātyāyanī-Durgā:
She has hands radiant with the Candrahāsa sword, and her excellent vehicle is a tiger.
May Kātyāyanī, the goddess who slays the Dānavas, bestow auspiciousness.
57. Now follows the meditation on Kālarātri as the Fortress: she has a terrifying form, and her body is shaped like a dark blue lotus.
May the goddess Caṇḍāṭṭahāsinī, the Night of Doom, bestow auspiciousness.
58. Now, the meditation on Mahāgaurī-Durgā: She is mounted upon a white elephant, wears white garments, and is pure.
Mahāgaurī shall bestow auspiciousness, O Mahādeva, she who grants supreme delight.
59. Now, the meditation on Durgā, the bestower of supernatural powers (siddhi):
[She who is worshipped] by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others, as well as by Asuras and immortals (gods).
Being constantly served, may she who bestows success be the giver of accomplishment. || 1 || 9 ||
60. Now, the meditation on the nine Durgās (according to the method stated in the *Skandayāmala* and the *Kāraṇāgama*):
There, in a place provided with a lotus, one should worship Durgā in her nine forms; one [form] has eighteen arms, a full chest, and broad arms and thighs.
Adorned with all ornaments, she bestows all accomplishments.
A head, a shield, a bell, a mirror, the threatening gesture, and a bow.
She holds a banner, a hand-drum, and a noose with her left hands.
A spear, a mallet, a trident, a thunderbolt, a conch, and then a lotus.
Holding a tally-stick, a search-staff, and a discus in their right hands.
The remaining sixteen hands should be present, excluding the arrow and the ḍamaruka drum.
These [goddesses] should be worshipped by wise men who desire victory. (Their names:)
Rudrā, Caṇḍā, Śacī, Īśā, Caṇḍī, Krūrā, and Anucaṇḍikā.
The ninth is Ugra-caṇḍā; these are proclaimed as the nine Durgās. (Their colors:)
The clouds are Pāvakābhāñjanā, Kṛṣṇā, Nīlā, Śuklā, and Dhūmikā.
They should be known as yellow and pale-white; those in the ālīḍha posture are surrounded by green. || 1 || 9 ||
61. Now, the meditation on the sixteen-armed Durgā (from the *Durgā-kalpa*):
[One should meditate on her] as having three eyes and being adorned with serpents, with her sixteen arms occupied by a trident and other weapons.
I bow to her who is adorned with a serpent-bracelet, whose neck is blue, and who is clad in the directions as her garment; she is of a dark complexion. || 1 || She is of a dark-blue color. || 1 ||
62. Now, the visualization of Durgā as a portion of Rudra (*Kāraṇāgama*):
She is clad in red garments, dark-complexioned, with two eyes, and adorned with golden ornaments marked by jewels on her crown.
Holding a trident, a sword, a conch, and a discus, she is mounted upon the king of beasts and adorned with the sun and the moon.
I meditate in my mind upon Durgā, who is a portion of Rudra, whose feet are worshipped by the gods, and who bestows desired objects; she is dark-complexioned. (1)
63. Now, the meditation on Eight-Armed Kālī (from the Kāraṇāgama):
She has eight arms and a massive body, with a radiance like that of a dark cloud.
He is endowed with the conch, the discus, the mace, the jar, the pestle, the goad, and the noose.
May she who bears the Vajra in her hand, Mahākālī, be for our delight; she whose complexion is dark like a rain cloud.
Holding a discus, conch, sword, shield, arrow, bow, trident, and the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
May that Durgā, who rests upon the head of the supreme buffalo and whose splendor resembles fresh dūrvā grass, grant me prosperity. [1] She is golden in color. [1]
65. Now, the visualization of Pratyaṅgirā (from the *Pratyaṅgirā-kalpa*):
One should visualize her as dark-complexioned, three-eyed, lion-faced, and four-armed; with hair standing upright, seated upon a lion, and with her locks of hair adorned [with jewels].
She is beautiful, holding a skull-cup, a trident, a hand-drum, and a snake-noose.
[One should worship] Pratyāṅgirā, who constantly destroys all enemies; she is dark-complexioned. 1-2.
66. Now, the meditation on Śūlinī (from her ritual manual):

Dark as a cloud, adorned with ornaments, and terrifying with a crown that shines like a water-bearing cloud, she holds in the tips of her hands a trident, arrows, a sword, a spear, a mace, a noose, and a bow.

May the wielder of the trident, who stands upon the shoulders of a lion, surrounded by four maidens equipped with swords and shields, and who has destroyed the Daityas, be the destroyer of our fear of worldly existence. She is dark blue in color like a rain cloud.
67. Now, the meditation on Dhūmrāvatī (from that *Kalpa*):

She has red limbs and wears red garments; her ears are adorned with earrings shining like elephant trunks; she has curved fangs and a garland of skulls rising from her neck; and around her is a radiant, shimmering host of *paiśācas*.

One should meditate upon Dhūmrakālī, who has three eyes, whose laughter is fierce and terrible, who is formidable with a skull held in her hand and a sword, who is the slayer of the lives of enemies, who wears a crown of the young moon, and who is red in color. 1. Red in color. 1.
68. Now, the meditation on Vaśyamukhī (*Mahālakṣmīratnakośa*):
She draws back a sugarcane bow, having fixed upon it an arrow made of flowers.
I worship the Goddess who conquers the world, who is crimson as the hibiscus flower, and whose face is ever-pleased. [1] Her color is red. [1]
69. Now, the visualization of Ugratārā (according to the Āmnāya):

She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, bearing a corpse upon her foot; she possesses a terrifying, loud laugh and holds a sword, a blue lotus, a trident, and a skull-cup; she is born from the seed-syllable *Hūṃ*.

Surrounded by matted locks that are short, dark blue, vast, and tawny, and by fierce serpents, Ugratārā herself destroys the dullness of the three worlds by placing it within her skull-bowl. [Her complexion is] the color of vermilion. 1. 1.
70. Now, the meditation on Kurukullā (from the Lalitopākhyāna):
Therein resides the goddess Naukeśvarī, renowned as Kurukullā.
She wore a dark bodice that was as black in appearance as the *tamāla* tree.
Her hands hold jewels and lotuses, and she is ever swelling with intense pride.
The jeweled boat of the Sage wanders all around; it is blue in color.
71. Now, the meditation on Vāruṇī (from the Lalitopākhyāna):
And there, the goddess Vāruṇī herself is the mistress of the boat.
Her whom they call Suvāmālinī, and her whom they call Amṛteśvarī; || 1 ||
There, situated upon that jeweled ship, she was surrounded by an army of Śaktis.
By its mere slight radiance, it bestows pride upon the three worlds.
Resembling the rising sun, with cheeks flushed with a slight redness.
Her mass of hair was entwined with the blood-red blossoms of the pārijāta tree. || 3 ||
She was carrying a goblet filled with wine, with a swaying blue lotus.
And pieces of cooked meat in jeweled vessels, as well as others.
The leader of the rows of boats crossing the Vāruṇī river shines there. [He is] red in color. 1.
72. Now, the meditation on Aparājitā (from the Nāradasaṃhitā):
[One should meditate upon] the Goddess who resembles a blue lotus, with her eyes sealed by sleep.
With the tips of her hair dark and curled, and possessing a deep navel and three folds [of skin on her waist]. || 1 ||
She whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness, who destroys the suffering of those who bow before her.
Clad in excellent yellow garments, she was adorned with ornaments and garlands.
She has the form of an excellent spear, is gentle, and destroys the splendor of the enemy army.
(18) With beautiful hands holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness, she has three eyes. || 3 ||
One should meditate upon that invincible Goddess Aparājitā, the bestower of all desires; she is blue in color. (1)
73. Now, the meditation on Śatruvidhvaṃsinī (from the Sudarśanasaṃhitā):
Śatruvidhvaṃsinī is fierce, three-headed, and has red eyes.
Her face was fierce with flames of fire, possessing terrible fangs and three eyes.
She is naked, with reddish hair and red hands, and has a large belly.
By means of these terrible rites performed with haste, one may swiftly cause enemies to be driven away. [1] Nīla... [2]
74. Now, the meditation on Svasthāveśinī (from the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā):
She has red limbs, dwells upon the corpse of Śiva, possesses three heads, and is fierce; she is the Great Bhairavī, smoke-eyed, the remover of fear, adorned with thick crests and dark locks of hair.

One should meditate upon her who holds a drum and a trident, who destroys enemies of great power, whose limbs are slender, who is the Earth, whose body is formidable, who has three matted locks, who consists of the fire of destruction, and who is praised by the wielder of the Pināka bow. [Her] color is red. 1. Color: Red. 1.
75. Now, the meditation on Daṇḍanāthāvārāhī (from the Lalitopākhyāna):
There, in the pavilion of the Goddess adorned with a hundred pillars, is the goddess Daṇḍanāthā.
He was seated in the center of the pericarp of a lotus made of refined gold.
[It consists of] a dot, a triangle, and a circle, enriched with a six-petalled lotus and a pair of circles.
There a wheel shines forth, resembling molten gold.
Her garments shimmered with the glow of twilight, and she was adorned with every ornament.
The conch, the discus, the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, as well as the plow and the mace.
Holding a noose and a goad, she is adorned with the crescent moon as her ear-ornament.
There dwells Daṇḍinī, joined with the face of a boar; she is golden-hued.
76. Now, the meditation on Svapnavārāhī (according to that *kalpa*):

She has the luster of a dark cloud, possesses enchanting breasts, is illuminated by three eyes, has the face of a boar, wears the moon as a crest-jewel, and is resplendent with the brilliance of her longing tusks.

One should meditate upon Vārāhī, who is mounted upon an excellent horse, adorned with auspicious ornaments, and holding in her lotus-like hands a sword, a shield, a noose, and a goad; she is dark as a rain cloud in complexion. (1) She is dark as a rain cloud in complexion. (1)
77. Now, the meditation on Śuddhavārāhī (from the Vārāhīkalpa):
[One should meditate on her] with a boar’s face radiant with tusks, and wearing a red cloth as an upper garment.
She bears in her hands a trident, a skull-bowl, a mace, and a serpent. || 1 ||
I worship that Vārāhī, whose head is adorned with a crest as languid as the line of the moon; she is blue in color. 1.
78. Now, the meditation on Laghuśyāmalā (from the Śyāmalākalpa):

One should meditate upon her who has the first flower as her crest-jewel, who is red, who wears a crimson garment, who holds a small vessel of honey, and whose corners of the eyes are rolling with intoxication.

She whose lute vibrates in her hands, who wears a stainless conch as an ear-ornament, who is languid from the weight of her full breasts, whose hair-knot has slipped down, and who is dark-complexioned—[she is] Śyāmalā. (1) [Her] complexion is dark. (1)
79. Now, the meditation on Rājamātaṅgī (according to that ritual manual): [She is] seated upon a jewel-throne, with dark-limbed body, listening to the speech of Śuka.
With one foot placed upon a lotus, she was adorned with a beautiful crescent moon as her head-ornament.
And she was playing upon a lute, her forehead illuminated by a tilaka mark.
He wore a crest of *saugandhika* flower garlands and was clothed in red garments.
I bow down to Mātaṅgī, adorned with ornaments; she is dark-complexioned. (1)
80. Now, the meditation on the Child-form (from the *Tripurasundarīkalpa*):
She resembles the *japā* flower, has blossomed [with beauty], and is seated upon the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
She has four arms, holding a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; she is red in color.
81. Now, the meditation on Bhuvaneśvarī (from the *Mahālakṣmīratnakośa*):

She possesses a luster equal to the rising sun, surpassing fresh hibiscus flowers and the crescent moon; she is encircled by a garland of light, has three eyes, wears earrings shining with various gems, and is seated upon a lotus.
82. Now, the meditation on Mṛtasaṃjīvinī (from the *Rudrayāmala*, *Kuhū-kalpa*):
[One should meditate upon] the Goddess Mṛtasaṃjīvinī, who bears a peaceful form.
[He holds] a noose, a goad, a hook, a mace, a sword, a trident, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I bow to the auspicious one, red in color, possessing eight arms, and seated upon a full-blown lotus. (1) [Red Color]
83. Now, the visualization of the goddess Bagalā (from her ritual manual):
[One should meditate on her] as four-armed, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus throne.
She holds a trident, a drinking vessel, a mace, and a tongue.
She had lips like the bimba fruit, a neck like a conch shell, and breasts that were perfectly full.
One should meditate upon the deity of the Brahmāstra weapon, clad in yellow garments and reeling with intoxication; her color is yellow.
84. Now, the visualization of the deity Prāṇa-śakti (from the *Śāradātilaka*):
Seated upon a red lotus that shines like a young fish in a sea of blood, she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a bow made of sugarcane, a rosary of gems, a goad, and five arrows.

May the Supreme Power of Life (Prāṇaśakti), who bears a skull filled with blood, who is enriched by three eyes and full, swelling breasts radiant like the morning sun, and whose complexion is that of the rising sun—may she grant happiness to my vital breath. (1) Her color is red. (1)
85. Now, the meditation on the goddess Śuddhavidyā (in the Somanāthavallīmantraśāstra):
She has a white form and holds a rosary and a book.
May Śuddhavidyā, whose hand displays the *cinmudrā* and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), protect me always. She is white in color. 1.
86. Now, the meditation on the Goddess Śrīvidyā (from the *Mahālakṣmīratnakośa*):

O You whose face is like the orb of the rising sun, who possess extremely fierce sprout-like fangs, who are the abode of infinite enjoyments through the playing of the lute, and who are fond of the singing of the lute and other instruments!

I worship you, O Śrī Śāṅkarī, who are honored for your great purpose, who move swiftly as the venerable Vidyā, who wear a manifest garland formed from the bones of men of various colors. || 1 || [The meter is Citravarga. || 1 ||
87. Now, the meditation on Kāmakaleśvarī (from the *Mahālakṣmīratnakośa*):
[One should meditate upon her] holding a lotus, a noose, a sugarcane bow, a *kiṃśuka* flower, and five arrows tipped with rice grains.
I meditate upon a certain Mother, who holds the boon-granting hand of constant fearlessness and possesses every artistic grace; she is red in color. 1. Red in color. 1.
88. Now, the meditation on Vanaśaṅkarī (from the Padma Purāṇa):

She possesses the splendor of the body of the fire at the end of the aeon, and holds a trident, a skull-bowl, an arrow, a bow, as well as the gestures of boon and fearlessness, a club, a conch, a discus, and a rosary.

I bow to that three-eyed Vanaśaṅkarī, who is praised by Vāgīśa and Viṣṇu, who wears a crown beautified by a mass of moonbeams, and who is adorned with jewels and garments. Her complexion is red. 1. 1.
89. Now, the meditation on Śākaṃbharī (from the Padma Purāṇa):
She holds a trident, a noose, a skull-bowl, a bow, a thunderbolt, arrows, a goad, a shield, a conch, a discus, a mace, a sword, the gesture of fearlessness, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a staff.

I praise Śākambharī, the mother of the three worlds and beloved of Maheśa, who protected the hosts of sages—stricken by the absence of rain—with vegetables (śāka). [She whose color is red. 1. [She whose color is red. 1.
90. Now, the meditation on the goddess Surā (from that *kalpa*):
While the excellent ocean of milk, Kṣīroda, was being churned by the gods and the asuras...
There, the goddess Surā was born, assuming the form of a maiden.
She is endowed with eighteen arms and has long eyes with reddish corners.
A conch, a sword, a bow, as well as a skull and a mace.
Holding a spear, a mace, a sword, and a bell with her left hands.
A discus, a fist, an arrow, a trident, an iron club, a shield, and a javelin.
Holding the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the small drum (bhiṇḍivāla) with her right hands.
One should worship her who has three eyes, whose limbs are long and slender, and who resembles the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having encircled Mount Mandara, it was terrifying with its frothy whirlpools.
She has the luster of the color of cow's urine and milk, yet she is another supreme goddess whose form is black.
She terrifies all the asuras and bestows fearlessness upon the gods.
She who is the goddess Umā, the companion of the gods, and he who is Mōha, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). (1) Citravarṇa. (1)
91. Now, the meditation on the Goddess of the sixty-four arts (*catuṣṣaṣṭikalādevī*) according to the *Śābaratantra*:
She holds in her hands a lotus, a discus, a bowstring, a deer, a book, a rosary, a chisel, a white skull-cup, a boon-granting gesture, and a golden jar shining with nectar.

I bow to Śāradā, whose five faces are as beautiful as pearls, lightning, clouds, crystal, and fresh *japā* flowers; who possesses breasts that resemble the moon and the fullness of a jar, and whose complexion is white. Her color is white.
92. Now, the meditation on Sarvavarṇeśvarī (from the Siddhaśābaratantra):
She has three eyes and incessantly holds in her hands a rosary of beads, a young deer, a raised ṭaṅka-axe, and a lore-script.
Bow down to the Mistress of Colors, who wears the crescent moon upon her head, who dwells within the red lotus, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts. (1) Her complexion is reddish. (1)
93. Now, the meditation on the twelve Ardha-devīs (from the Mahālakṣmīratnakośa): [One should meditate on her] as having five faces and three eyes, seated upon a corpse, and red in color.
She wears a garland of red lotuses on her head and has a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
[He holds] a rosary, a goad, a supreme trident, and a flower-arrow.
A noose, a sugarcane bow, the gesture of fearlessness, a skull-cup, and likewise a book.
I bow down to her who bears the twelve Ardha-devīs; she is red in color. (1)
94. Now, the meditation on the goddess Tiraskariṇī (from the Mahālakṣmīratnakośa):
Mounted upon a blue horse, she has a blue body and holds a sword.
May he who is the dark-blue curtain that conceals the world as it closes its eyes in sleep protect you. He is blue in color.
95. Now, the meditation on the Goddess mounted upon a horse (*Aśvārūḍhā*) [from the *Mahālakṣmīratnakośa*]:

She is mounted on a horse, holding in the tips of her hands a cane staff made of fresh gold; likewise, on the right and the left, she should be meditated upon with her slender body bound by a noose consisting of a horse-bit.

May the Goddess—who is eternally gracious, whose mass of hair shines like the moon, who possesses three eyes, and who is today beyond reproach—grant us the heart-pleasing fortune that brings about the attainment of the entire multitude of happiness. (1) [Her color is red. (1)
96. Now, the meditation on the goddess Indrākṣī (from the Indrākṣī-kalpa):
One should meditate upon the goddess Indrākṣī, who has two arms and is endowed with two yellow garments.
Holding a vajra in her left hand and granting boons with her right. || 1 ||
Indrākṣī, accompanied by her young companions and adorned with various ornaments.
Her lotus-face was serene, and she was attended by hosts of Apsarases; her complexion was yellow.
97. Now, the meditation on Tulajā-Bhavānī (from the Bhavānī-kalpa):
She has a reddish glow, is auspiciously clad in crimson garments, her face is full of bliss, she is adorned with pearl necklaces, and her waist-string is pressed by the weight of her breasts.

One should meditate upon the Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, who has three eyes, beautiful brows, and is lovely; she holds a water-lily and a ladle in her hands, and carries a jar filled with divine nectar. Her complexion is reddish-brown. || 1 || 1 ||
98. Now, the meditation on Candrāparameśvarī (from her *Kalpa*):
May she whose lotus-like hands hold beautiful lotuses, whose lotus-like eyes are lovely, and whose lotus-like face is smiling with the moon, dwell within my heart.
Her lotus feet are worshipped by the entire host of gods, and she is intoxicated by the exceeding fragrance of the honey [of her speech], which delights the swarms of bees.
Though her curved eyelashes were like a row of bees defeated by the terrifying movement of her gaze—terrible with the sword held in her hand—she was nonetheless crooked [in her ways].
She who wears garlands of blooming lotuses, whose nature is the song of yogis, whose graceful play is as beautiful as the moonlight, and who is the joy of the young.
The great goddess, golden-hued, seated upon a divine lion-throne.
And one should meditate upon the goddess Candirā, the supreme sovereign who bestows boons; she is golden-hued.
99. Now, the meditation on the goddess Tulasī (from the *Tulasīmāhātmya*):
One should meditate upon the goddess Tulasī, who is dark-complexioned and lotus-eyed.
She is serene, possessing four arms that hold a lotus, a white water-lily, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 1 ||
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments.
Clad in white garments and seated upon a lotus throne; [she is] dark-complexioned. 1–2.
100. Now, the meditation on Gāyatrī (from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa):
One should meditate upon the goddess Gāyatrī in the form of fire during the morning twilight.
A young maiden whose limbs were clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and red unguents.
She has four arms, four faces, bestows boons, and possesses eight eyes.
Holding a rosary of lotus seeds as a bracelet in her right hand. (2)
In his left hand he holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and in his other right hand a sacrificial ladle (sruva).
She holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her left hand and is established upon a lotus seat. || 3 ||
She whose form is the Rigveda, who is the morning libation, and whose vehicle is the swan.
And [he saw] the great Rasāyanā established upon the Gārhapatya fire; she was red in color.
101. Now, the meditation on Sāvitrī (from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa):
At the midday twilight, one should meditate upon the Goddess Sāvitrī, who possesses the form of Rudra.
A young woman, richly dressed in white garments, adorned with white garlands and white unguents.
She has four arms, four faces, bestows boons, and possesses twelve eyes.
Holding a rosary of rudrākṣa beads in her right hand.
In his left hand he holds a khaṭvāṅga, and in his right hand a trident.
In her left hand the goddess holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and likewise she bears the crescent moon.
Seated upon a golden throne, gentle, and having the form of the Yajurveda.
She who exists at the midday libation (mādhyandina-savana) and whose vehicle is a bull.
One of purified intellect should constantly meditate upon her, whose form is that of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire; she is white in color.
102. Now, the meditation on Sarasvatī (from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa):
One should meditate upon Sarasvatī at the evening twilight as having the form of Viṣṇu.
The elder woman, dark as a blue lotus, with hair that was black and curled. || 1 ||
She has four arms and one face, with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
The conch, the discus, the mace, and likewise again the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Wearing yellow garments and divine garlands and unguents.
And one should meditate upon her who is named the Third Extraction (Tṛtīyasavana) and who has the form of Viṣṇu. || 3 ||
Seated upon a blue pedestal in the north, she is the very embodiment of the Sāmaveda.
Bestowing boons, mounted upon Garuḍa, she was stationed at the Āhavanīya fire; she was dark-complexioned.
103. Now, the meditation on the two-armed Annapūrṇā (from the Kāraṇāgama):
She holds in her left lotus-hand a ruby vessel filled with sweet juices, and in her right lotus-hand, adorned with jeweled bracelets, she holds a jeweled ladle filled with divine foods.

I bow to Ambikā Annapūrṇā, who is red-clad, whose three eyes shine with a magnificent pearl necklace resting upon her full and lofty breasts, and whose face is the very image of the full moon. (1) Her color is red. (1)
104. Now, the meditation on the four-armed Annapūrṇā (from the Kāraṇāgama):

She has the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and bears the digit of the nectar-moon; she is a sky-faring goddess (*khecarī*), clad in red garments, endowed with full and lofty breasts, and beautiful with the onset of fresh, radiant youth.

I bow to the Goddess Annapūrṇā, who is adorned with various ornaments, whose eyes are like lotuses, whose form reflects the moon, who is enriched by the noose and goad, and whose hands grant fearlessness and boons. (1) Her complexion is the color of vermilion. (1)
105. Now, the meditation on Agnidurga (from the Śāradātilaka):

[One should meditate upon her] possessing a luster equal to a garland of lightning, seated upon the shoulders of the Lord of Beasts, terrifying, and attended by maidens whose hands shine with swords and shields.

I worship Durgā, who is composed of fire, who bears the moon, who has three eyes, and who holds in her hands a discus, an excellent sword, a shield, a bow, a goad, and a threatening gesture. Her complexion is like gold. 1. 1.
106. Now, the meditation on Goddess Śītalā (from the *Śītalā-kalpa* in the *Rudrayāmala*):
One should meditate upon Goddess Śītalā, seated upon a donkey and naked.
[She was] equipped with a broom and a water-pot, her head adorned with a winnowing basket; [she was] black in color. || 1 || || 1 ||

107. Now, the meditation on the deity Lopāmudrā (as per the Āmnāya): I worship the auspicious Lopāmudrā, who holds a noose, a goad, an arrow, and a bow; who has three eyes, possesses the luster of the sun, and has the moon as her crest-ornament. [Her complexion is] the color of vermilion. 1.
Now, the forms of the eight Mahālakṣmīs. 108. Among them, the meditation on the two-armed Lakṣmī (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): "O King, Lakṣmī, who is to be placed near Hari, is indeed two-armed."
Divine in form, with lotus-like hands, adorned with all ornaments; [her] complexion is like gold.
109. Now, the meditation on Gajalakṣmī (from the Pāñcarātra):
Lakṣmī, the goddess clad in white garments, appears in an incomparable form upon the earth.
The auspicious Goddess, possessing four separate arms, should be fashioned upon a lion-throne. || 1 ||
Upon her lion-throne, a beautiful lotus with a prominent pericarp should be fashioned.
O highly fortunate ones, she is well-established upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus.
The goddess should be depicted with four arms, seated like Vināyaka.
A large, auspicious lotus was to be fashioned as her ornament.
On the right, it rested upon the edge of the armlet of the best of the Yadavas.
O King, a beautiful jar of nectar should likewise be fashioned on the left.
O twice-born one, her other two hands should be made to hold a bilva fruit and a conch shell.
Behind that [deity] is a pair of elephants whose trunks are bent in a gesture of service.
And upon the head of the Goddess, a beautiful lotus should be fashioned; it is golden in color. (1)
110. Now, the meditation on Mahālakṣmī (as described by Viśvakarman in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): Wherever Mahālakṣmī is invoked, except at Kollāpura, [she is to be visualized as follows].
Then Lakṣmīvatī should be fashioned, adorned with all ornaments.
In the lower right hand he holds a bowl, and above it, the Kaumodakī mace.
In his upper left hand he holds a shield, and in the one below it, a bilva fruit.
Bearing a *liṅga* upon her head, she is worthy of worship for the sake of prosperity. She is golden-hued. (1)
111. Now, the meditation on Śrī Devī (in the Mayūrave):
[She holds] a noose, a rosary, a lotus, and a goad in her right and left hands.
One should visualize Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, seated in the lotus posture; she is golden in color.
112. Now, the meditation on Vīralakṣmī (from the Pāñcarātra):
May Vīralakṣmī, who bestows boons and fearlessness, protect [us]; she has a sword and a shield in her hands.
Her two hands hold upward-turned lotuses, and she is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana). She is golden in complexion.
113. Now, the meditation on the two-armed Vīraśrī (according to the *Pāñcarātra*):

In the right [hand] is the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and likewise in the left is the boon-granting gesture (*varada*). Her thighs have the form of lotus petals; such is the characteristic of the form of Vīraśrī. She is golden in color. 1.
114. Now, the meditation on the eight-armed Vīralakṣmī (from the *Pāñcarātra*):
She should be depicted with hands holding a noose, a goad, a rosary, the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a mace, a lotus, and a vessel. She is golden in color. 1. 1.
115. Now, the meditation on Prasannalakṣmī (from the Atharvaṇarahasya):
I praise Lakṣmī, who is identical with Paraśiva, possessing the luster of pure gold, whose form is radiant energy, clad in golden garments, and whose limbs are brilliant with every ornament.
[I salute] the primordial Śakti, the mother of all beings, who rests upon the left lap of Viṣṇu, holding a citron, a golden pitcher, and a golden lotus; she is golden-hued. (1)
116. Now, the meditation on the Śaktis of Viṣṇu’s retinue (from the Padma Purāṇa): Śrī shall have a splendor like gold, and Bhū shall have the luster of Arjuna (white) flowers.
Sarasvatī is white and red; Prīti has the appearance and form of a dark-blue hue. || 1 ||
Kīrti is red in appearance, while Śānti is said to have the luster of crystal.
Tuṣṭi is yellow and Puṣṭi is dark green; these goddesses are remembered as being thus praised. (2)
They are praised as having two hands holding lotuses, and their hands are shown in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 1 ||

117. Now, the meditation on Saubhāgyabhuvaneśvarī (from the Śāradātilaka): Her body is red like vermilion; she has three eyes; she wears a crest-jewel of rubies upon her head; she is adorned with the shimmering leader of stars (the moon) as her crown; her face is smiling; and her breasts are full.

One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle and seated upon a treasure of jewels; she holds in her two hands a jeweled goblet filled with gems and a red lotus, while her right foot rests upon that treasure of jewels. Her complexion is the color of vermilion.
118. Now, the meditation on Māyābhuvaneśvarī (from the Śāradātilaka):
She has a dark-blue body, bears the moon upon her crest, and eternally holds in her own hands a gift, a red lotus, a jewel-encrusted goblet, and that which removes supreme fear.
I bow to the consort of Hara, worshipped by the gods, who is seated upon a red lotus, whose breasts are radiant with pearl necklaces, and who shines with three eyes. [Her color is blue. 1. 1.

119. Now, the meditation on Vajraprastāriṇī (from the Śāradātilaka): She is seated within a blooming red lotus upon a red boat in a red ocean; she has a red body, a red crown from which a digit of the moon radiates, a smiling face, and three eyes.

I bow to Ambikā, whose limbs are slightly bent, who is stooped by the weight of her breasts, and who holds in her hands a citron, a noose, a goad, a mace, a bow, a garland, and a skull-cup. Her complexion is red. 1. Red in color. 1.

120. Now, the meditation on the goddess Trikaṇṭakī (from the Śāradātilaka): Blue from the navel downwards, bearing a reddish luster from the region of the neck upwards, she is white; with four faces, her limbs terrifying due to fangs set in gaping mouths that surround her belly.

May the three-eyed Goddess, who holds a lamp, an elephant tusk, a chariot wheel, and a lotus in her hands, and whose matted hair contains a shimmering crescent moon, be the remover of fear. (1) [The meter is Citravarna. (1)

121. Now, the meditation on the goddess Mohinīnityā (from the Śāradātilaka): She has the crescent moon upon her crest, is ruddy in hue, is worshipped by the immortals, and holds in her hands a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a full skull-cup.
One should meditate upon the consort of Śiva, whose limbs are overwhelmed with passion, who is three-eyed, and who is adorned with red unguents, garments, and ornaments. (1) Her color is red. (1)
122. Now, the meditation on Jayadurgā (from the Śāradātilaka):

She is vast in her dark hue, terrifying the hosts of enemies with her side-long glances, bearing upon her bound crest a crescent moon, and holding in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident; she possesses three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, surrounded by the gods, and served by those desiring spiritual perfection. [Her] color is black. 1.
123. Now, the meditation on Durgā Vindhyavāsinī (from the Śāradātilaka):

She resides in the center of a golden lotus, has three eyes, and resembles a flash of lightning; she holds a conch, a discus, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, and wears the crescent moon as an ornament.

One should meditate upon her who dwells on the Vindhya mountains, whose face is like the moon, who has five lions at her side, and who is praised by Indra and the other gods; she wears necklaces, armlets, strings of pearls, and earrings, and is golden-hued. || 1 || Golden-hued. || 1 ||
124. Now, the meditation on Ripumāriṇī-Durgā (from the *Śāradātilaka*):
Meditating upon her as red and terrifying, holding a threatening forefinger and a trident with her two arms, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times during the solar disc at dawn. || 1 ||
One shall slay one's enemies, together with their kinsmen, before long. [The deity is] red in color. 1.

125. Now, the meditation on Tripurabhairavī (from the Śāradātilaka): She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns; she wears a crown of scarlet silken cloth and a garland of flowers; her breasts are smeared with red pigment; and she holds a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

We worship the Goddess who stands upon a lotus, who possesses the splendor of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face, who wears a crown of jewels resembling the cool-rayed moon, and who holds the beauty of that very lotus with her lotus-like hands. [Her] complexion is red. 1.

126. Now, the meditation on Saṃvit Tripurā (in the Śāradātilaka): One should contemplate her within the heart—adorned with a crescent moon, as white as the autumnal moon, and consisting of fifty syllables.
She holds in her lotus-like hands a sacred book, a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and the gesture of exposition; she has three eyes and is white in complexion. || 1 ||
127. Now, the meditation on Bālā Tripurasundarī (from the Śāradātilaka):
She has the splendor of a thousand suns risen all at once, and her hand-emblems are the Vidyā [scripture], the rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness.
O Tripurā, those who worship you—whose lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes and who is radiant with the weight of your pearl necklaces—[attain their goal]. [The color is] red. 1.
128. Now, the meditation on the goddess Nityā (from the Śāradātilaka):
One should worship Nityā, who has the young moon as her crest-ornament, and who holds a noose, a goad, a wish-granting creeper, and a skull-bowl.
Carrying [it] with her hands, she is red-hued, three-eyed, and is striking that lute held in her hand. Her complexion is red.
129. Now, the meditation on the goddess Tvaritā (from the *Śāradātilaka*):
She is adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, wears a garment of leaves, possesses a necklace of *guñjā* seeds and shining breasts, and bears eight serpents.

I worship the three-eyed Goddess, adorned with the luster of bracelets, armlets, girdles, strings, and jingling anklets, whose hands are raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (1) Her complexion is dark blue. (1)
130. Now, the meditation on Kālarātri (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
She has a single braid of hair, wears hibiscus flowers as ear-ornaments, is naked, and stands upon a donkey.
She had long lips, ears adorned with earrings, and her body was anointed with oil.
Adorned with the thorns of the vine of her throbbing left foot.
She whose crest-banner increases, who is black as the Night of Doom, and is terrifying; she is black in color.
131. Now, the meditation on Vāgīśvarī (from the Kriyāpāda of the Pañcarātra):
Seated upon a white lotus throne, she is white in complexion and has four arms.
She was adorned with a crown of matted locks and decorated with jeweled earrings. || 1 ||
She wore a sacred thread as a necklace and was adorned with ornaments of pearls.
The goddess Dukkūlavasanā is endowed with three eyes. || 2 ||
In his right hand he holds a fine staff, and in his left hand a book.
And in his right hand he holds a rosary, and in his left hand a water-pot.
The form of Vāgīśī has been described; her color is white. 1.
132. Now, the meditation on Dhenuvāgīśvarī (from the Āśvalāyanakalpa):
[One should meditate on her] resembling pure crystal, clothed in white garlands and garments.
Holding a goad, a rosary, a noose, and a book. || 1 ||
The goddess, endowed with divine four arms, was adorned with strings of pearls.
Adorned with a new cloth that has the luster of a mirror polished by saliva.
She has breasts reaching to the middle of the altar and is adorned with a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She was endowed with a mass of matted locks, and her face resembled the full moon.
To the three-eyed Great Goddess, who wears golden anklets.
Adorned with bracelets rich in gold and jewels, she was further embellished with great bangles.
Illuminating the three worlds with her armlets, girdle, and other ornaments.
One should meditate upon the supreme Vāgīśvarī, who consists of the Śabdabrahman and is the Cow of Plenty; she is white in color.
133. Now, the meditation on Saubhāgyavāgīśvarī (from the Śāradātilaka):
She possesses the white luster of the full moon in its youth; her body is bent by the weight of her breasts, and she is seated upon a white lotus.

May the Goddess of Speech protect us—she whose splendor consists of a book and a writing stylus held aloft by her own lotus-like hands, and who is accompanied by all the hosts of prosperity. (1) She is white in color. (1)
134. Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī named Padmā (from the *Pāñcarātra*, *Kriyāpada*):
Padmā, seated upon a lotus throne, possessing the luster of a lotus, dwelling within a lotus.
The ear-ornament, consisting of earrings with crocodile-shaped ends, was radiant with gold and jewels. || 1 ||
Her face is as pure as the orb of the moon, and her two eyes are adorned with earrings.
Her limbs were as delightful as those of a young woman, and her well-arched eyebrows were beautifully expressive.
She has red lips, full cheeks, and breasts covered by a bodice.
The ornament of his head is the conch, the discus, the sectarian mark (sīmantaka), and the lotus.
His arms were like the trunks of elephants, radiant with armlets and bracelets.
The other goddess holds a lotus in her left hand and a bilva fruit in her right.
She was endowed with beautiful garments and possessed broad hips.
Marked by a girdle and a waist-cord, she is Lakṣmī who increases prosperity. [5] Padmavarṇa. [1]
135. Now, the meditation on the sixty-four Yoginīs (and their names, according to the Rudrayāmala):
I shall explain in brief the eight groups of eight Yoginīs.
The first eight [hands] are golden-hued, holding likewise a trident and a ḍamaru drum.
One should meditate upon Him, beautiful in all His limbs, holding a noose and a sword.
Then one should meditate on the second [form], holding a rosary and a goad.
Holding a book and a lute, he is white and adorned with jewel ornaments.
He is blue in complexion and holds a flame, a spear, a mace, and a lance.
One should meditate upon the third [deity], the bestower of auspiciousness, who possesses eight auspicious marks.
Holding a sword, a shield, a spear, and likewise an axe.
One should meditate with devotion upon that fourth [letter], which is smoke-colored, together with the eight [syllables].
A spear, a shield, an iron club, and likewise a bhindipāla; || 5 ||
This fifth Aṣṭaka is indeed white and very beautiful.
The sixth is yellow, the seventh is red, and the eighth has the brilliance of lightning.
The spear and other weapons are said to be equal, beginning with the sixth and ending with the eighth.
She is the Great Goddess of divine yoga, great yoga, and perfected yoga.
Piśācinī, Ḍākinī, Kālarātrī, and Niśācarī.
Kaṅkālī, Raudravetālī, Huṃkārī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 8 ||
With hair standing erect, with deformed eyes, with emaciated limbs, she was a devourer of human flesh.
Phaṭkārī, Vīrabhadrā, Dhūmrākṣī, and Kalahapriyā. || 9 ||
The Rakshasi Raktakshi is terrible, possessing universal forms and inspiring fear.
Kāmākṣī, Ugracāmuṇḍā, Bhīṣaṇā, and Tripurāntakā.
Vīrakaumārikā, Caṇḍī, Vārāhī, and Muṇḍadhāriṇī.
Bhairavī, Hastinī, Krodhadurmukhī, and Pretavāhinī. || 11 ||
Carrying a skull-topped staff, with long hanging lips, she is Mālatī, the Yoginī of mantras.
Asthinī, Cakriṇī, Grāhā, Kaṅkālī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 12 ||
Kaṇṭakī, Kāṭakī, Śubhrā, Kriyādūtī, and Karālinī.
Śaṅkhinī, Padminī, Kṣīrā, Hyasaṃdhā, and Prahāriṇī. || 13 ||
And Lakṣmī, fickle and longing for lovers, casts sidelong glances like a crow while keeping her face cast downward.
Dhūrjaṭī, Mālinī, Ghorā, Kapālī, and Viṣabhojinī. || 14 ||
Sixty-four yoginīs have been fully described, who bestow the supreme siddhis.
136. Now, the meditation on the deities of the six cakras situated within the body (according to the system of Vedānta Yoga):

in the Ādhāra, the Liṅga, the navel, the lotus of the heart, the root of the palate, and the forehead; in the two-petaled, sixteen-spoked, twenty-two-petaled, ten-petaled, twelve-petaled, and four-petaled [lotuses].

I bow to that which is in the form of letters, situated on all the petals: at the tip of the nose and in the middle of the forehead with the syllables *ḍa-pha-ka-ṭha-sa-ha*; in the middle of the throat, the vowels; and *haṃ-kṣaṃ* joined with the meaning of the principles (*tattva*).
Now, the meditations on the letters (*varṇadhyāna*) according to the *Siddhaśābaratantra* (137): Now, the meditation on the letter A:
I am Ajāmukhī, red in color, riding upon a swan, and clad in white garments.
He holds an excellent bow in his right hand, while in his two left hands he displays the arrow and the gesture of fearlessness. He is red in color.
138. Now, as for the meditation on Ākāra:
the Atharvaṇī known as Ākāra is dark-complexioned, clad in white garments, and emits rays of light.
He holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a shield (kheṭa), and likewise displays the gestures of boon-granting (vara) and fearlessness (abhaya) in succession; he is dark-complexioned.
139. Now, the meditation on the syllable *I*: the goddess known as *Ikārā* is white, mounted upon a rutting elephant, and auspicious.
In his right hands he holds the excellent sword Caṇḍahāsa and the mace; in his left hands he holds the shield and the gesture of fearlessness. He is white in color.
140. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ī*:
[the goddess] Īśvarī has the luster of gold, is mounted upon a bull, and wears white garments.
She holds a śārikā bird in her right hand, while in her left she holds a goad and the gesture of fearlessness; she is golden-hued.
141. Now, regarding the meditation on the syllable *U*:
the goddess Ugrā is indeed named after the syllable *U*; she has six arms, rides a lion, and is black in color.
In his right hands he holds a trident, a goad, and a boon-granting gesture; in his left hands, a noose, a mace, and the gesture of protection. He is white in complexion.
142. Now, the meditation on the syllable *Ū*: the goddess Ūkāra is radiant and has a noble tiger as her vehicle.
Red in color, she has four arms and holds a sword, a shield, the gesture of granting boons (vara), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). Her complexion is red.
143. Now, the meditation on the syllable Ṛ:
She who is named the syllable Ṛ is the abode of the seasons (Ṛtudhāmā), red in color, and seated upon a bull.
In his right hands he holds a noose and a sword, and likewise in his left hands an elephant goad and the gesture of fearlessness; he is red in color.
