144. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ṛ*:
This [goddess] named *Ṛkāra* has six faces and six arms, and is white in color.
In his right hands he holds a trident, a noose, and a shield; in his left hands, a sword, a mace, and the gesture of protection (abhaya).
She stands upon a red lion, holding [it], and is terrifying with her fierce gaze; she is white in color. 1.
145. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ḷ*:
she who is called *Ḷtaṃbhara-Ḷkāra* is dark-complexioned and stands upon an excellent tiger.
This [goddess], who has four faces and eight arms, holds protective implements in her remaining hands.
Likewise, he holds in his left hands a trident, a noose, and a ḍamaru drum.
She holds a sword, a skull-bowl, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is resplendent in yellow garments. [The other deity] is dark-complexioned.
146. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ḷ*: she who is named *ḷ* and *ḹṃjikā* is seated upon a flower-tusked elephant.
Red in color, with ten arms, she holds [various objects] in her hands starting from the right in successive order. || 1 ||
[He holds] the auspicious trident, noose, mace, sword, and the boon-granting gesture.
With his left hands, he likewise holds a sword, a shield, a mace, a spear, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; he is red in color.
147. Now, regarding the meditation on the letter *E*: she who is called *Ekārā* shall be Revatī, ten-faced, and garlanded with skulls.
She is red in color, has twenty arms, rides upon a lion, and possesses an eye in her forehead. || 1 ||
With his hands, he holds a discus, a trident, a noose, a sword, and a water-pot.
And he holds a rosary, the gesture of consciousness (cinmudrā), a water-purifier, a mallet, and the boon-granting hand.
In his left hands, he holds a conch, a bhindipāla, a crescent moon, and a shield.
The skull, the fire, the drying [wind], the staff, the mace, and the gestures of protection and fear; [the deity is] red in color.
148. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ai*: the constellation Aśvinī, preceded by the dry [constellation] Bharaṇī, and Revatī, are placed upon the three heads.
This six-armed goddess has the gait of a peacock and is surrounded by red hair.
With half [of his] hands, he holds a discus, a trident, and likewise a boon-granting gesture.
With his left hands he holds the conch, the mace, and the heavy club, as well as the gesture of granting fearlessness; he is white in complexion.
149. Now, regarding the meditation on the syllable *o*: from the syllable *o* arises the goddess Aśvinī, red in color and six-faced.
He should have the tail-feathers of a peacock on his left arm, and in his right hands, he should hold a lotus, a goad, and an arrow.
With a sword, a noose, the *cinmudrā*, and a bell, she gazes with a squint-eyed look.
In his left hands, he holds a spear, a bow, a shield, and a mace.
Holding a book and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), she causes terror to all enemies; her color is red. (1)
150. Now follows the meditation on the syllable *au*: This [syllable] called *au* is indeed Aghorī, Karālī, and Dīrghajihvikā.
She has one face, one eye, and a gaze made crooked by a frown. || 1 ||
Resembling a dark blue cloud, she is fierce, with Bheruṇḍa as her excellent mount.
With six arms like the rays of the sun, she holds a trident, a sword, and likewise a boon-granting gesture.
And Mahodarī holds a mace, a deer, and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands; she is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
151. Now, the meditation on the syllable Aṃ:
the goddess Añjanābhāñjanā has five faces, matted hair, and a slender form.
Mahodarī is mounted upon a noble vehicle that is a great tiger.
She is four-armed, holding a trident, a noose, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is black in color. 1.
152. Now, regarding the meditation on the syllable *Aḥ*:
the goddess A-ityākhyātvajā is three-headed and three-eyed.
She is clad in red and yellow garments and has as her excellent vehicle a most fierce female jackal.
She is adorned with six arms, holding a trident, a sword, and displaying the gesture of granting boons.
In her left hands, she holds, in sequence, an elephant goad, a great shield, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is red in color. 1. 2.
153. Now follows the meditation on the letter Ka:
she is white, adorned with ornaments of living beings, mounted upon an elephant, and possesses four arms.

He holds a trident and the boon-granting gesture (vara-mudrā) in his right hands, and an elephant-goad (aṅkuśa) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā) in his left hands. His complexion is white.
154. Now, the meditation on the letter Kha:
she is yellow, seated upon a wagtail, three-headed, and bearing a trident.
She is beloved, holding a sword that illuminates the darkness and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is yellow.
155. Now, the meditation on the syllable *ga*:
She is known as *Ga*, smoke-colored, four-faced, seated upon a lion, eight-armed, and auspicious.
Smoky-colored on the right, he holds a trident, a rosary, a sacrificial ladle, and the gesture of granting boons.
In the left [hands], however, he holds a book, a water-pot, a skull-cup, and the gesture of fearlessness in sequence; his color is smoky-gray. || 1 ||
156. Now, the meditation on the syllable Gha:
she has the form of a black female ogress, with the face of a sow and a slender waist.
With his six right arms, he holds in sequence a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a boon-granting gesture.
In her left hands she holds a sword and a shield; she is the destroyer of enemies and is black in color. (1)
157. Now, the meditation on the letter Ṅa:
The Mistress of Gods possesses infinite power and is mounted upon a red peacock.
In her six faces, she holds a bow, a sword, a shield, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is red in color.
Then he performed meditation upon Suṣumṇā, who has one face, is mounted on a horse, and possesses four arms.
She is known as the bearer of a sword and a shield, possessing auspicious hands that grant boons and fearlessness; she is golden-hued.
159. Now, the meditation on the letter Cha: she is as white as a waterfall, possesses Arundhatī, is yellow in color, and has a monkey as her vehicle.
The auspicious goddess holds a trident, a razor, a noose, and a shield; she is yellow in color.
160. Now, the meditation on the letter Ja:
she bestows the enjoyment of life, has a red face, three eyes, and rides upon a lion.
She has four arms, endowed with a sword, a shield, and hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is red.
161. Now, the meditation on the syllable Jha:
the goddess Jhonirjharanadī has a lotus resembling an autumn cloud.
Standing upon a peacock, he holds a noose, an excellent boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, bestowing auspiciousness upon men; his complexion is white.
162. Now, the meditation on the letter *ña*:
She who awakens through the name *ña*, she who is white, seated upon a lion, and whose nature is consciousness.
Her auspicious hands are endowed with the trident, the lotus, the *cinmudrā*, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is white in complexion.
163. Now follows the meditation on the letter *Ṭa*: the goddess Dhāraṇī named *Ṭā* holds a trident, a *ṭaṅka*-axe, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Standing upon a rutting elephant, she is clad in garments radiant as the *pāṭala* flower; her complexion is the color of the *pāṭala*.
164. Now follows the meditation on the syllable *ṭha*:
the ritual action is that of Sarasvatī; she is known as *ṭhā*, and she holds the *ṭaṃ* gesture, the goad, the boon-granting mudrā, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Mounted upon an excellent lion, she possesses a single face and is considered to be of a reddish hue; her complexion is the color of the dawn.
165. Now follows the meditation on the syllable *ḍa*:
Ḍakāriṇī has five faces and holds an axe and a mace.
She has four arms, holds a cock, a mountain, and displays the gesture of fearlessness; her complexion is white.
166. Now, the meditation on the letter *ḍha*:
She whose form is *ḍha* is named Śrīghanā, possessing five faces and riding upon a peacock.
With hands as white as lightning, she holds a trident, an axe, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. She is golden-hued. 1.
167. Now, the meditation on the letter *ṇa*:
The Mistress of the Gods (*Deveśī*) is of infinite power, red in color, and has a peacock as her vehicle.
She is beautiful, with one face, holding a trident, a spear, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is red.
168. Now, the meditation on the letter *ta*:
the goddess Sarasvatī, known as *Tā*, is white, seated upon a lotus, and clad in silken garments.
With the forms of a single face, he holds a lute, a trident, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; his complexion is white.
169. Now follows the meditation on the letter Tha:
Sarasvatī, known as Thā, has five faces, is black in color, and has a blue throat.
She holds a śārikā bird and a hand-drum (āṇḍamaru), is mounted upon a bull, and displays the gestures of boons and fearlessness; she is white in color.
170. Now, the meditation on the syllable *Da*:
she is known as Ekavaktrāruṇā, possessing eight arms and bestowing enjoyments.
She holds a lotus, a śārikā lute, and a ḍamaru drum, as well as the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness. She is of a reddish (aruṇa) complexion.
171. Now, the meditation on the syllable *Dha*:
she is known as Śyāmalā, Acamālā, and Dhā; she has one face and four arms.
Seated upon a bull, she holds a śārikā bird and a lotus in her [two] hands, and displays the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness. She is dark-complexioned. 1.
172. Now, the meditation on the letter Na:
Nonantashakti, the Goddess of the gods, is seated upon a rutting elephant.
With one face, she holds a lightning-bolt, a trident, a lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is golden.
173. Now, one should describe the meditation on the letter *pa*:
this [deity] has the form of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and holds a trident, a spear, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
She holds [the weapons] with her hands, has five faces, sits upon a seat of full-blown lotuses, and is reddish; she is red in color.
174. Now, the meditation on the letter Pha: she stands upon a fierce lion with five faces, as delicate as a pale-red parasol.
Holding a thunderbolt, a conch, a goad, a noose, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, as well as arrows; || 1 ||
He holds a noose and a deer with his ten hands in succession; he is pale-red in color. (1)
175. Now, the meditation on the syllable *baka*:
she has the pure, tawny luster of lightning, is mounted upon a lion, and possesses a beautiful form.
He holds weapons in his ten hands in the same manner as before; he is tawny in color.
176. Now follows the meditation on the syllable Bha:
the goddess Bhākhī is dark blue in color, has one face, and stands upon a bhadra seat.
She holds a bow and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, resembling the rising sun; she is the color of vermilion.
177. Now, regarding the meditation on the syllable *ma*:
the goddess Śyāmalā is the *movidyā*, horse-faced, and possesses the luster of crystal.
She is beautiful, holding a lute, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is white.
178. Now follows the meditation on the syllable *ya*: the goddess named Dīpinī is seated upon a lion, eight-armed, and black in color.
She holds a trident, a bow, a noose, a sword, a shield, a gift-bestowing gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness; she is white in color.
179. Now, the meditation on the syllable *repha*:
she who is called *repha* is *ārecikā*, dark blue in color, seated upon a lion, and clad in red garments.

She holds [these] with her eight hands, in the order of right and left: a sword, a shield, a goad, a mace, a noose, a trident, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. She is dark-complexioned. 1.
180. Now, the meditation on the letter *la*:
The goddess Mohinī, whose nature is *la*, has the luster of gold and is seated upon a lotus.
She possesses six arms, endowed with a goad, a trident, a sword, a shield, the gesture of giving, and the gesture of fearlessness. Her complexion is golden.
181. Now follows the meditation on the syllable Va:
the goddess Vākhyāpārāyaṇī has the luster of crystal and wears saffron-colored garments.
Seated upon a clearly manifest lotus throne, she holds two lotuses and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; her complexion is white.
182. Now, for the meditation on Śakāra:
Śākhyāmaṅgalagaurī has the luster of molten gold.
Seated upon a pedestal of a thousand lotuses, she is adorned with divine ornaments. || 1 ||
With his four-armed forms, he holds two lotuses and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he is golden-hued. || 1 ||
183. Now follows the meditation on the syllable *ṣa*:
The goddess Raktāṣānukriyā is seated upon a noble royal swan.
With her yellow-robed hands, she holds two lotuses and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she is red in color.
184. Now follows the meditation on the letter *sa*: she who dwells within the white lotus known as the *siddhakriyā-sakāra*.
With the radiance of the *pāṭala* flower, he holds the excellent lotus, the gesture of generosity (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). [He is] the color of the *pāṭala* flower. 1.
185. Now follows the meditation on the letter *ha*: she who meditates upon it is known as *Ādhyāyinī*, riding upon a rutting elephant named *Ha*.
With rays the color of the *pāṭala* flower, he holds the excellent lotus, the boon-granting gesture (*vara*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). [He is] the color of the *pāṭala* flower. 1.
186. Now, the meditation on the letter *la*:
the goddess Lobha-bandha-mocinī (the Liberatrix from the Bondage of Greed), golden-hued, is seated upon a lotus.
She possesses six arms, endowed with a goad, a trident, a sword, a shield, the gesture of giving, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is golden-hued.
187. Now, the meditation on the letter Kṣa:
the goddess Mālinī is dark blue in color and seated upon a five-faced lion.
The five-faced [deity] holds a sword, a trident, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness; she is the color of the *pāṭala* flower. She is the color of the *pāṭala*.
Now, the meditation on the deities of the letters beginning with *praṇava* (according to the *Pāñcarātrāgama*).
(In this [system], the arrangement of the weapons for all the deities must be performed in a clockwise direction.
188. Among those, [the meditation] on *oṃkāra*:

The deity is Śrī Nārāyaṇa (according to the *Śeṣasaṃhitā*): Nārāyaṇa has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus; he stands within a lotus, wears yellow garments, is adorned with all ornaments, is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus. || 1 ||

189. Now, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity of the letter *a* (according to the *Padmasaṃhitā*): he has the color of lotus filaments, wears yellow garments, is adorned with all ornaments, and holds a mace, a lotus, a conch, and a discus. || 1 ||

190. Now, according to the *Pādmasaṃhitā*, the presiding deity of the letter Ā is Madhusūdana: he is the color of a reddish lotus, wears yellow garments, holds a discus, a conch, a lotus, and a mace, is adorned with all ornaments, and stands [erect]. || 1 ||

191. Now, the deity of the letter *i* is Trivikrama (according to the *Pādmasaṃhitā*): he has the color of the fire of time (*kālānala*), wears yellow garments, holds a lotus-stalk, a discus, and a conch, is adorned with all ornaments, and stands [in a posture]. || 1 ||

192. Now, the deity of the vowel *ī* is Vāmana (according to the *Pādmasaṃhitā*): he has the color of the rising sun, wears yellow garments, holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, is adorned with ornaments, and stands [erect]. || 1 ||
193. Now, the deity of the syllable *u* is Śrīdhara; he is yellow in color, wears yellow garments, holds a lotus, a discus, a mace, and a conch, is adorned with ornaments, and stands upright. || 1 ||
194. Now, the letter Ū has Hṛṣīkeśa as its deity; he is the color of lightning, wears yellow garments, holds a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch, and stands adorned with ornaments. || 1 ||

195. Now, for the syllable *ṛ*, the deity is Padmanābha; he is blue-lotus colored, wears yellow garments, holds a conch, a discus, a lotus, and a mace, is adorned with ornaments, and stands upright. || 1 ||

196. Now, the deity of the letter *ṛ* is Dāmodara; he has the color of the Japā flower, holds a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a discus, and stands adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and the like. || 1 ||

197. Now, for the letter *ḷ*, the deity is Śambhu; he has three eyes, is reddish-brown in color, wears a crown of matted hair, holds the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a battle-axe, carries a deer and an elephant-goad in his hands, and is clad in a tiger skin. || 1 ||

198. Now, for the letter *ḷ*, the deity is Nārāyaṇa; he possesses the luster of a dark cloud, holds a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus, is adorned with ornaments such as a forest garland (*vanamālā*), and stands wearing yellow garments. || 1 ||
199. Now, for the letter *e*, the deity is Mādhava; he is white in color, wears yellow garments, holds a mace, a discus, a conch, and a lotus, and stands adorned with ornaments. || 1 ||
200. Now, for the vowel *ai*, the deity is Govinda; he is pale-red in complexion, wears yellow garments, holds a discus, a staff, a lotus, and a conch, and stands adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

201. Now, for the syllable *o*, Vāsudeva is the deity; he is dark as a rain-cloud, wears yellow garments, holds a lotus, a discus, a conch, and a mace, is adorned with ornaments, and stands upright. || 1 ||
202. Now, the deity of the vowel *au* is Saṃkarṣaṇa; he is red in color, wears yellow garments, holds a mace, a conch, a lotus, and a discus, and stands adorned with ornaments. (1)
203. Now, the deity of the syllable *Aṃ* is Pradyumna, golden-hued like shimmering gold, holding a discus, conch, mace, and lotus, adorned and standing. (1)

204. Now, for the syllable *Aḥ*, the deity Aniruddha is dark green like a blade of *dūrvā* grass, clad in yellow garments, holding a discus, mace, conch, and lotus, adorned with ornaments, and standing. (1)

205. Now, the rule for the letter *ka* and its deity: the four-faced one, golden in color, holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) in his hands; specifically, he bears the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his primary hands, while the other two hold a water-pot and a rosary; he wears a circle of matted locks (*jaṭāmaṇḍala*) and is seated comfortably. || 1 ||

206. Now, the deity of the letter *kha* is Sudarśana, having the color of a blazing fire, situated within a hexagon. He stands with his hair aflame, adorned with all ornaments, and bearing as weapons the conch, discus, bow, axe, sword, trident, noose, goad, lotus, vajra, shield, plow, mace, club, and spear. || 1 ||
207. Now, the speech-deity of the letter Ga is crystal-colored, holding a rosary, a lotus, a parrot, and a book; she is adorned with all ornaments and proceeds in a clockwise direction. (1)

Now, for the letter Gha, the deity is Śārṅgadhārī (the Wielder of the Bow), resembling gold in color and having a human form; he stands with his right hand in the tarjanī-mudrā and his left hand resting on his hip, his head marked by his own emblem. || 1 ||

209. Now, the presiding deity of the letter *ṅa* is Nandaka; he is dark green like a blade of dūrvā grass, has the form of a man, holds the tarjanī mudrā in his right hand, has his left hand placed upon his hip, and his head is marked with his own emblem. || 1 ||
210. Now, for the letter *ca*, Nandakodevatā is the presiding deity; the remainder is as before. (1)
211. Now, the deity of the letter *cha* is Yama; he is black in color, holds a staff and a noose in his hands while granting fearlessness, is mounted upon a buffalo, and has a terrifying face. (1)

212. Now, the deity of the letter *ja* is Musalī, dark as a crop of grain, having the form of a man; his right hand is formed with the *tarjanī-mudrā*, his left hand is placed upon his hip, his head is marked with his own seed-syllable, and he is adorned with all ornaments. (1)

213. Now, the deity Jhaṅkāradhāriṇī is golden-colored, human in form, holding the tarjanī mudrā in her right hand, with her left hand placed upon her hip, her head marked with her own emblem, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)

Now, for the letter Ña, Bhṛgu is the deity; he is dark green like a blade of dūrvā grass, holding the gesture of knowledge (vijñānamudrā) in his right hand and a book in his left, and is endowed with a sacred thread, matted hair, and other such attributes. (1)

215. Now, the presiding deity of the letter *ṭa* is Kūrma (the Tortoise), resembling gold; he holds the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), the wheel, the conch, and the boon (*varada*) in his hands, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

Now, for the letter *ṭha*, the presiding deity is Paṭṭābhirāma, who is dark-complexioned and seated comfortably upon a throne in the center. To his left is Sītā, golden-hued; in front is Hanumān, golden-hued; in the west is Lakṣmaṇa, golden-hued; on the two sides are Bharata, dark-complexioned, and Śatrughna, red-complexioned; in the northwest is Sugrīva, golden-piṅgala; Vibhīṣaṇa is black-complexioned; Aṅgada is red-complexioned; and Jāmbavān is golden-hued. He is surrounded by these [deities] and adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

217. Now, the deity of the letter *ḍa* is Garuḍa, possessing a golden luster; his right foot is drawn up, his left foot is cast behind, both wings are outstretched, his hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture at his heart, and he is adorned with various ornaments. (1)

218. Now, regarding the deities of the seven Mothers for the letter *ḍha*: therein, Brāhmī is golden-colored, holding in her hands the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, and a rosary; she wears a crown of matted hair, has a swan as her emblem and vehicle, and is adorned with all ornaments. (1)
Māheśvarī is red in luster, holding in her hands the gestures of fearlessness, a trident, a rosary, and a boon; she wears a crown of matted hair and has the bull as her emblem and vehicle. || 2 ||
Kaumārī has the luster of the dawn; she holds a spear and a cock in her hands, has a peacock as her banner and vehicle, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 3 ||

Vaiṣṇavī is dark-complexioned, holding the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons along with a conch and a discus in her hands, having Garuḍa as her vehicle, and adorned with all ornaments. || 4 ||

Vārāhī is dark-complexioned, with the face of a boar, and has eight arms; from the right side, she holds the gestures of fearlessness, a mace, a sword, a discus, a conch, a shield, a plough, and displays the gesture of granting boons; she is mounted upon a lion and adorned with all ornaments. || 5 ||

Māheṃdrī is red in color, four-armed, holding the gestures of fearlessness, a spear, and a vajra in her hands; she has an elephant as her emblem and vehicle, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 6 ||

Cāmuṇḍā is red in color, four-armed, holding the gestures of fearlessness, a skull-cup, a trident, and a boon-granting gesture in her hands; she wears a tiger-skin garment and is adorned with all ornaments. || 7 ||

219. Now, Viṣṇu is the deity of the letter *ṇa*; he resembles the filaments of a lotus, has four arms, and holds a lotus, a mace, a discus, and a conch. He is clad in yellow garments, adorned with all ornaments, and stands [there]. (1)
Now, for the letter *ta*, the deity is Acyuta; he is yellow in color, four-armed, holding a conch, a lotus, a discus, and a mace, accompanied by Śrī and Bhū, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)
221. Now, for the letter *tha*, the deity is Puruṣottama; he holds a discus, a lotus, a conch, and a mace, has four arms, the color of crystal, and is adorned with all ornaments. (1)

222. Now, for the letter *da*, the deity is Atri; he has the luster of the dawn, wears matted hair, and is seated. He holds the gesture of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*) in his right hand and a book in his left, and is adorned with all ornaments. (1)
223. Now, the deity of the letter *dh* is Kubera; he has white radiance, two arms, and holds a lotus and a bridle in his hands. He is mounted upon a horse and adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

224. Now, the deity of the letter *na* is Lambodara, with a ruddy luster, four-armed, having an elephant’s face, adorned with all ornaments, and holding in his hands a broken tusk, a noose, a goad, and a great fruit. || 37 ||

225. Now, the deity of the letter *pa* is Yoganṛsiṃha, who resembles gold; his two principal arms are extended over his knees, while with the other two he holds a discus and a conch, and he is adorned with all ornaments. (1)

226. Now, for the letter *pha*, the deity is Bhīmanṛhari, resembling molten gold; he holds four wheels with his four arms, possesses flaming hair, has a face formidable with fangs, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

227. Now, the presiding deity of the letter *ba* is Balarāma; he has a white radiance, two arms, holds a plow in his right hand, and his left hand is hanging down; he wears blue garments and is adorned with all ornaments. (1)
228. Now, for the letter *bha*, the deity is Nṛsiṃha according to the previously mentioned yoga; everything else is like that of the letter *pa*. (1)

229. Now, for the letter *ma*, the deity is Nārāyaṇa; he is dark-complexioned, seated upon a lotus throne, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)
230. Now, the deity of the letter *ya* is Vāyu (the Wind), smoke-colored, two-armed, holding a hook and a banner in his hands, mounted upon a deer, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)

231. Now, the deity of the letter *ra* is Dhūmadhvaja (Smoke-bannered), who is of reddish-brown color. He has four arms on the right and three on the left. In clockwise order, he holds a *sruk* ladle, a *sruva* spoon, a rosary, a spear, a javelin, a fan, and a vessel of ghee. He has three feet and two heads, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||

232. Now, the deity of the letter *la* is Indra; he is dark blue like a cloud, four-armed, with hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), holding a vajra and a conch, mounted upon an elephant, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)

Now, the deity of the letter *va* is Varuṇa; he is dark-complexioned, two-armed, mounted upon a crocodile vehicle, holding a noose in his right hand and granting fearlessness with his left, and adorned with all ornaments. (1)

Now, for the letter Śa, the deity is Umā, dark-complexioned, with two arms; she holds a lotus in her right hand, while her left hand hangs down, and she is adorned with the crescent moon as an ornament and embellished with all types of jewelry. (1)

235. Now, the deity of the letter *ṣa* is Lakṣmī; she has the luster of gold, sits upon a lotus throne, and has four arms. Her hands display the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and two lotuses, and she is consecrated by the nectar from the frontal globes of two elephants. She is adorned with all ornaments. (1)

236. Now, the deity of the letter *sa* is the Moon; he resembles crystal, sits upon a lion-throne, has two arms, and holds two white water-lilies (*kumuda*). He is accompanied by Rohiṇī, who is dark-complexioned and holds a water-lily, and is adorned with all ornaments. (1)

237. Now, the deity of the letter *ha* is Sūrya, red in color, seated upon an eight-petaled lotus in the midst of a circle of light; he has two arms, holds two lotuses, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||
238. Now, the deity of the letter *la* is Sūrya; everything else is as before. || 1 ||
239. Now, for the letter *kṣa*, the deity is the previously mentioned Bhīmanṛsiṃha; everything else is as before. || 1 ||

Thus, [he who is] seated upon the divine jeweled throne experienced by the entire circle of sovereign emperors, great kings, and principal lords of the earth—descended through an unbroken lineage of the treasury of all arts, shining resplendently in the midst of the illustrious Mahīśūra Great State, which is the seat of the prosperity of the Karṇāṭaka country, the crest-jewel of all lands, and the ornament of the entire circle of the earth.

In the work titled *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Great King Kṛṣṇarāja—the sovereign of Mahīśūra, adorned with numerous titles such as the illustrious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, Possessor of Unassailable Majesty, Peerless Hero among Monarchs, Ornament of the Sky, Sole Hero of the World, Moon in the Ocean of the Yadu Lineage, and Bearer of the Conch, Discus, Goad, Axe, Makara, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva, Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, Earth-Boar, Hanuman, Garuḍa, and Lion—the first treasury, entitled "The Description of the Nature of Powers such as Cāmuṇḍā," is complete. 1.
May this be offered at the lotus feet of Śrī Cāmuṇḍā.
May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the first Śaktinidhi within the venerable *Tattvanidhi* treatise. Prosperity!
Now,
In the *Śrītattvanidhi*, the second is the Viṣṇunidhi.
1. Now, the meditation on the Virāṭ Puruṣa (*Bhāgavata*, Skandha 2, Chapter 1).
For they declare that Pātāla is the root of his feet, while Sātala is his heels and forefeet.
Mahātala is the two beautiful ankles of the Creator of the universe, and Talātala is indeed the two shanks of the Supreme Person.
The two knees and the soles of the feet of the Universal Form are Sutala; the two thighs are Vitala and Atala.
They describe the surface of the earth as His hips, the expanse of the sky as His navel, and the celestial sphere as His chest, O Lord of the Earth.
The expanse of his chest is the multitude of lights; his neck is the day, and his mouth is indeed the intermediate space.
They know austerity to be the forehead of the Primal Being, and truth to be the heads of the thousand-headed one.
Indra and the others are his arms; the suns are his hands; the quarters are his ears; and sound is the hearing of that [Supreme Being].
The two Aśvins are the supreme nostrils, the sense of smell, and the fragrance; and Agni is the kindled mouth. || 4 ||
The two eyes became the sun and the moon, and the eyelashes became both day and night of Viṣṇu.
The expansion of his eyebrows was the abode of Parameṣṭhin; the palate was indeed the waters, and the tongue was the essence.
The Vedic hymns proclaim him as food; his fangs are Yama, the moon and the hosts of stars are his teeth.
And her glance from the corners of her eyes is an illusion that causes the madness of laughter and is a creation of endless variety.
Shame was his upper lip, greed his lower lip, and the path of dharma his back, while righteousness was his breast.
Mitra is his penis and testicles; the oceans and mountains are the collection of his bones.
The rivers are his channels, and the trees are the hairs on the body of this Universal Form, O Lord of Men.
Food, vigor, breath, the wind, movement, vitality, and the flow of the qualities of action [all arise from it]. || 8 ||
O Vidura, the clouds are the hair of the Lord, while the two twilights are the garments of that infinite one, the best of the Kurus.
They say the heart and the mind are the unmanifest; and that moon is the sheath of all transformations.
The wise call the power of consciousness "mati," the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of the Universal Self, O Girīśa.
Horses, mules, camels, elephants, and wild animals—all these beasts have their [vital] point in the region of the buttocks. || 10 ||
The speech of Manu, the abode of sages, is a diverse exposition of that wisdom.
The voices of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and Apsarases, as well as Smṛti and the foremost of the Asura hosts. || 11 ||
The high-souled one, whose face is Brahman, whose arms are the Kṣatriyas, and whose dark-colored feet rest upon the earth; (p. 46) [he is Viḍūru].

Endowed with the qualities of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, possessing the power of virility, he is the essence of the sacrificial oblation (*havya*), the application of the expansion of ritual action. || 12 ||
Such is the extent and configuration of this body of the Lord that I have described to you.
In this most massive body, the mind of one who does not lead it by means of his own intelligence is sustained [only] with difficulty. 13.1.
2. Now, the meditation on the form of Mahāvaikuṇṭha (from the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa):
In that place, amidst thousands of jewel-encrusted pillars possessing the brilliance of the sun...
The Blessed Lord Hari was seated within a beautiful, divine celestial chariot.
And there, upon a golden pedestal supported by the powers of the foundation (ādhāra-śakti) and the rest;
In that divine [palace] made of various jewels and endowed with many kinds of gems. || 2 ||
In the center of that is an auspicious eight-petaled lotus composed of the syllables of the mantra.
In the beautiful pericarp, within the auspicious syllable that is the seed-mantra of Lakṣmī.
In that [lotus], he was endowed with a splendor equal to ten thousand million rising suns.
The glorious and divine Nārāyaṇa was seated upon a lotus throne.
On his right side is the golden Mother of the World.
Endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with divine ornaments.
Holding a vessel of wealth and a citron in his hands, [he stands] upon a golden lotus.
To the left is the goddess Pṛthivī, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
Adorned with various ornaments and decorated with diverse garments.
With his two uplifted arms, he holds a beautiful pair of red lotuses.
Likewise, with the next two [verses], one should worship the Goddess, as well as the vessel of grain and the cloth.
The divine Śaktis, such as Vimalā and others, hold chowries.
Seated upon the tips of the petals, they were adorned with all auspicious marks.
Seated in their midst was the Blessed Lord Acyuta Hari.
With conch, discus, mace, and lotus in their hands, and adorned with divine ornaments.
He was adorned with ornaments such as armlets, bracelets, and necklaces.
He was resplendent with two earrings resembling the rising thousand-rayed sun at dawn.
Puruṣottama is eternally served by the aforementioned thirty gods.
He indeed dwells in the city of Kuṇṭha, eternally liberated and enjoying the singular bliss.
[This was] indeed [revealed] through the glorious eight-syllable mantras to the perfected ones who were wise.
Going to the world of Viṣṇu is not possible for others in any way whatsoever. [He is] red in color. (1)
3. Now, the meditation on Viṣṇu (from the *Pādmapurāṇa*):
The God of gods should be visualized as sleeping upon Śeṣa with two arms; one foot of the Lord should be shown resting in the lap of Lakṣmī. (1)
Likewise, another [digit] should be placed, situated upon the mark of the remaining enjoyment.
One [foot] should be placed in the *asana* (sitting) position, while the other is extended to the left side. || 2 ||
Another hand of his should likewise be placed upon the region of the head.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) is seated comfortably upon the lotus born from his navel. || 3 ||
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, however, should be depicted clinging to the stalk of the lotus.
One should place the conch, discus, mace, and other [emblems] in their embodied forms all around. [He is] cloud-colored. 1.
4. Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī (from the Ratnakośa):
She is seated upon a reddish lotus, her complexion like a mass of its pollen, holding in her hands a pair of lotuses that bestow the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
May the Mother of the World, adorned with various ornaments such as jeweled crowns and born of the Kalpas, grant us continuous prosperity and glory. (1) She is golden-hued. (1)
5. Now, the meditation on Bhūdevī (from the Pāñcarātra):
She is golden-hued, has two hands, and with her right hand bestows fearlessness.
Accompanied by pomegranate fruits, she is beneath the single wish-fulfilling tree on the left.
Her left foot is said to touch the ground where the treasure-pot rests.
Adorned with all ornaments, she should be meditated upon as the bestower of all fruits; her complexion is like gold.
6. Now, the meditation on Nīlādevī (according to the Pāñcarātra):
She is dark like the petal of a blue lotus and adorned with blue garments.
Four-armed and seated comfortably, she is endowed with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 1 ||
With her other two hands, however, she holds two white water-lilies.
Adorned with all ornaments, she is impelled by the goddess Nīlā; her complexion is dark-blue.
7. Now, indeed, is the meditation on Kuṇṭhanārāyaṇa (from the Aṣṭākṣarī-kalpa):

Having extended the left foot and drawn up the right foot—which removes the misfortunes of those who take refuge—placing it upon the knee, and having placed the other arm, which is not the left one, upon the coils of the serpent.

Holding the conch and the discus with his two rear arms for the subduing of adversaries, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha—adorned with divine ornaments and other regalia—brings about the welfare of the worlds. (1) [The meter is] Meghavarṇa. (1)
8. Now follows the meditation on Tārakarāma (from the Śrīrāmakalpa):

One should indeed visualize him here at the foot of the celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa), within a great golden pavilion, seated upon a jeweled vīrāsana throne situated in the center of the Puṣpaka chariot.

I worship that dark-complexioned Rāma, who, at the beginning, caused the sons of Prabhajana to recite the supreme reality to the sages, and who was surrounded by Bharata and the others. (1) [He is] of a dark complexion. (1)
9. Now, the meditation on the form of Śiṃśumāra (from the Mayūkhedānakhaṇḍa):
Śiṃśumāra has four arms and a luster resembling shimmering stars.
He whose hands shine with the conch, discus, boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and who is composed of the three Vedas. || 1 ||
Resplendent with hosts of deities resting upon his tail, which serves as the support for the wheel of light.
Hari, who is white in color, is the embodiment of Time, eternally to be meditated upon, and the bestower of the desired objects of his devotees. (1-2)
10. Now, the meditation on Trivikrama (from the *Mantrasāra* of the *Pāñcarātra* and the *Bhāgavata*):
Trivikrama is red in color and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
He shines resplendent with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and earrings.
With his shimmering crown, armlets, fish-shaped earrings, śrīvatsa mark, excellent jewel, girdle, and garments;
O King of kings, the Blessed One of wide strides was adorned with garlands and forest wreaths of honey-bees. || 2 ||
He strode across the earth with one foot, through the sky with his body, and across the quarters of the horizon with his arms.
From the second step, he gradually ascended to the third heaven; yet not even an atom of that [third step] belonged to him.
The foot of Urukrama has gone above and below the heavens, beyond Mahas, Janas, and Tapas; it is red in color. 1.
11. Now, the meditation on Hayagrīva (from the Pāñcarātra):
I salute him whose face is like a stage, who is seated upon the orb of the moon, as white as the moon, whose essence is nectar, and who [radiates] with rays on all sides.
Manifesting both within and outside the cosmic egg, his arms—adorned with a conch, an eye, a book, and a lotus—bear the marks of supreme awakening.

White in color. According to another version (*Vedāntācāryakṛtahayagrīvastuti*): May the Lord of Speech appear within my stainless mind, seated upon a white lotus as radiant as split crystal, holding in his lotus-like hands the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*), a book, a conch, and a discus, and flooding me with rays as pure as nectar and possessing unfading splendor. White in color. 1.
12. Now, the meditation on the form of Bhūvarāha (according to the Pāñcarātra):
He is dark-complexioned, bestowing the boons of the Discus, Fearlessness, and Excellent Boon, and accompanied by the Earth and all His own aforementioned retinues.
The object of meditation, endowed with all his own bodies, is the Boar (Kola), the Lord (Hari), who grants the fulfillment of all desires. He is dark-complexioned.
13. Now, the meditation on the form of Dharaṇīvarāha (from the Dānakāṇḍa of Hemādri): The Lord should be depicted in the form of a boar, standing upon Śeṣa.
The remaining [serpent] should be made four-armed and endowed with beautiful jewel-adorned hoods. || 1 ||
O Yādava, you should hold a sword and a mace in his two hands.
And he should be made in the form of a serpent, likewise with his hands joined in *añjali*.
The Blessed One should be situated behind him, standing in the ālīḍha posture.
The Earth, in the form of a woman, was situated at his left jewel.
One should perform auspicious prostrations to him with both hands.
In whose hand the goddess Earth is held, in that same hand there shall be a conch shell.
Other hands of his should be made holding a lotus, a discus, and a mace.
One should visualize Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, seated upon a lotus throne.
She was fair-complexioned, beautiful in form, and adorned with every ornament.
Her right hand, however, holds a golden lotus and is in the gesture of granting boons.
Varāha is dark-complexioned; Bhūmi is white-complexioned; Śrī is gold-complexioned; and Śeṣa is bright-white in complexion. || 1 ||
14. Meditation on the Śrīkara Mūrti (from the Pāñcarātra):
Holding the sun and moon as his conch and discus, and bearing the two treasures known as Śaṅkha and Prasūna;
He should be meditated upon as satisfying the Vasus with his two hands, with Lakṣmī seated on his lap and resting upon the shoulder of Garuḍa; he is golden-hued.
15. Now, the meditation on the form of Haṃsa (from the *Pāñcarātra*, *Mantrasāra*):
One should meditate upon Him who possesses the radiance of a thousand million moons, who holds the sun and moon in His hands, and who is seated together with His beloved upon the orb of the moon.
The Lord of Ramā, whose two arms hold a conch and a discus, is being sprinkled with nectar from the rising orb of the great moon; he is white in color. 1. 1.
16. Now, the meditation on the form of Dadhivāmana (from the *Pāñcarātra*):
One should meditate upon Him who has eyes as broad as the petals of a very white lotus, and who is eating nectar from a golden vessel filled with curds.
Holding [the moon] with both arms, accompanied by all the gods, seated within the orb of the cool-rayed moon, and united with Ramā; he is white in color.
17. Now, the meditation on Aśvattha-Nārāyaṇa (from the Aśvattha-kalpa in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa):
[He is] white in color, endowed with Lakṣmī, and adorned with eight arms.
The god who bears the conch and the discus, clad in yellow garments, the infallible one.
He bestows fearlessness and boons, is peaceful, and holds a sword and a shield.
One should meditate upon Puruṣottama, who is white in color and equipped with a bow and arrows.
18. Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha (within the meditation on His mantra):
One should meditate upon the Lord who resembles the autumnal moon, holding a conch, a discus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
[He saw] the lotus-eyed one, whose form was embraced by Lakṣmī. || 1 ||
One should meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, who has a lion’s face and a massive body, within the heart; he is white in color. 1.
50) Now, the characteristics of the twenty-four forms beginning with Keśava (in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Pāñcarātra*): 19. Among these, the meditation on Keśava.
Keśava has the luster of excellent gold and bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
He was gentle, wearing white garments and adorned with ornaments of pearls.

He should be depicted with a conch in his upper right hand, a discus in his upper left hand, a mace in his lower left hand, and a lotus in his lower right hand; he is clad in white garments, adorned with pearl ornaments, and is golden in color. || 1 ||
20. Now, the meditation on Nārāyaṇa:
Nārāyaṇa is dark as a rain cloud and bears the lotus, conch, mace, and discus.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with excellent ornaments made of jewels.
In the lower right hand is a conch, in the upper right hand a lotus, in the upper left hand a mace, and in the lower left hand a discus; his complexion is dark like a rain cloud. 1.
21. Now, the meditation on Mādhava:
Mādhava has the luster of a blue lotus and bears the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
Wearing variegated garlands and garments, his eyes resembled white lotuses. || 1 ||
In his upper left hand he holds a conch, in his lower left hand a lotus, in his upper right hand a discus, and in his lower right hand a mace; he is black in color. 1.
22. Now, the meditation on Govinda:
Govinda shall be moon-colored, bearing a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a discus.
His eyes were like red lotuses, and he was adorned with ornaments of molten gold.
In the lower left hand is a conch, in the lower right hand a discus, in the upper right hand a mace, and in the upper left hand a lotus. He is white in color. 1.
23. Now, the meditation on Viṣṇu:
Viṣṇu is white in complexion and holds the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
Wearing golden garments, adorned with garlands, and decorated with armlets and bracelets.
In the upper left hand is a conch, in the lower left hand a discus, in the lower right hand a mace, and in the upper right hand a lotus. He is white in color. 1.
24. Now, the meditation on Madhusūdana:
He resembles a lotus, is glorious, the conqueror of Madhu, and the refuge of Kamalā.
He eternally bears the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus in his arms.
In His upper right hand is a conch, in His upper left hand a lotus, in His lower left hand a mace, and in His lower right hand a discus. He is red in color. 1.
25. Now, the meditation on Trivikrama:
Trivikrama is red in color and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
He shines resplendent with a crown, necklaces, armlets, and earrings.
In the lower left hand is a conch, in the lower right hand a lotus, in the upper right hand a mace, and in the upper left hand a discus. He is red in color. 1.
26. Now, the meditation on Vāmana:
Vāmana should be of the color of a jasmine flower, with eyes as large as lotuses.
With his arms, he bears the conch, the mace, the discus, and the lotus.
In the lower right hand is a conch, in the upper right hand a discus, in the upper left hand a mace, and in the lower left hand a lotus; his complexion is white. 1.
27. Now, the meditation on Śrīdhara:
Śrīdhara has the luster of a white lotus; he holds a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus; his eyes are like red lotuses, and he is adorned with a necklace of pearls.
In his lower left hand is a conch, in his lower right hand a lotus, in his upper right hand a discus, and in his upper left hand a mace; he is white in color.

28. Now follows the meditation on Hṛṣīkeśa: Hṛṣīkeśa is the color of lightning, holding a discus, conch, mace, and lotus; he wears red garlands and garments, and has a white lotus as his ear-ornament. || 1 ||
In his lower left hand is a conch, in his lower right hand a mace, in his upper right hand a discus, and in his upper left hand a lotus. He is golden in color. 1.
29. Now, the meditation on Padmanābha:
Resembling a sapphire, bearing the discus, conch, lotus, and mace; Padmanābha is clad in yellow garments and adorned with variegated garlands and ointments. || 1 ||
In the lower right hand is a conch, in the upper right hand a lotus, in the upper left hand a discus, and in the lower left hand a mace. He is blue in color. 1.
30. Now, the meditation on Dāmodara:
Dāmodara holds a grass-blade, a lotus, the enemy of Padma (the conch), and a conch; he wears yellow garments, has large eyes, and is adorned with various jewels. || 1 ||
In his upper right hand he holds a conch, in his upper left hand a mace, in his lower left hand a discus, and in his lower right hand a lotus; he is greenish-black in color like dūrvā grass. || 1 ||
31. Now, the meditation on Saṃkarṣaṇa:

Saṃkarṣaṇa holds a white conch, a lotus, an enemy (sword), and a mace. The conch is in his upper right hand, the lotus in his upper left hand, the discus in his lower left hand, and the mace in his lower right hand. He is white in color. 1.
32. Now, the meditation on Vāsudeva:
Vāsudeva is white in complexion and holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
In his upper right hand he holds a conch, in his upper left hand a discus, in his lower left hand a lotus, and in his lower right hand a mace; he is white in color. 1.
33. Now, the meditation on Pradyumna:
Pradyumna shall be golden-hued and hold a conch, a lotus, a discus, and a mace.
In his upper right hand he holds a conch, in his upper left hand a mace, in his lower left hand a lotus, and in his lower right hand a discus; he is golden in color. 1.
34. Now, the meditation on Aniruddha:

Aniruddha is blue in color and holds a conch, a lotus, and a mace in his hands. The conch is in the upper left hand, the lotus in the lower left hand, the discus in the lower right hand, and the mace in the upper right hand. He is blue in color. (1)
35. Now, the meditation on Puruṣottama:
Puruṣottama is white, bearing the lotus, conch, mace, and discus.
In his upper left hand he holds a conch, in his lower left hand a mace, in his lower right hand a discus, and in his upper right hand a lotus; he is white in color. 1.
36. Then he performs meditation on Adhokṣaja, and [he visualizes] Adhokṣaja as possessing a blue mace, a discus, and a lotus.
In the upper left hand is a conch, in the lower left hand a discus, in the lower right hand a lotus, and in the upper right hand a mace; he is blue in color. 1.
37. Now, the meditation on Nārasiṃha:
Nārasiṃha is white in color and holds a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus.
In the lower left hand is a conch, in the lower right hand a discus, in the upper right hand a lotus, and in the upper left hand a mace. His complexion is white. 1.
Then Acyuta,
who is himself undecaying, assumes a golden hue and holds a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus.
In his lower left hand is a conch, in his lower right hand a mace, in his upper right hand a lotus, and in his upper left hand a discus. He is golden in color. (1)
39. Now, the meditation on Janārdana:
Janārdana is red in color and holds the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
In his upper left hand he holds a conch, in his lower left hand a mace, in his lower right hand a lotus, and in his upper right hand a discus. He is red in color. 1.
p.
53) 40 Now, the meditation on Upendra:
Upendra is blue in color and holds a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a conch.
In his lower right hand he holds a conch, in his upper right hand a mace, in his upper left hand a discus, and in his lower left hand a lotus; he is blue in color. 1.
41. Now, regarding the meditation on Hari: Hari shall be golden in color and hold the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
In his lower right hand is a conch, in his upper right hand a discus, in his upper left hand a lotus, and in his lower left hand a mace; he is golden in color. 1.
42. Now, the meditation on Kṛṣṇa:
Kṛṣṇa, however, is black in complexion and holds a mace, a lotus, a conch, and a discus.

In the lower right hand is a conch, in the upper right hand a mace, in the upper left hand a lotus, and in the lower left hand a discus. His complexion is black. || 1 || 24 The colors of Keśava and the others (according to the Padma Purāṇa):
Keśava is like gold, and his luster is equal to that of Arjuna. || 2 ||
Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned, while Mādhava has the luster of crystal. || 1 ||
Govinda, who resembles the filaments of a lotus, is declared to be Viṣṇu.
Resembling a reddish lotus, he is called Madhusūdana. || 2 ||
Trivikrama is like a peacock; Vāmana is like the rising sun.
Śrīdhara has the luster of yellow, while Hṛṣīkeśa has the brilliance of lightning.
Padmanābha is dark-complexioned, with the luster of the bandhūka flower.
These twelve, beginning with Keśava, have been declared as the incarnations of Dāmodara.
Whatever color has been proclaimed for the forms beginning with Vāsudeva, [that should be used].
That very [nature] belongs to the four, beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as to those born from them. || 5 ||
Puruṣottama is to be known as resembling pure crystal; Adhokṣaja is dark-complexioned, and Nṛsiṃha has the luster of gold.
Janārdana is yellow in color, fallen [from that state], and exceedingly red in color.
Upendra is declared to be dark-complexioned, while Hari is remembered as resembling gold in hue.
Kṛṣṇa, resembling a dark rain-cloud, possesses twenty-four forms.
Now, the meditation on the forms of the fourfold manifestation (*vyūhacatuṣṭaya-mūrti-dhyāna*) [according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara]:
43. Among these, the meditation on Saṃkarṣaṇa: "The Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa is to be manifested in the form of Vāsudeva."
The supreme messenger of the gods, whose body was white and radiant, was to be dressed in blue garments.
In the place of the mace, there is a club; in the place of the discus, there is a plow. [He is] white in color. 1.
44. Now, the meditation on Vāsudeva:
Vāsudeva is white and peaceful, seated upon a white lotus, and possesses four arms.
Yogamūrdhan is above, and Śaṅkha is remembered as being on the right, holding a bow. || 1 ||
One should hold the discus in the upper [hand] and the mace in the right [hand]. His color is white. (1)
45. Now, for the meditation on Pradyumna:
one should place a lotus in the upper right hand and a conch and mace in the lower hands.
Likewise, one should place a discus in the upper left hand and a mace in the lower left hand; [the deity] is yellow in color.
46. Now, [one should meditate on] Aniruddha, who is dark-complexioned, four-armed, holding a spear in his right hand and likewise a sword in his left.
They describe the hero Aniruddha as holding a bow and a shield; he is black in color. 1 || 4 ||
Now, the meditation on the forms of the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish (according to the *Pāñcarātra*; the colors, however, are according to the *Padma Purāṇa*):
47. Among these, the meditation on the Fish:
"Holding a conch in the left and a mace in the right, he has two arms and assumes the form of a fish."
Narāṅghri, or Matsyarūpa; Janārdana in the form of a fish; white in color.
48. Now, the meditation on the Tortoise (Kūrma):
The Tortoise has the form of a tortoise, possesses the form described for the Fish (Matsya), and is golden-colored. 1.
49. Now, the meditation on Varāha:
[He is] honey-tawny in color and endowed with four arms and weapons.
It had the body of a man and the face of a boar, slightly stout and very terrifying.
Śrī is stationed on the left elbow, accompanied by the attendants Ananta and Upadā.
I bow to this Varāha, who assumes this form and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; he is dark-complexioned.
50. Now, the meditation on Nṛsiṃha: [He] has the form of blazing fire, a lion’s face, and a human body.
With a mouth formidable with fangs and extremely terrifying with a flickering tongue. || 1 ||
With a round face, matted hair, and a broad chest, he was enraged and stood in the ālīḍha posture.
He made his own thigh into a Danava with unbendable and sharp claws.
And with his two hands and claws, he violently tore open its chest.
One should bow to the Lord Nṛsiṃha, who holds a mace and a discus with his two [hands]; he is white in color.
Now, the meditation on Vāmana:
Vāmana is described as holding a water-pot and an umbrella with his two [hands]. He is dark-complexioned. 1.
52. Now follows the meditation on Paraśurāma:
He who bears the terrible axe that brought about the end of the Kṣatriyas, with his face turned toward the axe.
Rāma, the slayer of enemies, the son of Jamadagni, should be fashioned; he is golden-hued.
53. Now, the meditation on Śrī Rāma:
He is youthful, with a gracious countenance, seated upon the shoulders of a lion, and possessing reddish-brown eyes.
Rāma, holding a bow and arrows, should be depicted with arms reaching down to his knees; he is dark-complexioned.
54. Now, the meditation on Balarāma:
[he holds] a wine-cup and a plow in his left and right hands respectively.
And Halīrāma, being white in color, holds a mace, a club, and a vajra. || 1 ||
The form of a mace (musala) means a thunderbolt; it is the color of milk. || 1 ||
55. Then, for the meditation on the Buddha:
[the practitioner] is clothed in saffron robes, with his monastic garment draped over one shoulder.
The Buddha is proclaimed as being meditated upon as seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) with two arms. || 1 ||
The color pāṭala is well known. || 1 ||
56. Now, the meditation on Kalki:
He is wrathful, with sword raised in hand, mounted upon a horse, and possessed of great strength.
The two-armed Kalki is proclaimed as the destroyer of the Mlecchas; his complexion is white.
(In another text, among the forms of the ten incarnations, Kṛṣṇa is seen in the place of Buddha.
57. Now, the meditation on Kṛṣṇa (from the *Padma Purāṇa*):
"The one known as Kṛṣṇa holds a conch and a discus, is dark-complexioned, and has two arms. [He is] of a dark hue. 11. 0.
The colors of the forms of the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish (according to the *Padmapurāṇa*):
the Fish is like crystal, and the Tortoise has the luster of gold.
The Boar [incarnation] is either dark-complexioned or has a white form. || 1 ||
Nṛsiṃha has the luster of the color of the moon, and Prahlāda has the radiance of gold.
Vāmana is dark-complexioned like a śyāmala tree, possessing a black hue and great strength. || 2 ||
The son of Jamadagni was golden-hued, while Raghava was dark-complexioned.
Bharata is said to be dark-complexioned, while Lakṣmaṇa has the luster of gold.
Śatrughna has the luster of red color, while Sītā has a form resembling the hue of gold.
Māṇḍavī has the luster of red, and Ūrmilā has a dark-complexioned form. || 4 ||
Śrutakīrti shall have a white body; Hanumān shall have the luster of gold; Aṅgada shall have the appearance of a red color; and Sugrīva shall be golden-tawny.
Jāmbavān is said to resemble a blue lotus, while [Hanumān] has the luster of gold.
The hymn of praise to Guha: He has the luster of silver, the color of time (black), and is terrifying.
Bala is like the color of milk, and Revatī is red in hue.
Kṛṣṇa should be dark like a cloud, and Urukmiṇī should have the luster of gold.
And their colors are proclaimed to be like those of Kalkī and Śveta.
58. Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
Nārāyaṇa has four arms; likewise, he holds the conch and discus in his upper [hands].
To the south, however, is Gadāpadmī, who resembles a dark blue cloud. || 1 ||
To the left is Śrī, holding a lute in her hand; Puṣṭā is in the other [hand], holding a lotus. [The deity] is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
59. Now, the meditation on Sūryanārāyaṇa (from the Tryṛcākalpa):

Nārāyaṇa, who always resides in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, a crown, and a necklace, possessing a golden body and bearing the conch and the discus—He is of a golden hue. 1.
60. Now, the meditation on Nṛsiṃha, the Eight-faced Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa (from the *Atharvaṇarahasya*, *Mantrasāra*):

I bow to the fierce, terrible, and most powerful Great Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa-Siṃha, who has eight faces including lions, tigers, boars, monkeys, the king of birds, and bears; who possesses thirty-two crores of arms and wields weapons such as the plow, mace, club, conch, and discus; who has fearsome fangs and devours śarabhas, birds, and elephants—this Nṛsiṃha.
The body is red in color, while the faces have their respective colors. || 1 ||
Alternatively, there is another way of meditating [on the deity] (in the *Mantrasāra*):
"He has three eyes resembling the fire and sparks of the thunderbolt at the end of an aeon;
he has a face with two tongues and fangs, with a beak and claws equal to a vajra. || 1 ||

One should always meditate upon Rudra, the destroyer of pride, who has eight faces, is terrifying, rides the bear and the seven horses of the wind, removes all suffering, and possesses the heart of a Śarabha, a Bheruṇḍa, and a lion. May that Hari protect us here—He who has eight mouths, eyes of fire, excellent claws like thunderbolts, and a lion’s mane blazing with lightning; whose two wings have the luster of diamonds; who has grasped within his heart and belly the eight Kālis and the eight Durgās; who has for thighs the Rudras and Kālas; who is the sky-goer (Garuda), the deer, and the man-lion; who has the face of a Bheruṇḍa; and who, wielding His discus, pierces the fierce enemies such as the Śarabhas.

With his pair of arms, his mouth wide open from drinking the abundant blood of the chest of the foremost asura, his enemy, which was brought to him in the hollow of his cupped hands, he tore apart the magnificent shoulder of the great śarabha with his claws, appearing most splendidly adorned.

With his two arms he has restrained the Asura, while with the pair of his feet and hands he raises up his claws, covering the bodies of his enemies; he possesses three eyes—the sun, the moon, and fire—and wings of thunderbolts.
[He holds] a lotus, a fire-sacrifice ladle, a goad, an arrow, a great noose, a spear, an intestine, a discus, a mallet, a raised pair of arms, the arm of an enemy, a sword, and a conch.
Holding in the tips of his hands a golden-bellied trident, a shield, a great noose with a head, the Pināka bow, a thunderbolt, the Kaumodakī mace, and an exceedingly powerful club.
The body is red in color, while the faces have their respective colors. || 1 ||
61. Now, the meditation on Pañcavaktranārasiṃha (from the Mantrasāra):
[One should meditate upon him] who has five faces, is most terrifying, and possesses a luster equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
He was fierce, wearing a garland of severed heads, and adorned with a necklace around his neck.
Richly adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, he is beautifully graced by a lion's face.
He has the moon as his crest-jewel, a dark-blue throat, and three eyes in every face.
And he was adorned with ten arms that resembled iron clubs.
He holds a rosary, a mace, a lotus, and a conch shell that resembles cow's milk.
A bow, a mace, and likewise a great, radiant discus.
And [he saw] the sword, the trident, and the noose, as well as Nṛsiṃha in the form of Rudra.
Having the luster of an indragopaka insect, the moon, and gold; with faces facing east and extending to the north, as well as an upward-facing face, he possesses every color.
O Daughter of the Mountain, he who bears the support of all the worlds has a body of red color and five colors upon his faces. 1.
62. Now, the meditation on Pratāparāma (from the *Mantrasāra*):

We worship Rāma, who is white in complexion, possesses three eyes, and crushes the hosts of the enemies of the gods with his splendors; he holds in his upraised arms a sword, trident, *ḍamaru* drum, scimitar, bow, staff, arrow, axe, conch, discus, dagger, plow, mace, club, *bhindipāla*, and noose, as well as a fist, and hands that grant fearlessness and boons. [He is] white in complexion. 1.
63. Now, regarding the beautiful meditation on [the Lord] together with his retinue (*saparivāra-paṭṭābhirāma-dhyāna*):

to the left is the son of the Earth (*Bhūmisuta*, Bhīṣma); behind him is Hanumān; and further back are the sons of Sumitrā—Śatrughna and Bharata—on the side petals and in the corners beginning with the northwest.
Together with Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, the crown prince Aṅgada, and Jāmbavān, I worship the dark-complexioned Rāma, whose luster is as soft as a blue lotus. (1) [He is] blue in color. (1)
64. Now, the meditation on Anantamūrti (from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa, in the section on the Ananta-kalpa):
He has the luster of fresh mango sprouts, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes; in his right upper hand is a lotus, and in the hand below that is a conch shell.
In his upper left hand he holds a discus, and in the one below that, a mace.
I worship the lotus-eyed one, who bears [the world] and is endowed with seven hoods. [The mantra] "gomūtravarṇaḥ" is the first.
65. Now, the meditation on Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa (from the Bhāgavata):
I bow to the one who is praised as the source of existence, whose garment is like lightning, who wears a guñjā berry as an ear-ornament, and whose face shines with the plumage of a peacock.

Salutation to the one who possesses the beauty of the forest garland, the *ekabala* fruit, the *vetra* cane, the horn, and the bamboo mark; to him whose feet are soft and who is born from the limbs of the cattle-herders. [1] He is blue in color. [1]
66. Now, the meditation on Saṃtānagopāla (from the Pāñcarātra):
[One should meditate upon Him] drinking at His mother’s breast and gazing with a beautiful smile at Her face.
And with the tips of her fingers, she touched that other breast again and again.
One should meditate upon the cowherd boy seated on Yaśodā’s lap, who always bestows sons.
Blue in color.
67. Now, the meditation on Madanagopāla (from the Pāñcarātra):
He is red in color, has ten arms, and is adorned with all ornaments.
The conch, discus, mace, lotus, noose, goad, and flower-arrows.
He was energetically playing a sugarcane bow with two [hands] and a flute with the other.
Seated upon a sixteen-petaled lotus, he is well-established above a hexagon. || 2 ||
This one named Madana, the cowherd, has a lotus-face with a gentle smile.
May he who was respectfully consecrated by the gopīs while seated upon a leaf of the *svarapa* tree protect us. He is red in color. 1.

68. Now, the meditation on Sudarśana (from the Pāñcarātra): He who bears the conch, the discus, the noose, the axe, the sword, the arrow, the trident, the bow, the goad, and fire; who holds the thunderbolt, the shield, the plow, the mace, the club, and the spear; and who possesses most fierce fangs.

One should meditate upon the wheel that destroys the life-breath of all enemies, which has flames for hair, three eyes, resembles a blazing fire, and is adorned with necklaces and armlets, situated within a hexagon; it is red in color. 1. 1.

69. Now, the meditation on the Discus (*cakradhyāna*) [according to the *Pāñcarātra*]: One should meditate upon the King of Discuses (*cakrarāja*), which has the form of fire with horizontal flames, its arms raised high with blazing crests of fire as armlets; it has tawny eyes and a flaming tongue, and is extremely fierce with hundreds of sharp-edged rays shining forth. It holds the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the lotus, the conch, the arrow, and the mace, burning all enemies. Situated within a hexagon, it resembles ten million suns and is gracious. It is red in color. 1.

70. Now, the meditation on Viṣvaksena (from the *Pāñcarātra-pādma-saṃhitā*): Viṣvaksena is dark-complexioned, possessing four arms with which he holds the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a conch, a discus, and a mace. His right foot is extended beneath the pedestal and his left foot is drawn up. Adorned with all ornaments such as a crown and so forth, Viṣvaksena is dark-complexioned. 1.

(59) 71. Now, the true form of Hanumān (in the meditation upon his mantra): I worship him who has the luster of crystal and the radiance of gold, who is two-armed and has joined palms in reverence; I worship him whose lotus-face is resplendent with a pair of earrings. || 1 || He is golden-hued. || 1 ||
72. Now, the meditation on the Five-faced Añjaneya (from the Sudarśana-saṃhitā):
[He is] five-faced, most formidable, and endowed with fifteen eyes.
Resembling ten million suns, with the face of a monkey and great splendor.
With a mouth formidable with fangs and eyes knit in a frown.
His single right face is that of Narasiṃha, most wonderful.
He possesses a body of exceedingly fierce splendor, both terrifying and the destroyer of fear.
In the west is the face of Garuḍa, Vakratuṇḍa of great splendor.
It bestows the siddhis of the netherworld (pātāla), is formidable, and destroys poisons, malevolent spirits, and the like.
His face was like that of a boar, black and blazing, radiant with a crest of flames.
It pacifies all beings and wards off the heat of fever.
With its face turned upwards, it was formidable, the supreme destroyer of the Dānavas.
A sword, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a noose, a goad, and two mountains.
Holding a drum, a cow's hoof-print, and a shaven head, he is worshipped by the gods; his complexion is like the color of gold.
73. Now, the meditation on Garuḍa (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara): Before Upendra, the bird Guḍākeśa stands with palms joined in reverence.
With his left foot placed upon the ground and his head adorned by a hooded serpent.
He had thick calves, a narrow neck, a prominent nose, and a slender body.
The son of Vinatā should be depicted with two arms and wings, and he is golden in color.
74. Now, the meditation on Śrī Kārtavīrya (from the Ḍāmaratantra):
May he who resembles the sun, who illuminates with his radiance, whose neck is encircled by a golden garland, and who wears a red garment and a turban, protect [us] from all fear.
Adorned with various ornaments, holding a bow in his five hundred hands and arrows in his other five hundred hands, may the Lord, the beloved of the Earth, protect us incessantly. He is red in color.
Alternatively, according to another method [in the *Kārtavīryārjunakalpa*], one should meditate upon the great Kārtavīrya on earth as follows:

"One should meditate upon the great Kārtavīrya on earth—possessing a thousand arms, holding arrows and a bow, clad in red garments, wearing a jeweled crown and earrings, the beloved destroyer of thieves and other wicked diseases. [He is] red in color. 1.
p.60) 75. Now, the meditation on Manmatha (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara): Kāmadeva, however, should be fashioned in the form of a statue upon the earth.
He should be fashioned with eight arms, adorned with a conch and a lotus.
With bow and arrow in hand, his eyes were rolling with intoxication.
Rati, Prīti, Śakti, Bhedaśakti, and likewise Ujjvalā. || 2 ||
Four wives, enchanting in their beauty, should be appointed for him.
His four wheels should be made of ivory, and his wife should be placed upon his chest. || 3 ||
In the case of Ketu, however, a great chariot drawn by five arrows (peacocks) should be fashioned in the form of a crocodile.
"Desire is like gold"—thus it is said in the Āgama; [he] is golden-colored. 1.
76. Now, the meditation on Dattātreya (according to that *Kalpa*):

One should meditate upon him seated in a jeweled pavilion at the foot of a *mandāra* tree, his initiation solely bound to the gift of gold; surrounded by the nine *nātha*-siddhas, he is like a dark cloud to the forest fire of poverty.

May Dattātreya, clad in an animal skin and white as ash, protect us—he who holds the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā) in his right lotus-hand, while his left lotus-hand rests upon his knee; whose left shoulder is raised; whose eyes are half-closed due to being overcome by the bliss arising from the stream of meditation; and who is clothed in a tiger skin. [He is] white in color. 1.

Thus ends the second treasury of Viṣṇu, titled "The Description of the Nature of Viṣṇu as Virāṭ and Other Forms," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja Mahārāja—the sovereign lord of the preeminent city of Mahīśūra; who is adorned by the entire circle of the earth; who is the crest-jewel of all lands; who is the seat of the prosperity of the Karṇāṭaka country; who shines resplendently in the midst of the great capital of glorious Mahīśūra; who has ascended the divine jeweled throne experienced by the circle of universal emperors (cakravartin) consisting of his own ancestral kings and foremost rulers; who bears the titles of Illustrious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, Possessor of Firm Prowess, Peerless Heroic Monarch, Forehead of the Sky, Sole Hero of the World, Moon in the Ocean of the Yadu Lineage, and is marked with numerous epithets such as Holder of the Conch, Discus, Goad, Axe, Makara, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva-Gaṇḍa, Bheruṇḍa, Earth-Boar, Hanuman, Garuḍa, and Lion.
Thus ends the second Viṣṇunidhi, contained within the Śrītattvanidhi treatise.
Śrī. Now, in the Śrītattvanidhi:
The third is the treasury of Śiva.
1. Now, the meditation on Maheśvara (in the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva):

[One should meditate on Him] as peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of the moon, five-faced, and three-eyed, holding in His right hands the trident, the thunderbolt, the sword, the axe, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.

I bow to the Lord of Pārvatī, who holds a serpent, a noose, a bell, the fire of universal dissolution, and a goad in his left hands; who is adorned with various ornaments, resembles a crystal gem, and is white in color. (1) [He is] white in color. (1)
2. Now, the meditation on Gaurī (from the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
The goddess Gaurī is clad in white garments, her beauty being peerless on earth.
The auspicious Goddess, possessing four arms, should be depicted separately upon a lion-throne.
Upon her lion-throne, a lotus with a beautiful pericarp should be fashioned.
O highly fortunate ones, it has eight petals and is well-situated within the pericarp.
The goddess Mahābhujā sits upon the body like Vināyaka.
A large ornament should be made for her, and a beautiful lotus as well. || 3 ||
On the right [side], it resembles the edge of the armlet of the best of the Yādavas.
O King, a beautiful jar of nectar should likewise be fashioned on the left side.
His other two hands hold a bilva fruit and a conch shell; he is emerald-colored. (1)
3. Now, the meditation on the form of Mahākailāsa (from the Upadeśakāṇḍa of the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā in the Skanda Purāṇa):
Listen, all you Brahmins, to this supreme [teaching], more secret than the secret.
To the north of Mount Meru lies the great Kailāsa mountain.
This belongs to Śambhu, who possesses attributes, who is accompanied by his consort, and who bears the moon upon his crest.
And its length is twenty koṭis of yojanas. || 2 ||
O best of the twice-born, its height should be known as double this.
In its center was an excellent pinnacle made of the nine precious gems.
Therein is the abode of Maheśa, variegated with various jewels.
It was resplendent with walls, gate-towers, watchtowers, and balconies.
Likewise, upon that lion-throne sat the great Śambhu, Sadāśiva.
Resplendent with twenty-five faces, he shines with the brilliance of a full-blown lotus.
Adorned with fifty arms resplendent with various held weapons.
He is radiant with the pair of feet of Śrī, which have arisen from a full-blown red lotus at his navel.
He was adorned even with ornaments inlaid with various kinds of jewels.
Possessing the radiance of many millions of suns, he is the embodiment of supreme bliss.
Possessing a non-ordinary body, glorious, and devoid of both the defined and the defining characteristics.
From which words turn back, along with the mind, unable to reach it.
His matted locks take refuge in the Gaṅgā, and he is adorned with the crescent moon.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes, he wore a serpent as his sacred thread.
He wears a garland of skulls and is clothed in a tiger skin.
Each face has three eyes, and he is the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals for his devotees. || 10 ||
Extending the right foot and contracting the other foot.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a discus, a trident, a mace, an arrow, and a club in his arms.
Swords, tomara-spears, śakti-missiles, axes, prāsas, and serpents.
A goad, a hook, a rosary, a small knife, and two flagstaffs. || 12 ||
Holding a vajra, a spear, a bone, fangs, a discus, a saw, and a bhiṇḍipāla weapon in his twenty-five auspicious right hands. || 13 ||
An excellent bow, a deer, a conch, a shield, a noose, and a battle-axe.
A mallet, a ḍamaru drum, a bell, a rudravīṇā lute, and a book.
He also held a skull, a severed head, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a bhuśuṇḍī weapon, and an iron club.
A wooden board, a cloth, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and a sacrificial fire.
Likewise, with his left hands, he holds a scissor, a pestle, and a peacock feather.
That great Sadāśiva shines there upon that mountain; he is white in color.
4. Now, the meditation on the form of Aghora with thirty-two arms (*Śivatattvaratnākara*):
One-faced, eternally blissful, and endowed with thirty-two arms.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, three-eyed, and having the moon as his crest-ornament.
The gesture of fearlessness, the sword, the trident, the discus, and likewise the ḍamaru drum.
And holding a bone-arrow, a mace, a lotus, and a skull-cup. || 2 ||
[He holds] the wisdom-mudrā, a spear in his hand, a goad, and a rosary.
Holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and an axe with his right hands. || 3 ||
A shield, a sword-blade, an axe, a noose, and a mallet.
The elephant, the fire, the deer, the bell, the bow, and the hand upon the hip.
And [he holds] a jewel, a lily, a water-pot, a pestle, and likewise a book.
This [form] is equipped with weapons and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
It is situated upon the head of Kālamuṇḍa and bestows fearlessness upon all.
Blue in color. || 1 ||
63) 5. Now, the meditation on the ten-armed form of Aghora (according to the Pāñcarātra):
[He holds] an axe, a ḍamaru drum, a sword, a shield, an arrow, and a bow.
Holding a trident, a skull-cup, and granting fearlessness and boons, he bestows all that is desired. || 1 ||
He has three eyes, a terrifying face, a dark blue body, and is clad in red garments.
We worship Him whose entire body is adorned with serpents, who is not terrible, and who is blue in color. || 1-2 ||
6. Now, the meditation on Mahākāla accompanied by Mahākālī (from the Lalitopākhyāna): Mahākāla is dark as a rain cloud, his form embraced by Kālī.
Wearing a dark tunic and possessing eyes red with intoxication. || 1 ||
Drinking the full wine of universal essence from the goblet of the cosmic egg.
Glancing with sidelong glances at Mahākālī, who was dark as a rain-cloud and moist with passion.
Seated upon a lion-throne, which is of the nature of auspicious conceptualization.
Endowed with the jaws of Time and Death, he is the sole devourer of all the worlds.
Lalita is perfected in meditation; Lalita is eager for worship.
Bestowing exceedingly long life upon his devoted followers, he is blue in color. 1. 4.
7. Now, the meditation on Amṛtamṛtyuñjaya (from the Kāraṇāgama):
He is resplendent in the lotus posture, joined above by the moon.
He has the complexion of the moon, from whom divine nectar flows, and who bears the digit of the moon.
Accompanied by two lower hands joined together in the single yogamudrā.
With both hands holding a golden pitcher filled with nectar. || 2 ||
His eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and he wears matted locks that are bound and tawny.
Adorned with various ornaments and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
The god who wears a tiger-skin garment and is compassionate toward his devotees.
One should meditate upon this Rudra, the conqueror of death, who is smeared with ashes; he is white in color.
8. Now, the hymn to Nīlakaṇṭha (from the Pāñcarātra):
