[I salute him] whose crescent moon is bound in matted locks, and who is adorned with ornaments of serpents.
And holding a rosary, a trident, and a skull-cup with his hands. || 1 ||
He also holds a khaṭvāṅga staff and wears a tiger skin as his garment.

I worship the blue-throated Lord (Nīlakaṇṭha), who has three eyes, whose abode is the lotus, whose splendor resembles the rising sun, and who is the bestower of the desires of his practitioners. [Verse 2] His complexion is reddish-brown. [1]
9. Now, the meditation on the form of Rudra (from the Pañcarātra): [He is] like Kailāsa, five-faced, accompanied by the Goddess, and three-eyed.
He has a blue throat, is adorned with serpents, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
Her hands hold a rosary, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and a shining water-pot.
I bow down to Rudra, who wears the moon and the Ganges in his matted locks. [He is] white in color. 1. 2.
(p. 64) 10. Now, the meditation on Māmaheśvara with his retinue (*kāraṇāgama*):

To the left is the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī), and behind is the bull; in front are Surendra and the others, while Daityāri and Vidhi are on the side petals in the corners starting from the northwest.

I worship Śambhu, who is white and possesses the delicate luster of a pale lotus situated between Bhṛṅgin, Nārada, Bāṇa, Bhairava, Gajānana, Skanda, Vīreśvara, and Amadhyeśvara. (1) [He is] white in color. (1)
11. Now, the meditation on the Lord of the Assembly (*sabhāpati-dhyāna*) [from the *Kāraṇāgama*]:
Having seated Gaurī, the mother of the three worlds, upon a jeweled throne encrusted with gold on the peak of Mount Kailāsa;
All the gods worship that Primordial Being, the moon-crested Lord, as he dances at the time of dusk.
Brahmā holds the tāla; Hara holds the ḍamaru-drum; Bhāratī holds the vīṇā; and the two auspicious ones, Mārtaṇḍa and Soma, hold a pair of flutes with their radiant hands.
May Gāyana, Kautumburu, Nārada, Sāma, Rājju, Nandī, Kumāra, and Rudra the dancer—whose dance is born of their own nature—protect us always. [1] He is fair-complexioned. [1]
Now, the meditation on the five forms beginning with Sadyojāta (from the *Śaivakāraṇagama*): First, the meditation on Sadyojāta:
He has the luster of a kunda flower, the moon, a conch shell, and crystal; he holds the Vedas, a rosary of beads, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
May the three-eyed, four-faced one of vast power, born instantly, protect me in the western direction. He is white in color.
13. Now, the meditation on Vāmadeva:
he holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a *ṭaṅka* in his hands, and his complexion is like the filaments of a lotus.
May Vāmadeva, the three-eyed one with beautiful four faces, protect me in the northern direction; he who is golden-hued.
14. Now, the meditation on Aghora:
[He] holds an axe, a goad, a noose, a trident, a skull-cup, a drum, an eye, and a rosary.
May the four-faced Aghora, blue-hued and three-eyed, protect the southern direction. He is blue in color.
15. Now, as for that meditation on the *tatpuruṣa* [face]: he has the luster of blazing lightning and gold, and holds in his hands the [mudrās of] knowledge and fearlessness, as well as a sword.
Four-faced, that Puruṣa with three eyes, stationed in the east, may he protect me constantly. He is golden-hued.
16. Now, the meditation on Īśāna:

he holds in his hands the Vedas, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), the ṭaṅka, the skull-bowl (*kapāla*), the drum (*ḍhakkā*), the eye, and the trident (*śūla*).
May the five-faced Īśāna, white in luster and the supreme light above, protect me; he is white-complexioned. (1) (5)
Now, regarding the forms of the seventy *tāṇḍava* manifestations (in the *Śaivaikāraṇāgama*),
first is the meditation on the *ānanda-tāṇḍava*:
[He is] four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with flowing matted hair.
Endowed with a fair complexion and possessed of peacock feathers. || 1 ||
It is adorned with a blue lotus, a right-facing dhattūra flower, and a crescent moon.
On the right, at the tip of his own matted locks, he was adorned by the Jāhnavī.
In his left ear he wears a lotus leaf, and in his right an earring shaped like a crocodile.
Adorned with all ornaments and provided with a sacred thread. || 3 ||
Clad in a tiger skin garment and equipped with small bells upon his feet.
With his left arm extended and his right hand in the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā). || 4 ||
One should hold a hand-drum (ḍamaru) in the right hand and indeed fire in the left hand.
But the right leg is bent and positioned above the apasmāra [demon]. || 5 ||
The left foot should be raised upward, with the tip of the foot following behind the right one.
The Ānanda-tāṇḍava has been described; he is fair-complexioned. 1.
18. Now, the meditation on the Egg of the Twilight (Sandhyātāṇḍava):
I meditate upon Him who has four arms, three eyes, and wears a crown of matted hair.
In his right hands he holds the gesture of fearlessness and the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and in his left hands the peacock-feather whisk and a look of wonder. || 1 ||
Even without Apasmāra, she stands upon the pedestal with her left foot drawn up.
But above, one should blow [the breath] following the path of the right foot in a counter-clockwise direction.
That foot was either clenched or adorned with a bracelet of mustard seeds.
Thus should be the *tāṇḍava* of the twilight; the colors and other details are as before. || 1 ||
19. Now, the meditation on Umā: she has one face, three eyes, and is adorned with a circle of matted locks.
Fair-limbed and endowed with six arms, he likewise holds the gesture of fearlessness and the damaru drum.
A trident on the right side, as well as a skull and an expression of wonder.
He blew [the conch] with his hand, which resembled an elephant’s trunk and was positioned along his left side.
And indeed, that same left foot is positioned above the apasmāra [demon].
The right foot is raised, following along with the left foot.
On the left side, indeed, is Goddess Umā together with Jāhnavī.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a tiger skin as an upper garment.
The *umātaṇḍava* is here concluded. The remainder is as before. 1.
20. Now, the visualization of Gaurītāṇḍava: peaceful, endowed with four arms, red in color, and with a smiling face.
The karoti-baka flower, the dhuttūra, and the arka flower. || 1 ||
He has the crescent moon in his mass of matted hair, which is beautifully spread out.
Adorned with a serpent-bracelet and standing upon a person afflicted by epilepsy.
The right foot is bent, while the left foot is raised above it.
Holding the gesture of granting fearlessness in one left hand and a *ḍamaru* drum in the other hand.
In another [direction], to the east, there is a serpent, and to the west, a vessel of fire.
Gaurī is joined on the left, and Nandikeśin is on the right.
With his mass of matted locks well-spread, he is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
On the left [hand] he is endowed with a crown; the rest is as in the first dance. || 5 ||
This is called the Gaurī-tāṇḍava; it is red in color. (1)
21. Now, the meditation on Kālikātāṇḍava: [he has] one face, two eyes, and his head is covered with matted locks.
Endowed with eight arms, his right foot was raised aloft. || 1 ||
With his left foot slightly bent, he stands upon the person afflicted by epilepsy.
In his right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness, a trident-noose, and a hand-drum.
And he holds a skull-cup, a fire-vessel, and a bell in his excellent left hands.
His hand was like an elephant's trunk, extended and following the right side.
Endowed with the characteristic of *dadhaṃ*, the remainder is like the first dance.
The Kālikātaṇḍava has been proclaimed; it is fair-complexioned. 1.
22. Now, the meditation on Tripura-tāṇḍava:
[He is] endowed with sixteen arms and seated upon Gaurī to his left.
Skanda, however, was on the right side, with his joined palms held in reverence in his left hand.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness, a hand-drum, a thunderbolt, and a trident.
Likewise, he holds a noose, a hammer, a staff, and a serpent in his right hands.
The right hand follows [the first], and likewise the left hand is placed in front.
[He holds] a fire, a book, the gesture of granting boons (varada), and a banner with a skull-topped staff (ketukheṭaka). || 3 ||
And a water-pot and a skull with his eight left hands.
Endowed with all the [auspicious] marks, the remainder is like the first dance. || 4 ||
The Traipura-tāṇḍava has been described; his complexion is fair. || 1 ||
23. Now, the meditation on the Saṃhāra-tāṇḍava:
[He is] three-eyed, eight-armed, and endowed with well-disheveled matted locks.
The left foot is drawn up and placed upon the top of the apasmāra [demon]. || 1 ||
With his right foot raised, he wore a tiger skin as an upper garment.
And in his right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a trident, a noose, and a hand-drum (ḍamaru).
Holding a skull-cup and a fire-vessel, he displays his hands in a gesture of wonder.
Resembling an elephant's trunk, he is endowed with four arms on the left side. (3)
The left [hand] is like an elephant's trunk, and likewise follows the right.
Nandīśa is on the right side, while on the left he is accompanied by Gaurī.
The seventh dance has been described; it shall bring about the prosperity of the world.
The rest is like the first dance. He is fair-complexioned. 1.7.
Now, the names of these seven tāṇḍavas [are given] in the Śaivakaraṇāgama:
first the Ānandatāṇḍava, and then the Saṃdhyātāṇḍava.
Thus there is the Umā-taṇḍava, and likewise the Gaurī-taṇḍava.
The Kālikā, the Tāṇḍava, and the sixth is the Tripuratāṇḍava.
The seventh is the Saṃhāra-tāṇḍava; thus there are seven tāṇḍavas. || 2 || 7 ||
24. Now, the meditation on the eight forms of Bhava (from the *Śaivāgama-śekhara*): Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Ugra, and likewise [Bhīma, Rudra, and Mahādeva].
Rudra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva—these are proclaimed as the eight forms (mūrtis). || 1 ||
They have four arms and three eyes, and they wear crowns of matted hair.
They likewise hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as the ṭaṅka and the sword.
These two are adorned with all ornaments and wear red silk garments.
These are their colors.
White, dark, red, black, and resembling cow’s milk.
And the coloring for those who speak of saffron, coral, and blue is as follows. || 1 || 8 ||
Now, the names and so forth of the eleven Rudras (according to the Śaivāgama):
Śambhu, Pinākin, Giriśa, Sthāṇu, Bharga, and Sadāśiva.
Śiva, Hara, as well as Śarva, Kapālī, and Bhava. || 1 ||
These eleven Rudras, who are devoted to the welfare of the world, have been described.
25. First, regarding the meditation on Śambhu:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśāna, the gods, the Dānavas, and the Rākṣasas—
I bow down to that Śambhu, from whom the gods were born. He is crimson in color.
26. Now follows the meditation on the wielder of the Pināka bow:
[he is] mounted upon the chariot of forbearance and endowed with the sacred thread.
I worship the wielder of the Pināka bow, accompanied by the four Vedas.
He is yellowish-green in color. || 1 ||
27. Now, the meditation on Giriśa:
Seated in the midst of a jeweled pavilion shining atop the peak of Kailāsa, [he is visualized].
May Giriśa, the beloved life-breath of Girijā, be for eternal joy. He is blue in color.
28. Now, the meditation on Sthāṇu, which brings happiness to the Daughter of the Mountain who is reclining upon his left side.
I bow my head in salutation to Sthāṇu, who is honored by all the gods. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
29. Now follows the meditation on Bharga:
he who has the moon as his crest-ornament, who wears matted hair, who has three eyes, and who is white with ashes.
May Bharga, the destroyer of all fear, ever abide within my heart. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
30. Now follows the meditation on Sadāśiva:
having become Brahmā, he creates the world; then, having become Viṣṇu, he protects it.
Having become Rudra, he devours at the end; may Sadāśiva be my refuge forever. || 1 ||
Dark green in color. || 1 ||
31. Now, the meditation on Śiva:
Obeisance to the one whose abode is established by the syllable Om, who is the object of realization for the Gāyatrī.
I offer my salutation to Śiva, the abode of auspicious qualities. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
32. Then follows the meditation on Hara, whose feet are bowed to by the multitude of gods, for the purpose of consuming venomous serpents.
Let there be salutation to Hara, whose hand is marked by the Pināka bow. || 1 ||
He is black in color. || 1 ||
33. Then there was the meditation on Śarva, the destroyer of the three cities, who crushed the pride of Kṛtānta.
May he who holds a sword in his hand, possesses sharp fangs, and is named Śarva, bring me joy. || 1 ||
The tawny-colored one. || 1 ||
34. Now, the meditation on Kapālin:
He who brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice has a lotus-face filled with wrath.
May the trident-bearer Śūlapāṇi grant happiness; may Kapālī protect me day and night. || 1 ||
The color of the pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
35. Now, [I shall describe] your meditation, whose lotus feet are praised by the lords of yogis, which transcends duality, and which is the refuge of all beings.
I take refuge in you, who have traversed the depths of Vedānta. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
Alternatively, their true forms [are described] in the Padma Purāṇa:
they resemble three-eyed Rudras and wear matted hair and crowns.
Rudra, the three-eyed, the ruddy one, who wears a mass of matted locks. || 1 ||
Four-armed, blue-throated, and adorned with the crescent moon.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with all ornaments. || 2 ||
With his two principal hands, he is steadfastly bestowing boons and fearlessness.
And with his other two hands, he holds an axe and a deer.
Their colors are as follows: crimson, green, blue, white, dark-brown, and black.
Yellow, black, as well as brownish-brown, pale-red, and white. || 1 ||
This description of the eleven Rudras has been fully declared.
Now, the meditation on the twenty-five Līlāmūrtis (according to the Śaivaikāraṇāgama):
First, the meditation on Candraśekhara:

[He who has] hands in the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, possessing a gentle and amorous expression, with broad face and eyes, and a crest-jewel consisting of a portion of the lunar orb.
With a straight body and feet standing evenly, having the luster of coral, holding a deer and an axe in his hands, and seated upon a lotus pedestal. || 1 ||
The color of coral. || 1 ||

37. Now, this is the meditation on Gaurī standing at his side: she is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, two-armed, and posed in the *tribhaṅgī* stance, with her feet bent and positioned to the right and left.
In her right hand she holds a beautiful blue lotus, and she stands upon a lotus pedestal to the left of the God. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
38. Now, the meditation on Umāmaheśvara:
[He is] seated upon a comfortable throne of white lotuses, holding a young deer, a water-pot, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
This is indeed the form of Umā’s consort, who has a beautiful face, eyes like lotuses, and bestows boons. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
39. Now, the meditation on [the Lord] mounted upon the bull:

On the right side, the hand of the Lord of Cows (Nandin) holds a curved-tusked elephant-goad; he stands upon the back of the bull, his left half being white, while his two upper hands hold a battle-axe and a black [object].

Bow down to that Lord who brings about auspiciousness, who is mounted upon a bull, whose eye is fixed on his forehead, who is graced by three eyes, who wears a crown of matted locks, and who is joined with Gaurī on his left side. [He is] white in color. 1.
40. Now, the meditation on the form of Nāṭya:
He who stands upon the head of a dancing serpent, his left foot raised and resting upon a large, thick lotus in the midst of a garland of flames, while his right foot is placed in a graceful pose.

I worship Naṭeśa, who resembles a tree with limbs smeared with ashes, holding fire at the tips of his hands and feet, and bearing the *dolavara* (the boon-granting gesture), the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling gesture), and a *ḍamaruka* drum; he is red in color.
And Śivakāmavallī should be depicted like Ambā, situated near Candraśekhara. 1.

41. Now, the meditation on the wedding-form, or alternatively, the meditation on the form of Kalyāṇasundara: [He is] the color of vermilion, three-eyed, endowed with four arms, adorned with necklaces and armlets, his limbs clothed in divine garments, and beautified by excellent bracelets and golden kalhāra ornaments.
I bow to Śambhu, who with his right hand grasps the palm of Pārvatī’s right hand, who holds an axe and a black antelope in his other hands, and who wears the moon upon his crest with affection.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, and decorated with the crescent moon.
I bow to the three-eyed, four-armed one, who is proud of his fresh youth.
The deity’s standing posture is proclaimed as being endowed with symmetrical limbs.
With the left foot tucked in and the right foot standing [extended], he is the color of vermilion.
Now, the forms of the deities associated with the marriage ceremony (42): first among them is the meditation on Girijā—
[one should meditate on her] possessing full thighs, full cheeks, and endowed with full hands.
She has two arms and two eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should place the goddess, dressed in fine linen (dukūla), to the left of the god; she is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
43. Now, the meditation on Brahmā:
[one should meditate upon him] with four faces, four arms, and bearing a water-pot and the sacred thread.
He wore a sacrificial thread as an upper garment and was adorned with a crown of matted locks. || 1 ||
In his right hand he holds a rosary of beads, and in his left hand a water-pot.
He holds a *sruva* ladle in his right hand and a book in his left.
Brahmā, seated upon his lotus throne, intent on destroying sin.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be square and provided with three girdles (mekhalās).
It is characterized by the marks of being joined at the navel and the yoni, and is free from [defects].
One should place the Fire-god in the center, surrounded by five flames.
One should properly worship the fire placed in the front portion of Brahmā; it is pale-red in color. || 1 ||
p.
71) 44. Now, the visualization of Menakā: On the right side of the Goddess is Menakā, whose face is graced with a beautiful smile. || 1 ||
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by every kind of decoration, she was the color of gold. || 1 ||
45. Then, one should practice the meditation on Himavat, assuming the form of one holding golden jars of water in both hands.
And she was seated upon a lotus throne, while Himavat stood at her side.
In the midst of that, by standing upon a bull, it then takes the form of a water-vehicle.
On the left side of the God, however, are Sanaka and Sanandana.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, their matted hair was bound up, and they were ever dear to him.
And the foremost of the immortals, headed by Viṣṇu, were present at the wedding, engaged in service.
It is declared to be beautiful and auspicious; Himavat is white in color.
Sanaka and Sanandana are pale-red (pāṭala) in color; the colors of Viṣṇu and the others correspond to their respective [descriptions]. || 5 ||
46. Now, the meditation on the form for wandering for alms: [one should meditate on the deity] with four arms and three eyes, naked, and with a smiling face.
Smeared with ashes, resembling coral in hue, and encircled at the waist by a serpent.
The Bhṛṅgī-pāda [mudrā] is adorned with a looped ornament and joined with sandals.
That tip of his right hand, however, should follow after the face of the deer.
In the right hand, one should likewise have a ḍamaru drum depicted.
In his other left hand, however, he holds a trident and a peacock feather fan.
The right foot is drawn up, while the left foot is firmly planted.
And the posture with even legs is that which is ready for movement. || 4 ||
And with a hand endowed with a skull, he arises equal to the navel of a bull.
Thus has the wandering for alms been described; now hear about Guṇḍodara.
To the left side of the god, however, Guṇḍodara is situated below.
One should place a skull, joined with two hands, upon the head.
One should place the two earrings, joined with the form of the elements, upon the ears.
And [he saw] his face with fangs that were formidable, endowed with the characteristics previously described.
Devī is the color of coral; Guṇḍodara is dark-complexioned. 2.
47. Now, the meditation on the form of the burner of desire: one should contemplate the Enemy of Desire (Kāma) in a fierce form, endowed with four arms.
Adorned with a black mark (kṛṣṇa-ṭaṅka), and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. || 1 ||
But that which consists of the restraint of desire is situated upon a lotus seat.
The right foot is extended downward, while the left foot is laid down.
Thus, one should perform the ritual for the Enemy of Desire (Kāmaripu); I shall now describe the destruction of Time (Kālanāśana), which is red in color. 1.
48. Now, the meditation on the form of Kālahara:

one should meditate upon him who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, possesses three eyes and eight arms, is radiant with a trident, a lotus, a ṭaṅka, a fine thread, and a noose, and whose face is terrifying with protruding fangs.
With his left foot drawn up with its sole raised against the chest of Kāla, bearing matted locks that are neither severed nor broken, and united with Girijā, he is the deity of the universe. || 1 ||
Having raised the left foot, it should be placed upon the chest of Kāla.
One should worship the fierce-faced [deity] standing upon the head of the linga with his left foot; he is red in color.
Now, the forms of the limbs (49).
Next, the meditation on Mārkaṇḍeya:
Mārkaṇḍeya stands to the right, touching the base of the liṅga.
He has two arms and two eyes, and is adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
Devoted to the worship of Śiva and tranquil, he should be intent on meditation upon Śiva; his complexion is white. || 1 ||
50. Now, as for the meditation on Death:
on the left side of the Lord is Kāla, whose form is that of Death.
Adorned with a crown and earrings, possessing excellent tusks and a formidable form.
In both hands, he has the form of one drawing a staff and a noose. || 5 ||
In the midst of that, the form of Kālarūpa seated upon a buffalo is described here; he is dark-complexioned. 1.
51. Now, the meditation on the form of Tripurāri:
[He is] four-armed, three-eyed, and holds a deer and an axe.
Equipped with a bow and arrows, and likewise accompanied by Umā.
Adorned with all ornaments and clothed in divine garments.
He placed a leaf upon his left ear and a jeweled earring upon his right.
It is endowed with the sacred thread (upavīta) and possesses the three-fold bend (tribhaṅga), which is auspicious.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, his body radiant with coral; thus [is the form] for the destruction of Tripura. He is the color of coral. 1.
52. Now, the meditation on the form of Hara as Jalandhara: [He is] red-hued, with fierce eyes, two arms, and three eyes.
Equipped with the sacred thread and adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||
(On page 73:
[He is] equipped with sandals on his feet, truly intent upon departing.
A parasol is held in his right hand, and a full water-pot in his left.
With his mass of matted hair beautifully disheveled, he was accompanied by Gaṅgā and Candra.
Adorned with earrings, and equipped with necklaces and anklets.
He has two arms and two eyes, and is adorned with a crown and bracelets.
Adorned with all ornaments and equipped with a sword at his side.
With palms joined in reverence, he held a supreme discus in his hand.
Then Jalandhara is described: the god [Jalandhara] is red in color; Jalandhara is yellow in color. 2.
53. Now, the meditation on the Threefold Form (Mūrti) for the severing of Brahma’s head: [He is] fair-complexioned, three-eyed, and resplendent with a crown of matted locks.
And bearing earrings upon his right and left ears. || 1 ||
Wearing a tiger-skin garment and endowed with four arms.
In his left hands, he holds a vajra and an axe in the front, and the skull of Brahmā. || 2 ||
Others have a trident in their hand; perform the rest as previously described. He is fair-complexioned. 1.
54. Now, the meditation on the form of the destroyer of Gajāsura:

Standing upon the head of the elephant with his right foot, his left limb raised by the right [hand], his skin wrapped upward around his tail, with his uplifted hand holding a trident and a sword, blazing with the tips of his horns.

I bow to Hara, who holds an axe and a black antelope skin in his hands, whose face possesses the brilliance of the moon, who is accompanied by his daughter who looks toward him with great fear, and whose left hand is adorned with a needle; he is white in color. 1. 1.
55. Now, the meditation on the form of Vīrabhadra: [He is] four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with a crown of matted hair.
In his right hands he holds a sword and an arrow, and in his left hands he bears a bow and a mace.
With a face made terrifying by formidable fangs, he was fearsome with a dreadful roar.
Adorned with a garland of severed heads, he stands firmly upon a pair of sandals.
One should place Karāla, joined with Bhadrakālī, upon the heart; he is blue in color. (1)
The nature of Dakṣa-Brahmā: one should establish Dakṣa-Brahmā on the right side of the Vīra.
It has the face of a goat, two eyes, and is adorned with two horns.
He offered salutations with palms joined to the Brahmin who was devoted to the meditation on Śiva; he was dark-complexioned. 1 || 2 ||
56. Now, the meditation on Hari-Hara:

On the right side [is the form] with the luster of coral, wearing a crown of the moon and adorned with ashes and rudrākṣas; on the left side [is the form] with a dark-blue luster, endowed with a jeweled crown and exceedingly beautiful in yellow garments.

May the left hand display the *iṭakā* (thunderbolt) and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), while the other pair of hands holds the conch and the *kaumodakī* mace; may the glorious half-body of Hari, with a slightly visible eye on the forehead, shine forth before me. || 1 ||

On his right side is a sword, while on the other [left] is a beautiful lotus encircled by the Ganges; on the left half is a magnificent crown, resembling a pool of blood, and he is clothed in a tiger skin.

I bow to Śambhu, who bestows all auspiciousness and is enriched by the granting of all prosperity; he whose equal feet are marked by half a ploughshare and half an eye, who wears a beautiful sacred thread, and who possesses half the form of Hari. (2)
The portion belonging to Īśvara is red in color; the portion belonging to Viṣṇu is dark blue in color. || 1 ||
57. Now, the meditation on the form of Ardhanārīśvara:
He has four arms and three eyes, and the portion belonging to Śiva is on the right side.
The left half, however, on the left side, possesses the hairline, the tilaka, and the mole.
Half of an eye, however, is joined upon the forehead in its southern portion.
On the right ear he wore an earring, while on the left was a leaf-shaped ornament.
Or she may have a sword at her waist, with the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the gesture of protection (ṭaṅka) in her left and right hands respectively.
In his left hand, he holds a wish-granting lotus, adorned with armlets and bracelets. || 3 ||
On the portion of Umā, however, one should fashion a breast, joined with the utterance "svāhā."
Śambhu has the southern half of his hip covered by a tiger-skin garment.
Her waistband is half-umā, and she is adorned with garments of variegated cloth.
The left foot is adorned with an anklet, while the right foot is drawn up and bent.
It should be coral-colored itself, with its left side being very black.
The Ardhanārīśvara form has been described; the portion belonging to Īśvara is red in color.
The portion belonging to the Goddess is dark-colored. || 1 ||
58. Now, the meditation on the form of Kirātārjuna:
[He is] four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with matted hair and a crown.
Adorned with all ornaments and clothed in divine garments. || 1 ||
He is red in color, equipped with a bow and arrows, and joined by a black axe.
Make it endowed with an upper garment (upavīta) and a body of even proportions. || 2 ||
On the left is Gaurī joined [with him], and on the right stands Arjuna.
The form of Arjuna: having one face and two eyes, and endowed with matted hair and a crown.
Adorned with all ornaments, he stands with his palms joined in reverence. || 1 ||
Thus it was told regarding the Kirāta: the god was red in color, and Arjuna was dark in color. 2.
59. Now, the meditation on the form of Kaṅkāla:

He who bears the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), who holds a beautiful peacock-feather fan and a skull-topped staff in his right hand, and a chisel in his left lotus-hand, and who possesses the splendor of dense vermilion.

I bow to Hara, who holds a trident and has the face of a black antelope, whose hand is extended, who wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, who is clothed in a tiger skin, and who is surrounded by gods and the lords of sages. 1.
Four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
On his feet were joined sandals, and he was somewhat intent on departing.
Adorned with all ornaments, with a sacrificial thread and an upper garment.
He wore a conch on his left ear and bird-shaped and crocodile-shaped earrings.
With a face slightly smiling and endowed with various graceful gestures.
Holding a dagger at his right hip, he was accompanied by spirits.
It was filled with deer, birds, and other creatures that had come seeking alms-food.
One should fashion the Great Being on the left side of the god.
He has two arms, two eyes, and is endowed with a formidable face.
Having placed the skull upon his head, he remained stationed to the left of the deity.
Thus the skeleton has been described. The deity is red in color; the spirit is black in color. 2.

60. Now, the meditation on the form of Caṇḍeśa as the embodiment of grace: One should meditate upon Caṇḍeśa, who is yellow in complexion, possesses two arms, holds a *ṭaṅka* (axe) in his right hand and a black [object] in his left, and stands by the left side of Pārvatī.

I praise him who has placed his hand upon the head of Caṇḍeśa, who possesses three eyes on his right side, who is adorned with all ornaments, who wears the crescent moon, and who is joined by the Gaṅgā. || 1 ||
One should likewise place Caṇḍeśa on the right side of the deity.
The length of Caṇḍeśa is said to be equal to the height of the god's arm. || 2 ||
And by the grace of Nyasta-vyoma, Caṇḍeśa was endowed with devotion.
Caṇḍeśvara, golden-hued and adorned with the ornaments of a child.
The head of Caṇḍa, adorned with the god, was graced by his playful sport.
The favor of Caṇḍeśa has thus been declared. || 4 ||
And the god Caṇḍeśa is yellow in color. || 2 ||
61. Now, the meditation on the form that removes poison: [the deity] has one face, three eyes, and is endowed with a crown of matted hair.
Having four arms, deep red in color, accompanied by a deer, and bearing an axe.
Holding poison in his right hand, with his gaze directed upward toward the wind (apāna), he looked at me alone.
In his left hand, he holds the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā) and is adorned with all ornaments.
On the left side of the god, one should likewise have the goddess fashioned.
Dark-complexioned, with two eyes and two arms, she is posed in a triple-bend (tribhaṅgī), with her feet tucked one on each side.
Pressing it against her throat, she stood with her right arm hanging down, overwhelmed with anxiety, bestowing satisfaction upon the Lord.
She is clad in yellow garments, possesses two eyes, and bestows the fruits of all desired objects.
The god is red in color; the goddess is dark blue in color. 2.
62. Now, the visualization of the form for the gift of the discus (cakradāna):

Standing before Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sattva, with hands joined in *añjali* at the lotus-feet of the God, one should constantly meditate upon Him who wears yellow garments and the Kaustubha gem, and whose eyes are fixed upon a beautiful garland.
I worship that supreme Paśupati, who out of compassion gave him the name Padmākṣa, who bears the excellent black antelope skin and the axe, and who bestows the discus. || 1 ||
He has one face and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
And in his left hands, he holds a water-pot and an excellent axe.
On the right, joined with a wheel, the form of the giver is described here.
On the left side of the god, however, there was one of dark complexion, well-established [there]. || 3 ||
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a yellow upper garment.
One should place the joined palms (añjali) on the north, accompanied by the conch and the discus.
Thus, the form of Viṣṇu endowed with these characteristics is described here.
The god Śveta is white in color; Viṣṇu is dark blue in color. 2.
63. Now, the meditation on the form of Vighneśvara, pleased by his boon: [he is] four-armed, three-eyed, and endowed with a crown of matted hair.
He should place the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) on his head and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in his left hand.
Vighneśa stands to the right, joined with Kṛṣṇa’s axe.
Lying down, he placed his right foot down while his left was suspended.
Adorned with all ornaments, dark-complexioned, and most beautiful.
On the left side of the god, however, was the goddess with a smiling countenance. || 3 ||
Adorned with all ornaments, she holds a blue lotus in her right hand.
She has two arms and three eyes, and her left hand is joined in the gesture of granting boons.
One should place the foot resting on the right side, while the left is extended.
Place the goddess Umā seated on a single seat, as described in the words of Skanda.
And Vighneśa, red in color and adorned with a crown and diadem.
He performs salutation with palms joined in añjali, and is endowed with a noose and a goad.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, it bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
Thus it is said regarding the Vighnaprasāda. The God and the Goddess are dark-blue in color; Vighneśa is red in color. 3.
64. Now, the meditation on the form of Somāskanda:

resembling the rising sun, endowed with four hands, divine and wearing garments along with armlets, necklaces, and other ornaments, possessing matted hair and a crown, and beautifully adorned with three eyes.

I worship the Lord who is joined by Gaurī on his left, seated comfortably between the two, the youthful Kumāra, the pervasive one who is both Soma and Skanda, holding the deer, the gesture of fearlessness, the boon-granting mudrā, and an axe.
Somāskandeśvara is proclaimed as being endowed with the power of enjoyment.
He has four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Adorned with all ornaments, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
And he holds a black chisel in his right hand and likewise in his left.
He should place the leaf-ornament on his left ear and the crocodile-shaped earring on his right.
And likewise, he was wearing the sacred thread and lying down on his left side.
With the right foot extended and accompanied by Gaurī on the left.
Between those two was Skanda, endowed with all auspicious marks.
This is declared to be the Somāskanda [liṅga], accompanied by Gaṅgā and Candra.
Beside Somāskanda, however, Bhogaśakti is on the left side.
But the Hero (Vīra) is on the right side, either seated or standing.
Among the twenty-five forms, Soma, Āskaṇḍa, and Mahān are considered [the foremost].
At the time of commencing the festival, however, [the worship] of Soma and Skanda is especially [important].
One should [visualize] the goddess Dharā as Kumudā, holding a boon-granting gesture in her left hand.
Lying down with the right foot extended and the left foot hanging down.
The meditation on Skanda.
Skanda stood there in the form of a child, with two eyes and endowed with two arms.
Holding a straight lotus in his hand, he was adorned with all ornaments.
This is declared to be the Soma-Skanda [mantra]. The god is red in color; the goddess is dark blue in color; Skanda is blue in color. 3.

65. Now, one should meditate upon the form of the Lord with one leg: the All-pervading One, possessing the luster of ten million suns, three-eyed, bearing the moon and the Gaṅgā, holding a trident and a deer in his hands, granting boons and fearlessness, and endowed with a single foot.
He stands between the right and left armpits and arms of Śambhu—namely Brahmā and Acyuta—surrounded by their respective characteristic weapons, with his two hands joined in añjali. || 1 ||

The Lord who abides firmly even during the dissolution of the universe, who is situated within the cosmic egg, endowed with such characteristics, and who is the destroyer of the cities—He has been made into the single form of one foot.
Known as Ekapāda, he is seated comfortably; his color is red, though in another tradition, white is also well-known. || 1 ||
66. Now, the meditation on the form seated in ease:
[He is] reddish in luster, smeared with beautiful white ashes, holding the earth-touching and boon-granting gestures, and bestowing fearlessness.
This form possesses beautiful eyes and auspicious limbs, shining with a garment as red as the dawn, and is seated comfortably. || 1 ||
Four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
He holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his right hand and the gesture of granting boons (varada) in his left hand.
In the left and right hands, he holds a black axe.
Lying down, he placed his right foot forward while keeping the left bent.
Everything together with Umā, excluding Skanda and Gaurī.
"He is said to be seated comfortably; his color is red. || 1 ||

67. Now, the meditation on Dakṣiṇāmūrti, or alternatively, the meditation on Vyākhyānamūrti: His body is slightly pale like the color of ash, he wears a crescent moon, and his lotus-like palms shine with the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), a rosary, a lute, and a book; he is beautiful with a yogic cloth (*yogapaṭṭa*).
May the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti—who is seated upon the throne of exposition, served by all the best of sages, exceedingly gracious, and clad in the skin of a serpent—protect us forever. || 1 ||
Nārada and Jamadagni are to the right of Vasiṣṭha and Bhṛgu.
Bharadvāja, Śaunaka, Agastya, and likewise Bhārgava. || 2 ||
On the left side, it should be arranged, well-served by Kinnaras and others.
On that Mount Kailāsa, at the foot of a banyan tree.
[He saw] Maheśvara, the lord of all, seated there, possessing a peaceful form.
It is called Dakṣiṇāmūrti. One should cause Apasmāra to lie down below.
Of bright complexion. || 1 ||
68. Now, the meditation on the Liṅgodbhava form:
situated in the center of the linga-shape, he stands like Candraśekhara.
The foot situated below Nālaka is endowed with the emergence of the Liṅga. || 1 ||
Viriñci, in the form of a swan, is indeed above on the left side.
Hari, in the form of the Lord Varāha, descended below in that very form. || 2 ||
Standing on the left and right sides of the mouth, they both have their palms joined in the añjali gesture.
In their own essential nature, the two-footed, the stationary, the unborn, and Viṣṇu abide in the Supreme.
Thus, the descent of the *liṅga* always brings about peace for all.
With arms reaching down to his broad, high-shouldered chest, and possessing the various colors and ornaments that serve as his distinctive marks;
May he bestow that which is endowed with splendor, brings auspiciousness to all subjects, and causes the increase of sovereignty and the assembly. || 1 ||
In another view, he is also well known as being white in color. || 1 ||
69. Now, the meditation on the form of Śarabha:
having a form equal to Mount Meru, eight feet, and the radiance of the sun.
Possessing thirty-two arms and having the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes. || 1 ||
It was difficult to approach, with the two elephants as its adversaries, and possessed the deep roar of thick clouds.
With hair standing erect, mighty-armed, and adorned with various ornaments. || 2 ||
The thunderbolt-fist, the gesture of fearlessness, the wheel, the spear, the staff, and likewise the goad;
A sword, a khaṭvāṅga staff, axes, a rosary, bones, and a trident. || 3 ||
Holding a bow, a mace, and fire in his right hands.
Likewise, [he holds] the boon-granting gesture, a noose in his hand, a mace, an arrow, and a banner.
The saw, the chest, the conch, the white elephant, and the lotus.
[He holds] a skull, a book, and a spear, with his lotus-like hands embracing Durgā.
And holding a ploughshare in his left hand, he is formidable with his lotus-like hands.
With his fangs bared, he was being crushed by the fierce lashing of a great lion's tail.
Red in color. || 1 ||
Now, the thirty-two names of the Gaṇapatis (from the Mudgala Purāṇa):
Bāla, Taruṇa, Bhakta, Vīra, Śakti, and likewise Dvija.
The one named Hiraṃba was sent by the Siddhas, Ucchiṣṭa, and Vighneśa. || 1 ||
Lakṣmī, Gaṇapati, and likewise Mahāvighneśvara;
Vijaya and Kalpanṛtta are also said to be above Vighneśa. || 2 ||
The single-syllable mantra is supreme, and the three-syllable mantra is the swift bestower [of results].
And [the one] named Haridrā, Ekadanta, Sṛṣṭi, and the one named Uddaṇḍa. (3)
The debt-releasing Koḍhuṇḍi, as well as the two-faced and the three-faced [deities].
The Siṃha-yoga, Durgā, and the God who removes all distress.
Now, the meditation on those known as the thirty-two Vighnarājas is described.
First, there is the meditation on Bālaganapati:
holding in his hands plantains, mangoes, breadfruit, sugarcane, and sweetmeats.
I bow to this youthful sun, the god who is the leader of the youthful Gaṇas. He is red in color.
71. Now, the meditation on the youthful Gaṇapati:
[He who holds] in his own hands a noose, a goad, a cake, a kapittha fruit, a jambu fruit, his own tusk, rice, and sugarcane.
May that youthful Gaṇeśa, who possesses the luster of the ever-youthful dawn and whose complexion is red, protect you all. (1) [He is] of red color. (1)
72. Now, the meditation on Gaṇapati, the Lord of Devotees: [He is] holding coconuts, mangoes, plantains, molasses, and milk-rice porridge.
73. Now, the meditation on Vīragaṇapati:
[He holds] a vetāla, a spear, an arrow, a bow, a discus, a sword, a khaṭvāṅga, a mallet, a club, a goad, and a snake-noose.
I constantly remember the red-colored Lord of the hosts of heroes, who bears a trident, a spear, an axe, and a banner. [1] He is red in color. [1]
74. Now, the meditation on Śaktigaṇapati:
[He is] embracing the Goddess, whose body is green, with their hip regions mutually locked together.
I praise Gaṇeśa, who is as red as the twilight, who wields the noose and the goad, and who removes all fear; he is the color of vermilion. || 1 || He is the color of vermilion. || 1 ||
75. Now, the meditation on the Lord of the Host of the Twice-born (Brahmā):
He is moon-colored, his hands adorned with a book, a rosary, a staff, and a water-pot, and shining with the splendor of sacred knowledge.
O Lord of the assembly of the twice-born, blessed is he who meditates upon you, whose splendor is measured by the four faces of the elephant-faced one, and whose complexion is white.
76. Now, the meditation on Siddhagaṇapati:
[He is worshipped] together with ripe mango fruits, flower clusters, stalks of sugarcane, sesame seeds, and sweetmeats (modakas).
May he who bears the axe, endowed with the prosperity of splendor, be golden-hued; may he be of a tawny color.
77. Now, the meditation on Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati: [He holds] a blue lotus, a pomegranate, a lute, a stalk of rice, a guñjā berry, and a rosary.
May this dark-hued Gaṇeśa, who bears the name Ucchiṣṭa, protect me. || 1 ||
In another way, he is blue-colored, being infatuated by desire and greedy for the taste of the woman’s womb. 1.
78. Now, the visualization of Vighnagaṇapati:
[He is] with a conch, sugarcane bow, flowers, arrows, axe, noose, discus, his own tusk, goad, cluster of blossoms, and shafts, and so forth.
Victorious is Vighneśvara, whose splendor of ornaments is perfectly arranged upon his hands, who is as fair as refined gold, and who possesses a golden complexion.
79. Now, the meditation on Kṣipragaṇapati:
[He is] resplendent with a tooth, a wish-fulfilling creeper, a noose, a jewel-pot, and a goad.
One should meditate upon the swift Lord of the Gaṇas, who possesses a lovely luster like the Baṃdhūka flower; he is red in color.
80. Now, the meditation on Heraṃba Gaṇapati:
He has hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and he holds a noose, a tusk, a rosary, a goad, an axe, a mallet, and a modaka sweet.
May Gaṇapati, named Heraṃba—who has attained the state of a lion, whose face is like that of a five-tusked elephant, and who is exceedingly fair—protect [us]. (1) He is of a white complexion. (1)

81. Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī and Gaṇapati: He bears a parrot, a citron, a māṇikya jewel, a water-pot, a goad, a noose, and a wish-fulfilling creeper; he possesses a sword and a shimmering stream of light and nectar.

May the two goddesses, Lakṣmī and Gaṇeśa—fair-limbed, accompanied by Śyāma who holds a lotus, and holding hands in the gestures of granting boons—protect us from all sides. [They are] fair-complexioned. 1.
82. Now, the meditation on Mahāgaṇapati:

He has the face of a lordly elephant, wears the crescent moon upon his crest, and possesses a reddish glow; he has three eyes and is constantly embraced with passion by his beloved, who holds a lotus in her hand and rests upon his lap.

I worship Him who carries in His hands a citron, a mace, a sugarcane bow, an excellent discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, His own tusk, and a jewel-filled jar; He is red in color. 1.
83. Now, the meditation on Vijaya Gaṇapati:
He holds a noose, a goad, his own tusk, and a mango fruit, and has a mouse as his vehicle.
May the red-colored Vināyaka destroy all obstacles here. (1) [Red-colored] (1).
84. Now, the meditation on Nṛttagaṇapati:
His hands, with their beautiful fingers, are fashioned to hold a noose, a goad, a sweetmeat offering (*apūpa*), and a battle-axe, as well as his tusk.
I worship Gaṇeśa, who possesses a yellow radiance, resides beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), and is accompanied by the dance, [who is] red in color. 1. 1.
85. Now, the meditation on the upward-moving Gaṇapati: His limbs are radiant with gold, [holding] a white lotus, a sugarcane bow, arrows, and the sprouts of his tusks.
May that Lord of the Gaṇas, whose body is green and who has his hands raised to embrace the goddess Yaṣṭī, bestow auspiciousness upon me. He is golden-hued. 1. 1.
86. Now, the meditation on Ekākṣaragaṇapati:
He is red, adorned with red unguents, garments, and flowers; he is pot-bellied, has the moon upon his crest, is endowed with three eyes, has short hands and feet, and holds a citron fruit.

May the Lord Vighnarāja—the king of obstacles—bestow happiness for the sake of prosperity; he who has an elephant’s face, who is adorned with ornaments, who sits upon a lotus throne, and whose hands hold a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and a rosary. He is red in color. 1. 1.
87. Now, the meditation on the excellent Gaṇapati:

I worship him who has the luster of vermilion, the face of an elephant, and three eyes; who holds a noose and a goad in his hands, and constantly bears a honey-filled skull-cup; and who is adorned with a beautiful crescent moon upon his crest.

His body is embraced by Puṣṭi, who holds a lotus at the tip of her hand like a banner; her hands shine with that [lotus] as her source. His hand, placed upon her lap, holds a splendid water-lily (*vasumat-pātra*) that shines like a lotus. He is red in color. 1.
88. Now, the meditation on the Three-Syllable Gaṇapati: [He who has] the face of the lordly elephant, with his moving ears like excellent whisks.
Golden-hued, four-armed, holding a noose and a goad, and most excellent.
He holds a sweetmeat in his right hand and likewise a mango fruit in his left.
One should meditate upon him holding a lotus and a modaka sweetmeat; he is golden-hued. 1–2.
89. Now, the meditation on Gaṇapati of Swift Faith:
He holds a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, a rosary, and a citron.
He whose crown is adorned with a crescent moon, who has three eyes, who is tawny-hued, and who has the face of an elephant. || 1 ||
Resplendent with shining ornaments, possessing a large belly, and radiant upon a lotus seat.
May he who is red in color, whose wind-like breath dispels obstacles, and who always holds a lotus in his hand, grant me prosperity. || 1 || || 2 ||
90. Now, the meditation on Haridrā-Gaṇapati:
[one should meditate upon] the Lord who is turmeric-colored, four-armed, and has a face like turmeric.
The god holds a noose and a goad, and likewise possesses a sweetmeat for his tooth.
I salute the bestower of devotion and fearlessness, the destroyer of obstacles, who is turmeric-colored. 1.
91. Now, the meditation on Gaṇapati Ekadanta:
One should meditate upon Gaṇeśa, who has a large belly, a dark body, holds an axe and a rosary, and has his trunk raised upward.
I praise him who holds a *salaṭṭu* flower and a tusk in his two lower hands, the left and the right; he is dark-complexioned. || 1 || He is of a dark hue. || 1 ||
92. Now, the meditation on Sṛṣṭigaṇapati:
He holds a noose, a goad, his own tusk, and a mango fruit, and has a mouse as his vehicle.
May the red-hued Vināyaka, who is skilled in creation, destroy our obstacles here. (1) [He is] red in color. (1)
93. Now, the meditation on Uddaṇḍagaṇapati:
He holds a white water-lily, a lotus, a citron, a mace, an elephant-goad, a sugarcane bow, arrows, a jeweled jar, a śālī-grain measure, a noose, a goad, and a lotus.

May the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), whose body is crimson and who is embraced by the Goddess with fair limbs and beautiful lotus-like hands, bestow auspiciousness upon those who worship Him. [1] He is red in color. [1]
94. Now, the meditation on Gaṇapati Ṛṇamocaka:
He has a noose, a goad, and an elephant-goad in his hands, and possesses the luster of crystal.
Gaṇapati, clad in red garments, shall be for the sake of joy; he is the liberator from debt. [He is] white in color.
95. Now, the meditation on Dhuṇḍhi Gaṇapati:
[He holds] a rosary, an axe, a jewel-bowl, and his own tusk.
May the Lord of Obstacles, named Ḍhuṇḍhi, who holds [his weapons] in his hands, grant us joy. He is red in color.
96. Now, the meditation on Dvimukha Gaṇapati:
He has a greenish-blue body and, with his hands, holds his own teeth, a noose, a goad, and a vessel of jewels.
May Gaṇeśa, who wears a red garment and a crest-garland of jewels, always turn his face toward me for prosperity. He is green in color. 1. 1.

97. Now, the meditation on Trimukha Gaṇapati: He joyfully holds in his right hands a lotus, a sharp-tipped goad, a rosary, and the gesture of granting boons; and in his left hands, he holds a noose, a jar filled with nectar, and the gesture of fearlessness.

May he who sits upon a throne resplendent with a golden lotus possessing a beautiful pericarp, who has three faces, whose countenance is like a *palāśa* flower, and who has the face of a serpent, protect us. (1) He is red in color. (1)
98. Now, the meditation on Siṃhagaṇapati:

With his right hands he holds a lute, a wish-fulfilling creeper, an enemy [of obstacles], and displays the gesture of granting boons; with his left hands he holds a lotus, a jewel-filled jar, a beautiful cluster of blossoms, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.

May Gaṇapati—whose face is like a lion with a trunk like a young elephant, who is as white as a conch or the moon, and whose auspicious garments resemble shining jewels—protect us from calamity. (1) [He is white in color. (1)
99. Now, the meditation on Yogagaṇapati:
He is established in yoga, beautiful with his yogic cloth, radiant like the rising sun, and adorned with garments of sapphire-blue.

Resembling molten gold, with eight hands and a large body, he holds in his right hands a blazing goad, an arrow, a rosary, and a tusk.
In her left hands, she holds a noose and a bow, while her moving hands support a lotus.
May Durgā and Gaṇapati, who are golden-hued and always clad in red garments, bring delight. 1-2.
101. Now, the meditation on Gaṇapati, the remover of distress:
He has the luster of the rising sun and carries a young girl on his lap.

Resembling a cluster of blue lotuses, he stands upon a seat that is as red as a lotus.

she has one face and two eyes, and is endowed with a crown of matted hair.

he has two faces and eight arms, and is white and dark-blue in complexion.
