1. Now, the meditation on the Four-faced One (according to the Śaiva Āgama):
[One should meditate on Him] who has four faces and four arms, and who holds a water-pot and the *akṣamālā* (rosary).
He wears a sacrificial thread as an upper garment and is adorned with a crown of matted locks. || 1 ||
A rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left hand.
He holds a sruva ladle in his right hand and a book in his left hand.
Seated upon the lotus throne, with eyes momentarily closed in meditation.
One should meditate upon this four-faced deity, who has the luster of the tip of a lotus petal; his color is pale-red (pāṭala).
2. Now, the meditation on Sarasvatī (from the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
The goddess Sarasvatī should be visualized adorned with all ornaments.
She should be depicted with four arms and likewise standing firmly upright. || 1 ||
And a book and a rosary are in his two right hands.
And likewise, in the two left hands, a flute and a water-pot should be fashioned.
She stands with feet together, not resting [on a seat], her face is gentle, she is white, and her complexion is white. || 1 ||
Now, the meditation on the five Brahmans (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
First, the meditation on the Primordial Brahman.
The wise man should visualize the god Brahmā as gentle and four-faced.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, joyful, and likewise clothed in a black antelope skin.
Wearing matted locks, possessing four arms, and seated upon a chariot drawn by seven swans.
When Vāmana was offered as a gift, one pair of his arms became the means of crossing over [the ocean].
Holding a rosary of beads in his single right hand.
And in the second [hand], he holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), wearing all ornaments.
O King, he was endowed with all the auspicious marks and possessed a tranquil form.
For a moment, with eyes closed in meditation, his face shone like the tip of a lotus petal. || 4 ||
The preceptor should thus perform [the rite] either in a painting or in the construction of a temple; [the deity is] the color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
4. Now, the meditation on the World-Protectors and Brahmā:
Seated upon a lotus-petal throne, Brahmā has four faces and performs his divine activities.
He was the color of the sun, a knower of dharma, and likewise wore a rosary and a sacred thread.
Form (rūpa) is the effect previously mentioned; everything else belongs to the Lord of the World. [His] color is pale-red (pāṭalavarṇa). || 1 ||
5. Now, for the meditation on Prajāpati as Brahmā, he should be performed with a swan as his vehicle, and he should not be made four-faced.
The auspicious Sāvitrī should be made his wife, seated upon his lap.
The supreme form spoken by Brahmā is the entire creation of Prajāpati; it is the color of the Pāṭala flower. 1.
6. Now, regarding the meditation on Brahmā according to the ritual rule: the Lord Viśvakarman should be visualized as assuming the form of the Sun.
Having two arms and ten hands, the great one who bears a form of splendor is pale-red in color.
7. Now, the meditation on Viśvakarman as Brahmā:
He has four faces, four feet, and four arms, and is clad in white garments.
Having satisfied all desire for ornaments, he performed religious duties without waste. || 1 ||
Holding a rosary in his right hand and a book in his left.
But Resolve, embodied, [arose] from the right side of Kārya. || 2 ||
The face situated on the left side should be made exceedingly beautiful in form.
Their two lotus-like hands should be placed upon their heads; they are pale-red in color. (2, 5)
Now, the names of the nine lords of progeny (as found in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*):
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Kardama, Kaśyapa, and Dakṣa—these nine are the sons of Brahmā.
8. First, regarding the meditation on Marīci:
I bow to the primordial Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, who was born from the mind [of the Supreme].
Holding a rosary and a water-pot in his hands, he was adorned with matted hair and bark garments.
Resembling a mountain of gold, he was chanting the supreme *praṇava*; he was golden-hued.
9. Now, the meditation on Aṅgiras:
I bow to the sage Aṅgiras, whose head is marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra).
The Lord of Creatures, possessing the luster of gold, holds a rosary and a water-pot in his hands; he is golden-hued.
10. Now, the meditation on Atri:
[one should meditate upon] Atri, the son of Marīci, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
I worship incessantly the one with matted hair and a beard, who is peaceful and has a dark-complexioned body. [1] He is of a dark hue. [1]
11. Now, the meditation on Pulastya: I bow my head to Pulastya, the mind-born son of Brahmā.
He is peaceful, having conquered the group of six internal enemies, and holds a rosary and a staff in his hands.
He had a black antelope skin as an upper garment, wore matted hair, and possessed a tawny radiance; he was of a tawny complexion. (1)
12. Now follows the meditation on Pulaha:
I perpetually bow to Pulaha, the treasure-house of austerity, who is exceedingly peaceful.
He was dark as a rain cloud, holding a rosary and a water-pot; he was blue in color.
13. Now follows the meditation on the seasons (ṛtudhyāna): [one should meditate upon] the season, which is preeminent among the seasons and praised by the hosts of Brahman-sages.
He had matted hair and a beard, carried a staff and a water-pot, and was radiant.
I meditate upon that storehouse of ascetic powers, resplendent like the seven-rayed sun; he is red in color. 1.
14. Now, regarding meditation on the mud:
I bow to the one whose head is not mixed with mud, who dries up the mud of sin.
Richly adorned with the splendor of a crown of matted locks, his body was as ruddy as the clouds of twilight.
Holding a rosary and a water-pot in his hands, clothed in rags and a black antelope skin, he is the color of vermilion. 1.
15. Now follows the meditation on Kaśyapa:
I bow to Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, who is pure and whose head is like the sun.
His mind was firmly attached to the Praṇava-Brahman, and he possessed the luster of pure gold.
Clad in rags and bark garments, radiant with a mass of matted locks.
Golden-hued, he was intent on creating progeny, holding a rosary of beads and a water-pot.
16. Now, the meditation on Dakṣa:
he has the face of a goat, two eyes, and is adorned with two horns.
I salute with palms joined in reverence him who is devoted to meditation on Śiva—Svāyaṃbhuva, dark as a rain cloud, Dakṣa, initiated for the sacrifice. He is of a dark complexion. 1–9.
17. Now, the meditation on the Seven Sages (from the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
They are indifferent [to worldly affairs], wearing sacred threads, and carrying water-pots and rosaries.
Those with matted hair and beards, peaceful, seated and intent on meditation. || 1 ||
The seven ṛṣis, with Vasiṣṭha at their head, should be depicted together with their wives.
Their names are: Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Kaśyapa.
Jamadagni and Vasiṣṭha appeared twenty-one times during the Vaivasvata Manvantara.
18. First, there [is] the meditation on Gautama, the son of Rahūgaṇa, who is peaceful and whose head is marked with the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra).
I worship Gautama, who holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff; he is golden-hued. 1. Golden-hued. 1.
19. Now follows the meditation on Bharadvāja:
[one should meditate upon] Bharadvāja, who is greatly tranquil, the husband of Suśīlā, and powerful.
I worshipped the sage Aṅgiras, who held a rosary and a staff in his hands and was dark-complexioned.
20. Now, the meditation on Viśvāmitra:
[one should meditate on him] resembling Hiraṇyagarbha, wearing a crown of matted locks.
I worship Viśvāmitra, the peaceful lord of Kumudvatī; he is yellow in color.
21. Then one should meditate upon the meditation of Kāśyapa, [visualizing] the son of Marīci wearing matted hair and bark garments.
[He saw] that bull among sages, accompanied by his wife, holding a rosary of prayer beads; he was black in complexion.
22. Now follows the meditation on Jamadagni:
[one should meditate upon] the son of Bhṛgu, who is peaceful, who has conquered the group of six internal enemies, and who possesses great splendor.
I bow to Jamadagni, who holds a staff and a rosary in his hands; he is red in color.
23. Now follows the meditation on Vasiṣṭha: [the sage] who is a treasury of austerity, an ocean of compassion, and born from Mitra and Varuṇa.
I bow down to Vasiṣṭha, who holds a garland and a staff in his hands and grants boons; he is white in color.
24. Then, [he meditated] upon the god Atri, the son of Viriñci, who held a rosary and a water-pot.
I worship Atri, the husband of Anasūyā, who is peaceful, stainless, and dark-complexioned. 1 || 7 ||
p.
95) 25. Now, the meditation on the fourfold set beginning with Dharma (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): "Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and likewise sovereignty."
White, reddish, yellow, and black; these are proclaimed to be the forms of lions. || 1 || 4 ||
26. Now, the meditation on the four deities who preside over the fourfold set beginning with *dharma* (according to the *Pāñcarātra*):

Yama, Vāyu, Śiva, and Indra are to be known as the deities of *adharma* and the others. (Their characteristics are to be seen among the guardians of the directions [in the section on] the treasure-house). 4.
27. Now, the meditation on the fourfold [set] beginning with Adharma (from the Pāñcarātra’s Pādmasaṃhitā):
"The forms of Puruṣas are situated within those very [worlds] that are produced from desire."
They have four arms and lion faces; some are white and others are reddish-brown.
With both hands turned toward him, they formed hollowed palms in the gesture of añjali.
And with two other hands, they hold two yogapīṭhas.
They have white color on their faces and ruddy color on their bodies. 4.
28. Now, the meditation on the four deities presiding over the fourfold set beginning with Adharma (as found in the *Pādma-saṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*):

Nirṛti is the lord of Adharma; Durgā is the lord of Ajñāna (Ignorance); Kāma is the lord of Avairāgya (Lack of Dispassion); Rudra is the lord of Anaiśvarya (Lack of Sovereignty). Those who do not worship [the Lord] are of such a nature as to be the appropriators of Adharma and the rest.

Nirṛti, Durgā, Kāma, and likewise Rudra. (The forms of these [deities], whose characteristics have been previously stated in their respective iconographic descriptions, will be described in sequence [in chapters 4, 5, 2, and 5 of the Nidhi section]. Rudra is like the deity of the Ārdrā asterism; Durgā is like the deity of the year.)
29. Now, the characteristics of a meritorious person (*puṇyapuruṣalakṣaṇa*) [from the *Kāraṇāgama*]:
[He is] seated upon a lion-throne, golden-hued, and wearing a crown.
I meditate upon the meritorious lotus-feet of the Son of the Gods within my heart. He is golden-hued.
30. Now, the meditation on the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣadhyāna*) [according to the *Pañcarātra*]:
He has the murder of a Brahmin for his head and the theft of gold for his two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher’s bed.
The pair of words connected to that [name] is the sin against the limbs and minor members.
His body hair was like that of a minor sinner, and his eyebrows, beard, and eyes were tawny.
One should visualize the sinner as black-complexioned, bearing a sword and a shield, with [the sin] in his belly. He is black in color. (1)
p. 96) 31. Now, the meditation on the Brahmāstra (according to its ritual manual):
[He is seen] pressing down enemies with his left hand, and with his upper [hand], a mace.
I remember Bagalāmukhī, who has a long tongue and wears yellow garments; she is well known for her yellow complexion. (1)
Now, the nature of the four Vedas (*Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*, verse 32): First among them, the nature of the *Ṛgveda* is as follows:
"The *Ṛgveda* shall be white in color, two-armed, and with the face of a donkey."
Wearing a rosary, gentle, joyful, and intent upon exposition; he is white in color.
33. Now, as for the nature of the Yajurveda:
its face is that of a goat, it is yellow in color, and it holds a bull and a sacred thread.
In his left hand he holds a vajra; he bestows prosperity, oblations, and auspiciousness. He is yellow in color.
34. Now, as for the nature of the Sāmaveda:
the Sāmaveda has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and has the face of a horse.
He is remembered as holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left; his complexion is white.
35. Now, as for the nature of the Atharvaveda:
the Veda named after Atharvan is white in color and has the face of a monkey.
He is described as being endowed with a rosary in his left hand and holding a water-pot in his right; his complexion is white.

Now, the forms of the wives of the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda (from the *Skanda Purāṇa*, *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā*), chapter 36: First among them, the form of Sāmidhenī, the wife of the Ṛgveda, is as follows: she has the face of a peacock, is white in complexion, and is adorned with two bracelets.
Holding a lotus with her two hands, she is clad in incomparable yellow garments.
She is designated as the *sāmidhenī* [verse]; she is of brilliant complexion. 1.

37. Now, listen to the nature of the *sṛgā* who is the consort of the Yajurveda, and to the characteristics of the *sṛgā*: she is red in color, large-eyed, with a lotus in her hand and a slender waist. (1) She is red in color. (1)
38. Now, the form of Kuhū, the wife of the Sāmaveda:
she has a face as radiant as the full moon and is adorned with two arms.
Likewise, he should place a white flower on the left side and a cluster of grain on the right.
The goddess Sākambharī, white in color, bestows [blessings]. 1.
(p. 97) Now, regarding the nature of the fuel for the wife of the Atharvaveda—the characteristics of the fuel are stated.
She has the face of a sow, eyes like those of a cakora bird, and is radiant with garments the color of campaka flowers. || 1 ||
With his four arms, he holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a lotus, and a water-pot.
They are golden-colored. || 1 ||
40. Now, the forms of the ancestral lineages (*gotra*) and presiding deities (*adhidaivata*) of those who take pride in the four Vedas (from the *Dānakāṇḍa* of Hemādri):
"The wise know that the lineage of the *Ṛgveda* is Ātreya and its deity is Soma."
They know that the Yajurveda of Kāśyapa has Rudra as its presiding deity. || 1 ||
The Sāmaveda also, by lineage, was Bharadvāja Puraṃdara.
One should understand the fire-altar (Vaitāna) with respect to the deities; it belongs to the Atharvans.
One should know Brahma as the deity; O noble one, hear now its forms.

(Ṛgveda-personification Soma, like the Moon among the nine planets; 5 niyamas). (Yajurveda-personification Rudra, like the Sun with its presiding deity; 5 niyamas). (Sāmaveda-personification Indra, like Bṛhaspati with his presiding deity; 5 niyamas).
(Then Brahmā, the presiding deity of the Atharvaveda, together with Bṛhaspati as his subordinate deity; 4th [section], Nirukta). || 1 ||
41. Now, the nature of Āyurveda (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
Āyurveda is yellow like turmeric, with the face of a monkey and large eyes.
Holding a rosary and a jar of nectar, he bestows abundant health. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
42. Now, the meditation on Dhanvantari, the presiding deity of Āyurveda (from the Bhāgavata):
Then, from the ocean being churned by the descendants of Kaśyapa who were seeking the nectar of immortality...
A most wonderful man arose, O Great King. || 1 ||
With long and stout staff-like arms, a neck like a conch shell, and reddish eyes;
Dark-complexioned, youthful, wearing a garland, and adorned with all ornaments. || 2 ||
Clad in yellow garments, broad-chested, and adorned with polished jeweled earrings.
He has lovely, dark-blue, curly hair at the ends of his locks, and possesses the majestic stride of a lion.
Holding a jar filled with nectar and adorned with bracelets.
He was born as a partial incarnation of the Lord Viṣṇu himself.
Dhanvantari shall be renowned as a seer of Ayurveda through his sacrificial rites; he is dark-complexioned.
Another classification (in the treatise of Āyurveda).
He is richly adorned with a yellow garment, his hands manifesting a lotus, a water-lily, a jewel, and a pitcher of nectar, while his face is as beautiful as the moon.
May Dhanvantari protect us—he who shines with white garments, whose crown bestows health, and whose complexion is like that of the jewel of Indra. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||

Another form [described in the Mantrāgama] holds a conch, a discus, a leech, and a jar of nectar with his four arms; he is subtle, pure, and heart-pleasing, with a crown resplendent with a goad and lotus eyes.

I bow to that Dhanvantari, whose body is radiant like a dark rain-cloud, who is adorned with beautiful yellow garments shimmering upon his hips, and who displays the grace of a forest fire to the thicket of all diseases. || 1 ||
p. 98) Meditation according to the various types [as described] in the medical treatises (vaidyaśāstra).

In his upper and lower hands he holds a conch and a discus; in the right [upper] hand a divine herb, and in the left [upper] hand another hand holding a vessel of stainless nectar and a row of leeches.
May the Blessed Lord Dhanvantari—the mine of compassion, the creator of auspiciousness, and the destroyer of all maladies—constantly sever all your misfortune. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
43. Now, the nature of Dhanurveda (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
Dhanurveda is yellow in color, has the face of a cuckoo, and possesses a large body.
Fierce, bearing a bow and arrows, with tawny matted locks upon his head. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||

44. Now, the meditation on Indra, the deity presiding over the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), [as found] in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda* and the *Mayūkha*: "I visualize in my heart Indra, who is mounted upon a white elephant, whose hands are skillful with the thunderbolt and the goad, who possesses a thousand eyes, and who has a golden-yellow luster. (1)
Yellow in color. (Like the presiding deity of semen; 5th initiation. || 1 ||

Now, the forms of the deities who preside over the nature of the Vedas and their six ancillaries (*veda-ṣaḍaṅga*) [are described in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*, verse 45]. Among them, the form of *Śikṣā* is as follows:
Śikṣā is white, endowed with the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*) and the gesture of teaching (*jñāna-mudrā*).
She has three eyes, wears a rosary, possesses a water-pot, and has six arms holding a staff and a lotus.
She is of a bright white complexion. || 1 ||
46. Now, the meditation on Prajāpati, the deity presiding over the Śikṣā:
he should be depicted as riding upon a swan, and he should not have four faces.
Sāvitrī, auspicious and seated upon his left lap, should be fashioned for him.
The supreme form spoken by Brahmā is the entirety of the activity of Prajāpati.
The color is pale red. || 1 ||
(As with the five Brahmans, Suprajāpati, and Brahman; 4th initiation. || 1 ||
47. Now, the nature of the Kalpa: The Kalpa, moreover, has the luster of a white water-lily, a face like a crow's, and a large belly.
Holding an axe, a staff, and a lotus in his hands, he was adorned with a girdle and earrings.
The color of a white water lily. || 1 ||
48. Now, regarding the meditation on Brahmā, who is identified with the Kalpa (according to the Śaivāgama):
[One should meditate on him] as four-faced and four-armed, holding a water-pot and the Akṣamālā (rosary).
He wore a sacrificial thread as an upper garment and was adorned with a crown of matted locks. || 1 ||
In his right hand he holds a rosary of beads, and in his left a water-pot.
He holds a sacrificial ladle (sruva) in his right hand and a book in his left hand.
Seated upon a lotus throne, the Brahmin is facing upward with a smile.
The color is pale-red (pāṭalavarṇa). (Like Brahmā within the Trimūrti, 4th definition. || 1 ||
49. Now, the nature of Vyākaraṇa: Vyākaraṇa should be known as white, with a belly like the plumage of a peacock.
It was divine, held a lute, and was adorned with celestial garments.
Of brilliant white color. || 1 ||
50. Now, the meditation on Sarasvatī, who takes pride in grammar (from the Hemādri):
She is endowed with four arms; with one hand she holds a rosary made of crystal beads, with another a white lotus, with another a parrot, and with the remaining hand a book.

May this goddess of speech, shining with a luster resembling jasmine, the moon, a conch, crystal, and a gem, who is ever-constant and gracious, dwell forever within our mouths. (1) She is white in color. (1)
51. Now, the essential nature of Nirukta: it is as stainless as the moon, peaceful, with a face like that of a crane and a slender belly.
He is joined with a noose and a lotus, and holds a rosary along with a book.
The etymological explanation has been thus determined: it is of a bright color. || 1 ||
52. Now, the nature of Varuṇa as the presiding deity according to the Nirukta (from the Mayūkha):
He holds the serpent-noose, is adorned with jewels, and is the beloved of the lotus-lake.
Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, is golden-hued and has a sea-monster as his vehicle.
Kanaka-varṇa (like Varuṇa among the guardians of the quarters; 4th invocation). || 1 ||
53. Now, the nature of *chaṃdas*:
*Chaṃdas* should be known by the wise as resembling the *japā* flower.
Holding a *japā* flower with a *cakora*-like face and a spear adorned with a crest. || 1 ||
It was equipped with iron rings and adorned with ornaments made of coral.
Of red color. || 1 ||
54. Now, the nature of Aditi, the deity presiding over the *chandas* (according to the Śaiva Āgama): Aditi is yellow in color, and she holds a *sruk*, a *sruva*, an *akṣamālā*, and a *kamaṇḍalu*.
Bearing an auspicious flame, she shall be the illustrious mother of the gods.
Yellow in color. (Like the presiding deity of Punarvasu, 5th *niyuta*). || 1 ||
55. Now, the nature of the *jyotiṣa* [breath]:
the *jyotiṣa* is like the mouth of a cat, resembling an *indragopa* insect, and auspicious.
He bears a rosary of beads for recitation in his right and left hands.
Red in color. || 1 ||
100) 56. Now, the nature of Hari as the presiding deity of light (according to the Pāñcarātra): Hari shall be golden-hued, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Golden-hued; [the twenty-four forms are like those of the chariot-steed of Hari] (Ni0 2). || 1 ||
57. Now, the nature of the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
"The supreme Mīmāṃsā-śāstra possesses a splendor equal to that of the moon."
Holding a rosary in his right hand and a jar filled with excellent nectar in his other [left] hand.
White in color. || 1 ||
58. Now, the nature of Soma, the presiding deity of Mīmāṃsā, according to the Śaiva Āgama:
He is white, clad in white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments.
The moon-crested Lord should be depicted with two arms, holding a mace in his hand and granting boons. || 1 ||
White in color, like the moon situated among the nine planets. (5th Nibandha) || 1 ||
59. Now, the nature of the Nyāya-śāstra (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda): "The wise man should know that Nyāya resembles the flax flower."
Lion-faced, he holds a thread in his right hand and a banner in his left hand. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
60. Now, the nature of Vāyu, who takes pride in the Nyāya-śāstra, [as described] in the Śaiva Āgama: He is mounted upon a running deer, has two arms, and carries a banner.
I worship the Wind-god, smoke-colored and bestowing boons. || 1 ||
Smoke-colored; [like the wind residing in the five elements] (4th initiation). || 1 ||
61. Now, the nature of the Dharmaśāstra (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): The Dharmaśāstra is white, peaceful, fair-faced, and seated upon a *kuśa* grass mat.
Wearing a rosary of pearls and beads in his right hand, he holds a balance scale in his left.
White in color. || 1 ||
62. Now, the nature of the Dharma-Puruṣa, who takes pride in the Dharmaśāstras (from the *Dānakāṇḍa* of Hemādri):
He has four faces, four arms, four feet, and wears white garments.
The wise man should represent Dharma as white and adorned with all ornaments. || 1 ||
In his right hand there should be a rosary, and in his left a book.
He should be depicted as holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
White in color. || 1 ||
63. Now, the nature of the Purāṇa (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
The Purāṇa has the luster of a campaka flower, a parrot-like face, and four bellies.
She holds a rosary and should be known as holding [the gesture of] fearlessness, adorned with various ornaments. || 1 ||
The color of the campaka flower. || 1 ||
101) 64. Now, the nature of Svāyambhuva Manu among the ancient presiding deities (as established in the Śaiva Āgamas):
The first is known as Svāyambhuva Manu, the son of Brahmā.
White in color. (All else is to be seen as in [the section on] humans, sūtra 14; 4th initiation. || 1 ||
65. Now, the nature of Itihāsa (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
Itihāsa has the luster of kusha grass, the face of a boar, and a large belly.
Holding a rosary and a water-pot, he is endowed with a lotus and a garment. || 1 ||
His complexion is dark like the dūrvā grass. || 1 ||
66. Now, regarding the form of Prajāpati, the presiding deity of Itihāsa (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
He should be depicted as having a swan-vehicle, and he should not be made four-faced.
The auspicious Sāvitrī should be depicted on his left lap.
The supreme form spoken by Brahmā is the entirety of the activity of Prajāpati.
The color is pale-red (*pāṭalavarṇa*). (Like Prajāpati and Brahmā established in the five Brahmas; 4th *niyama*. || 1 ||
67. Now, the nature of the Bharata-śāstra (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda): This delightful science of dance is [personified as] Mṛgavaktra, who bears matted locks.
Holding a rosary and a trident, and possessing three eyes. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
68. Now, the nature of Umāmaheśvara, who takes pride in the Bharata-śāstra (according to the Kāraṇāgama):
[He is] joined by the goddess on a white, radiant throne, with a young deer, a *ṭaṅka*, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands.
O God, this form of Yours, together with Umā, has been made to face us by the lotus-eyed Goddess who grants boons. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
69. Now, the nature of the Pāñcarātra scripture (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
"The scripture named Pāñcarātra has Lāvaṇya as its bull-vehicle."
He holds a rosary and a plow, and is adorned with a forest garland.
White in color. || 1 ||
70. Now, the nature of Saṃkarṣaṇa as conceived in the Pāñcarātra scriptures (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
"The Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa is to be produced from the nature of Vāsudeva."
But that best of messengers should be made with a white body and blue garments. || 1 ||
And in the place of the mace, there is a club; in the place of the discus, there is a plow.
In the upper right hand is a conch shell; in the lower right hand, a mace; in the lower left hand, a bow; and in the upper left hand, a plow. || 1 ||
White in color; like the form of the cosmic array (vyūhamūrti). (2, niyama 1)
71. Now, the nature of the Pāśupata scripture (*nṛsiṃhaprāsāde*):
The auspicious Pāśupata scripture has the face of a serpent and a slender belly.
He was formidable, holding a bowl for alms, and was clothed in a garment of tiger skin.
White in color. || 1 ||
72. Now, the nature of Rudra, who takes pride in the Pāśupata scriptures (from the Mayūkha):
He has five faces, is mounted upon a bull, and possesses three eyes in each face.
The Supreme Lord holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident, an eye, and a thread. || 1 ||
White in color. (Like the secondary deity of the Sun; 5th initiation. || 1 ||
73. Now, the nature of the Pātañjala-śāstra (in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
The one named Pātañjala is red, has the face of a serpent, and possesses great luster.
Holding a rosary and a banner, and adorned with earrings. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
74. Now, the form of Ananta, the presiding deity of Pātañjala (from the *Anantavratakalpa*):
He has the luster of nine mango sprouts, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes.
In her upper right hand is a lotus, and in the one below that is a conch shell.
In his upper left hand he holds a discus, and in the one below that, a mace.
I worship the lotus-eyed one who bears seven hoods.
The color of cow’s urine. || 1 ||
75. Now, the nature of the Sāṃkhya scripture (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): "Sāṃkhya is that [teaching] of Kapila, O tawny one, with a face adorned by radiant earrings."
He was tall, holding a rosary and a staff, and was certainly not one who wore matted locks.
The color is tawny. || 1 ||
76. Now, the nature of Kapila, who takes pride in the Sāṃkhya treatise, [is described] in the *Mantrādhyāya* of the *Pāñcarātra*:
"He whose body is equal to the rising sun, who has pervaded the entire world with the rays of a thousand risen suns..."
One should meditate upon Datta, whose hand is marked with the symbols of knowledge and fearlessness, who is tawny-hued, and who awakens the assembly of Brahmā and the other gods. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
77. Now, the names of the sixty-four arts (*catuṣṣaṣṭi-kalā*) according to the *Śivatattvaratnākara*:
all the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs (*vedāṅga*), as well as the Epics (*itihāsa*) and the Agamas.
Likewise, the science of logic, poetry, poetics, and drama. (1)
Poetic skill, the science of erotics, and proficiency in gambling as well.
Thorough knowledge of regional dialects, knowledge of scripts, and the art of calligraphy. || 2 ||
Likewise, the *Samastāvadāna* and the *Svaraśāstra* are the exponents [of this].
And [he taught] palmistry, the science of omens, and the examination of the succession of precious gems.
Likewise, the examination of gold, and likewise the characteristics of a sick horse.
The science of elephants, the art of wrestling, and thereafter the practice of cooking.
The ten sciences of pregnancy-longings (doḍhaka) and the origin of the Vāda-gandhaka.
The doctrine of alchemy, the doctrine of mining, and thereafter the doctrine of elixirs. || 5 ||
The pillarization of fire, the pillarization of water, and likewise the pillarization of poison.
Likewise, the pillar of wind, as well as subjugation, delusion, and attraction.
Exorcism, inciting enmity, killing, and the cheating of death.
Trade, cattle-rearing, agriculture, and one's own specific duty.
Proficiency in wrestling with gourds and skill in ram-fights.
Skill in amorous arts, hunting, and likewise the art of making oneself invisible; || 8 ||
The crafts of painting, metallurgy, stonework, masonry, carpentry, basketry, and leatherwork;
Likewise, [the sin of] gambling and likewise that of being a thief. || 9 ||
Likewise, there is success with mantras and medicinal herbs, as well as in deceiving others through the observation of voice and gaze.
The accomplishments of walking on water, the power of speech, and likewise the accomplishment of the medicinal pill.
In the same way, there is the accomplishment of the sandals (pādukāsiddhi), and after that, the art of sorcery (indrajāla).
These sixty-four [vidyās] are considered to be the net of Mahendra. || 11 ||
(Also seen in another manner in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Bhāgavata*, 10th Skandha, Purva-khaṇḍa, Chapter 45, Verse 36, with the commentary of Śrīdhara, and in the *Śukra-nīti*, Chapter 4.
Now, the natures of the five elements (*pañcabhūta-svarūpa*). (According to the *Śaiva Āgama*, 78): First among these, the nature of the deity Earth (*pṛthvī-devatā-svarūpa*):
One should meditate upon the Earth, white in color and adorned with divine ornaments.
She has four arms and a gentle form, and her garments are like the fierce-rayed sun.
Below and above, he holds a jewel-vessel with his two hands, and a vessel of grain.
Likewise, with his two right hands and two left hands, he holds a lotus.
Holding a vessel filled with medicinal herbs, her lotus-like face is beautiful.
And she is mounted upon the backs of four Diṅnāgas, possessing four arms. || 3 ||
I take refuge in the Goddess Bhū, who is white and the abode of all crops.
She is of brilliant white complexion. || 1 ||
79. Now, the true nature of the water-deities:
they resemble the surface of a mirror, are auspicious, and are the revivers of the world.
Endowed with the quality of sweetness and adorned with all poetic ornaments. || 1 ||
They assumed the forms of women, radiant and adorned with two arms.
Always holding a noose and a jar, they have makaras as their vehicles.
One should joyfully contemplate her, whose entire body is adorned with pearl ornaments.
They are of bright complexion. || 1 ||
Now, the essential nature of the deity Tejodevatā:
[One should meditate on her] as having limbs the color of fire and gold, possessing seven flames, and free from all affliction.
Mounted upon a ram, with seven arms, and accompanied by the goddess Svāhā. || 1 ||
One should meditate upon Vibhāvasu, whose hands are endowed with weapons such as the Śakti and others.
Golden-hued. || 1 ||
81. Now, the true form of the deity Vāyu: he is mounted upon a running deer, has two arms, and carries a banner.
I worship Vāyu, smoke-colored and with hands granting boons. || 1 ||
Smoky-colored. || 1 ||
82. Now, the nature of the deity of space:
I meditate upon the pervasive Lord as the blue sky, wearing blue garments.
Having two arms with the moon and sun in his hands, he is adorned with all ornaments.
Blue in color. || 1 ||
Now, the nature of the ten directions (*nṛsiṃhaprāsāde*, 83): First, the nature of the eastern direction—
*Pūrvāgajagatābālā* (the young girl who has gone to the eastern mountain) shall indeed be the eastern direction, red in color.
Red in color. || 1 ||
84. Now, the nature of the southeastern direction:
she who moves in a water-fowl, large-bodied, with the luster of a lotus, resides in the southeast.
The color of a lotus. || 1 ||
85. Now, the nature of the southern direction: situated on a vulture, yellow, with the face of a vulture, and having attained youth.
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
86. Now, the nature of the direction of Nirṛti:
Mounted on a camel, dark-yellow in color, and youthful, she stands between the southern and western directions;
she is greenish-yellow in hue. (1)
87. Now, the nature of the western direction: the western [deity] is a young woman, two-armed, black, and mounted upon a horse.
Black in color. || 1 ||
88. Now, the nature of the quarter of Vāyu:
she is dark-complexioned like a woman whose husband is near, and is intent upon playing the bow.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
89. Now, the nature of the northern direction: the North is white-faced, likewise red, and wrathful.
Red in color. || 1 ||
90. Now, the nature of the direction of Īśāna:
she is very aged, seated upon a bull, white in color, and situated to the north-east.
White in color. || 1 ||
91. Now, the nature of the direction above (ūrdhvadik):
It resembles the upper sky; it is blue in color. 1.
92. Now, the nature of the downward direction:
it is equal to the earth situated below; its color is white. 1.
93. Now, the forms of the eight nāgas (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, and Padmaka;
Mahāpadma and Śaṅkha—these eight are the Kulikas and the families. || 1 ||
The two Brahmins, Aṭaṅka and Kulika, are declared to be of white complexion.
Each of those two was adorned with eight thousand hoods.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are Kṣatriyas of red complexion.
Each of their hoods, moreover, shone with seven hundred jewels.
Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are declared to be of the Vaiśya caste.
They were yellow in color, with five hundred hoods raised high upon their excellent heads.
Padma, Karkoṭaka, and Auśūdra are blue-colored and are held in the hands.
The two [serpents] with three hundred hoods are to be known as renowned according to their true nature. || 5 || 8 ||
94. Now, the forms of the eight elephants of the quarters—(in the Mayūkha and the Āgneya Purāṇa):
The glorious Airāvata elephant is white in luster and possesses four tusks.
Puṣpadanta is large and dark-complexioned; he has six tusks and possesses the Puṣpadanta [elephant]. || 1 ||
The elephants of the remaining directions are traditionally remembered in the form of a common elephant.
(The names [of the elephants] are completed by the addition of *āgneya*: Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana.)
Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, Supratīka, and Aṣṭa are the elephants of the directions. || 1 || 8 ||
95. Now, the names of the wives of the elephants of the eight directions (according to the Āgneya Purāṇa): [they are] Bhramu, Kapilā, Piṅgalā, and Anupamā, in order.
Tāmraparṇī, Sudaṃtī, Añjanā, and Añjanāvatī. || 1 || 8 ||
Now, the meditation on the eight guardians of the directions (96). First among them is the meditation on Indra (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
One should meditate upon Indra as having a thousand eyes, yellow in color, and four arms.
He displays the gesture of fearlessness in his right hand and the gesture of granting boons in his left hand.
A vajra in the right hand, and likewise a hook in the other.
Adorned with divine ornaments, including the jewel Kaustubha and various gems.
Wearing earrings and a sacred thread, and possessing divine splendor.
I bow down to the beloved of Śacī, who is mounted upon the elephant Airāvata.
He is golden-colored. || 1 ||
97. Now, the meditation on Agni (from the *Siṃhābhaṭṭīya* regarding the preliminary ritual):
He has seven cubits, four horns, seven tongues, and two heads.
Three-legged, with a serene countenance, seated comfortably, and possessing a pure smile. || 1 ||
He should place the goddess Svāhā on his right side and likewise Svadhā on his left.
Holding in his right hand a spear, food, a *sruk* ladle, and a *sruva* spoon.
Holding a trident and a fan in his left hands, and a vessel of clarified butter as well.
Mounted upon a ram, with matted hair tied up, of terrible appearance and large-bellied. || 3 ||
He whose banner is smoke, whose eyes are red, who possesses seven flames, and who is free from ailment.
One should meditate upon the fire in this manner as seated facing toward oneself.
He is red in color. || 1 ||
98. Now, the meditation on Yama—(according to the Śaivāgama and the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda):
Furthermore, [one should meditate on him] mounted upon a formidable buffalo and holding the staff of death.
I bow down to Kṛtānta, who is dark-complexioned and holds a noose in his hand. || 1 ||
Yama, the beloved of Ilā, the wielder of the staff, has a buffalo for his vehicle.
For he is red in color, bestowing upon the worlds the fruits of their respective karmas.
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
99. Now, the meditation on Nirṛti—(in the Mayūkheḍānakaṇḍa):
Nirṛti is blue, bearing a sword and a shield, and having a man as his vehicle.
He has upright hair, deformed eyes, and is formidable; he is dear to Kālikā. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
100. Now, the meditation on Varuṇa—(from the Mayūkha of Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
He holds a serpent-noose, is adorned with red ornaments, and is beloved by the lotus-lake.
Varuṇa is the lord of the waters, golden-hued, and has a makara as his vehicle.
He is golden-colored. || 1 ||
101. Now, the meditation on Vāyu—(according to the Mayūkha of Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
Vāyu is indeed the kinsman of the world, seated upon a black antelope skin.
He has a golden staff upon his banner, is dark in complexion, and is the beloved of Mohinī. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
102. Now, the meditation on Kubera—(from the Mayūkhabhaṭṭabhāskarīya):
Kubera is mounted upon a horse, holds a spear in his hand, and is fond of Citriṇī.
The Lord of Treasures (Nidhīśvara) is golden-hued, a bestower of wealth, handsome, and powerful.
Golden-colored. || 1 ||
p.
107) 103 Now, the meditation on Īśāna—(in the Mayūkheḍānakhaṇḍa):
The Lord of Gaurī, whose vehicle is the bull, resembles pure crystal.
The Supreme Lord holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a trident, an eye, and a thread.
White in color. || 1 ||
Now, the meditation on the eight Vasus— (according to the Śaivāgama) (the color according to the Kāraṇāgama) 104. Therein, first, the nature of Dhruva Vasu:
He wore a rosary of beads, and his chest was radiant with a sacred thread.
I always contemplate Dhruva for the sake of eternal glory with constant joy. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
105. Now, the nature of Adhvaravasu: he holds a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in his hand, wears a tiger-skin garment, and is pure.
I bow daily to the sacrifice that is devoted to the service of the sacred fire.
Dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
106. Now, the true nature of Soma and Vasu: [He is] the generator of bliss for the world, whose eyes stream with nectar.
I meditate upon Soma seated upon a jeweled lion-throne within my heart. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
107. Now, the nature of the water-vessels: they destroy all sins and are filled with seawater and gold.
May the Waters, who are accompanied by the one whose vehicle is a fish, bestow auspiciousness. || 1 ||
They are white in color. || 1 ||
108. Now, the nature of Anilavasu: May Anila, the purifier of the world, always be present for the sake of auspiciousness.
His lotus feet are being worshipped by the entire host of gods.
He is yellowish-green in color. || 1 ||
109. Now, the form of Analavasusvara:
mounted upon a goat, auspicious, and joined with the goddess Svāhā.
I meditate upon Anala, whose head is radiant with a crown. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
110. Now, the true form of Pratyūṣavasu: he wears white garments, and his body is anointed with white sandalwood paste.
At dawn, I shall again contemplate the cause that uproots all obstacles. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
111. Now, regarding the nature of Prabhāsa-Vasusvara: I meditate upon Prabhāsa, whose body is completely filled with radiance.
His hand is radiant with a rosary of beads, and he is clothed in a tiger skin. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
Now, the descriptions of the colors and characteristics of the eight Vasus (from the *Kāraṇāgama*):
Dhruva is yellow, Adhvara is dark-blue, Soma is white, and Anila is green.
The waters are declared to be white, while fire is remembered as red. || 1 ||
He is like the dawn, possessing white light; he is radiant and white in color.
They have serene faces, are gentle, grant boons, and hold tridents in their hands.
The Vasus should always be depicted seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) with two arms.
Now, the forms of the seven Maruts— (according to the Śaivāgama and the Varṇas-tupāda-kāraṇāgama)—
112. Among these, first is the form of the Āvaha wind:
May the best of the Maruts, Āvaha, always bring me happiness.
Moving everywhere around, he was mounted upon a very fierce Garuḍa.
Smoke-colored. || 1 ||
113. Now, as for the true nature of the *vivahara* (the playful dance):
it effects the destruction of the worlds through its backward-rushing movements.
The wind situated in the middle of the sky is the Vivaha yoga; it causes the destruction of prosperity for the native. || 1 ||
He is red in color. || 1 ||
114. Now, the nature of the rising winds:
they cause the oceans to overflow and uproot the mountains and trees.
Constantly agitating the world, this Upholder is served by me. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
115. Now, the nature of the Saṃvaha wind:
it gradually produces joy for the world and carries away fragrances.
May that wind, which carries droplets of cool water and brings happiness, blow upon me. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
116. Now, the nature of the host of Maruts: [the wind] by its fierce movements shook and caused the mountains to flee.
I bow my head in reverence to Nivaha, the foremost of the winds. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
117. Now, the nature of the Anuvaha wind:
it runs in opposition [to the preceding wind], causing the three worlds to whirl.
One should always take refuge in the wind of the Maruts, known by the name Anuvaha. || 1 ||
Asitavarṇa (the Black-colored One). || 1 ||
118. Now, the nature of the Vyavahāra-maru: pervading and enlivening the world in the form of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth.

The color is reddish-orange. || 1 ||
119. Now, the seven names of the Maruts (according to the Śaiva Āgama): Āvāha, Vivaha, Udvaha, and likewise Saṃvaha; [and Parivaha, Pravaha, and Udvaha].
By the names Nivaha, Anuvaha, and Vyavaha. || 1 ||
These seven Maruts have been declared, each divided into seven groups.
Their colors (as stated in the Padma-kāraṇāgama) are: smoky, red, yellow, dark blue, white, black, and rosy.
This is the description of the seven Maruts, stated in their proper sequence. || 1 || 7 ||

Prāṇa (1), Apāna (2), Vyāna (3), Udāna (4), Samāna (5), Nāga (6), Kṛkara (7), Kūrma (8), Devadatta (9), Dhanañjaya (10), Pravaha (11), Vivaha (12), Śambhu (13), Saṃvaha (14), Parivaha (15), Udvaha (16), Āvaha (17), Śaṅku (18), Kāla (19), Prāvaha (20), Śāsa (21), Anila (22), Anala (23), Pratibha (24), Kumuda (25), Kānta (26), Śibi (27), Śveta (28), Rakta (29), Kṛṣṇa (30), Jita (31), Ajita (32), Jhañjhādyota (33), Kratu (34), Siddha (35), Piṅga (36), Śuci (37), Saumya (38), Kāmya (39), Māruta (40), Hanu (41), Kampana (42), Maṇḍūka (43), Bhīma (44), Kapi (45), Saṃvartaka (46), Jaḍa (47), Atijaḍa (48), and Saṃtata (49). || 49 ||
Now, their essential natures are as follows: (in the Mayūkha) "The Maruts, the brothers of Puruhūta, possess the brilliance of the sun."
Adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
Always bearing swords and shields, they were the constant attendants of Śakra.
The colors and forms of these principal Maruts are as follows. (2.49)
121. Now, the nature of the ten Viśvedevas (according to Bhaṭṭabhāskara):
"And all the Viśvedevas have arrows in their right hands."
We two, white-complexioned and bearing bows, must be made [to stand] upon the left hand. || 1 ||
The names of these [are as follows]: p. 110).
Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, Dhuri, and Locana.
Purūravas and Ārdrava—these are remembered as the ten Viśvedevas. || 1 ||
They are white in color. || 10 ||
Now, the forms of the seven oceans—(from the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*, verse 122): Among them, the form of the salt ocean (*lavaṇasamudra*) is as follows:
"The Salt Ocean should be fashioned with two arms and adorned with jewels."
In her right hand she holds a rosary of beads, and in her left a vessel filled with many jewels.
With an upper garment and a sacred thread, possessing the hue of the Pāṭala flower, he sits comfortably.
The color is pale red. || 1 ||
123. Now, the nature of the ocean of sugarcane juice:
the ocean and the stalk of sugarcane have a complexion resembling cow's urine.
I meditate upon the God holding a water-pot and a staff within my heart. || 1 ||
The color of cow’s urine. || 1 ||
124. Now, the nature of the ocean of wine: the liquor-ocean is situated within the Gaṇḍakāru mountain and possesses a luster like that of the gomeda gem.
I should meditate upon him in my heart as bearing both a mallet and a water-pot.
The color of a gomedaka gem. || 1 ||
125. Now, the true nature of the Ocean of Ghee: Ghṛtoda is to be known as tawny (kapila), situated in the sign of Cancer, and wearing matted hair.
Vidūratha was carrying a vessel and a jar filled with Kaśeru grass. || 1 ||
He is of a tawny color. || 1 ||
126. Now, the nature of the Ocean of Curd:
This auspicious Ocean of Curd-mass indeed exists, possessing the color of water-lilies.
Holding a staff and a spear, he has two arms and is endowed with matted locks.
Of bright complexion. || 1 ||
127. Now, the nature of the Ocean of Milk:
Kṣīroda is white in color, has two arms, and wears jeweled earrings.
Seated upon a crocodile, she holds a lotus in her right hand and a water-pot in her left.
White in color. || 1 ||
128. Now, the true form of Śuddhodakasamudra: he has the luster of pearls from the ocean of sweet water, possesses two arms, and wears red earrings.
Seated upon a makara, she holds a lotus in her right hand and a water-pot in her left.
The color of a pearl. || 1 || 7 ||
129. Now, the forms of the eight rivers—(according to the Śaivāgama): In the right hand, a water-pot; in the left, the noose of Varuṇa.
The rivers, possessing two arms, riding upon crocodiles, and holding [offerings], are to be worshipped. || 1 || 8 ||
130. Therein, first, the nature of the river Gaṅgā:
[She is] born from the foot of Trivikrama and follows the path of Bhagīratha.
I bow to Bhāgīrathī, the river Gaṅgā who flows through the three paths.
She is of radiant white complexion. || 1 ||
Another method (from the *Dharmābdhisāra-paśupāpaharā-kalpa*).
Seated upon a white makara, white in complexion, with three eyes, holding a jar from which an utpala lotus emerges in her hand—she who is most beloved.

I bow to that Jāhnavī, who embodies the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; who is adorned with a crest-jewel of the moon, and who is clothed in white silken garments. She is white in color. 1. — 1. — ||
Another version (in the twenty-seventh chapter of the first half of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa).
Four-armed and three-eyed, she is attended by rivers and streams.
Whose three folds of skin were embraced by the flowing nectar of her loveliness.
Holding a full water-pot and a white lotus, and with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
In this way, one should meditate upon her who is exceedingly gentle and possesses a radiance equal to ten thousand moons.
She was being fanned with yak-tail whisks and graced by a white parasol.
The surface of the earth was flooded with nectar and anointed with divine fragrant unguents.
Her feet are worshipped by the three worlds and she is praised by divine sages.
White in color. || 1 ||
131. Now, regarding the nature of the Yamunā river:
I bow my head to the Kālindī, who is dark blue and who takes refuge at the feet of Rāma.
One should meditate in the heart upon the Yamunā, purified by the dust of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Black in color. || 1 ||
132. Now, the nature of the Godāvarī river:
I revere the great river Godā, the Pāṭalā, frequented by sages.
It is the purifier of all the worlds and the key to the gate of heaven. || 1 ||
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
133. Now, the nature of the Kṛṣṇā river: Obeisance to you, O Kṛṣṇaveṇī, who are dark-hued and endowed with auspicious marks.
Salutations again and again to you, whose impurities have been shaken away by the dust from Kṛṣṇa’s body.
She is black in color. || 1 ||
134. Now, the true nature of the river Revā: [I shall describe] the Revā, which originates from the Vindhya mountain and is frequented by Raivata.
I bow to her who possesses a golden luster, the mother of all that is auspicious in the world. || 1 ||
She is golden-colored. || 1 ||
135. Now, the nature of the river Tāpī: [I praise] the Tāpī, who is to be resorted to by ascetics, who is red in hue, and who scorches the flood of sins.
I bow to the great river that pacifies internal torment. || 1 ||
She is red in color. ||1||
136. Now, as for the nature of the river Veṇī: she possesses cool water that brings peace to the mass of the torments of worldly existence.
I worship her braid, which resembles a sprout of coral, for the attainment of happiness. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
137. Now, the nature of the river Sarasvatī: she is like a braid of hair, with whirlpools of water, possessing the luster of pearls, and flowing in a hidden manner.
I bow with manifold joy to her who bestows auspiciousness and bliss. || 1 ||
Having the color of a pearl. || 1 ||
138. Now, the true nature of Parjanya—(according to the Śaiva Āgama): He who is to be known by the name Parjanya is endowed with three elephant faces.
He who sustains the best life-force of all living beings and yet is the desiccator of that very life-force. || 1 ||
The axe, the lotus-born [sword], the wish-fulfilling gem, and the great pure one.
[He holds] a noose, a discus, a sprout, and a water-pot with his ten hands.
White in color. || 1 ||
139. Now, the form of the two Aśvinī deities (according to the Śaiva Āgama): both of them wear the sacred thread and bear crests and crowns.
Their eyes are like full-blown red lotuses, and they wear yellow garlands, garments, and unguents. || 1 ||
The two physicians known by the names Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the Aśvins.
They are white in color. || 2 || - ||
Another method—(in the medical science, the treatise of Āyurveda).
I shall describe the forms of the Aśvins, adorned with all auspicious characteristics.
One should visualize the form of a horse from the feet up to the throat.
Having first fashioned two eyes with mouths and endowed them with crowns.
They have two ears, thick necks, and are endowed with four arms.
Each is endowed with two horse-feet; the one on the left holds the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) mudrā and a medicinal herb.
Holding a basket and an amṛta-pitcher in his left hand. || 3 ||
The two Aśvins, known as physicians, should not be depicted in the nine-tāla measurement.
The two Aśvins of the gods, white in form, were addressed by name.
The two are white in color. || 2 ||
140. Now, the nature of the Kāmadhenu—(in the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda): Surabhi, Gomukhī, and Gaurī, in female form, adorned with all ornaments.
Likewise, holding a handful of grass and a water-pot, she is the bestower of nourishment to all beings.
She is fair-complexioned. || 1 || - ||
Another version (in the Mahābhārata, Ādiparvan, chapter 176).
One with six protuberances, beautiful flanks and thighs, three broad parts, and five well-concealed parts.
She had eyes like a frog, a well-formed nose, and was praised even by the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu.
She beheld that beautiful and enchanting cow, which had a fine tail, pointed ears, and lovely horns;
she was gazing with wonder at her, whose head and neck were exceedingly long.
She is fair-complexioned. || 1 ||
141. Now, the nature of the twelve weapons—(according to the Śaiva Āgama):
the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), and likewise the goad (aṅkuśa).
The mace, trident, discus, and lotus—these constitute the ten weapons. || 1 ||
They have two arms and two eyes, and are adorned with all ornaments.
With palms joined in reverence, they were adorned with crowns and caskets.
Each [deity] is endowed with a form corresponding to the respective weapon, according to the measurement of its particular face.
It possessed great lightning of various colors and had the hue of a dark blue cloud.
A ruby, a lotus-red gem, ice, and a sapphire.
Śāra, dābhra, and rakta are the pigments for diamonds and the other [gems]. || 4 ||
One should know that the female [seed-syllable] consists of the spear and the mace, while the male [seed-syllable] consists of the noose and the lotus.
The remaining ones are renowned as male and are celebrated as having the form of weapons.
In the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda, however: "The arrow should be a divine man, with a red body and divine eyes."
The bow has the luster of a woman's red lotus and is adorned at its head; it is the bearer of the bow. || 1 ||
In this way, O Supreme Goddess, one should understand the weapons as being embodied.
And for all those [deities] mentioned, there is the mark of their own weapon upon the head.
Then, two arms should be fashioned, with weapons resting upon the shoulders.

Now, the essential natures of the three powers—(from the *Kāraṇāgama*, verse 142): First among them is the nature of the power of sovereignty (*prabhu-śakti*): "The power of sovereignty, known as majesty (*prabhāva*), is the goddess who follows the quality of sovereignty."
She has the form of a woman, the hue of the Pāṭala flower, and possesses white horses as her excellent vehicle.
In his crown is a basket-shaped ornament, and he holds a discus, a spear, a sword, and a goad.
In the right and left [hands], there are a conch and a bell, a shield, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise a mace.
Bearing [weapons] with ten hands, she is the destroyer of enemies.
Clad in saffron-colored garments and worshipped, she grants the desires of men. || 3 ||
The color of the *pāṭala* flower. || 1 ||
143. Now, the nature of the power of mantra (mantra-śakti): The power of mantra has a golden face, the luster of saffron, and wears a crown.
A sword, a bow, a bhṛśuṇḍī, a trident, a spear, a choice weapon, and a plow.
[He took] the bows, arrows, staffs, swords, nooses, and goads of fear.
With fourteen arms, she holds [attributes] individually in each of her right and left hands. || 2 ||
Mounted on rutting elephants, wearing diamond armor and jeweled girdles.
Red in color. || 1 ||
144. Now, the nature of the power of enthusiasm (utsāha-śakti): Power, in the form of enthusiasm, has a face like vermilion and is auspicious.
Having the luster of Jāmbūnada gold, she dances, mounted upon a magnificent peacock.
With six arms, she holds a spear, a bow, an excellent noose, an arrow, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
Wearing various garments in succession and radiant with a crown, she shines forth.
And this goddess of pure smiles subdues her enemies through skillful means.
She is red in color. || 1 ||

Now, the nature of the deities of the four means (*upāya*): (Kāraṇāgama) 145. Among these, first is the definition of the deity of the *sāma* means: Mounted upon an elephant, with a smiling face, and clothed in garments radiant like gold.
With six arms, he holds a discus, a conch, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a bow, and an arrow. || 1 ||
Constantly honored, she brings the circle of enemies under one's control.
Golden-colored. || 1 ||
146. Now, the nature of the means of giving (dānopāya):
The deity known as Dānopāya has a magnificent palanquin as his vehicle.
With eight hands as red as the twilight, he holds a discus, a lotus, and a supreme treasure-vessel.
In the left hand, a bow; in the right, a conch, a lotus, an arrow, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Wearing yellow garments and adorned with a crown and armlets, he appeared resplendent. || 2 ||
When worshipped, it bestows auspiciousness and brings the circle of enemies under one's control.
Red in color. || 1 ||
147. Now, the nature of the means of differentiation (bhedopāya):
The deity known as the Means of Differentiation has the noble hyena as his vehicle.
Meghavarṇa, Karālāsya, and Krūradaṃṣṭra, with ten arms. || 1 ||
A discus, a trident, a bow, and a noose are held in the right or left hands.
Holding a conch, a staff, an arrow, and a skull-topped club, he brought his enemies under his control.
Or he should rub it, shining with his crown and armor.
Meghavarṇa. || 1 ||
148. Now, the nature of the expedient of punishment (*daṇḍopāya*):
[the deity] is red in color, has the face of a lion, and rides upon a corpse.
The discus, trident, mace, staff, sword, bell, shield, and bow. || 1 ||
A whip, a goad, an arrow, fire, a shield, a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus.
Holding [them] with sixteen hands, he is clothed in blue and white variegated garments. || 2 ||
Worshipped in Mardaga, he is the crusher of enemies in battle after battle.
He is red in color. || 1 ||

Now, the essential natures of the fourteen Manus—(from the *Siddhāntaśekhara* in the *Śaivāgama*)—first, the meditation on Svāyaṃbhuva Manu: "The first is Svāyaṃbhuva Brahmā; he is remembered as the pure Manu."
Śatarūpā was his wife; he was devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were his [sons], as were three daughters.
Ākūti, Devahūti, Prasūti, and Śvetavarṇavat. || 2 ||
But he who wields weapons worthy of a kṣatriya is the lord of all the worlds.
Wherein there are various auspicious dharmas based upon the four castes.
White in color. || 1 ||
150. Now follows the meditation on Svārociṣa: Svārociṣa was the second Manu; he was the son of Agni.
And his sons were Dyumatsena, Suṣeṇa, Rociṣmat, and others as their leaders.
Ūrjā was his wife, and he remained devoted to the dharma of a Brahmin.
He has the luster of molten gold and is the Lord of all worlds.
He is golden-colored. || 1 ||
151. Now follows the meditation on Uttama: the third Manu, named Uttama, was the son of Priyavrata.
His sons were Bhārya, Uṣas, Ṛñjaya, Jaya, Hotraka, and others.
He was red in color, bearing a bow, and devoted to the duty of the kṣatriya.
The Lord Īśvara is the master of four times seventy yugas.
Red in color. || 1 ||
152. Now follows the meditation on Tāmasa:
The fourth elder brother was named Manu, and he was Tāmasa.

This son of Priyavrata, however, was devoted to the duty of a Kshatriya.
He is tawny-colored, holds a bow, and is the Lord of all the worlds.
He is yellowish-green in color. || 1 ||
Now follows the meditation on Raivata:
The fifth, named Raivata, is remembered as the younger brother of the two preceding ones.
His wife was Vindhyāvalī, and his sons were headed by Dattaka and Arjuna.
The son of Kṣatrapriyavrata, Śyāma, resorted to the shoulder.
Always bearing weapons such as the sword, he is the Lord of all worlds.
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
154. Now follows the meditation on Cākṣuṣa:
the sixth son of Cakṣus was renowned by the name Cākṣuṣa.
Listen to [the account of] Āditya’s grandson, his wife Kānti, and their offspring. || 1 ||
Likewise, Tāmravarṇa had Sudyumna and others as his sons.
The god who upholds the vow of Brahmā is the lord of all the worlds.
Red in color. || 1 ||
155. Now follows the meditation on Vaivasvata Manu:
the son of Sūrya named Manu Vaivasvata is the seventh [Manu].
His sons were headed by Ikṣvāku, and his wife was named Iṣṭi.
Resorting to both the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa dharma, he was the lord of the earth and the author of the Smṛti.
He is described as golden-hued, lotus-eyed, and the Lord of the worlds.
He is golden-colored. || 1 ||
156. Now, the meditation on Sūryasāvarṇi:
The eighth Manu will be Sāvarṇi, the son of the Sun.
Nirmoha, Virāja, and others were his sons, while Devikā was his wife.
The Kṣatriya is world-renowned and has taken recourse to a dark complexion.
He is declared to be the lord of seventy-four yugas.
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
157. Now, the meditation on Dakṣasāvarṇi Manu: The ninth Manu, Dakṣasāvarṇi, was born from Varuṇa.
Patnīpara, Adhṛṣṭakētu, and others are recorded as his sons. || 1 ||
The Kṣatriya is world-renowned, having resorted to the dark complexion.
He is declared to be the lord of seventy-four yugas.
Red in color. || 1 ||
158. Now follows the meditation on Manu Brahmasāvarṇi: The tenth [Manu] is Brahmasāvarṇi, the son of the sage Upaśloka.
His sons were Bhuriṣeṇa and others, and his wife was considered to be Bṛhatī.
The Brāhmaṇa, renowned throughout the world, has taken recourse to a white complexion.
He is the sustainer of all worlds, just like the Manus previously mentioned.
White in color. || 1 ||
159. Now, the meditation on Dharmasāvarṇi:
Manu Vaidharmasāvarṇi is declared to be the eleventh.
Dharmaputra was his son, and Satyadharma and others are considered to be his sons. || 1 ||
Dīkṣāpatnī was red in complexion and devoted to the duties of the Kṣatriya order.
He is declared to be the lord of seventy-four yugas.
He is red in color. || 1 ||
160. Now follows the meditation on Rudrasāvarṇi Manu: "Rudrasāvarṇi shall come to be; he is of the nature of Rudra and consists of twelve [deities]."
The gods and the antigods were his sons, and Āryā is remembered by men as his wife. || 1 ||
Resorting to the duty of a Kshatriya, he was dark-complexioned and full of prowess.
Caṇḍapraśāsana, however, was the lord of all the worlds. || 2 ||
Dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
161. Now, the meditation on Vedasāvarṇi Manu:
"The thirteenth Manu to come shall be the self-possessed Vedasāvarṇi."
He had a son named Vedaśiras, who was devoted to the dharma of Brahmā.
Citrasena and others were his sons, and Trayī was his highly esteemed wife.
The Lord Īśvara is the master of four times seventy yugas.
White in color. || 1 ||
162. Now, the meditation on Indrasāvarṇi:
Manu Indrasāvarṇi is declared to be the fourteenth.
Indraputra and his sons, such as Urugaṃbhīraka and others, [were there]. || 1 ||
Blue in color and wielding a bow, he was devoted to the duty of a Kshatriya.
He, the lord of all the worlds, had a wife named Mati.
Blue in color. || 1 || 14 ||
Now, regarding the forms of the nine Cirajīvis (as described in the *Śaivāgama*, specifically the *Pādme*):
first, the meditation on Aśvatthāman:
"With arms radiant with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), he shone, clothed in a black antelope skin."
May Aśvatthāman live long; may he grant me a long life. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
164. Now, the meditation on Bali:
Bali is the king whose abode is Pātāla, and who bears a bow and arrows.
May he whose head is marked with the footprint of Viṣṇu live long; may he be gracious. || 1 ||
He is black in color. || 1 ||
165. Now, the meditation on Vyāsa:
Vyāsa is the speaker of all dharmas, praised by the best of sages.
May the matted-haired one grant me long life and a long lifespan.
He is black in color. || 1 ||
166. Now, the meditation on Hanumān:
Hanumān, the pure and excellent devotee who clings to the lotus feet of Rāma.
May he who took away my life restore it to me, granting me long life here. || 1 ||
The color of crystal. || 1 ||
167. Now, the meditation on Bibhīṣaṇa: Bibhīṣaṇa is devoted to righteousness and dedicated to the worship of Rāma.
May Cirañjīvin, who has conquered his senses, grant long life. || 1 ||
He is black in color. || 1 ||
168. Now, the meditation on Kṛpa: Kṛpa is one whose hope lies in compassion, an ascetic wearing garments of bark.
May he, with a serene soul, grant freedom from disease for as long as life lasts. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
169. Now, the meditation on Paraśurāma:
His lotus-hand holds a blazing axe, and he is adorned with a mass of matted locks.
May the descendant of Bhṛgu, with a serene soul, grant long life.
Golden-colored. || 1 ||
170. Now, the meditation on Prahlāda: [one should meditate upon] the devotee of Viṣṇu, the highly wise, the two-armed, the best of Rākṣasas.
I meditate upon the very gentle Prahlāda, who is long-lived. || 1 ||
He is golden-colored. || 1 ||
171. Now, the meditation on Mārkaṇḍeya:
[One should meditate on him] as glorious, tranquil-minded, and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
I worship Mārkaṇḍeya, who knows the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras. || 1 ||
Of bright complexion. || 1 || 9 ||
The complexions of these long-lived ones are described in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Aśvatthāman is white in complexion; Mahābali is black in complexion."
Vyāsa is Kṛṣṇa, while Māruti is proclaimed to have the luster of crystal. || 1 ||
Bibhīṣaṇa is black in color, while Kṛpa is remembered as white.
Jāmadagnya is golden-hued, while Mārkaṇḍeya is remembered as white. || 2 ||
And Prahlāda is golden-hued; these are proclaimed to be their respective colors. (10)
172. Now, the forms of the ten sages beginning with Marīci—(in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu;
He, as well as Veda, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada [were there]. || 1 ||
They had matted hair and beards, were tranquil, emaciated, and always devoted to dharma.
Ten sages with two arms should be depicted, holding staffs and water-pots.
Nārada, the celestial Gandharva, was there with his rosary and water-pot.
Like two friends, we two [shall play] with lutes embraced by the roots of our arms. || 3 ||
But the sages, O King, should be fashioned in white form.
They are white in color. || 10 ||
Then the group of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras: (In the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda) 173. First, among them, the group of Bhṛgu:
"The Bhṛgus and Vāmadeva are to be fashioned in white form."
Bhṛvaṇa, Bhāvana, Sujanya, and likewise Sujana. || 1 ||
And likewise Kratusarvasva, Sūri by name, as well as Vyaśruta.
Pravāsa, Avyaya, and Dakṣa—these are the twelve. || 2 ||
The twelve deities designated as Bhṛgus are those who are performers of sacrifice.
They are white in color. || 12 ||
174. Now, as for the host of Aṅgirases: "The gods and likewise the Aṅgirases should be fashioned in the form of living beings."
Ātman, Āyu, Manas, Dakṣa, Pāda, and Prāpa likewise. || 1 ||
Haviṣya, Gaviṣṭha, Ṛta, Satya, and Devala.
They are yellow in color. || 9 ||
Now, the names of the deities presiding over the Śāstras are as follows (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): Śikṣā is to be known as Prajāpati, and Kalpa is proclaimed to be Brahmā.
Sarasvatī gave grammar, and the Lord Varuṇa gave the Nirukta. || 1 ||
Likewise, the Lord Hari is the manifestation of desire, the fire, and the light.
The Blessed One Soma is Mīmāṃsā, and the Wind is the Path of Logic (Nyāya). || 2 ||
And Manu is likewise the authority for the Dharma and the Dharmaśāstras as well as for the Purāṇa.
He is history, the presiding lord of progeny, the science of archery, and the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Likewise, the Lord Dhanvantari himself is Āyurveda.
Mahādeva is the Veda of fruits; Maheśvara is the science of dance. || 4 ||
Saṃkarṣaṇa [revealed] the Pāñcarātra, and likewise Rudra [revealed] the Pāśupata.
Ananta is the author of the Pātañjala [Yoga], and the sage Kapila is the author of Sāṃkhya. || 5 ||
All treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra) are proclaimed as pertaining to the Superintendent of Wealth.
Kāmadeva, the teacher of the world, [taught] all the arts and sciences. || 6 ||
Whatever other various treatises they proclaim to have been composed by him;
He alone is the deity for him; his scripture and his poetry are like the Veda.
175. Now, the true form of the Yakṣas:
all Yakṣas are preservers of virtues, auspicious, and bearers of swords and shields.
I pay homage to those who move through the sky and those who move among the gods, for the attainment of happiness. || 1 || 1 ||
176. Now, the form of Viśvakarman—(from the Dānakhaṇḍa of Hemādri):
"The creator of all (Viśvakartṛ) should be depicted with a beard and wearing a lower garment."
Holding tongs in his hand, he has two arms; he is the great one who bears splendor as his very form.
Golden-colored. || 1 || 1 ||

Thus ends the fourth treasury, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Four-Faced One, the Five Brahmas, the Guardians of the Quarters, and Others," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign of the preeminent city of Mahīśūra; he who is adorned with numerous titles such as: the ornament of the entire circle of the earth, the crest-jewel of all lands, the abode of the prosperity of the Karṇāṭaka country, the one resplendent in the midst of the great seat of Mahīśūra, the one seated upon the divine jeweled throne experienced by the circle of universal emperors and chief royal protectors descended through an unbroken lineage of masters of all arts, the king of kings of kings, the supreme lord, the monarch of incomparable heroism and mighty majesty, the one whose fame reaches the vault of heaven, the sole hero of the world, the moon in the ocean of the Yadu dynasty, the one marked with the conch, discus, goad, axe, crocodile, fish, śarabha, sālva, gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, earth-boar, Hanuman, Garuḍa, lion, and many other titles.
Thus ends the fourth treasury of Brahman, named the Exposition of the Four-Faced One, the Five Brahmans, and so forth, in the treatise known as the *Śrītattvanidhi*.
Śrīḥ.
Now,
in the venerable *Tattvanidhi*, the fifth treasury, the Treasury of Planets (*Ugrahanidhi*).

Now, the forms of the nine planets together with their presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) and secondary presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatā*) [are described]. (According to the words of Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa in the *Prayogaratna*, and in verse by Mayūkha:
First among these is the meditation (*dhyāna*) on the Sun:

O Blessed One, Lord of the Sun-planet, of the Kāśyapa lineage, Sovereign of the Kaliṅga country, born on the seventh lunar day under the Viśākhā asterism, whose bodily luster resembles the hibiscus flower, two-armed with hands holding a lotus and the gesture of fearlessness, crimson in color, clad in garments, garlands, and unguents, with all your limbs adorned with ornaments set with blazing rubies, O treasury of radiant splendor, embodiment of the three deities who illumines the three worlds—salutations to you! Arriving upon a single-wheeled chariot drawn by seven horses, adorned with armor, ornaments, and banners, circumambulating Mount Meru, come and preside over the copper image facing east upon the circular pedestal at the center of the lotus, together with Agni and Rudra; one should meditate upon you thus, complete with your limbs, weapons, powers, and consorts.
Seated in the lotus posture, with hands like lotuses, he possesses a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus.
He should have two arms, be accompanied by his wife, and be joined with a chariot drawn by seven horses. || 1 ||
The color is pale red. || 1 ||
2. Now, the meditation on the four-faced Sūrya (from the Śāradātilaka):

He whose innate luster resembles a golden lotus and coral, who holds in his beautiful hands the khaṭvāṅga, the lotus, the discus, the spear, the noose, the goad, the most lovely rosary, and the skull-cup.

We worship Him who holds [the sun] with His lotus-like hands, who is beautiful with three eyes and the four Vedas shining upon His faces, who is enriched by His beloved, who wears a crown of jewels, and who is radiant with diamonds. || 1 ||
The color of coral. || 1 || — ||
(Śāradātilaka, p. 122) Meditation in another manner:
I worship the Sun, who sits upon a red lotus, who is the unique ocean of all virtues, and the sovereign of all worlds.

Holding a pair of lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons with his lotus-like hands, he wears a crown of rubies, possesses a reddish bodily luster, and has three eyes. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
3. Now, the meditation on Agni, the presiding deity of the Sun:
He has tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair; his three eyes are tawny and his body is ruddy.
Seated upon a goat, holding a rosary, bestowing boons, and bearing a spear; || 1 ||
The color is reddish-brown. || 1 ||
4. Now, the meditation on Rudra, the presiding deity of the Sun:
He has five faces, is mounted upon a bull, and possesses three eyes in each face.
Śiva holds a skull, a trident, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and the Pināka bow; he has the crescent moon upon his head. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
5. Now, the meditation on the moon (candradhyāna):

"O Blessed One, Lord of the Moon and the twice-born, whose body consists of nectar, of the lineage of Atri, Sovereign of the Yāmuna region, whose limbs possess the luster of white cow’s milk, with two arms marked by the mace and the gesture of granting boons, adorned with white garments, garlands, and unguents, beautiful with pearl ornaments, the deity who nourishes all the worlds and whose form is to be tasted by the gods—salutations to You! Arriving while circumambulating Mount Meru on a three-wheeled chariot drawn by ten horses and graced by a firmly fixed white banner, come and occupy Your place upon the square pedestal in the middle of the eastern petal of the lotus, facing east, together with Umā, seated upon a crystal image. Thus one should meditate upon the Moon, accompanied by His consort and son, equipped with weapons, and complete in all His limbs.
He was white, clad in white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments.
He should be depicted with two arms, holding a mace in his hand, and as a moon-like bestower of boons.
White in color. || 1 || — ||

Another method of meditating on the Moon (from the *Śāradātilaka*): With a face like the orb of the full moon, white as camphor and crystal, and with a body adorned with strings of pearls that utterly eradicates darkness— [thus one should meditate].

I worship the Moon, who holds a white water-lily and a blue lotus in his two hands, who is illuminated by dark curls of hair, who possesses the qualities arising from the deer situated upon his lap, and who is the ocean of nectar.
White in color. || 1 ||
6. Now, the meditation on the waters, whose presiding deity is the Moon:
The Waters assume the form of women, white in color, and have crocodiles as their vehicles.
Holding nooses and water-pots, they were adorned with ornaments of pearls. || 1 ||
They are white in color. || 1 ||
p.
123) 7 Now, the meditation on the respective presiding deities (pratyadhidevatā):
[He holds] a rosary, a lotus, a mirror, and a water-pot.
Uma, who is honored even by the thirty gods, carries [these] in her hands. || 1 ||
Golden-colored. || 1 ||
8. Now, the meditation on Aṅgāraka:

O Blessed Aṅgāraka, having the form of fire, of the Bharadvāja lineage, Lord of the Avanti country, born under the Śravaṇa asterism on the eighth lunar day, whose bodily luster is like a mass of flames, holding in your four arms a spear, a trident, a mace, and a khaṭvāṅga staff; you who wear red garments, garlands, and unguents, whose entire body is adorned with the luster of coral ornaments, and who are radiant with light—to you, salutations! Adorned with a fastened red banner, riding upon a chariot drawn by eight red rams, come circling Mount Meru clockwise; together with Bhūmi and Skanda, occupy the middle of the southern petal of the lotus, presiding over a triangular seat upon which is an image of red sandalwood facing south—thus one should meditate upon you, complete with your limbs, weapons, and consort.
Wearing red garlands and garments, he holds a spear, a trident, and a mace.
The son of the Earth (Mars), having four arms and riding upon a ram, should be depicted as granting boons. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
9. Now, the meditation on the Earth, the presiding deity of Aṅgāraka:
The Earth is to be visualized as white in color, adorned with divine ornaments.
Four-armed and of gentle form, she was clothed in garments resembling the sun.
A vessel of jewels, a vessel of grain, and a vessel filled with medicinal herbs.
And a lotus-hand gesture should be made, O delighter of the Yadu dynasty.
Likewise, she should be placed upon the backs of the four world-elephants (diggajas).
She is white in color. || 1 ||
10. Now, the meditation on Skanda, the presiding deity of Aṅgāraka:
The youth should be visualized as six-faced, adorned with peacock feathers.
The god, wearing red garments, has the excellent peacock as his vehicle. || 1 ||
And likewise, a cock and a bell are in his two right hands.
A banner and a victory-standard (vaijayantī) should be depicted, and a spear (śakti) should be held in the two left hands. || 2 ||
The color is pale red. || 1 ||
11. Now, the meditation on Budha:

O Blessed One of gentle luster, composed of all-knowledge, born of the Atri lineage on the twelfth lunar day under the constellation Dhaniṣṭhā, Lord of the Magadha country, whose body and radiance are the color of saffron, four-armed, with hands marked by the sword, shield, mace, and the gesture of granting boons, adorned on all limbs with emerald ornaments and yellow garlands and unguents, O you of wise intellect, homage to you! Arriving while circumambulating Mount Meru in a chariot drawn by four lions and adorned with a fastened green banner, please take your seat upon the arrow-shaped pedestal facing north, amidst the lotus petals of Īśāna, together with Viṣṇu and Puruṣa—one should meditate upon [the deity] along with his limbs, weapons, consort, retinue, and powers.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, he possesses a luster equal to that of the *karṇikāra* flower.
Buddha, holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, stands upon a lion and bestows boons.
Golden-hued. || 1 ||
12. Now, the meditation on Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of Mercury:
Viṣṇu holds, in sequence, the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus.
One should always perform circumambulation, beginning from the lower right hand. || 1 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
