Kārttika is indeed Ūrja, Mārgaśīrṣa is Śveta, and Sahas is Sita.
Puṣya is Sahasya and the month of Māgha is also remembered as Harita. || 3 ||
Phālguna is also its name; it is recorded as being pale-red in color.
O Lord of the Earth, you have described those gods according to their respective colors. || 4 ||

Now, regarding the baths, gifts, worship, offerings, and so forth to be performed in each of the twelve months beginning with Caitra— as found in the works of Bhaṭṭabhāskara, the Padma Purāṇa, Vāmana Purāṇa, and Mahābhārata— first, concerning Caitra: "In the month of Caitra,
there are various kinds of baths and seats."
For the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, these should be given to Brāhmaṇas. || 1 ||
(Vaiśākha) —
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform an external bath according to the prescribed rite in a divine river or similar body of water.
Eating sacrificial food, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, and steadfastness in self-restraint. || 1 ||
O Goddess, there is the joy of vows, the joy of giving, and the worship of Madhusūdana.
It also burns away even the terrible sin arising from thousands of previous births. || 2 ||
(In the month of Jyeṣṭha:
Water-pots, water, cows, palm-leaf fans, and sandalwood.
And in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it should be given for the pleasure of Trivikrama.
In Āṣāḍha—
one pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt, and myrobalan fruits.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, these should be offered with devotion here for the pleasure of Vāmana.
(In the month of Śrāvaṇa: Ghee, jars of milk, and fruits cooked in ghee.
These should be offered day by day for the pleasure of Śrīdhara in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should offer milk-rice along with honey and clarified butter.
For the sake of pleasing Hṛṣīkeśa, he [offered] a mirror and rice with jaggery.
(In the month of Āśvayuja:
One should consume a bull that has well-stabilized limbs, along with curd, sour gruel, and similar substances.
For the sake of pleasing Padmanābha, men should give [offerings] in the month of Āśvayuja.
(In Kārtika)—
silver, gold, lamps, jewels, pearls, and so forth.
A person should give [this] during the month of Kārttika for the sake of pleasing Dāmodara. || 1 ||
(In Mārgaśīrṣa)—
Donkeys, camels, horses, men, goats, and cattle, as well as carts, goats, and sheep.
It should be given by the best of men in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for the propitiation of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
O son of Kuntī, he who passes the month of Pauṣa by eating only one meal a day—
He becomes fortunate, handsome to behold, and a partaker of fame. || 1 ||
And he who bathes continuously during the month of Māgha, O Bhārata—
For him, there shall be the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice day after day. || 1 ||
(In Phālguna)—
In Phālguna, one should give a garment together with a black antelope skin and rice.
O bull among men, it should be given for the sake of pleasing Govinda. || 1 || 12 ||
Now, the gifts for the twelve months beginning with Māgha—(from the *Dānacintāmaṇi*, based on the *Viṣṇudharmottara*).
Among these, first, in *Māgha*:
"By the gift of sesame seeds in *Māgha*, one does not go to the world of Yama."
157) (In Phālguna)—
by offering priyaṅgu in Phālguna, one becomes beloved on the earth.
In the month of Caitra, by giving variegated garments, one enjoys good fortune.
By the offering of cakes in the month of Vaiśākha, one attains heaven.
Likewise, by the gift of an umbrella in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one attains all desires.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, sandalwood mixed with camphor should be offered; it yields great fruit.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is proclaimed that the fruit of giving cloth is exceedingly great.
In the month of Bhādrapada,
likewise on the full moon day, the gift of that [substance] is phāṇita.
(Regarding Āśvina):
By the gift of ghee during the month of Āśvina, one is born handsome.
In Kārttika—
by the offering of lamps in Kārttika, one shall attain all radiance.
In Mārgaśīrṣa— by giving salt in Mārgaśīrṣa, one enjoys good fortune.
In Pauṣa—by the gift of gold in Pauṣa, one likewise attains supreme nourishment. || 11 ||

Now, the qualities of those born in the months beginning with Caitra—(from the *Jātakābharaṇa*): First, regarding Caitra—a man will be endowed with virtuous deeds, learning, and discipline; he will be an enjoyer of life and a consumer of sweet food.
And the minister, born in Caitra, was devoted to giving to worthy recipients and possessed of wonderful mantras. || 1 ||
In Vaiśākha,
the man is one who has excellent offspring, is endowed with the quality of nourishment, is powerful, and is devoted to the twice-born and the gods.
In the month of Mādhava, one will have long life, be fond of water and travel by boat, and be endowed with happiness from kinsmen. || 1 ||
In Jyeṣṭhā,
one is endowed with patience yet possesses a fickle state of mind, has a strong inclination for living abroad, and is intense in temperament.
Indeed, one born under Jyeṣṭhā will possess a versatile intellect, be somewhat procrastinating, yet be the most excellent among men. || 1 ||
In Āṣāḍha—
one who is extravagant in spending, lacking in verbal eloquence, prone to negligence, yet affectionate toward his teacher.
One born under the conjunction of Āṣāḍha will always suffer from weak digestion, perform auspicious deeds, and possess very intense pride. || 1 ||
(Śrāvaṇa:
"Together with sons, grandsons, wife, and friends, he shall be happy and a fulfiller of his father's commands."
He was world-renowned for his phlegmatic temperament, yet he was generous and filled with meritorious virtues in the month of Śrāvaṇa. || 1 ||
In Bhādrapada, one becomes illustrious, though with a diminished physical frame; yet he is a donor and endowed with the happiness of a beloved wife and sons.
For a mortal who is transformed by pleasures and pains and is born as a base person in the month of Bhādrapada shall become a rogue. || 1 ||
In the month of Āśvayuja, he will be learned, wealthy, beloved by the royal family, a performer of virtuous deeds, and possessed of many servants.
One born under Āśvinī will be a donor, a connoisseur of virtues, possessed of a lineage of many sons, and endowed with prosperity such as horses and other wealth. || 1 ||
(Kārtika) —
One who performs virtuous deeds, possessing the wealth of many verbal delights, with beautiful, dark, and well-arranged locks of hair.
Granted that this desire, born under the constellation Kārttika, brings about the performance of good deeds for the sake of buying and selling. || 1 ||
(In Mārgaśīrṣa:
Devoted to pilgrimages to sacred sites, virtuous, skilled in the entire range of arts, and elegant.
A benefactor of others, one who maintains the path of the virtuous, one born on the right path, and indeed one endowed with prosperity. || 1 ||
In Puṣya,
one is a benefactor to others, devoid of paternal wealth, a spender of riches acquired with difficulty, and a knower of the sacred rites.
One who has well-guarded mantras, is endowed with the application of the scriptures, is distinguished in the month of Pauṣa, and possesses the arts; || 1 ||
In the month of Māgha—
one who knows the true mantras, is devoted to the company of Vedic sages, and is intent on practicing the knowledge taught in Yoga.
Through the excellence of his awakening, that sinless man born in the month of Māgha shall have conquered the hosts of his enemies. || 1 ||
(Phālguna)—
One who assists others, possesses a compassionate disposition, is endowed with strength, and has a delicate physique.
He whose nature is the practice of amorous play with graceful women, and whose speech in the month of Phālguna is full of playful charm. || 1 || 12 ||
182. Now, the visualization of the deities presiding over the months beginning with Caitra—(in the *Śāradātilaka*):
"The deities beginning with Keśava indeed correspond to the months from Mārgaśīrṣa through Ūrja."
These worship rituals, performed in sequence throughout the months, are for the sake of the complete abundance of all prosperity.
(Their characteristics, like the twenty-four forms beginning with Keśava, are as follows: Ni0 2) || 12 ||
Now, the forms of the twelve solar transits (*saṃkrāntis*) beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces (as described in the *Jyotiṣārṇava*):
First, the form of the Aries transit (*meṣasaṃkrānti*):
She has matted hair and the form of fire, possesses three eyes, and has a tiger as her vehicle.
Holding a skull and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, she has one face and is of a terrifying appearance. || 1 ||
May this first Aries transit (meṣa-saṃkrānti) be for our constant joy.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
184. Now, the nature of the Vṛṣabha-saṃkrānti:
she has one face, two arms, and three eyes, and she rides upon a lion.
White in color and most formidable, she holds a skull and the gesture of fearlessness. || 1 ||
May the second transit of the sun into Taurus always bring me joy.
She is white in color. || 1 ||
185. Now, the nature of the conjunction with Mithuna:
Virūpākṣī is green in color, three-eyed, and seated upon a boar.
Holding both the gesture of fearlessness and the skull-bowl, she is auspicious with her single face. || 1 ||
May that which is called "concordant" (muthuna), being well-connected, always be for the sake of the accomplishment of your desired goals.
Yellow-colored. 1.186 Now, the nature of the Karkātaka transit:
Mahodarī, Ekavaktrā, and Kaṭakā are situated in the sign of Aries.
She has a body the color of the Pāṭala flower, two arms, and she holds a skull and the gesture of fearlessness.
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
187. Now, the nature of the Leo transit (siṃhasaṃkrānti): She has a skull and a fly-whisk in her hands, is red in color, and is seated upon a donkey.
May Ekavaktrā, who has transferred her essence into Jihmikāsiṃha, be gracious. || 1 ||
She is red in color. || 1 ||
188. Now, the nature of the Kanyā-saṃkrānti:
She has a dark face and a reddish body, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon an elephant.
She is unknowable even to the Siṃhikās, adorned with a skull and the gesture of fearlessness. || 1 ||
This is called the Kanyā-saṃkrānti; it brings delight to the ancestors and is auspicious.
The face is black in color; the body is red in color. (1)
189. Now, the nature of the transition of the Libra (tulā) [sun]:
She is named Tulā, dark blue in color, with a ram's face, and seated upon a cock.
Accompanied by Maṇḍātrinetra, she holds a skull and displays the gesture of fearlessness. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
190. Now, the nature of the Scorpio transit (vṛścikasaṃkrānti):
She is mounted upon a goat, blue in color, three-eyed, and considered to be Āhlādinī.
And Saṃkrānti, known as Vṛścika, holds a skull and a spear in her hands. || 1 ||
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
191. Now, the nature of the transition to Dhanus: she is seated upon a buffalo, possesses three eyes, and is named Citravarṇojjvalā (Resplendent with Variegated Colors).
And she who holds a skull and the gesture of fearlessness is called Dhanussakrānti. || 1 ||
The multicolored one. || 1 ||
192. Now, the nature of the Makara-saṃkrānti: she has the color of a hibiscus flower, possesses three eyes, and has a face with protruding fangs.
And the Rākṣasī Kapālavajrahastā has a camel as her vehicle. || 1 ||
Furthermore, the Makara-saṃkrānti bestows highly desired fruits.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
193. Now, the nature of the Aquarius (Kumbha) transit: She is mounted upon a horse, has a large belly, and is blue in color.
And she who holds a skull and the gesture of fearlessness is declared to be Kumbhasaṃkrānti. || 1 ||
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
194. Now, the nature of the transit into Pisces (Mīna-saṃkrānti):
She is named Avakrā, three-eyed, and mounted upon a supreme bear.
She who is named Mīnā has a face of reddish-brown color and is joined with the gestures of holding a skull and granting fearlessness. || 1 ||
The color is reddish-brown. || 1 || 12 ||
Now, the names of the twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*)—(according to the *Jyotiṣārṇava*): Karālī, Mahāghorā, Virūpākṣī, and Mahodarī.
Jihmikā, sihmikā, mandā, hlādinī, and ujjvalā are considered [her forms]. || 1 ||
Rākṣasī, Bhañjikā, and Vakrā are the transitions (saṃkrāntis) in sequence. || 12 ||
Now, the vehicles for the twelve transits (as stated in the *Jyotiṣārṇava*):
the tiger, lion, boar, dog, donkey, and goat; [and the elephant, horse, camel, bull, ram, and cat].
The cock-fight, and likewise the buffalo, the camel, the horse, and even the bear. || 1 ||
These would be the mounts for the Saṃkrāntis beginning with Meṣa (Aries). || 12 ||
Now, Viśvāmitra (in the Bhaṭṭabhāskarīya) states the gifts to be given during the transits [of the sun]: "At the transit of the sun into Aries, the gift of a ram yields great fruit."
Likewise, the gift of cows is prescribed for the transit of the sun into Aries.
Indeed, clothing, food, drink, and vehicles are ordained for the couple.
The gift of a cow filled with ghee is highly praised during the month of Karkaṭa.
The gift of a bowl together with gold is always prescribed for a lion.
Likewise, at the entrance of a maiden, there should be garments and fragrant substances.
Upon the entry of the sun into Libra, it is most excellent for grains and seeds alike.
And when insects enter one's clothes or dwellings, the giving of gifts is indeed prescribed. || 4 ||
At the entry of the bow (the Dhanus zodiac), there is great fruit for garments and vehicles.
Likewise, there is the offering of wood for the fire at the time of the deer's entry. || 5 ||
Upon the entry into the pitcher, however, one should give grass and water to the cows.
Indeed, at the entry of the Fish [sign], even for those with unfading garlands, this is the most excellent.
Now, the names of the twelve Ādityas, who preside over the twelve months—(according to the Śaiva Āgama):
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Mitra, Aruṇa, and Candra.
Vivasvat, Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Aṃśu, Bhaga, and Pūṣan as well. || 1 ||
And Parjanya—these twelve are indeed the deities of the solar transits (saṃkrāntis).
161) Now, the meditation on the twelve Āditya deities who preside over the twelve months—(in verses from the Śaivāgama;
in passages from the Śrī Viṣṇu Bhāgavata; and the rays [of light] according to the Kūrma Purāṇa).
194. First, there is the meditation on Dhātṛ and Sūrya: "O Sage, [he] whose weapon is the earth made by Dhātṛ, who fashioned Vāsuki as his chariot."
Pulastya, Tuṃburu, Ṛtumat, and Madhumāsa—these are the ones who lead [the way].
May he, the bestower of what is auspicious for me, grant it to me again and again, and in ever greater measure.
Enveloped by a web of rays, he is the destroyer of the mass of darkness.
The sun has placed the sheep within the blades of the sword.

The Apsaras is Kṛtasthalī; the Gandharva is Tuṃbaru; the Ṛṣi is Pulastya; Vāsuki occupies the position of the noose; the chariot-maker is named Vardhaki; the Rākṣasa is named Heti; there are eight thousand reins; and its color is red. 1.
195. Now follows the meditation on the Asūryas:
Aryaman, Aṅgiras, Atharvan, Ūrja, Praheti, and Puñjikasthalī.
Nārada and Kacchanīra lead Mādhava here.
Moving within the peaks of Mount Meru, he is the kinsman of the lotus-pools.
May Aryaman grant ever-increasing prosperity to me, who am bowed before him. || 2 ||

The month is Vṛṣabha; the Āditya is Aryaman. The seer is Pulaha; the Apsaras is Puñjikasthalī; the Gandharva is named Nārada; the Nāga is named Kacchanīra; the carpenter is named Ūrja; the Rākṣasa is Praheti. There are ten thousand rays; the color is yellow. 1.
196. Now, the meditation on Mitra-Sūrya:
Mitra, Atri, Pauruṣeya, Atharvan, Takṣaka, Menakā, and Ahā.
These sounds of chariots are heard; they are bringing the bright month.
Skilled in warding off the night, he has taken his refuge on the mountain of sunrise.
May Mitra, the destroyer of the darkness that obstructs my joy, be my friend. || 2 ||

The Sun is the friend of the month of Mithuna. His sage (ṛṣi) is Atri; his Apsaras is Menakā; his Gandharva is Hāhā; his Nāga is Takṣaka; his carpenter is named Rathasvana; his Rākṣasa is Pauruṣeya; his rays are seven thousand; and his color is reddish-brown (aruṇa). 1.
197. Now, the meditation on Aruṇa-Sūrya:
Vasiṣṭha, Aruṇa, Ambhas, Sahajanya, and likewise Āhuhū.
The parrot and Citrasvana likewise bring about the month of Śuci. || 1 ||
Mounted upon the chariot of the sun, garlanded with flames, he was full of majesty.
Indeed, Aruṇa, who has become Time and can assume any form at will, is served by me.

In the month of Karkaṭaka, the sun is Aruṇa. The seer is Vasiṣṭha; the Apsaras is Rambhā; the Gandharva is Hūhū; the Nāga is named Śuka; the carpenter is Citrasvana; the Rākṣasa is Sahajanya; the rays are five thousand; and the color is dark green (śyāma). 1.
198. Now, the meditation on Indra and Sūrya:
Indra, Viśvāvasu, Śrotṛ, Celāputra, and likewise Aṅgiras.
Pramlocā, Rākṣasa, Śaryā, and Nabhas—these bring about the month of Māsa. || 1 ||
I take refuge in Indra, the granter of boons, who is enveloped by a thousand rays.
Today, with my head bowed, I prostrate before the one who bestows the increase of spiritual welfare.

In this month of Siṃha, Indra is the Sun; Aṅgiras is the Ṛṣi; Viśvāvasu is the Gandharva; Pramlocā is the Apsaras; Ilāputra is the Nāga; the carpenter is named Śrotra; the Rākṣasa is named Śarya; there are seven thousand rays; and the color is white. 1.
199. Now, the meditation on Vivasvat-Sūrya:
Vivasvat, Ugrasena, Vyāghra, Āsāraṇa, and Bhṛgu.
Anumlocā, Śaṅkhapāla, and those known as Nabhasya lead [the breaths].
The creator of the universe, whose splendor pervades all directions.
I bow to Vivasvat, the great lamp for grasping the celestial spheres. || 2 ||

Vivasvān Sūrya [beheld] Kanyā as his wife. The seer was Bhṛgu; the Apsaras was Anumlocā; the Gandharva was Ugrasena; the Nāga was Śaṅkhapāla; the carpenter was Āsāraṇa; the Rākṣasa was Vyāghra; his rays numbered ten thousand; and his color was tawny (babhru). 1.
200. Now, the meditation on Tvaṣṭṛ and Sūrya:
Tvaṣṭṛ, Ṛcīka, Rakṣa, the one named Kambala, and Tilottamā.
Brahmarātī, Athaśatajihvā, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Iṣambharā. || 1 ||
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is served by the remnants of the bali offering, become auspicious for me.
Performing various arts, he assumes various elemental forms and is the maker of light. || 2 ||

The sun is situated on the Libra zodiac sign. The seer is Brahmarāta; the celestial nymph is Tilottamā; the gandharva is Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the nāga is named Kambala; the carpenter is named Śatajit; the rākṣasa is named Ṛcīka; there are eight thousand rays; and the color is variegated. 1.
201. Now, the meditation on Viṣṇu-Sūrya:
Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Ambhas, Sūryavarcas, and Satyajit.
Viśvāmitra is a great preta; these [beings] are bringing forth vital energy.
He who dwells in the center of the solar orb and is served by the three Vedas.
With devotion, I bow to Viṣṇu, who is the one to be propounded by the Gāyatrī.

In the month of Vṛścika, the Sun is Viṣṇu. Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi). Rambhā is the Apsaras. Sūryavarcas is the Gandharva. Satyajit is the name of the carpenter (vardhaki). Aśvatara is the Nāga. Mahāpreta is the Rākṣasa. There are six thousand rays. His color is tawny (aruṇa). 1.
202. Now, the meditation on Aṃśu-Sūrya:
Next, Aṃśu, Kāśyapa, Tārkṣya, Ṛtasena, and likewise Urvaśī.
Vidyutchatru, Mahāśaṅkha, and Sahomā—these are being brought together.
Always delighted in driving away [suffering], he is the lamp of auspiciousness for the world.
May the auspicious ray of light, praised by the assembly of lords of sages, bring prosperity to me.

In the month of Dhanus, the sun is Aṃśu; the seer is Kāśyapa; the apsarā is Urvaśī; the gandharva is Ṛtaseṇa; the nāga is Mahāśaṅkha; the vardhaki is Tārkṣya; the rākṣasa is Vidyucchatru; there are nine thousand rays; and its color is yellowish-green (hari). 1.
203. Now, the meditation on Bhaga and Sūrya: Bhaga, Sphūrji, Ariṣṭanemi, Ūrṇa, and Āyus as the fifth.
Karkoṭaka and Pūrvacitti—these bring about the month of Pauṣa. || 1 ||
And also of the lunar days, months, and seasons, as well as of the years and solstices.
And he who is the maker of the ghaṭikās, may that Lord bestow fortune and good luck upon me. || 2 ||

In the month of Makara, the Sun is Bhaga; the Ṛṣi is Ariṣṭanemi; the Apsaras is Pūrvacitti; the Gandharva is Ūrṇa; the Nāga is Karkoṭaka; the Vardhaki is Āyu; the Rākṣasa is Sphūrja; the rays are eleven thousand; and the color is red. (1)
204. Now, the meditation on Pūṣan and Sūrya:
Pūṣan, Dhanañjaya, Dhātṛ, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Suruci.
Ghṛtācī and Gautama—these two bring about the attainment of the power of asceticism. || 1 ||
May Pūṣan become the satisfaction for you through the removal of all evils.
Enveloped by a thousand rays, he whose inner self is entirely peaceful.

The sun is in the month of Kumbha (Aquarius). The seer is Gautama. The Apsaras is Ghṛtācī. The Gandharva is Suruci. The Nāga is Dhanañjaya. The carpenter is Suṣeṇa. The Rākṣasa is Dhātṛ. There are six thousand rays. Its color is that of lac. 1.
205. Now, the meditation on Parjanya and Sūrya:
Kratuvarcas Bārhadrāja, Parjanya, and likewise Senajit.
Viśva and Airāvata—these lead the one called Tapasya.
Scorching the world of manifold phenomena once more, and then again gladdening it with rains.
The rain-cloud, which produces joy for the world, is worshipped by me.

In the month of Mīna, Parjanya is the Sun; Bharadvāja is the seer (ṛṣi); Varcas is the gandharva; Airāvata is the nāga; Senajit is the vardhaki; Viśva is the rākṣasa; there are nine thousand rays; and the color is reddish-brown (aruṇa). 1.
Now, regarding the chariot-horses of these twelve Ādityas (in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*):
they are green in color; they are named after the Vedic meters (*chaṃdas*); they are seven in number; and there is one principal horse named Sapti who precedes them.

Herein are the names of the twelve Ādityas and their role as the instigators of the twelve months (*Viṣṇupurāṇa*). (It should be understood that where they are mentioned elsewhere in a different order, this is due to a difference in *kalpa*).
206. Now, the characteristics of these twelve Ādityas (*Padmapurāṇa*).
Mārtaṇḍa is two-armed, red in color, wearing red garments, and standing.
On the back part is the head-wheel (śiraścakra), and in its place is the stainless mandala.
Wearing a crown and holding a pair of lotuses in his two hands.
Upon the region of his chest [he wore] the stainless, great Syamantaka jewel.
And one should meditate upon him as mounted on a chariot with a single wheel, which has been brought to rest. || 1 ||
Now, their colors— (in the Padma Purāṇa)—
are red, yellow, rosy, dark-blue, white, tawny, and variegated.
Aruṇa, Harita, Śoṇa, and Kāntanibha-aruṇa. || 1 ||
These colors are traditionally taught as belonging to the twelve Ādityas in their respective order.
207. Now, regarding the characteristics of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) and the omitted month (*kṣayamāsa*)—(in the Śiromaṇi):
A month without a solar transit (*asaṃkrāntimāsa*) is clearly an intercalary month; a month with two transits is sometimes called an omitted month (*kṣaya*).
If [the intercalary month] occurs during the three months beginning with Kārttika, there will be a depletion [of days]; otherwise, there would be two intercalary months within a single year. || 1 ||

(For the intercalary month as well, the deity is indeed the same as the deity of its own corresponding month; its essential nature is also like the essential nature of its own corresponding month. (6, Niḥśeṣa)
Now, the gifts to be performed during an intercalary month—(in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa): "When an intercalary month has arrived, [one should give] thirty-three cakes."
One should give a fruit with jaggery and ghee, placed within a vessel of bell-metal.
And for the sake of pleasing Janārdana, he fashioned an image of him made of gold.
(p. 165) 208 Now, the nature of the Makara-saṃkrānti—(in the Jyotiṣaratnākara): [He is] two-faced, black in color, four-armed, and three-eyed.
It is seven cubits tall, has three feet, two heads, and its gaze is directed upward. || 1 ||
In his right hands, he holds seven weapons: a mace, a sword, and two arrows.
Holding a mace in his left hand, as well as a shield, a vessel, and a bow.
It is renowned as having a cruel form, characterized by the "crocodile-entrance" (makarakrānti).
He is black in color. || 1 ||

Alternatively, the specific forms of the seven types of Capricorn transits according to the distinction of days of the week (*jyotiṣārṇava*, 209): [All are black in color]. First, the form of the transit named *Ghorā* occurring on Sunday:
"The Capricorn transit on Sunday is indeed named *Ghorā*, while it resides in Leo."
A lute, a sword, a worn winnowing basket, a white lotus, and a bow. || 1 ||
And she holds the king of mountains, which serves as the beam of the scales, with her seven hands.
210. Now, the nature of the *dhvāṅkṣī* transit on Mondays:
O Śārdūlavāhana, a transit occurring on a Monday is indeed *dhvāṅkṣī*.
A sword, a sieve, a lotus, a balance-beam, and a bow.
Holding a serpent, a discus, and a sword, may they grant me boons. || 1 ||
211. Now, the nature of the Mahodarī-saṃkrānti on Tuesday: likewise, when the transit occurs on a Tuesday, it is known as Varāhavaravāhanā (the one whose excellent vehicle is the boar).
She is renowned as Mahodarī; she holds a worn winnowing basket and a white lotus.
The balance-beam, the bow, the serpent, the saw, and likewise the knife.
Bearing [these], may she be the bestower of boons for the pacification of all misfortunes. || 2 || 1 ||
212. Now, the nature of the transit of the Mandākinī on Wednesday:
On a Wednesday, the Mandākinī is situated in the Kharapravara [nakṣatra].
And [he holds] a white lotus, a bow, a balance-beam, and the lord of serpents.
Always bestowing auspiciousness, she bears the saw, the dagger, and the arrow.
213. Now, the nature of the transit on Thursday (Guruvāra) during the period known as Mandā:
On Thursday, the transit called Mandā is auspicious, involving the movement of excellent elephants.
A bow, a balance-beam, a lordly elephant, a saw, and arrows.
Joyfully wielding a dagger and a bhindipāla with her arms.
Now, the nature of the Miśrikā-saṃkrānti on Friday:
On the day of the preceptor of the lords of the Asuras (Venus), [the goddess] Miśrikā is seated upon a buffalo throne.
And the great lord Tulādaṇḍa, as well as Krakaca and Kṣurikā. || 1 ||
He also carries an arrow, a bhindipāla weapon, and a spear.
215. Now, the nature of the Rākṣasī-saṃkrānti on Saturday:
On the day of the Son of the Sun (Saturn), the Rākṣasī is mounted upon a horse.
They also carried a curved saw, a razor-edged knife, and even an arrow.
And she bears in her hands a bhindipāla, a spear, and a bhuśuṇḍī.
216. Now, the general characteristics of the *saṃkrānti* (transits)—(from the *Jyotiṣasaṃgraha*):
She indeed has eight arms, four faces, eight ears, and eight eyes.
It is sixty yojanas in width and one hundred yojanas in height.
She is to be worshipped with seven weapons in her hands; she has protruding lips and three feet.
She has hair standing on end, deformed eyes, is the personification of the transition (saṃkrānti), and possesses a masculine form. || 1 ||
She is blue in color. || 1 ||

Now, specifically regarding their eleven forms according to the distinctions of entry into the *karaṇas*—(from the *Jyotiṣasaṃgraha*) 217: First, the form of the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) when it has entered the *bava-karaṇa*:
Seated upon a lion, holding a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, [the deity] wears white garments and coral, and is adorned with *puṃnāga* flowers.
Indeed, on the day of the sun Bava, one eats musk, fine golden vessels, and food. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
218. Now, the nature of the *saṃkrānti* (transit) that has entered the *bālavakaraṇa*:
[the deity] is seated upon a tiger, wearing garments of dawn-red color, and [carrying] flowers, pearls, and sandalwood.
And when Bālava is present, the Sun holds a bronze vessel together with a water-strainer and partakes of milk-rice.
The blue veil. || 1 ||
219. Now, regarding the nature of the transit that has entered the *kaulava* karaṇa:
having stood upon a boar, wearing variegated garments, bearing *kunda* flowers, and accompanied by laughter, he holds *bakula* blossoms.
Indeed, he who eats boiled rice, whose ornaments are adorned with gold, and who possesses a copper vessel, is truly a Kaula; he is blue-complexioned.
220. Now, the nature of the *saṃkrānti* when entering Taitila:
[the deity] holds a staff in his hand, resembles a *mallikā* flower, and wears yellow garments like yellow pigment (*gorocana*).
The Sun holds an iron vessel, eats cakes, and adorns his body with perfumes and oils; he is blue in color.
221. Now, the nature of the *saṃkrānti* (transit) when one has entered *gara*:
Seated upon *gara*, holding a bow and a *salākā*, with *gomedhika* as his time-measure (*kālakaraṇa*), he drinks milk.
He wears blue garments, carries a vessel of lead, and wears garlands of *japā* flowers. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
222. Now, the nature of the transit from the Vaṇig to the Parvīṣṭa:
this [transit] occurring in the Vaṇig [navāṃśa] is seated upon a buffalo; it resides in a blanket and in divine sandalwood.
The eater of curd-rice (dadhyanna) holds a blue lotus and a sapphire, and carries a vessel made of copper. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
223. Now, the nature of the Bhadrā-praviṣṭa-saṃkrānti:
[The deity] is seated on a horse, holding a spear, clad in a hide, and adorned with the flowers of the mādhavikā.
The Sun holds a vessel of bell-metal filled with turmeric, eats variegated food, and wears golden ornaments. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
224. Now, the nature of the transit (saṃkrānti) entered by the bird:
[The deity] is seated on a dog, holds a noose, wears a patched garment, vermilion, copper-colored robes, and carries a vessel for perfumes.
That Campaka, having gone in the direction of Pīśi, is a bird-eater (guḍāśana) and would be a Ravi-śākunika. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
225. Now, the nature of the transit when it has entered the four-footed [sign]:
wearing garments of leaves, carrying a wooden vessel with a reddish-brown garland, and adorned with *kuśa* grass ornaments.
And the Sun, followed by a ram, having eaten honey, sleeps soundly among the quadrupeds. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
226. Now, the nature of the transit (saṃkrānti) when entering the Nāga [zodiacal sign]:
situated in Taurus, wearing garments of bark, and possessing a clay vessel, weapons, and ornaments of reeds.
Carrying a foul odor like that of a cesspool, he who is known as a "Nāga" eats only what has been offered. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
227. Now, the nature of the *saṃkrānti* that has entered *Kiṃstughna*:
one situated in a rooster, bearing the sign of Taurus (*ṛṣabha*), wearing a bodice, and possessing the red fragrance of the *ketakī* flower.
In the age known as Antya, he will subsist on sugar, wear copper ornaments, and carry a bamboo vessel. || 1 ||
Blue in color. ||1||
228. Now, the nature of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa): (In the Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda)—the Śuklapakṣa is a white man, endowed with matted hair and a crown.
Clad in red garments, with matted hair and reddish-brown eyes, he was adorned with a large tilaka mark.
This [being] places the sun on the right and the orb of the moon on the left.
He is to be worshipped with great devotion on every white and black lunar day.
White in color. || 1 ||
229. Now, the nature of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*): (In the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*) "The dark fortnight is dark-complexioned, yet powerful, wearing white and red garments."
Holding a sun-disk in his right hand and an imperishable lotus in his left. || 1 ||
He is to be worshipped every month according to the specific divisions, for the sake of attaining power.
Black in color. || 1 ||
Now, the gifts to be performed during the bright and dark fortnights—(from the *Dānacintāmaṇi*, based on the *Viṣṇudharmottara*):
"The gift of flowers during the bright fortnight is remembered as bestowing prosperity."
Likewise, the giving of fruits during the dark fortnight yields great fruit. || 1 ||

Now, the qualities produced in the bright and dark fortnights (according to the *Jātakābharaṇa*): one who is born during the bright fortnight possesses a long life, excellent character, prosperity, sons, and a soft body and luster.
If the time of birth occurs during the bright fortnight, then it is a time when the Kali age has been overcome by eternal and true bliss.
One who is prone to idle chatter, weak, fickle, fond of poetry, and arrogant toward his own kin;
For that man whose birth occurs under the other (Mars), there is an extreme excess of mental passion. || 2 ||
230. Now, the nature of the Moon, who presides over the bright fortnight—(according to the Śaiva Āgama):
"Day by day, [he is honored] by the gods, led by Agni, Indra, and Yama..."
Salutations to the one of white form, who is the northern course during the waxing fortnight.
White in color. || 1 ||
231. Now, the nature of the Moon, who presides over the dark fortnight—(according to the Śaiva Āgama):
"Day by day, he nourishes the hosts of gods with a stream of nectar."
Salutations to you, O Asitā, who indeed brings delight to the ancestors. || 1 ||
He is black in color. || 1 ||

Now, regarding the essential natures of the thirty lunar days (*tithis*) divided by the bright and dark fortnights (as stated in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*, verse 232), first, the names of the lunar days (according to the *Śaivāgama*):
I shall describe the days: the first (*pratipad*), the second, and the third.
The fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and likewise the eighth [lunar days]. || 1 ||
And likewise the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [days].
The thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon occurring in the bright fortnight; || 2 ||
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight is likewise considered a mirror, as is the fifteenth.
A month, consisting of thirty days, is formed by both fortnights.
233. First, regarding the nature of the first day of the bright fortnight: the lunar days shall now be described; the first day (pratipad) is ruddy and two-armed.
She who dwells in Aries, whose vessel is power, and who possesses white wings—this is the first lunar day.
The color is reddish-orange. || 1 ||
234. Now, the nature of Śuklā-dvitīyā: She rides upon a swan on the second lunar day, holding a white and non-white book; she is white in complexion. (1)
235. Now, the nature of Śukla-tṛtīyā:
She who stands upon a bull on the third lunar day is fair-complexioned, holding a trident and a vessel in her hands. She is of a fair complexion. (1)
236. Now, the nature of the White Fourth [Day]: She has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and is seated upon golden ground on the fourth day.
Holding an axe and a vessel, she was clothed in garments of bark.
The color of a blue lotus. || 1 ||
237. Now, the nature of Śukla-pañcamī: She has the luster of coral and rests upon a lotus; she is adorned with ornaments for the neck and the head.
The fifth [form] is considered to be bearing a conch, a mudrā, and likewise a vessel.
The color of coral. || 1 ||
238. Now, the nature of Śukla-Ṣaṣṭhī: she holds a peacock, a red lotus, a water-pot, and a cock.
The color is reddish-orange. || 1 ||
239. Now, the nature of Śukla-saptamī:
She is considered to be the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) who is cloud-colored, holds a Brahman’s vessel, and is seated upon a lion.
Meghavarṇā || 1 ||
240. Now, the nature of the White Eighth (Śuklāṣṭamī):
Holding a bell and a vessel, Goṣṭhā is white as cow's milk on the eighth lunar day.
The color of milk. || 1 ||
241. Now, the nature of Śuklanavamī: She is considered to be seated upon a lion, white in complexion, and holding a noose and a vessel.
She is white in color. || 1 ||
242. Now, the nature of Śukladaśamī: She is dark-complexioned, seated upon a buffalo, and holds a staff in her hand.
Black in color. || 1 ||
243. Now, the nature of Śukla-ekādaśī: When the eleventh lunar day is conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras and the signs of Libra and Gemini.
With a white face and reddish eyes, she possesses a luster like that of a sapphire.
Multicolored. || 1 ||
244. Now, the nature of Śukla-dvādaśī:
Dvādaśī is mounted upon Garuḍa, cloud-colored, and holding an enemy as her vessel.
Meghavarṇā || 1 ||
245. Now, the nature of the White Thirteenth Day (Śukla-trayodaśī): The White Thirteenth Day is fair-complexioned, holds a bow and arrows, and is situated in Capricorn.
She is fair-complexioned. || 1 ||
246. Now, the nature of the White Fourteenth [Day]: She has the luster of a pale-red lotus, and her hands hold a fruit and a vessel.
And the fourteenth [digit] has the throat of a blue-necked peacock and eyes like the ceṃdragopa insect. || 1 ||
The color of the *pāṭala* flower. || 1 ||
247 Now, the nature of the full moon of the bright fortnight: she is as white as the full moon, adorned with ornaments of pearls.
In her left hand she holds a jar filled with nectar, and in her right, a vessel of grain.
White in color. || 1 || 15 ||
248. First, the nature of the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapratipat): She has a greyish-black appearance, stands upon a crane, and is four-faced.
With her four arms, she holds a missile, a vessel, a sruva-spoon, and a bow. || 1 ||
Smoke-colored. || 1 ||
249. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇadvitīyā:
Dvitīyā has the luster of a white water-lily (kumuda), stands upon a bull, and holds a staff and a water-pot.
She is white in color. || 1 ||
250. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇatṛtīyā: she is remembered as blue, riding upon Garuḍa on the third lunar day, and holding a conch-shell vessel.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
251. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇacaturthī: She has the luster of black collyrium, stands upon a buffalo, and possesses four arms.
In his right hands, he holds a rosary of beads, a staff, a noose, and a bowl.
Black in color. || 1 ||
252. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇapañcamī: She who dwells in the crocodile, who is as fair as moonlight, the fifth day [personified], and she who holds a water-pot in her hand.
White in color. || 1 ||
253. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇa-ṣaṣṭhī:
she has three eyes, rides upon a peacock, is red in color, and holds a spear and a cock.
She has one face, two arms, and is adorned with a red garment. || 1 ||
She possesses dark blue earrings and is adorned with matted locks and the crescent moon.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
254. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇasaptamī: she is fair-complexioned, seated upon an elephant, two-armed, and holds a vajra and a *yaṃtri*.
She is fair-complexioned. || 1 ||
255. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī: Pretagācāṣṭamī is red, while Kṛṣṇagrīvā is considered inauspicious.
The four-armed goddess holds an akṣamālā, a conch, a sword, and a bowl. || 1 ||
She is red in color. || 1 ||
256. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇanavamī:
she is considered to be dark-complexioned, possessing fangs, and having the *tāla* rhythm of a serpent’s gait.
She is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
257. Now, the form of Kṛṣṇadaśamī: She is seated upon a throne, radiant white, and adorned with yellow earrings.
This [goddess] holds the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), wears yellow garments, and is adorned with a garland of lotuses. || 1 ||
She is of brilliant white complexion. || 1 ||
258. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇaikādaśī:
Ekādaśī is mounted upon a bull, blue in color, and bearing a trident.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
259. Now, the nature of Kṛṣṇadvādaśī: She is copper-colored, mounted upon a chariot, and holds a bowl, a shield, a sword, and a lotus.
This [goddess] wears bright garments on the twelfth day and is adorned with blue earrings.
She is red in color.
260. Now, the nature of the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇatrayodaśī):
she is considered to bear the bud of the Aśoka tree, an arrow, a bow, and a vessel.
The thirteenth [digit] is dark-complexioned, two-armed, and mounted upon a serpent. (1)
Black in color. || 1 ||
261. Now, the nature of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇacaturdaśī):
Kṛṣṇacaturdaśī is seated upon a sword, deep blue in color, and possesses two arms.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
262. Now, the nature of the dark new moon (kṛṣṇāmāvāsyā):
the new moon is to be fashioned with two arms, possessing the luster of emerald.
And she is seated upon a seat of darbha grass, emaciated and holding a bundle of darbha grass.
She is the color of emerald. || 1 ||
Now, the duties to be performed on the lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright and dark fortnights— (from the *Daivajñavilāsa*): On the first day (*pratipad*),
[one should perform] the acquisition of metals, stones, trees, beds, and so forth, as well as agriculture and the art of painting.
The equipment for battle on that lunar day is declared to be the first day (pratipad).
(On the second lunar day)—
the investiture with the sacred thread, marriage processions, and so forth, as well as consecrations, ornaments, and the like.
Rites for nourishment, the consecration of dwellings, and so forth, are prescribed for the second lunar day.
(On the third lunar day)— concerts, instrumental music, all arts and crafts, boundary-marking, tonsure ceremonies, food offerings, and the consecration of houses.
Whatever task is to be done on the second day shall likewise be accomplished on the third day as well. || 1 ||
(On the fourth day)—
the killing or binding of one who has performed empty rites, as well as [the mastery of] weapons, poison, fire, spirits, and so forth, attain accomplishment.
Whatever auspiciousness and merit one has performed goes to destruction month by month. || 1 ||
(On the fifth lunar day)— processions, initiations, marriages, consecrations, rites for peace, and rites for prosperity.
It is declared that [the rite] performed on the fifth lunar day brings long-lasting stability for all undertakings.
(In the sixth [house]:
Service, ornaments, cattle, real estate, war, and buying and selling.
Adorning oneself with ornaments and the administration of all medicinal treatments are prescribed for the sixth lunar day.
(In the seventh [house]):
Building sites, moving in, marriage, consecrations, and so forth—both movable and immovable.
The battle for the ornament of agriculture is proclaimed to take place on the seventh day.
(Another method)— those [planets] mentioned for the second, third, and fifth [houses] are also [considered] here.
All those tasks whatsoever are accomplished on the seventh lunar day.
(On the eighth day:
— [It governs] battle, grain, all types of building sites, arts, livelihoods, quarrels, and all forms of writing.
On the lunar day sacred to Maheśa, all activities such as women, jewels, merchandise, and ornaments—whether they be proper or improper—[should be avoided]. || 1 ||
(Ninth day)—
The seizing and the subduing, as well as the cutting off and the sowing of dissension among enemies.
On the ninth day, one should also cause many rites for the spirits (bhūta-karmāṇi) to be performed.
173) (In the tenth [lunar mansion])—
nourishing rites, auspicious ceremonies, journeys, entries, and water-related activities.
On the tenth day, a wise person should perform visits and household duties.
(On the eleventh day:
Marriage, agriculture, commerce, fasting, and so forth, as well as ornaments.
The laying of foundations, architecture, dance, and so forth are prescribed for the eleventh lunar day.
On the twelfth day,
one should perform rites for prosperity and expenditure, as well as those that promote righteous conduct.
One should perform the Carasthiras on the twelfth lunar day, except for the Śravaṇa nakṣatra. || 1 ||
(On the thirteenth day:
Kṣema, Dhruva, Saubhāgya, Maṅgala, and Nāṭyabhūṣaṇa.
One should likewise have the training of horses and painting performed on the thirteenth day.
On the fourteenth day:
brushing the teeth, oil, meat, a procession, and the investiture with the sacred thread.
On the fourteenth day, one should not perform this nor any other auspicious rite. || 1 ||
On the full moon day:
sacrificial rites, auspicious ceremonies, and nourishing rituals; all architectural works suitable for battle.
The rite, richly adorned with all the ornaments of marriage and craftsmanship, should indeed be performed on the full moon day. || 1 ||
(On the new moon day)— on the new moon day, only the rite for the ancestors should be performed, and no other.
Now, the time of entry into the poisonous nāḍīs on the lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright and dark fortnights—(in the Sārāvalī):
[The sequence is] horse, both, lion, elephant, woman, excellent man, donkey, and excellent man.
Kha-raṃ-va-raṃ, Ka-viṃ-vi-ṣṇuṃ, Rā-laṃ-sā-kaṃ, Vi-yat—these are [the syllables] in sequence. || 1 ||
In another way.
(Regarding the lord of the muhūrta-groups:
The lunar days [are represented by] the arrows, the eight, the seven, the limbs, the five, the Vedas, the eight, and the mountains.
The *ghaṭikās* [of the respective periods] are, in order: ten, three, twelve, fourteen, seven, and eight. (1)

263. Now, the gifts to be performed on the lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*): (From the *Dānacintāmaṇi*, based on the *Viṣṇudharmottara*)—On the first day, flowers; and on the second day, ghee.
On the third [lunar day], [the offering] should be of priyaṅgu seeds, and on the fourth, of silver.
Indeed, by the offering of fruits on the fifth day and by the gift of a bath on the sixth day, [one obtains the fruit].
On the seventh [lunar day], one should give garments, and on the eighth, indeed, molasses.
On the ninth day, however, there is [the offering] of kulmāṣa, and on the tenth day, that of food.
On the eleventh day, [the gift] of gold; on the twelfth day, of clothing. || 3 ||
And on the thirteenth day, [one should offer] white perfumes; immediately after that—
And the gift of excellent food on the fifteenth day yields great fruit.
Now, the qualities of those born on the lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright and dark fortnights— (from the *Kālaprakāśa*): (On the first day)—
A man born on the first day (*pratipat*) shall be wealthy and devoted to merit.
(On the second day):
Viśoka, however, is a poet, handsome, lustful, and fond of quarreling.
But one born on the second lunar day shall become a lord of cattle and grain. || 1 ||
(On the third lunar day)— one who is victorious by nature, rich in wealth, virtuous in character, and possessed of a beautiful form.
One born on the lunar day of Jayā is intelligent, skilled in speech, learned, and pure. || 1 ||
(On the fourth day:
one who acts miserably, is of bad character, has deformed nails, and is a knower of mantras and tantras.
And one born on the fourth lunar day is even-tempered and skilled in daring deeds.
(Fifth stage)—
He is gentle, amorous, skilled in the arts, patient, and affectionate toward those who depend on him.
Born under the lunar mansion of Oṣadhīśa, he was a poet whose conduct was characterized by compassion. || 1 ||
(On the sixth day:)—
The lord of men is invincible, possessed of great courage, renowned, and quick to anger.
On the sixth day, a man is born with a birthmark on his face, back, or thighs. || 1 ||
(In the seventh [bhūmi]):
He is wise, possessed of spiritual strength, illustrious, with limbs free from blemish, and the embodiment of all arts.
The Lord, who is capable of creation, preservation, and destruction, was born on the lunar day sacred to Indra (the twelfth).
(On the eighth day:
One who is joyful yet miserable, deceitful, prosperous, of base conduct, and dominated by phlegm (kapha).
On the eighth day, a man is born who is lustful, possesses a wife, and is generous.
(In the ninth [house]):
He is famous as one fearless of nihilism, long-standing in enmity, and learned.
On the ninth [tithi], a man is born who is brave, possessed of bad sons, and submissive. || 1 ||
(In the tenth house: One who is righteous, wealthy, affluent, and possessed of sons, friends, and a wife.
On the tenth day, a man is born who is ethical, truthful, and learned.
On the eleventh day,
one should possess devotion toward the ancestors, the gods, and others, and be diligent in one's duties and eager for victory.
A man born under the asterism of Govinda becomes wealthy, powerful, and successful in his undertakings. || 1 ||
On the twelfth day:
Kāmī, Kalāpī, Vikrānta, Kānta, Śānta, and Dhanādhipa.
On the twelfth day, a man is born who is wise, generous, happy, and heroic. || 1 ||
(On the thirteenth day)—
one born under Saumya will be desirous, victorious, wise, learned, and of a restless nature.
One born on the thirteenth lunar day becomes wealthy, a patron of dance, and an enjoyer of cattle. || 1 ||
On the fourteenth day:
one who is like a thief, of unsteady mind, not slow [to act], grateful, an atheist, and wealthy.
And one who is devoted to another's wife—such is the birth on the fourteenth day. || 1 ||
(From the *Pañcadaśī*):
One who worships gods, brahmins, and kings shall be an enjoyer of pleasures, possessing cattle, wealth, and grain.
Born on the fifteenth lunar day (Pañcadaśī), he became rich with sons, friends, and a wife.
In another way.
Now, the qualities of those born on the lunar days beginning with the first day of the bright and dark fortnights— (from the *Jātakābharaṇa*): (On the first day)—
one who has a large retinue of followers, is charmingly learned, discerning, adorned with gold and jewels, and possessed of excellent character.
If the birth of a living being occurs on the first lunar day (pratipad), he will possess exceedingly beautiful splendor and will obtain wealth from a ruler of the earth. || 1 ||
(Regarding the second [lunar day]):
A donor who is compassionate, virtuous, and well-provided with prosperity, blessed with the conduct and discernment of a lovely son;
With a serene form and widely sung fame, he shall become born on the second lunar day. || 1 ||
(On the third [lunar day]):
One will be preeminent in desire, possessed of blameless knowledge, endowed with strength, wealthy, and born from a royal family.
A mortal born under the third lunar mansion is habitually inclined toward travel, clever, playful, and full of pride.
(On the fourth day:
There will be the onset of debt; he will be very bold in battle, skilled in combat, yet miserly by nature.
If a non-human being should speak to one whose mind is excessively addicted to gambling, that would be the fourth cause for birth [as a ghost]. 1.
(Fifth stage)—
With his limbs fully developed, accompanied by sons, wife, and friends, and endowed with compassion for all beings.
A man who is honored by kings and is generous shall indeed become a king at the time of his birth on the fifth lunar day. || 1 ||
(On the sixth day:
A man of great luster, true to his promise, possessing the wealth of a son, with long thighs and knees.
One born on the sixth lunar day will possess distinguished fame, be clever, most excellent, yet have a body covered with wounds.
(In the seventh stage)—For he who possesses the eye of wisdom knows the qualities [of others]; his mental disposition is directed toward honoring worthy recipients and the gods.
One who abducts a maiden, one who steals another's wealth, and a man who kills a cow or a Brahmin shall become a consumer of the seventh hell.
(On the eighth [lunar day])—
one who possesses the happiness of various riches and sons, is compassionate, and has attained wealth and prestige through the favor of a ruler of the earth.
For one whose birth occurs on the eighth lunar day, there arises affection for a beloved woman and a fickle disposition of mind. (1)
(p. 176) (On the ninth [day])—
one who is turned away from kinsmen, whose speech is harsh toward those with a single purpose, and who is hostile to the wise.
A man should always be devoted to right conduct if his birth falls on the ninth lunar day.
(In the tenth [month]):
One whose mind is solely intent on Dharma, enriched by great prosperity, with a long neck, and a reciter of many scriptures.
One who is noble-minded, thoroughly disciplined, delightful, and yet possesses desire shall be in the tenth stage. || 1 ||
(On the eleventh day)—
one who is devoted to the worship of gods and brahmins, observant of vows and charitable giving, whose internal organ is perfectly pure, and who is proficient [in these matters].
With a mind solely intent on merit, performing weighty deeds, observing the Ekādaśī vow, emaciated by fire-like austerities, and free from anger—[such a person attains the goal]. || 1 ||
(On the twelfth day:
He is indeed fond of water, habituated to business, and inclined toward the pleasures of dwelling in lowly abodes.
A man who observes the Dvādaśī vow becomes a constant giver of food, attains wealth from the earth, and possesses progeny. || 1 ||
(On the thirteenth day)—
endowed with beauty, characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), liberated, with a long neck, and born from the feet.
Nara was a hero, skillful and exceedingly capable, born on the thirteenth lunar day. || 1 ||
On the fourteenth day— [he is] cruel, exceedingly brave, clever, and laughing, with the movements of his mind agitated by the play of Kandarpa.
A man born on the fourteenth lunar day (Caturdaśī) may be difficult to endure, prone to speaking extreme contradictions, and full of wrath. || 1 ||
(On the full moon day)—
one whose body is exceedingly graceful, who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is accompanied by many young women, and who is constantly filled with joy.

He whose merit arose from the display of exceedingly powerful strength, who was filled with ultimate compassion, who was replete with a multitude of virtues, and whose birth occurred on the full moon day. || 1 ||
On the new moon day:
one who is peaceful, wise, devoted to his father and mother, having acquired wealth through hardship, and desiring to travel back and forth.
A man born under Mānyojaṇa destroys the luster of his kinsmen; he is thin-limbed and possesses a joyful disposition. || 1 ||

Now, the names of the deities presiding over the lunar days (*tithi*) of the bright and dark fortnights—(from the *Kālāmṛta*): Fire, Tvaṣṭṛ, Himādrijā (Pārvatī), Gaṇapati, Sarpa, Kumāra, Arka (the Sun), Gaurīśa (Śiva), Vasu, Nāga, Dharma, Hari, Kāma, Kali, Indu (the Moon), and Pitṛ. These are the lords of all the days.

264. Now, the forms of the deities presiding over the lunar days (*tithi*) of the bright and dark fortnights: first, the meditation on Agni, who presides over the first day (*pratipad*) of both the bright and dark fortnights—Come here, O Agni, in person; you are the carrier of oblations for the gods.
Enter this image for the purpose of worship during the rite of pacification.
Red in color. || 1 ||
Now, the meditation on the deity Tvaṣṭṛ, who presides over the second lunar day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
O Tvaṣṭṛ, creator of the three worlds, purify this earth with your heart.
O Four-faced One, establish your presence within this image.
He is red in color. || 1 ||
266. Now, the meditation on Pārvatī, who presides over the third lunar day of both the bright and dark fortnights: "Come here, O Daughter of the Mountain, to this golden image!"
I pay homage to your lotus feet for the attainment of the supreme goal of human life.
Yellow in color. || 1 ||

267. Now, the meditation on Gajānana, the presiding deity of the fourth lunar day of both the bright and dark fortnights: O destroyer of obstacles, [you who are] like the rising sun, born from the luster of Pārvatī!
"Accept this incomparable image of Gajānana," he said with great respect.
Red in color. || 1 ||
268. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*) of the serpent deity presiding over the fifth day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
O Lord of Serpents, invoked by me, please take your seat upon this image!
I worship your lotus feet for the attainment of all prosperity. || 1 ||
He is of brilliant white complexion. || 1 ||
269. Now, the meditation on the six-faced deity who presides over the sixth day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
"At the conclusion of the salutation to the Six-Faced One, [I place my] hands upon his lotus feet."
O beloved of my heart, come here to this golden image of the vine.
Red in color. || 1 ||
270. Now, the meditation on the Sun, who presides over the seventh day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
O thousand-rayed one, O fierce-beamed one, come before me with respect!
At the conclusion of my prostrations to the embodiment of the three Vedas, I offer them again and again. || 1 ||
He is red in color. || 1 ||
271. Now, the meditation on Sadyojāta, who presides over the white and black eighth days (of the lunar fortnight): "Obeisance to you, O Sadyojāta; obeisance to you, O Lord of Gaurī."
O Śambhu, show me favor; indeed, look upon me with respect.
White in color. || 1 ||
272. Now, the visualization of Durgā, who presides over the ninth day of both the bright and dark fortnights: O Durgā, three-eyed one, whose hair is adorned with a digit of the moon!
O Goddess of the gods, come here quickly and show me your favor.
She is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
p.
178) 273 Now, the meditation on the presiding deity of the tenth lunar day (tithi), whether white or black:
To him whose neck is bent low by the weight of the earth, and whose crown is marked with the foot of Viṣṇu.
Homage, homage be to the Naga; for my image is indeed held with reverence. || 1 ||
Of bright complexion. || 1 ||
274. Now, the meditation on the Dharma-deity who presides over the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of both the bright and dark fortnights:
To her whose essential nature is to be known through the Vedas, and who is the embodiment of sacrifices and other rituals...
Salutation to Dharma, the great one, who is the means for attaining abundant well-being. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
275. Now, the meditation on the deity Hari, who presides over the twelfth day of both the bright and dark fortnights: O Hari, Lord of the three worlds, Beloved of Lakṣmī, Mādhava!
"O Lord, come to this image and quickly grant me your grace. || 1 ||
Golden-hued. || 1 ||
276. Now, the visualization of the deity Manmatha, who presides over the thirteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
"O you who are born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, whose flower-bow is dear to Rati!"
"Come quickly to this image; be gracious to me, O Manmatha! || 1 ||
Golden-colored. || 1 ||
277. Now, the meditation on the personification of the Kali age (kalipuruṣa), who identifies with the fourteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights:
[one should meditate on him] as the proclaimer of all unrighteousness and the instigator of all sins.
I bow to King Kali, who is skilled in deception, for the sake of prosperity. || 1 ||
Black in color. || 1 ||
278. Now, the meditation on the deity Moon, who presides over the full moon: To the one served by all the gods, the lover of Lakṣmī, whose eyes are [the moon].
Salutations to you, who are praised as the Moon, the beloved son of the Ocean of Milk.
White in color. || 1 ||
279. Now, the meditation on the ancestral deities presiding over the new moon:
"Repeated salutations to the ancestors who dwell in the world of the Pitṛs."
Having obtained this golden image, may you always be gracious toward me, O Mother. || 1 ||
They are black in color. || 1 || 30 ||
Now, the characteristics of the days of the week—(from the *Mayūkheḍānakhaṇḍa*, verse 280):
First among them, the nature of Sunday:
Seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in his hand, with a luster equal to the interior of a lotus.
The Sun, together with his wife, should have two arms and be joined to a chariot drawn by seven horses. || 1 ||
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
281. Now, the nature of Monday: He is white, wearing white garments, having ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments.
The moon-crested Lord should be depicted with two arms, holding a mace in his hand and granting boons.
White in color. || 1 ||
282. Now, the nature of Tuesday:
[The deity] wears red garlands and garments, and holds a spear, a trident, and a mace.
The son of the Earth (Mars) should have four arms, be mounted on a ram, and be in the gesture of granting boons. || 1 ||
He is red in color. || 1 ||
283. Now, the nature of Wednesday:
wearing yellow garlands and garments, with a luster like that of the karṇikāra flower.
Buddha holds a sword, a shield, and a mace in his hands; he stands upon a lion and bestows boons. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
284. Now, regarding the essential forms of Jupiter and Venus:
when Jupiter and Venus are pure, they are yellow and white respectively, and both have four arms.
The two [deities] should be depicted holding staffs, granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
The two are golden-colored. || 2 ||
285. Now, the nature of Sthiravāra:
He has the form of a sapphire, holds a trident, bestows boons, and has a vulture as his vehicle. (1)
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted holding arrows and a bow.
Blue in color. || 1 || 7 ||
Now, the rites to be performed on the seven days of the week beginning with Sunday—(according to the *Nāradīya*):
first, regarding Sunday (*ravau*)—one should perform such acts as the coronation of a king, auspicious ceremonies, service, travel, and so forth.
On Sunday, one should enter a dwelling containing medicinal herbs, grains, and other such provisions.
[Some]—
the resorting to conch-shells, pearls, water, silver, trees, sugarcane, and women.
On the day of Puṣpa, Gīta, Kratu, Kṣīra, Kṛṣi, Karma, and Indu. || 1 ||
(Maṅgala):
Poison, fire, imprisonment, theft, treachery, war, and combat.
On a Thursday, one should engage in the work of mines, precious stones, coral, and weapons.
(When Mercury is strong: [One obtains] dance, craftsmanship, arts, song, writing, books, and statues.
On the day of the Moon, who is gentle in his deeds and a conqueror in the battle of disputes. || 1 ||
180) (Regarding the Guru:
Sacrificial rites, prosperity-bringing ceremonies, auspicious acts, and ornaments such as gold and fine garments.
On the day of the tree, the shrub, the creeper, the vehicle, the ritual, and the deity. (1)
(When Venus is strong: dance, song, instrumental music, gold, women, clothing, and ornaments.
On a Saturday, one should perform activities such as trade festivals and the cultivation of cattle and grain.
(On Saturday: Cotton, lead, iron, weapons, stones, poison, sin, liquor, and falsehood.
All stable construction work and the gathering of materials should be undertaken on a Saturday. || 1 || 7 ||
Now, the times of entry into the poison-veins (viṣanāḍī) during the seven days beginning with Sunday—according to the *Muhūrtagaṇapati*:
twenty on Sunday, two on Monday, and twelve on Tuesday; on Wednesday...
If Jupiter is there, there are ten; if Venus, seven; and if Saturn, five. || 1 ||
Twenty-five ghaṭīs beyond that are proclaimed as the lethal nāḍīs.
(In another text:
The twenty-first [digit] belongs to Jupiter, and the twenty-second to Mercury and Mars.
Twenty-five nāḍīs for Venus and the Sun, and eight nāḍīs for Saturn and the Moon. || 1 || 7 ||
Now, the gifts to be performed on the seven days of the week beginning with Sunday—(in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*): "He who, having fashioned the planets out of gold, bestows them upon Brahmins..."
That very jewel, that very grain, and that very colored garment. || 1 ||
On those days, one shall obtain all desires according to one's capacity.
Now, the specific gifts to be performed on each respective day [are described] individually— in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
first, regarding Sunday— on the day of the Sun, one should offer a cake (*apūpa*) combined with salt, clarified butter, and molasses.
By giving it along with gold, a person is not overcome by diseases. || 1 ||
On a Monday— by giving [this] on such a lunar day, one shall obtain good fortune.
On a Tuesday—
by giving wood on a Tuesday— one shall attain the destruction of the enemy.
On Wednesday— on this day,
the giving of toys to children is recommended.
On Thursday,
by the gift of garments, one attains supreme nourishment.
On Friday—
one obtains a white horse by giving [a gift], and sexual pleasure to women by giving [the fruit of] the *śukra*.
On Saturday—by applying oil massage on the day of Saturn, one shall obtain long life. || 8 ||
181) Now, the qualities of those born on the seven days beginning with Sunday—(from the *Jātakābharaṇa* and elsewhere). First, among them, regarding [Sunday] (*ravau*):
A hero with sparse hair who is victorious at the front of battle, dark-red in complexion, possesses an accumulation and provocation of pitta.
The man who gives [this] shall possess great enthusiasm and great vigor, and his crops shall flourish day by day. || 1 ||
Born at dawn, sweet-spoken, knowledgeable in the rules, and always possessing a conduct that provides refuge for lords of men.
A man born under Śītakara is of an even nature toward both pleasure and pain. || 1 ||
In Maṅgala,
one will be fond of excessive crooked speech, a minister to a king, and live by means of clouds.
Endowed with goodness and possessing an exceedingly intense nature, he was born during the day to the delight of the earth. || 1 ||
(When Mercury is strong: One who possesses a handsome form, whose speech is characterized by gentle playfulness, who is illustrious, and endowed with proficiency in the arts.
For he who is born under Jñādinī (Jyeṣṭhā) becomes wise, a knower of qualities, and skilled in the business of trade. || 1 ||
(Regarding the Guru: He is learned, wealthy, endowed with all virtues, charming, and has attained his desires from the king.
And the person whose birth occurs during the period of Jupiter shall become a preeminent teacher and beloved by the people.
In the case of Venus: one with a very dark, yet true and moving mass of hair, possessing a serene appearance, and especially endowed with intelligence.
A man born on a Saturday in the month of Bhādrapada, following the auspicious path, shall wear white garments and possess a joyful disposition. || 1 ||
(When Saturn is present: There is the onset of premature old age; one is deprived of strength, with a frail body like a mere stick.
A person born on the day of Saturn is overcome by the quality of darkness (tamas) and by cruelty. || 1 || 7 ||
Another classification— (from the *Kālaprakāśikā*) regarding the Sun:
one with tawny eyes and yellow hair, skilled in the arts, virtuous, and a lord.
The man born on Sunday has a temperament consisting of bile and wind. || 1 ||
(Someone) with a soft, lovely, and gentle body, possessing arts and small amounts of wealth and grain.
A man born on Monday is phlegmatic and desires the wives of others.
(Maṅgala):
A hero is indeed one who speaks with confidence and performs daring deeds.
A man born on Tuesday will be dwarfish, a thief, and possessed of a great army. || 1 ||
(If Mercury is in the ascendant: One who is an expert in the distinctions of song and instrumental music, and a worshiper of gods and Brahmins.
But the man born on Wednesday is always devoted to the Dharma. || 1 ||
182) (Regarding the Guru: He is possessed of knowledge, has kinsmen, is renowned, virtuous, and beloved by the king.
A man born on a Thursday will be a renouncer, an enjoyer, and a knower of the future.
In Śukra:
one who is beloved due to his natural phlegmatic temperament, a poet, and a teacher skilled in statesmanship.
And the man born on Friday is a consumer of perfumes and garlands. || 1 ||
(When Saturn is there,) one has reddish eyes, large ears, is wealthy, and follows a base path.
A man born on a Saturday will have deformed nails and be slow in his actions. || 1 || 7 ||
Now, the names and forms of the presiding deities of the days: (according to the Śaiva Āgama) Rudra, Durgā, Ṣaṇmukha, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Svarāṭ, and Yama.
The presiding deities of the days of the week, beginning with Sunday, have been proclaimed. || 1 ||
286. First, the nature of Śiva, who presides over Sunday:
mounted upon a bull, holding a trident in his hand, and attended by beautiful women.
Today, with my head bowed low, I prostrate before Śiva, the lord of the sun and the day.
He is of brilliant white complexion. || 1 ||
287. Now, the form of Durgā, who presides over Monday: [I meditate on] Durgā, adorned with eight arms, for the destruction of calamities.
I meditated upon that woman who was intent on tasting blood. || 1 ||
Meghavarṇā. || 1 ||
288. Now, the form of Ṣaṇmukha, who presides over Tuesday:
he has a single arm blazing with power, wears a crown of the moon, and is mounted upon a peacock.
We praise the six-faced one, the lord of Aṅgāraka, the commander of the army of the king of the gods.
Red in color. || 1 ||
289. Now, the form of Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of Wednesday:
he is accompanied by four [emblems]—the radiant crown and the beautiful discus, bow, and mace.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the East (the Sun), the sovereign of the quarters and lord of Wednesday, seated upon an infinite throne with his rays. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
290. Now, the form of Caturmukha, who presides over Thursday:
Caturmukha has four faces and four arms, and he holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a sacred thread (akṣasūtra).
He is considered pure, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is the presiding deity of Thursday.
The color of a lotus. || 1 ||
291. Now, the essential form of Indra, who presides over Friday:
Indra is mounted upon an excellent elephant, holding a thunderbolt, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I take refuge in Him who, with His four hands, holds Śukra, the lord of the intellect. || 1 ||
Yellow in color. || 1 ||
292. Now, the essential form of the goddess who identifies with Monday: she has two arms radiant with noose and staff, and she rides upon a buffalo.
I worship Yama, who has a dark-blue body, is formidable, and is known by the name Śanivāra. || 1 ||
Blue in color. || 1 ||
Now, the forms of the deities presiding over the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*)—(in the *Śaivāgama*).
Regarding the number of stars, forms, worship, and so forth of those lunar mansions—(in the *Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi*).
Therein, the names of the lords of the lunar mansions—(in the *Jyotiṣaratnākara* by Nārada).
The lords of the lunar mansions are, in order: the Aśvins, Yama, Agni, Pitṛs, and Vāyu.
The Moon, Rāhu, Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, the Pitṛs, Aryaman, and Bhaga; || 1 ||
Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Maruts, Indra and Agni, Mitra and Vāsava.
Yātudhāna, Ambu, Viśva, Viṣṇu, Vasu, and Toyapa. || 2 ||
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are thus proclaimed. || 27 ||
293. Now, regarding the Aśvinī constellation:
I praise those two deities of the Aśvins, who are white in color, each possessing two arms.
With lotus-hands holding jars filled with nectar, they have horses as their vehicles.

White in color; the Aśvinī deities preside over: the tethering of elephants and horses, the establishment of chariots and vehicles, cities, medicine, mantras, houses, palaces, and the consecration of gods. (In the *Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi*) [these are the matters].
In the Aśvinī nakṣatra, they perform pilgrimages, consecrations, sacrifices, initiations, tonsure ceremonies, the investiture of the sacred thread, and rites for peace.

Aśvinī consists of three stars—Cū, Ce, and Col—and is horse-headed. Its color is black. It has three stars and the form of a horse's face. Its location is Paṭṭana. It is masculine and belongs to the class of deities. Its face is turned sideways and its eyes are small. It is quickly externalized. Its tree is the Viṣamuṣṭi. Its bird is the Bheruṇḍa. It belongs to the Vaiśya caste, has four feet, and its source is the horse. Its presiding deities are the Aśvins. Its vowel is the letter 'a'. Aśvatthāman was born under this asterism. Beyond fifty ghaṭikās, there are four poisonous nāḍīs (periods). Eating powdered black gram (*māṣapiṣṭa*) is auspicious for setting out toward the east or north. In cases of fever, there are nine days of danger. For its pacification, the ritual for worshipping the deity Aśvinī involves white cloth and sandalwood paste.

An *utpala* flower; *guggulu* incense; an offering (*naivedya*) of milk-rice (*kṣīrānna*). Having worshipped with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) using the mantra "devasya tvā," one should offer oblations (*homa*) one hundred and eight times with milk, sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) while reciting the *Gāyatrī*. One should present a *bali* offering in the northern direction consisting of sandalwood paste, flowers, and black gram (*māṣa*) rice mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*). From the ninth day, one becomes well. Under this asterism (*nakṣatra*), a woman experiencing her first menses will have a son. Under this asterism, sowing seeds, capturing horses, wearing clothes and ornaments, piercing the ears, tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), medical treatment, battle, and so forth are auspicious. The qualities of one born under this asterism are: long-lived; large-bodied; having fine nails; large-eyed; fortunate; handsome; honored by kings; long-faced; possessing a very sharp mind; fond of ornaments; a friend to the wicked; impulsive; fickle; greedy; having a portion of enjoyment (*bhogyāṃśa*); firm in undertakings; marked with a fish on the region of the hips; possessing the quality of laziness; and having a maximum lifespan of eighty-six years. All such details are to be found in this treatise (*grantha*). (In this [section], the subjects are written according to the manuscript.)
294. Now, regarding the lunar mansion Bharaṇī:
[the deity] has two arms blazing with a noose and a staff, and rides upon a buffalo.
One should worship the formidable Yama, who is dark blue in color and seated upon a golden throne. || 1 ||
Blue in color; the deity is Yama. — (In the *Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi*):
[It governs] combat, assault, killing, imprisonment, poison, fire, weapons, piercing, obstacles, and other such fears, as well as acts of violence, robbery, and criminal deeds.
Under the Yamabha constellation, one attains success in incantations for splendor, rites of sorcery, mantras, entering subterranean caverns, and obtaining daughters. || 1 ||

Bharaṇī is the womb (yonī). It consists of three stars: lī, lū, and le. Its color is white. It has three stars. Its shape is triangular. It belongs to the Vaiśya caste. It is female. It belongs to the human class. It is downward-facing. Its gaze is dull. Its location is a village. It is fierce. It is quadrupedal. Its mandala is that of fire. Its tree is the Āmalaka. Its bird is the crow. Its womb is the elephant. Its presiding deity is Yama. Its seed-syllable is the letter *ya*, its vowel is *u*. In this [asterism], Duryodhana was born. Beyond twenty-four *ghaṭikās*, there are four poisonous *nāḍīs* (veins); these must be avoided for a journey. Alternatively, beyond seven *ghaṭikās*, if one eats sesame and rice, it is auspicious for a departure toward the east or north. In the case of fever, there is danger to life; in the final quarter (of the asterism), death occurs; in the third quarter, there is danger for two days; or otherwise, there are eleven days of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*). For its pacification, the following is the procedure for the worship of the deity Yama: blue clothing; red oleander flowers (*karavīra*); black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāgaru*) as fragrance; buffalo-axle incense (*mahiṣākṣī*); and an offering of molasses and rice (*guḍānna*). Having worshipped with the sixteen services using the mantra "Yamāya somaṃ," one should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter one hundred and eight times while reciting the Gāyatrī.
One should offer a bali-oblation in the southern direction— or in the north— with perfumes, garlands, and food mixed with jaggery and sesame seeds.

After eleven days, she becomes comfortable. Under this asterism, a woman who experiences her first menses becomes a widow. Under this asterism, fierce undertakings are commended. The qualities of one born under this asterism are: he is fickle; has many sons; is learned in the scriptures; has a pleasant countenance; is happy; long-lived; truthful; eats well; is dear to women; has deep sleep; has red eyes; has red hair; possesses a body fit for enjoyment; and is marked with sesame seeds and fish on the region of the navel. His maximum lifespan is eighty-six years. All such details are to be found in this treatise. 1.
295. Now, regarding the lunar mansion Kṛttikā: [one should worship] Agni, the deity of Kṛttikā, seated upon a ram-vehicle.
I bow to him who holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons in his four hands. || 1 ||
Red in color; Agni is the deity. — (In the *Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi*):

The rites of establishing the sacred fire (*ādhāna*), the oblation (*homa*), initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*), worship of the fire (*vahnipūjā*), the bestowing of gifts (*dāya*), the depositing [of the fire], and the wearing of prescribed ornaments (*vihitābharaṇa*) and so forth.
Mantras, medicinal herbs, elixirs, and the practices of alchemy succeed when performed with fire under the constellation of Hutāśana (Kṛttikā). || 1 ||

Kṛttikā consists of six stars: Ā, Ī, Ū, E, Kṛttikā. Its color is red. It has six stars. Its shape is like a razor (kṣura). Its gender is feminine. Its class of beings is the Rākṣasa gaṇa. Its source is the goat (aja). Its caste is Brāhmaṇa. It has three feet. Its presiding deity is Agni. It is downward-facing. Its eye is beautiful. It is common (sādhāraṇa). Its stars are equal in number. Its end is Aṃ. Its position is empty. Its mandala is that of fire. Its tree is the Udumbara. Its bird is the peacock. Its vowels are the letters *i* and *u*. Beyond thirty ghaṭikās, there are four poisonous nāḍīs; travel during these is to be avoided. After nineteen ghaṭikās, eating curd and setting out toward the east or north is auspicious. In cases of fever, there is danger to life, or otherwise, misfortune for nine days. To pacify this, the ritual for worshiping the deity Agni is as follows: red cloth, red sandalwood paste, red karavīra flowers, incense of guggulu mixed with ghee, and an offering of rice cooked in ghee. With the mantra "Agnināgnissamidhyate" and "Agneye samidhamahārṣam," one should worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and offer oblations of ghee and honey one hundred and eight times while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra. In this asterism, cruel deeds are recommended. One becomes well after nine days. A woman who experiences her first menses under this asterism will become poor. The qualities of one born under this asterism are: radiant, intelligent, famous, a great eater, fond of women, powerful, possessing wealth earned by his own arms, yet a partaker of suffering.
He has white hair; his body is deep-set; he is marked with a fish on his left side; his maximum lifespan is eighty years—all such details are to be found in this very text. || 1 ||
296. Now, regarding the Rohiṇī asterism:
Prajāpati has four arms and holds a water-pot and a rosary.
May the deities Śuddhā and Rohiṇī, who grant boons and fearlessness, protect me. || 1 ||

The color is pale red (*pāṭalavarṇa*); the presiding deity is Brahmā. (In the *Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi*, one should perform the rites for the consecration of a king, the entry into a house, palace, or city, fire-offerings (*homa*), propitiatory ceremonies (*śāntika*), and the marriage ritual.)

In the asterism of Rohiṇī (Abjaja), there is the cultivation of rice and sugarcane, the tying of trees for ritual purposes, the yoking of draft animals, and the wearing of new garments, ornaments, and jewelry. || 1 ||

Rohiṇī has the shape of a cart (śakaṭa). Its seed-syllables are *ū*, *vā*, *vī*, *vū*. It is black in color. It consists of five stars. Its form is that of a cart. It is masculine.
