Jaṭāyu was born under this asterism. Beyond twenty-four *ghaṭikās*, there are four *viṣanāḍīs*. It is auspicious for a journey toward the northeast after preparing an offering of rice grains. In cases of fever, there is danger for seven days. To pacify it, the procedure for worshiping the deity Ahirbudhnya is as follows: white cloth; agallochum (*agarū*) incense; *śatapatra* flower; guggulu resin with ghee as incense; an offering (*naivedya*) of molasses and boiled rice. Having performed worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) using the mantra "Viṣṇuryonim," one should offer oblations (*homa*) one hundred and eight times with black gram mixed with milk and ghee while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra. One should present an offering of molasses and rice along with perfumes and garlands. Within seven days, one becomes well. Under this asterism, a woman experiencing her first menses becomes fortunate and possessed of sons. Under this asterism, rites such as conception (*ṛtu*), the *sīmanta*, *puṃsavana*, naming, first feeding (*annaprāśana*), ear-piercing, tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), graduation (*samāvartana*), adorning with ornaments, royal consecration, propitiatory (*śāntika*) and nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rites, the bringing of the throne and the fourfold army, mounting a palanquin, establishing a bed, entering a city, sowing seeds, and the collection of wealth and grain are all highly recommended. The qualities of one born under this asterism are: skilled in action; fond of dance and song; beloved by young women; courageous; valorous; long-sighted in intellect; terrifying to people; wealthy; excessively indulgent; fond of perfumes and garlands; slow-moving; hunchbacked; hateful toward his own wife; a reviler of kinsmen; and a maximum lifespan of ninety years. All such details are to be found in this entire treatise. 1.
320. Now, for the sake of prosperity, one should constantly worship Pūṣan and Revatī, the lord of the Revatī constellation.
His hands are radiant with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.
The color is lotus-like; the presiding deity is Pūṣan. — [In the Nakṣatracūḍāmaṇi:
Initiations, the rite of shaving, marriage, and the settling of dwellings such as houses and cities.
Even the mounting of elephants, horses, and so forth is said to be auspicious during the nakṣatra of Puṣya.
Revatī has the form of a fish and possesses thirty-two [stars]. She is Revatī; her color is red; she has thirty-two stars; her shape is that of a fish. (p. 208)

[The asterism] Revatī: its presiding deity is the host of gods (*devagaṇa*); it is feminine; its source is the womb of the elephant; its presiding deity is Pūṣan; it consists of four feet; its face is turned sideways; its eyes are blind; it is soft; it is external; its stars are equal in number; its position is empty; its mandala is that of Varuṇa; its tree is the *madhūka*; its bird is the peacock; its letter is the syllable *kṣa*. In this [asterism], Abhimanyu was born. Beyond thirty *ghaṭikās*, there are four poisonous *nāḍīs*. Eating flour (*piṣṭa*) during travel toward the east or north is auspicious. In case of fever, death occurs within a month. For its pacification, the procedure for the worship of the deity Pūṣan is as follows: a garment of ruby-red color; red sandalwood paste as fragrance; *mandāra* flowers; *guggulu* incense; an offering (*naivedya*) of sesame-rice; one should worship with the sixteen services using the mantra "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" and offer oblations (*homa*) one hundred and eight times with sesame, rice, and clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī. One should present an offering of sesame-rice along with perfumes and garlands. After a month, one becomes well. In this asterism, a woman experiencing her first menses will have a son. In this asterism, the following auspicious rites are recommended: the *ṛtu* (conception), *puṃsavana* (male-impregnation), naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), first feeding (*annaprāśana*), tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), study of the Vedas and Shastras, beginning of letters, oil massage, wearing of clothes and ornaments, the return home (*samāvartana*), coronation of a king, audience with a king, mounting the throne, palanquin, riding elephants and horses, propitiatory (*śāntika*) and nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) rites, great festivals, practice of mantras, medicine, performance of dance, song, and instrumental music, sowing of seeds, journeys, and so forth. The qualities of one born in this asterism: endowed with good fortune; radiant; large-bodied; complete in limbs; prone to anger; an enjoyer of pleasures; a spender of wealth; learned; long-lived; surrounded by various enemies; bilious (*pittavat*); a giver of food; envious; a performer of cruel deeds; steadfast; a traveler to foreign lands; red-haired; marked slightly with sesame and fish; his maximum lifespan is eighty-four years. All such details are to be found in this entire treatise. 1, 27.

Now, the tasks to be performed during the twenty-seven lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā— (according to another source, the *Nāradīya*, and in the *Dānacintāmaṇi* and *Mahābhārata* regarding *Kṛttikā*):
[One should undertake] the consecration of the sacred fire (*agnyādhāna*), the taking up of missiles and weapons, and fierce matters concerning peace or war.
Battles, medicinal preparations, musical performances, and auspicious rites are recommended when the fire asterism (Kṛttikā) is ascendant.
(Regarding the gift:
O highly fortunate Kṛttikā, [one should offer] milk-rice with excellent clarified butter.
By satisfying virtuous brāhmaṇas, one attains unsurpassed worlds.
209) (In Rohiṇī:
The parting of the hair, marriage, clothing, ornaments, and stable undertakings [should be performed].
The laying of the foundation for an elephant, the consecration of a king, and the installation of a horse are auspicious when performed under the constellation Brahmā (Jyeṣṭhā).
(Regarding charity)—
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should give gifts of beans, food, and clarified butter.
Milk should be given as a drink to the twice-born for the sake of discharging one's debt.
Under Mṛgaśīrṣa:
the rites of consecration, ornamentation, marriage, parting the hair, and the investiture of the sacred thread.
Shaving, as well as journeys by elephant, camel, or horse, are recommended during the lunar mansion of Mṛgaśiras.
(Regarding giving:
A man should give a milch cow together with her calf under the lunar mansion presided over by Soma.
Having given [this], one abiding in a divine celestial chariot attains the unsurpassed heaven. || 1 ||
Under Ārdrā:
raising a banner, constructing an archway, engaging in battle, building a wall, and employing weapons are auspicious.
In the Śārva [year], the conjunctions, military expeditions, sacrificial pavilions, tastes, and so forth, are auspicious. || 1 ||
(Regarding giving):
Having given kṛsara mixed with oil under the constellation Ārdrā, one should remain composed.
A man crosses over difficult terrains and mountains with edges as sharp as razors.
In Punarvasu:
the installation of images, the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony, the acquisition of clothing, the consecration of a dwelling, and the initiation (*upanayana*).
Under the asterism Āditi (Pūrvaphalgunī), one should perform the rites of shaving and weapons, as well as obtain grain and ornaments. || 1 ||
(Giving)
— having given a cooked offering filled with ghee during the Puṣya and Punarvasu constellations.
He is born into a family that is illustrious, endowed with beauty, and possesses abundant food. || 1 || 1 ||
(Puṣya)— Departure, consecration, the simantonnayana rite, the tying of the sacred thread, and entry [into a new house].
All rites performed during the asterism of Devejya (Jupiter) are auspicious, provided they are done without the payment of taxes. || 1 ||
(Regarding giving):
By giving gold, whether wrought or unwrought, during the Puṣya asterism, one attains great merit.
In worlds devoid of light, he shines like the moon. || 1 || 1 ||
(At Āśleṣā) —
[One gains] addiction to nectar, gambling, alchemy, medicinal herbs, and battle.
In the Bhujaṅga-lagna (Cancer), there is auspiciousness for disputes, trade, and commerce. || 1 ||
(Regarding giving)—
under Āśleṣā, one gives a son, or likewise silver, or a bull.
Freed from all fear, he is born possessed of the Teacher. || 1 || 1 ||
(When the moon is) in Maghā—
agriculture, trade, cattle, grain, medical instruments, and so forth [are auspicious].
All activities such as marriage, dancing, and singing should be performed under a lunar mansion presided over by the ancestors (Pitṛs).
(Regarding giving)—
a man [should offer] increasing vessels filled with sesame seeds under the Maghā asterism.
By giving [this], one is born indeed possessing cattle and endowed with sons. || 1 || 1 ||
(When the moon is in Pūrvaphalgunī:
There will be disputes, poisons, weapons, fire, and fierce, terrible crocodiles or adversaries.
In the first three [periods], all actions should be performed, including the sale of meat. || 1 ||
(Regarding giving: Having fasted, one should give to Brahmins during the time of the Pūrvaphalgunī constellation.
By giving edible foods mixed with molasses, one attains good fortune.
210) (Under Uttaraphalgunī)—
the consecration with garments, the *sīmantonnayana*, marriage, and the binding of the sacred thread (*vratabandhana*).
Entering, establishing, horses, elephants, and architecture—these three [are governed by] Uttara. || 1 ||
(As for the gift:
rice mixed with flour, combined with ghee and milk, according to the prescribed ritual.
Having given [a gift] in the region of Uttara, one is glorified in the heavenly world. || 1 ||
Or rather, that gift which is bestowed by men upon a superior object.
It is certain that in this world, it becomes eternally fruitful and infinite. || 2 || 1 ||
(Haste)— [the rites of] consecration,
marriage, the parting of the hair, the journey, the investiture of the sacred thread, and initiation.
Shaving, consecrations, and the wearing of ornaments are auspicious during the periods of Karmabhānu.
(Generosity)—
Having fasted, he indeed gave a chariot drawn by four elephants into his hand.
A man crosses over difficult terrains and even mountains with edges as sharp as razors.
(Under Citrā)— The entry [of a new house],
the wearing of new clothes, the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony, the consecration of images, and the binding of the sacred thread (*vratibandhana*).
There should be the sciences of Tvāṣṭra and Bheṣaja, as well as the craft of shaving and ornamentation. || 1 ||
(Regarding giving):
O Bhārata, by giving a bull and a pair of meritorious cows under the asterism Citrā, one attains [great merit].
He wanders in the world of the Apsarases and delights in the Nandana grove.
(Under Svāti) – One may perform the installation of deities,
the investiture of the sacred thread, marriage, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and the wearing of ornaments.
In the Aśvinī nakṣatra, one should undertake activities concerning cattle, water, horses, elephants, agriculture, and the work of milking. || 1 ||
(Dāna)—
Now, having given wealth under the Svātī asterism, whatever is most dear to oneself [should be given].
He attains auspicious worlds and great fame even in this very world. || 1 || 1 ||
(When the moon is in Viśākhā:
There will be trade in clothing and ornaments, and the accumulation of wealth, grain, and other goods.
Under the asterism Indrāgnibha (Jyeṣṭhā), one should perform dancing, singing, crafts, and the art of writing.
(Generosity)—
Having given a bull and a milch cow that yields milk during the asterism of Viśākhā.
And a cart together with its yoke-halter, filled with grain and provided with clothing. || 1 ||
He gratifies the ancestors and the gods, and after death, he attains infinity.
He does not encounter difficulties and goes to the heavenly world. || 2 ||
Having given what has been prescribed to the Brahmins, one obtains the desired fruits.
And it is certain that one does not incur the afflictions pertaining to the hells. || 3 || 1 ||
(In Anurādhā:
Auspicious rites such as entering a new home, consecrating a deity, marriage, and the tying of the sacred thread are performed.
In the Maitra nakṣatra (Anurādhā), [one should undertake] clothing, ornaments, real estate, and so forth, as well as peace and war.
(Dāna)—
Under Anurādhā, one who has fasted should give a fine upper garment as a superior cloth-offering.
Even by giving for a hundred yugas, a man is glorified in heaven.
(When Jyeṣṭhā is ascendant:
— The business of hair-cutting, missiles, weapons, trade, and work involving cattle, buffaloes, and water.
Indrabhūti [perceived] dance, instrumental music, the arts, and the properties of metals, stones, and eyes. || 1 ||
(Dāna)—
Having given black potherbs along with radishes to the Brahmins, he becomes immortal.
By [worshipping] Jyeṣṭhā, one destroys death and attains the desired state. || 1 || 1 ||
(In the Mūla asterism:
marriage, agriculture, trade, fierce battles, and medicine.
Dancing, acting, crafts, weaponry, treaties, war, and writing. || 1 ||
(Dāna)—
Having given root and fruit to the Brahmins with a concentrated mind.
O God, he pleases his own ancestors and attains his desired goal. || 1 ||
(When the moon is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā:

In Gemini, there is an abundance of buffaloes, sheep, and service to kings. || 1 ||
In Cancer: the construction of ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as the damming and releasing of water.
Whatever nourishing rite (pauṣṭika-karma) there may be, all of it succeeds during the month of Karkaṭa.
(Sihme) — agriculture, trade, merchandise, and so forth; service to the king and royal consecration.
One should always perform the rites concerning the mines of the elements and so forth during the rising of Leo.
In the case of a maiden: [the results pertain to] ornaments, auspicious rites, medicinal knowledge, merchandise, crafts, and so forth.
In matters of marriage, rites for peace and prosperity, and [the acquisition of] elephants, horses, camels, and daughters; || 1 ||
(In the case of Libra:)— In the rising of Libra, there is the work of refining metals, trade, and journeys.
And all things dependent upon the scales and the balance-bowls become perfected. || 1 ||
In Scorpio: fierce, reckless, and violent deeds, as well as service to the king and royal consecration.
Acts of theft involving steady undertakings should be performed during the rising of Scorpio.
(In the case of the bow: The arts of warfare, craftsmanship, painting, and manual skills are served by Maṅgalā.
The manufacture of garments and weapons, as well as agriculture and trade, should be undertaken when the bow (Kārmuka) rises. || 1 ||
In Makara,
one should perform the binding and releasing of waters, as well as work related to its mechanical devices.
There would be the apprehension of women, quadrupeds, and so forth, at the rising of Mṛgaśiras. || 1 ||
(In the Kumbha [sign])— whatever there is, such as horses, agriculture, crafts, and so forth, as well as water, jewels, and the like.
The installation of stable ornaments, the laying of foundations, and so forth, should be performed during the rising of the pitcher (ghaṭodaya).
In Pisces:
the binding of water, the releasing of water, journeys, jewels, and other ornaments—such are the activities.
The acquisition of chariots, horses, camels, and cattle is most excellent when the ascendant is Pisces. || 1 || 12 ||
435. Now, the forms of the zodiac signs (*rāśis*)—(from the *Bṛhajjātaka*):
A pair of fish, a water-jar, a man and woman, a man with a staff, a man with a lute, an archer, a man with the hindquarters of a horse, a crocodile, and a deer-faced being.
The planets Taurus, Sagittarius, Scorpio, and Pisces, as well as all the remaining signs beginning with Virgo, are like their own names; and all the sky-goers (planets) are likewise. || 1 || 12 ||
Now, the nature of the decans (*drekkāṇa*) beginning with Aries— (from the *Bṛhajjātaka*,
verse 436). First, among those, the natures of the first, second, and third decans of Aries— (the first):
Krishna, his waist wrapped in black cloth, was like Shakti himself in providing protection.
The fierce man with blood-red eyes holds aloft a raised battle-axe. || 1 ||
The person is black in color. || 1 ||
(Second:
Her mind is attached to red garments and ornaments; she has a pot-belly, a face like that of a horse, and is afflicted by thirst.
And according to the teaching of the Yavanas, the form of the middle decan of Aries consists of one foot and one half-foot. || 1 ||
Woman: red in color. || 2 ||
(Third:
Krūra, Kalājña, Kapila, Kriyārthin, Bhagnavrata, and Udyatadaṇḍahasta.
Caṇḍa wears red garments; he is declared to be the third part, the ram. || 1 ||
The person is tawny-colored. || 3 || 1 ||

437. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇas*) of Taurus: (The first)—one with a wretched, shorn head of hair, a body like a broken jar, wearing a burnt garment, thirsty, and having a mind fixed on food.
Gaurī desires ornaments; this is the first form of the Bull. || 1 ||
The woman has a complexion like that of a cow. || 1 ||
(Second)—
and skilled in fields, grain, houses, cows, arts, knowledge, plows, axes, and carts.
Bearing a burden like that of a bull, intent on eating, with a face like a goat and clad in dirty rags. || 1 ||
The person is white in color. || 2 ||
(Third)—
He whose body is like that of an elephant, whose tusks are white, whose feet are like those of a śarabha, and whose form is tawny.
With hair not matted and a mind free from agitation, he has reached the presence of the most excellent Bull. || 1 ||
The person is golden-colored. || 3 || 2 ||
p.
243) 438 Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇa*) of Gemini—
(the first):—
A woman endowed with a beautiful form, who is attentive to her duties of maintenance, desires to resort to a needle.
Those who know [the matter] say that the first [son] born to a woman of low lineage during her fertile period, who has soft and long arms, belongs to the third abode. || 1 ||
A woman; yellowish-green in color. 1.
(The second:
Standing in the garden, clad in armor, bearing a bow and arrows, and possessing weapons, he is mounted upon Garuḍa with his wings raised high.
By means of the ornament of the net of play, he makes that mind [his own] in the midst of the pair. || 1 ||
The person is yellowish-green in color. || 2 ||
(Third)— Adorned with many jewels like Varuṇa, equipped with a quiver, armor, and a bow.
He was an expert in the arts of dance and instrumental music, and a composer of poetry at the conclusion of the sign of Gemini.
The person is golden-colored. || 3 ||
439. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decanates (*dekkāṇa*) of Cancer:
(The first)—A two-legged creature that eats leaves, roots, and fruits, with the feet of a *śarabha* in the Malaya forest.
They declare that the first form in the sign of Cancer has a face like a boar's and ears like those of a horse.
The person is the color of the trumpet-flower (pāṭala). 1.
(Second)—
One who is occupied with the head-like [splendor] worshipped by Padmā cries out upon the surface of the forest, harsh for women.
And she is seated upon the branch and foliage of the Palāśa tree, situated in the middle of the zodiac sign known as Karkaṭaka. || 1 ||
A woman; the color of the *pāṭala* flower. 2.
(Third)—
One who has boarded a ship for the ocean to provide for his wife's maintenance goes forth enveloped by a serpent.
Adorned with golden ornaments, he has a flat face and has gone to the end of Cancer. || 1 ||
The person is the color of a lotus. || 3 || 4 ||
440 Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇas*) of Leo:
(The first)— a vulture, a jackal, and a monkey atop a *śālmali* tree, clothed in soiled garments.
This first form, in the likeness of a lion, is said to arise from the separation from one's mother and father. || 1 ||
The person is smoke-gray in color. || 1 ||
(The second:
A man with the form of a horse, wearing a crest of white garlands, bears the strength of a black antelope skin.
Like an unassailable lion with his bow drawn, he stood in the midst of the kings like a lord of beasts with his lowered crest.
The person is smoke-gray in color. || 2 ||
(Third verse)—
One who acts like an ignorant monkey bears punishment, blows from a weapon, and [the loss of] his prey.
A man with a beard and curly hair, possessing three parts at the end like that of the lord of beasts (a lion), [is auspicious]. || 1 ||
The Puruṣa is smoke-colored and pale. || 3 || 5 ||
441. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇas*) of Virgo:
(The first)—a maiden with her limbs covered in long garments, [standing] before a jar strewn with flowers.
Desiring union with clothing and wealth, the young maiden first goes to the family of her father-in-law.
The woman has variegated colors. || 1 ||
(Second)—
A man, dark-complexioned, holding a pen, with his head wrapped in a cloth and his body smeared with ashes.
He carries a large bow, and his body is covered with hair; such is the middle type. || 1 ||
The person is dark-complexioned. || 2 ||
(Third:)— Clad in a fore-edge silk garment washed by Gaurī, with her hand raised holding a water-pot.
They say that for the construction of a temple, one should take the final third part of the ground from where women have not been active.
Golden-colored. || 3 || 6 ||

442. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇa*) of Libra: (The first)—A man standing in the middle of a marketplace stall, a Libra-ascendant person skilled in weighing and measuring, holding a balance in his hand.
He considers the vessel, and the Yavanas first state its value according to the scale. || 1 ||
The person is black in color. || 1 ||
(Second)—
Having let go of the jar and rushed out, the foolish man desires to seize the vulture.
Hungry and longing for his wife and children, he stood amidst the merchants, weighing them in his mind.
The person is black in color. || 2 ||
(Third)—
He stands there, striking terror, adorned with jewels in the forest, bearing a golden quiver and a shield.
A man bearing the form of a monkey and wielding a bow is described by the Yavanas as occurring at the end of Libra. || 1 ||
The person is black in color. || 3 || 7 ||
443. Now, the forms of the first, second, and third decans (drekkāṇas) of Scorpio: A woman, adorned with garments and ornaments, comes from the great ocean to the shore.
The first [period] belongs to the sign of Scorpio; it is delightful, with feet bound by crawling snakes that have fallen from their place. || 1 ||
A woman, golden-colored. || 1 ||
(Second:)—
For the sake of her husband, she whose body is entwined by serpents longs for the pleasures of various positions.
They describe a body resembling a tortoise-shell, with the form of a scorpion in the middle. || 1 ||
A woman, golden-colored. || 2 ||
(Third)— One with a face like a broad, flat tortoise, causing terror to dogs, deer, jackals, and boars.
The lord of beasts (Leo) protects the region of Malayākara, and Scorpio is situated at the end. || 1 ||
The person is golden-colored. || 3 ||
444. Now, the forms of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇas*) of Sagittarius (*dhanuḥ*):
(The first)—a human-faced being with a body like that of a horse, holding a bow, standing in an extensive hermitage.
O ascetic, wander about protecting those engaged in their sacred rites; let the front portion of my bow remain as it was before. || 1 ||
The person is tawny in color. || 1 ||
(Second)—
She of beautiful form sits upon an auspicious seat, her complexion like that of a charming *caṃpaka* flower.
The middle third of the bow, which does not strike the jewels of the ocean, is prescribed [as the range]. || 1 ||
Woman; golden-colored. || 2 ||
(Third:
Seated, holding a staff, he has the luster of campaka flowers growing on a *kūrcīna* tree, and is adorned with a *vārāsana* [necklace].
It bears silken garments and a deerskin; this is the third form of the constellation Dhanuṣ. || 1 ||
The person is golden-colored. || 3 || 9 ||
445. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans of Capricorn: (The first)—having a face like that of a hairy crocodile with tusks, and a body resembling that of a boar.
Therein is the first Makara, fierce-faced, holding a net and a binding cord. || 1 ||
The person is of variegated color. || 1 ||
(The second:)—
A dark-complexioned woman with eyes as long as lotus petals, skilled in the arts, was searching for paintings.
In the midst of the Makara, she was pointed out by a woman with iron ears adorned with ornaments. || 1 ||
Woman: dark-complexioned. || 2 ||
(Third):
Equipped with a body like that of a Kinnara, a quiver, a bow, and armor.
The last [sign] of the zodiacal sign Capricorn (makara-rāśi) carries upon its shoulder a pitcher adorned with jewels. || 1 ||
The person is of variegated color. 3.10.
p.
246) 446 Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decans (*drekkāṇa*) of Aquarius (*kumbha*):
(the first)—
Sukambala’s mind was distracted by oil, wine, water, food, and meat.
Clad in a silkworm's cocoon, covered in a deerskin, with a face like a vulture, he was one who had not yet attained the [first] stage. || 1 ||
The Puruṣa is tawny-colored. || 1 ||
(Second)—
O you who bring iron and other metals from the forest of the Anga country, where the grassy meadows have been scorched by the burning of the cart!
The middle [type] has his head covered with dirty cloth and carries vessels upon it. || 1 ||
The woman is tawny-colored. || 2 ||
(Third)—
Dark-complexioned, with lotuses for ears and wearing a crown, he bears bark, leaves, resin, and fruit.
The potter, having reached the final stage, distributes vessels mixed with various metals such as bronze and iron.
A man, dark-complexioned. || 3 || 11 ||
447. Now, the natures of the first, second, and third decanates (drekkāṇas) of Pisces: (The first)—with hands occupied by garlands, vessels, pearls, gems, and shells, and well-adorned with ornaments.
For the sake of adorning his wife, he went by boat upon the ocean, like a fish leaping into the waters.
The person is white in color. || 1 ||
(Second)—
Accompanied by her retinue, she approaches the ship with its banners and flags raised very high, and it proceeds toward the shore of the ocean.
A woman whose complexion resembles the campaka flower is declared by the sages to be a third part of a fish; the second [part] is likewise described. || 1 ||
A woman; golden-colored. || 2 ||
(Third):
A man in a forest, naked and with his limbs entwined by a serpent near a chasm.
With his inner self agitated by the fire of thieves, he cries out in distress as he reaches the final stage of the fish.
The person is white in color. || 3 || 12 ||
448. Now, the nature of the day and night—(in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
"And here, that which is called day and night is Kṛṣṇagrīva, who has two heads."
He has two arms reaching from his navel to the tips of his feet, and he has long, lizard-like fingers. || 1 ||
He has the moon as his crest-jewel upon matted locks, and he is tawny-eyed with beautiful eyes.
Adorned with a circle of eyebrows and locks of hair, he was clothed in black and white garments.
He holds the sun in his right hand and likewise the moon in his left.
For the sake of the fulfillment of one's sacrifices and charitable works, he should be worshipped by the wise. || 3 ||
Golden-hued. || 1 ||
449. Now, the true nature of Divā (the Day-Goddess) [as described in the *Madanaratna*]:
I bow to her who has two arms, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is seated upon a lotus.
The god was wearing white garments and bore matted hair and bark clothing. || 1 ||
He was mounted upon a pigeon and adorned with every kind of ornament.
One should visualize [the deity] with a lotus-like face, white in color, and possessing a radiant form. || 2 ||
The Sun is well known as the presiding deity of the day, like the Sun situated among the nine planets. (Ni. 5) || 1 ||
Now, the duties to be performed during the day—(according to Mādhavīya):
naming, the *puṃsavana* rite, shaving, sowing seeds, the installation [of the sacred fire], and so forth.
The consecration of a king, the first eating of solid food, the commencement of learning, and the initiation ceremony (upanayana). || 1 ||
The house-entry ceremony, the sīmantonnayana, the śrāddha, and others are prescribed for the daytime.
450. Now, the nature of Rātri—(in the Madanaratna):
She has four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, her face resembles the moon.
One should meditate upon Rātri, who has a jackal as her vehicle and is endowed with the digit of the moon.
The deity of that [day] is the Moon, as is well known, like the Moon among the nine planets. (Ni. 5) || 1 ||
Now, the duties to be performed at night—(from the *Smṛtimuktāphala*, *Dharmaśāstra*): the meeting with a friend, the fire-ritual, the entry for the bridegroom, and the marriage ceremony.
The depositing of the embryo, the offering of oblations, the worship of deities, the consecration of the water-pot, and indeed rites of sorcery; || 1 ||
And when there is affliction by Piśācas, one should perform the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) once [the child] has been born.
451. Now Bharadvāja states the essential natures of the *saṃdhyās* (in the *Mādhavīya*):
"The *paiśācī* is the western *saṃdhyā*, while the eastern *saṃdhyā* is said to be *raudrikī*."
The Rākṣasī [period] occurs at midnight, while the Brāhmī is said to be at midday. || 1 || 4 ||
Now, Manu (in the *Bhaṭṭabhāskarīya*) declares the activities to be avoided during the twilights:
"One should avoid these four actions during the twilight."
Food, sexual intercourse, sleep, and likewise the constant practice of self-study. || 1 ||
Disease arises from food, and miscarriage results from sexual intercourse.
From sleep, misfortune arises; from Vedic study, the depletion of life-span occurs. || 2 ||
452. Now, the nature of the morning twilight (as described in the Śekharatantra of the Śaiva Āgama):
"I bow to the auspicious morning twilight, which bears the orb of the sun as its hand."
A young woman with a white and reddish luster, adorned with various ornaments. || 1 ||
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
p.
248) 453 Now, the nature of the evening twilight—(in the *Śaivāgama-śekhara*):
"I bow to the evening twilight, which possesses the rays of the orb of the moon."
She has a complexion reddish like saffron, a prominent nose, and is adorned with variegated ornaments. || 1 ||
The color of vermilion. || 1 ||
454. Now, the true form of Mahākāla (according to the Śaiva Āgama): [He is] Kāla with a scattered face, terrifying, and the subduer of enemies.
I bow my head to the Lord, whose hands hold a noose and whose body hair consists of lotuses. || 1 ||
He is black in color. || 1 ||
455. Now, the true form of Ugradevatā (according to the Śaiva Āgama):
[She has] a terrifying face, three deformed eyes, and is fierce, seated upon a tiger.
I meditate upon him holding a trident and a deer in his hands, [and] in his heart. || 1 ||
Red in color. || 1 ||
456. Now, the nature of the deity of Death (according to the Śaiva Āgama):
Her lotus-like hands manifest as holding a noose, a sword, a goad, and a mace.
I bow to him whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, who is Death himself, and who has a buffalo as his vehicle.
Blue in color. || 1 ||
457. Now, the essential form of Kuhū—(in the Rudrayāmala): I meditate upon the goddess Kuhū, whose form is terrifying and who is born from Yama.
Her hair-ends were like blazing fire, and her radiance was equal to a dark blue cloud.
Adorned with ornaments made of iron, she was of terrifying form.
Her face is formidable with fangs, and she is seated upon a buffalo. || 2 ||
Three-eyed, with eight hands holding a sword, a trident, a goad, and a boon-granting gesture;
Indeed, [he holds] the shield, fire, fearlessness, and the serpent, on the right and left sides respectively.
She possessed a massive body and had eyebrows that were arched and knitted together in a frown.
I bow down to her whose form arises from the poison of the Kuhu-Kuhu snake.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
458. Now, the true nature of Kṛtyā—(in the *Pāñcarātra*):
She is terrifying with a trident in her hands and possesses seven heads and three feet.
With her tongue, red and blazing, she was licking her own mouth.
As if vomiting from his two eyes the sacrificial fire drenched with clarified butter.
Wearing a garland of human bones and having serpents as her girdle. || 2 ||
Accompanied by Kapālakuṇḍalā, she was laughing and terrifying.
A staff, a bell, as well as a winnowing basket, a broom, a noose, and a small water-pot.
She was bearing down with her two hanging breasts, and her hair was disheveled.
She was mounted upon the shoulders of a man, appearing like thick darkness.
And she stands within a circle of sparks, terrifying with her released fury.
Thus, I bow to the Kṛtyā who assumes such a form and destroys enemies. || 5 ||
Black in color. || 1 ||
459. Now, the true nature of Mahākṛtyā—(in the Śābaratantra): She is black in color, of massive body, with black, curly hair.
In the lower right hand is a sword, and likewise, in the upper right hand is an axe.
In the upper left hand there is always a goad, and in the lower left hand a mace.
And one should worship her who bears a great form, the destroyer of enemies.
She is black in color. || 1 ||
460. Now, the true form of Rākā—(in the Rudrayāmala):
She resembles a crystal, is mounted upon a hare, and possesses four arms.
She displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, the digit of nectar, and holds the vessel of nectar.
May she, adorned with a pearl necklace, protect [us] always, bestowing [all blessings].
White in color. || 1 ||
461. Now, the true form of Sinīvālī (according to the Rudrayāmala):
She is black in complexion and has four hands, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
I worship Sinīvālī, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness. || 1 ||
Black in color. || 1 ||
462. Now, the true form of Kālarāhu (according to the Śaiva Āgama): [He has] the feet of a serpent, the face of a hyena, and a massive body.
I meditate upon the bestower of what is desired by the world for the cessation of all misfortunes. || 1 ||
Black in color. || 1 ||
463. Now, the nature of apasmāra (epilepsy)—(in the Siddhāntaśekhara): "He is dark-complexioned with reddish hair, and his form and appearance are like that of a bhūta (spirit)."
In his left hand he holds a serpent, and in his right a snake-seal ring.
Its height is thirty-six finger-breadths, measured by the same unit of four finger-breadths.
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
Now, the forms of the fifteen muhūrtas of day and night— (in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*,
verse 464): First among them, the muhūrta of the day called Raudra is dark blue, with a white and reddish luster.
Clad in white garments and exceedingly tall, he holds a serpent in his right hand.
In the left hand, a vessel filled with nectar for the accomplishment of minor rites.
He is dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
465. Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* called Śveta during the day: The second is named Śveta; he is white in color and has a large belly.
This one has garments with white and red luster, and is adorned with white pearls. || 1 ||
In his right hand is a bright lotus, and in his left, indeed, a water-pot.
He who bestows existence is worthy of worship for the increase of yoga and for happiness. || 2 ||
Of bright complexion. || 2 ||
466 Now, the nature of the Divājayamuhūrta: it is called Tṛtīyotrajaya, and its body is large, being both black and white.
In the right [hand] is a blue lotus; in the left, a serpent with a great hood. || 1 ||
O lord of men, you are worthy of worship as you bear the fruits of victory.
The color of a dark blue cloud. || 3 ||
467. Now, the nature of the Muhūrta called Āryabhaṭṭa during the day:
The fourth [Muhūrta] is named Āryabhaṭṭa; he is dark-blue and white, and possesses great strength.
In his right hand he holds a book, and in his left a trident.
Maintaining it for the sake of excellence, prosperity, victory, and happiness.
The color of a dark blue cloud. || 4 ||
468 Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* of the Sun during the day is as follows:
"And thus, I shall now describe the fifth [period], that of the Sun (*sāvitra*)."
Clad in white garments and appearing dark blue, he was accompanied by great beings.
In the right hand he holds a book, and in the left, a flawless water-pot.
He should indeed be worshipped day and night for the destruction of diseases. || 2 ||
He is black in color. || 5 ||
469 Now, the nature of the muhūrta called Divāvirāja:
here, Virāja is indeed the sixth [deity], dark-complexioned and wearing matted hair.
In his right hand he holds a staff, and in his left, the gesture that inspires fear.
Bearing [this] for the sake of the happiness of one's own clan, it should be worshipped with devotion as "the one worthy of worship."
Dark-complexioned. || 1 || 6 ||
470. Now, the nature of the muhūrta Divāgandharva:
here, the seventh Gandharva is copper-colored, emaciated, and has matted hair.
One should have her hold a lute in her right hand and a spear in her left.
For the increase of happiness and the increase of fame, he should be worshipped with devotion.
Red in color. || 1 || 7 ||
471. Now, the nature of the *abhijit* muhūrta during the day is described: next, the auspicious eighth [muhūrta] named *abhijit* is indeed explained.
He is yellow in color, short in stature, wears copper-colored garments, and has a large belly. || 1 ||
Endowed with two hands holding a balance, he should be worshipped for the attainment of happiness.
That alone is to be known by the wise as Kutupa. || 2 ||
He is indeed very dear to the ancestors, or else he holds the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) in his hand.
Yellow in color. || 8 ||
472. Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* called Rauhiṇeya during the day is described: the ninth *muhūrta*, known as Rauhiṇeya, is now being told.
He was of fair complexion, large-eyed, and wore golden earrings set with sapphires.
In his right hand there is a lotus, and in his left hand there is a modaka.
Wearing it for the attainment of beauty, and for the sake of achieving victory, health, and success. || 2 ||
He is of brilliant white complexion. || 9 ||
473. Now, O dear one, the nature of the Gadādhara Muhūrta during the day is being described; Gadādhara is indeed the tenth [muhūrta].
He was fair-complexioned, tawny, dressed in white garments, and wearing white earrings.
Holding a conch in his right hand and a lotus in his left.
He is fair-complexioned. || 10 ||
474. Now, the nature of the *divāvijaya* (victory of the day) *muhūrta*:
"The eleventh *muhūrta* is now to be known by the name Vijaya."
He was golden-hued, possessed large plows, and wore garments that were black, white, and reddish-brown. || 1 ||
He should carry a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left.
Bestowing [this] for the sake of attaining the bliss of wisdom, he is worthy of worship by the wise.
He is golden-colored. || 11 ||
475. Now, the nature of the twelfth muhūrta of the day, called Nairṛtya, is to be known as follows: the twelfth muhūrta is indeed named Nairṛtya.
Blue-complexioned, with matted hair upon his head, clad in yellow garments, and possessed of great strength. || 1 ||
He holds a wheel in his right hand and displays the gesture of fearlessness in his left.
Blue in color. || 12 ||
476. Now, the nature of the hundred-sacrifice (śatamakha) muhūrta during the day: here, the thirteenth [muhūrta] is red and is named Śatamakha.
Clad in red garments, broad-chested, and adorned with jeweled golden earrings.
His right eye is like a red lotus, and he is endowed with a kundala on his left [ear].
He is red in color. || 13 ||
477. Now, the nature of the morning hour (muhūrta) called Taruṇa is described here: the fourteenth [muhūrta] is known as Taruṇa.
He resembles a pearl and is adorned with a necklace of pearls. || 1 ||
One should know that he who bears a bow and arrows shall likewise attain happiness.
White in color. || 14 ||
478. Now, the nature of the auspicious Muhūrta called Subhaga during the day: furthermore, the fifteenth [Muhūrta] is to be known as Subhaga, which is dear to Hari.
He wore garments with blue, white, and reddish borders, and was adorned with blue earrings.
On the right, however, a banner is to be known, and on the left, a vessel filled with nectar.
Blue in color. || 15 ||
479. Now, the essential natures of the *muhūrtas* of the night—(according to the verses in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*, the *Mayūkha* of the *Śaivāgama*, the *Pāñcarātra*, and the *Kāraṇāgama*, verse 480).
Among these, first is the nature of the *atiraudra-muhūrta* during the night:
The first is extremely fierce—(like Rudra, according to the Nirukta 3).
(In the Śaiva Āgama):
Adorned with the moon, wearing matted hair, three-eyed, and white with ashes.
May Bharga, the destroyer of all fear, always abide within my heart. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. (Like Bharga residing in the eleven Rudras; Ni0 3) || 1 ||
481. Now, the nature of the Muhūrta of Mahāgandharvarāja at night: Mahāgandharvarāja is the second [Muhūrta] (like Gandharva; Ni0 4). ||-||
(In the Śaiva Āgama):
The Gandharva is of auspicious form and is devoted to the Gandharva-Āgama.
He is known as Aruṇa, who possesses wings and knows the true essence of playing the lute.
He is the color of dawn. || 2 ||
482. Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* known as Draviṇaparivṛḍha during the night:
Draviṇaparivṛḍha is the third [muhūrta] (like Kubera; Niśvāsa-tattvasaṃhitā 4).
In Mayūkha:
Kubera is mounted on a horse, holds a spear in his hand, and is beloved by Citriṇī.
The Lord Nidhīśvara is golden-hued, the bestower of wealth, and possessed of beautiful form. || 1 ||
He is golden-colored, like Kubera, the guardian of the quarter. (Ni0 4) || 3 ||
483. Now, the nature of the *śrāvaṇa* muhūrta at night:
*Śrāvaṇa* is the fourth [muhūrta] (like Viṣṇu; Ni0 2).
In the *Mayūkha*: Viṣṇu holds the Kaumodakī mace, the lotus, the conch, and the discus in succession.
One should always perform circumambulation, beginning from the lower right hand.
The color is white (like that of washed cloth). (As in the case of Viṣṇu residing in the twenty-four forms; Ni0 2) || 4 ||
484. Now, the nature of the Vāyu-muhūrta at night: Vāyu is the fifth [deity] (like the wind, Ni0 4). (In the Mayūkha:
For Vāyu is the kinsman of the breath of the world, seated upon a black deer.
He holds a golden staff, is dark in complexion, and is the beloved of Mohinī. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned, like Vāyu among the guardians of the directions. (Ni0 4) || 5 ||
p.
253) 485 Now, the nature of the *agnimuhūrta* at night: Agni is the sixth [deity] (*agnivat*, Ni0 4).
(In the Mayūkha):
He has tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair; his three eyes are tawny and his thighs are reddish.
Seated upon a goat, holding a rosary, possessing seven flames, and wielding a spear. || 1 ||
He is red in color. (As with the presiding deity of the sun, see sūtra 5. || 6 ||
486. Now, the nature of the Rākṣasa muhūrta of the night: the seventh [muhūrta] is Rākṣasa (like Nirṛti; cf. Nirukta 4).
(Regarding the *mayūkha*):
Nairṛti is blue, bearing a sword and a shield, and having a human for his vehicle.
He has hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and is formidable; he is the beloved of Kālikā.
He is blue in color. (Like Nirṛti among the World-Guardians; Ni0 4) || 7 ||
487. Now, the nature of the *dhātṛ* muhūrta at night:
*Dhātṛ* is the eighth [muhūrta] (like the sun; *Niśvāsa*, 5).
(In the Mayūkha):
Seated in the lotus posture, with hands like lotuses, possessing a luster equal to the interior of a lotus.
He should have two arms, be accompanied by his wife, and be joined with a chariot yoked to seven horses. || 1 ||
The color is pale red, like the sun situated among the nine planets. (Ni0 5) || 8 ||
488. Now, the nature of the Saumya Muhūrta at night: Saumya is the ninth [muhūrta] (like Budha; Ni0 5).
(On the ray: Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with a luster like that of the karṇikāra flower.
Bearing a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, the planet Mercury (Budha) stands upon a lion and bestows boons.
(As Mercury situated among the nine planets; Ni0 5) || 9 ||
489. Now, the nature of the *brahmamuhūrta* at night:
"The *brahmamuhūrta* is the tenth [period]" (*brahmavat*, Ni0 3). (In the *Śaivāgama*:
"He has four faces and four arms, holding a water-pot and a sacred thread.")
Pure, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, he is to be known as the eternal Brahmā. || 1 ||
The color is pale red (*pāṭalavarṇa*). (Like the deity of the Rohiṇī asterism; Ni0 5) || 10 ||
490. Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* Vākpati during the night:
Vākpati is the eleventh [lord] (like Bṛhaspati; see *Nirukta* 5).
(From the Mayūkha): When the preceptors of the gods and the Daityas are pure, they are yellow and white, each having four arms.
The two attendants should be depicted holding staffs and granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots.
Golden-colored, like Jupiter situated among the nine planets. (Ni0 5) || 11 ||
p.
254) 491 Now, the nature of the *paila-muhūrta* at night—*paila* is the twelfth [muhūrta] (like *pūṣan*; Ni0 5). (In the Śaiva Āgama)
May Pūṣan grant me satisfaction for the removal of all evils.
Enveloped by a thousand rays, he fills the entire space between all the quarters of the sky.
The color is pale-red (pāṭalavarṇa). (Like Pūṣan among the twelve Ādityas; Ni0 5) || 12 ||
492. Now, the nature of the Vaikuṇṭha-muhūrta of the night: the thirteenth [muhūrta] is Vaikuṇṭha (like Nārāyaṇa; Ni0 2).
In the Pāñcarātra,
Nārāyaṇa is dark as a rain cloud and bears the lotus, conch, mace, and discus.
Clad in yellow garments and adorned with excellent ornaments made of jewels. || 1 ||
His complexion is dark like a cloud. (As in the case of Nārāyaṇa residing in the twenty-four forms; Ni0 2) || 13 ||
493. Now, the nature of the *samīraṇa* muhūrta during the night:
the fourteenth [muhūrta] is *samīraṇa* (like the wind; *niyama* 4).
In the [sixth] ray: Vāyu, the life-kinsman of the world, whose seat is the black antelope.
He holds a golden staff, is dark in complexion, and is the beloved of Mohinī. || 1 ||
He is dark-complexioned. (Like Vāyu among the guardians of the directions, Ni0 4) || 14 ||
494. Now, the nature of the *muhūrta* Nir-ṛti during the night:
Nir-ṛti is the fifteenth [lunar day] (*nir-ṛtivat*, see *niyama* 4).
In the [southern] ray: Nirṛti, blue in color, bearing a sword and shield, and having a man as his vehicle.
He has upright hair, deformed eyes, and is formidable; he is the beloved of Kālikā.
He is blue in color. (Like Nirṛti among the World-Guardians; Ni0 4) || 15 ||
495. Now, the natures of the *ghaṭikās*—(according to the *Kāraṇāgama*):
(In that regard, they are threefold by way of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*)—the *Sārā* and others are associated with *sattva*, while the *Māyā* and others are joined with *rajas*.
Ugra and the others are joined with tamas and bestow fruits corresponding to their own nature. || 1 ||
Indeed, they move in succession according to the progression of their respective watches.
O Pārvatī, hear their names and forms according to their true nature.
Therein, first, the names of the *sāttvika* ghaṭikās: Sārā, Dhārā, Kalā, Viśvā, Vidyā, Śakti, Prabhā, and Dhruvā.
Peace, forbearance, victory, wisdom, permission, gentleness, fearlessness, and the supreme boon.
Faith, intelligence, retention, and eloquence—these are the qualities of sattva.
And they are the color of pure crystal, endowed with the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā). || 2 ||
Each was adorned with ornaments corresponding to her own name.
They are white in color. || 20 ||
(p. 255) Now, the names of the royal ghaṭikās:
Māyābalāpramodā, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, and Śubhā.
Piṅgalā, Bhadrakā, Dhanyā, Samṛddhi, Harṣaṇā, and Dhṛti. || 1 ||
Attachment, clinging, enthusiasm, aversion, and likewise approval.
Rati, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi are the Yoginīs associated with the quality of rajas. || 2 ||
And these should be red in color, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
They are red in color. || 20 ||
Now, O Pārvatī, listen as the names of the Tāmasa Ghaṭikās— the Tāmasa Kālayoginīs— are told.
Then Ugrājyeṣṭhā, then Raudrī, and after that Śeṣaraudrī. || 1 ||
Kālīvikarṇī, and likewise Kalapūrvāvikarṇikā.
Balapūrvāvikarṇī and likewise Balapramathinī. || 2 ||
It is cruel, likewise extremely sharp, envious, and stingy.
Envy, hypocrisy, egoism, delusion, and likewise the perilous state of confusion.
They are to be known as the Ulkikās, yoginīs endowed with darkness.
I shall describe their characteristics; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the truth.
(Since the *sāttvika* and *rājasa* forms are not mentioned here, and only the characteristics of the purely *tāmasa* form are described, their specific natures are set forth below:
496. Among those, first is the nature of Ugrā:
she stands upon a bull, has matted hair, three eyes, and a radiance equal to the flames of fire.
Terrible with a skull and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, she bestows various fruits upon those who seek them.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
497. Now, the true nature of Jyeṣṭhā: Jyeṣṭhā has the luster of a trumpet-flower (pāṭala), is auspicious, and holds a skull as her excellent attribute.
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
498. Now, the form of Raudrī:
likewise, Raudrī is red in color and holds a skull and a chowrie in her hands.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
499. Now, as for the nature of Śeṣaraudrī:
Śeṣapūrvā is to be known as having a black face and being exceedingly terrifying. [Her weapons are stationed upon her body, as before.]
Her body is red in color; her face is black in color. (1)
500. Now, the form of Kālī:
Then Kālī is deep blue-black, with a face resembling a long, hanging copper-colored [object].
She should be known as the destroyer of fear, holding a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her hands. || 1 ||
Her body is cloud-dark in color; her face is red in color. || 1 ||
501. Now, the nature of Vikarṇī:
Vikarṇī is to be known as blue; she is considered to have the power of the shaven-headed one (Muṇḍaśakti) in her hand.
She is blue in color. || 1 ||
502. Now, the nature of Kalavikarṇī:
Kalavikarṇī is white in appearance; she removes fear, wretchedness, and grief.
White in color. || 1 ||
503. Now, as for the nature of Balavikarṇī: she is multicolored, large-eyed, and holds a skull-cup and a rosary.
Bestowing peace for the sake of prosperity, she possesses a pericarp preceded by power.
Multicolored. || 1 ||
504. Now, as for the true form of Balapramathinī: the auspicious Balapramathinī has a copper-colored body and a white face.
She is the bearer of the skull-noose, the one who strikes fear into all enemies.
Her body is red in color; her face is white in color. (1)
505. Now, the nature of Dāruṇā:
Dāruṇā resembles the hibiscus flower and has a large belly.
She who wields the vajra in her skull-bowl is proclaimed as the terrifier of all enemies. || 1 ||
She is red in color. || 1 ||
506. Now, as for the true form of Tīkṣṇā: she has sharp, dark-blue, and copper-colored faces; she has broad shanks and is terrifying.
She who holds a skull and a sword, a servant [of the Lord], who increases the fear of enemies. || 1 ||
In the body she is blue in color; at the mouth she is red in color. 1.
507 Now, the true nature of Madā: she is considered to be dark-complexioned, with a protruding belly, her eyes wide and intoxicated with passion.
She was terrifying with the light from her hand, which was equipped with a sword-edge.
Dark-complexioned. || 1 ||
508. Now, the nature of envy (asūyā): [The goddess] has copper-colored hair-ends, is smeared [with ashes], and has a contracted face.
Vibhīṣaṇā holds a bowl in the hand of Kṛśodarī and a sword.
She is red in color. || 1 ||
509. Now, as for the true nature of Matsarā:
Matsarā has the luster of a dark-blue color, with a red mouth and a large belly.
Holding a sword and a shield, she has long limbs and a contracted face.
In the body she is blue in color; in the mouth she is red in color. 1.
510. Now, the nature of envy (*īrṣyā*):
[the goddess] has the corners of her eyes curved with envy, is blue in luster, and has white teeth.
She has a protruding belly and a high nose, and she is adorned with a skull and a pestle.
She is blue in color on the body and white in color on the face. (1)
511. Now, the true nature of hypocrisy (dambha): she has a face reddened by hypocrisy, variegated colors, is hunchbacked, and has a large belly.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), she holds a sword and a water-pot.
Multicolored. || 1 ||
512. Now, the nature of *ahaṃkṛti* (the gesture of self-assertion):
*Ahaṃkṛti* consists of a contracted mouth, with eyebrows knitted and eyes squinting.
With a straight body and a nose as high and pale-red as a trumpet-flower, she has a large belly. || 1 ||
And she stood upon a yogic lotus seat, holding a skull and a staff in her hands.
The color of the Pāṭala flower. || 1 ||
513 Now, the true nature of Bhrāmarī:
Bhrāmarī has the luster of a dark blue cloud, long shanks, and a slender waist.
Holding a bell and a staff in her hands, she is fierce, with a gaping mouth and matted hair.
Blue in color. || 1 ||
514. Now, as for the nature of Saṃkaṭā: she has a neck that is both constricted and broad, a sunken nose, and a slender waist.
Her complexion is dark and white; she is youthful and bears a sword and a shield. || 1 ||
Her complexion is black and white. || 1 ||
515. Now, the true nature of the Ulkikā [deity]: Ulkikā has the luster of a firebrand, a blue neck, and a large belly.
Holding a firebrand as her staff, she was terrifying to the world.
Her body is red in color; her throat is blue in color. (1)
516. Now, the nature of the deities of the *kalās*—(in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*):
The *kalā* is to be known as white in color, wearing blue garments, and having three eyes.
A single rudrākṣa garland from the sky was suspended from her ear.
In her left hand she holds a rosary of pearls joined with a lotus.
They are especially worthy of worship for the sake of attaining knowledge and higher realization. || 2 ||
White in color. || 1 ||
Now, the essential nature of the deity of the North (Kāṣṭhā): (In the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda* [it is said]:
"The North should have the luster of a blue color, wear yellow garments, and possess three eyes."
She is endowed with eighteen arms and possesses the *jñānamudrā*.
Blue in color. || 1 ||
518. Now, the nature of the Nimeṣa deity—(in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): "The Nimeṣa, however, should be thus: having eyes like a crow, half-blue."
He holds a rosary in his right hand and likewise the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) in his left.
One who maintains this for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga should be honored by the wise.
He is black in color. || 1 ||
159. Now, the nature of the deities of the *kṣaṇas*—(in the *Nṛsiṃhaprāsāda*): The one named *Kṣaṇa* should be white, having the form of a sage (*muni*), and wearing a beautiful crown.
He was endowed with matted hair and three crests, his body smeared with sandalwood paste.
In his right hand he holds a pearl rosary, and in his left he carries a water-pot resting against him.
He is of brilliant white complexion. || 1 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treasury of Planets" (*Ugrahanidhi*), concerning the description of the essential nature of the respective deities associated with the gross and subtle divisions of time—beginning from the nine planets and the start of the Yuga—within the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*. This work was composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign of the preeminent city of Mahīśūra; he who is adorned by the entire circle of the earth; the crest-jewel of all lands; the very seat of the prosperity of the Karṇāṭaka country; the one resplendent in the center of the great kingdom of Mahīśūra; the one seated upon a divine jeweled throne experienced by a circle of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) consisting of the ancestral lineages of kings who were repositories of all arts; the one endowed with the titles of Illustrious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, Possessor of Majestic Valor, Matchless Heroic Monarch, and the "Forehead of the World" (*Anteṃbaragaṇḍa*); the sole hero among men; the moon in the ocean of the Yadu lineage; the one marked by numerous titles such as Conch, Discus, Goad, Ploughshare, Makara, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva, Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, Earth-Boar, Hanuman, and Garuḍa-Lion.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Respective Deities according to the Distinctions of the Coarse and Subtle Kalās of the Nine Planets and the Beginning of the Yuga," in the work known as the *Śrītattvanidhi*. The "Treasury of Planets" is complete.

Now, the eight self-manifested forms:
And at the beginning of this manifestation, in these celestial chariots known as Aṅgas.
At Śrīmuṣṭi, on the Veṅkaṭa mountain, at Sāligrāma, and at Naimiṣa; || 1 ||
And at Totādru and Puṣkara, as well as at the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There are eight forms of mine that are self-manifested upon the surface of the earth.
Now, the verse concerning the four divine places (as spoken by Śrī Rāmānujācārya):
[I bow to] the auspicious jewel of Śrī Raṅgam, the abode of compassion, and the dark cloud dwelling upon the peak of the venerable Veṅkaṭādri mountain.
I bow my head to Śrīśa, who shines like a pārijāta tree upon the peak of the glorious Hastiśaila mountain, and who is the lamp of the mountain of the Yadus. || 1 ||
Now begins the *Prapattisopāna*:
In the land of Pāṇḍya, in the city named Kuṇḍina, there is a place called Tūla, situated between the Tulasī and the Mūlatārā.
I take refuge in the venerable Sage Saumyajāmātṛ, who is perceived as having the nature of a serpent upon his couch. || 1 ||
I worship Kāśāra-bhūta, Mahādāhvaya, Bhaktisāra, Antseva, Īśaṭhārika, Kulaśekhara, and Viṣṇucitta.
I bow to those lords of sages whose feet are the dust for devotees, who are the foremost among the great ascetics, and who have emerged from the lotus-like Tulasi of sweet poetry.
Or else, at the end of the Dvāpara age, in the month known as Āśvayuja, there shall be Hemāmbuja in Śravaṇa at Kāñcī.
Śrī Pāñcajanya was born as a divine yogi; I take refuge in the one named Sāra. || 3 ||
In that month, he descended from there onto the far shore of the ocean at the place named Purimala.
I take refuge in the venerable Gadāṃśa, the sage who is the true designation of all beings, whose name ends in "Utpala. || 4 ||
He was born in that month, under the Śatatārakā constellation, in the city of Māyūrapurī, from Maṇikairava.
With devotion, I take refuge in that great portion (known as Mahat), who is a portion of the illustrious Nanda. || 5 ||
In the month of Taiṣya, under the Maghā asterism, Bhārgava was born on earth in Mahīsārapura from a celestial woman.
I take refuge in that Sudarśana, whose fame is noble, who is the essence of devotion. || 6 ||
In the intermediate periods of the Kali and Dvāpara ages, [the lifespan] turns back for seven thousand years on the earth.
And I take refuge in him (Bhaktisāra), who has assumed the form of the Sudarśana [discus]. || 7 ||
In the beginning of the Kali age, in the city of Hikurika in the Pāṇḍya country, during the month of Vaiśākha, he was born under the Maghā constellation and the Anala lagna.
I take refuge in Śrīśāspada (Śaṭharipu), who descended into the house of the potter, the wife of the army commander. || 8 ||
He made his descent in the city of Kolapura under the asterism Punarvasu in the month of Māgha, among the thickly forested Keralas.
I take refuge in the protector of the earth known as Kulaśekhara, who is a portion of the glorious Kaustubha gem. || 9 ||
In the city known as Śrīdhanvinavyākhyapura, there was a pair of kings celebrated for their brilliance, which was like the flame of a fire fanned by the wind.
I take refuge in Śrī Viṣṇucitta, the son-in-law of Murāri, who is a portion of Garuḍa. || 10 ||

273) Then appeared the son of Mahendra, adorned with a small bow and a sword, from the splendor of the forest garland of the Boon-Granting Lord.

I take refuge in the Lord of Raṅga, whose joy is in divine play, whose crest-lock points upward, who is the king of the twice-born, whose feet are the dust for his devotees, and whose nature is endowed with faultless qualities.
He who descended like the planet Scorpio into Rohiṇī at the city of Nicula on the banks of the Kāverī, born of a noble lineage.
I take refuge in the one known as Pāṇa, who possesses devotion for Him who reclines upon the serpent Śrīvatsāṃśaka, and who has the excellent sage as His vehicle. || 12 ||
In the fourth syllable, there is the rising form of the fallen Śārṅga-arrow within the skin of Kārttikeya.
I take refuge in the Lord of the Fourfold Assembly, whose limbs are made to tremble by the service of the masters of the various arts. || 13 ||
To him whose descent is celebrated in the land of Pāṇḍya, who has Citroḍuja as his crest-jewel while residing in Caitra, and whose topknot is turned upward;
I take refuge in the lord of poets Madhurakavi, the disciple of Śaṭhakopa, who partakes in the portions of the Gaṇas. || 14 ||
In the month of Śuci, on the auspicious ground of the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, from within a grove of fresh Tulasī plants;
Let us worship Vasumatī, the beloved of the Lord who is the chief actor upon the stage of noble virtues, as she rises. 15.
In the lineage named Āsurī on the earth at Toṇḍīra, under the asterism Ārdrā in the month of Caitra, by the power of Śeṣa, the lord of serpents.
I take refuge in [the author of the Bhāṣya], who has appeared for the sake of establishing the flourishing tradition of Śrī Śaṅkara’s teachings. || 16 ||
To him who, while on the way, beheld Rāmānuja at a certain place called Yamunādvaya;
I praise him who, out of affection, gave away his secret treasure for the sake of protecting the world when [the vessel] was completely full.
Born from a portion of Siṃhānana, perfected through the yoga of Īśvara, the pearl among those liberated, the grandson of the honored lord of sages;
Meditate in your heart upon the noble one of the Yamunā, who is the abode of distinguished wisdom and a gale-force wind to the cotton-wool of opposing disputants. 18.
Having defeated King Yāmuna on earth through debate, he then made that detached king the ruler of half the kingdom.
I take refuge in that Rāmamiśra, whose eyes are like water-lilies, who possesses power, and who is the disciple of Padmākṣa. || 19 ||
Having obtained the eloquent utterance of Śaṭhāri from the sacrifice of the lord of yogins, Śrīnātha, in a manner worthy of being sung by the gods;
O Jayatsena, I take refuge in the wise portion, the illustrious Puṇḍarīkākṣa. || 20 ||
From the most excellent of the twice-born, Īśvarapūrvabhaṭṭa, the ornament of the Colakṣitauśoṭṭa lineage.
I take refuge in Nāthamuni, who possesses a radiant splendor, who is a portion of the divine Gajavaktra (Gaṇeśa), and who stands at the forefront of devotees. || 21 ||
Having bowed to Aśaṭhāri, who is the essence of the teachings of all the Āgamas, and having served Senāpati, the friend of the feet of Murāri;
Having bowed to Padmā, the mother of the entire world, I take refuge in Śrīkānta (the Primal Being). || 22 ||
Those who, with undistracted minds, constantly read and hear this "Staircase of Surrender" (Prapattisopāna), [attain their goal].
For them, there shall be a powerful ascent to the blissful palace of Hari’s eternal sovereignty. || 23 ||

274) 1. Now, the procedure for wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*—(as found in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas).
First, in that regard, [it is stated] in the Mahopaniṣad:
Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, [one should meditate upon] Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, who is accessible through Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
"Having known Viṣṇu thus, a person shall be liberated from all the bonds of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
(In the Kaṭha-śākhā):
That noble-souled person who, having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and bearing the discus, meditates upon Viṣṇu as the Supreme.
By means of the sound of the mantra, [one perceives] that which always resides in the heart, higher than the highest, greater than the great.
(From the Atharvaṇa):
He who, for his own welfare, wears the Ūrdhvapuṇḍra with a central cavity in the shape of Hari’s foot becomes dear to the Supreme Being.
One becomes a partaker of merit; one becomes a partaker of liberation.
(In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): "The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic."
One must certainly always wear a very beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).

2. Now, the five types of clay suitable for wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* (as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* and other texts): [clay] from a mountain peak, from a riverbank, and especially from my sacred field (*kṣetra*).
And on the bank of the Sindhu river, at an anthill situated at the root of a Tulasī plant.
These clays alone are to be collected; other types of earth are to be avoided.
Now, regarding the deities residing on the *urdhvapuṇḍra*: (In the thirty-first chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"One should place Keśava on the forehead and Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen."
One should worship Mādhava on the chest and Govinda at the hollow of the throat.
And Viṣṇu in the right side of the belly, and Madhusūdana in the arm.
Trivikrama on the region of the shoulder, and Vāmana on the left side.
One should place Śrīdhara between the arms and Hṛṣīkeśa on that arm.
And on the back, one should place Padmanābha, and at the three joints (trikā), Udarabhaṭa.
And with the water used for washing that [image], one should sprinkle Vāsudeva on the head. || 13 ||
3. Now, he states the measurement for those who wear the vertical *puṇḍra*s:
on the forehead, the pair of arms, the two backs, and the hollow of the throat.
One should wear the ūrdhvapuṇḍra marks, four finger-breadths in length.
It is taught that the length from the navel to each of its two sides is ten finger-breadths.
On the two arms and the chest, the *puṇḍra* is said to be twelve finger-breadths in length. || 2 || 12 ||
4. Now, the differences in the number of vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) according to the distinction of castes: "In this manner, a Brāhmaṇa should always wear twelve marks."
Having meditated upon that specific form within each respective mark (puṇḍra), one should apply it while reciting the mantra. || 1 ||
It is declared that four marks [of the forehead] are for kings, while two marks are traditionally prescribed for Vaiśyas.
However, a single sectarian mark (ekapuṇḍra) is prescribed for women and for Śūdras.
5. Now, regarding the deities of the places for wearing the vertical *puṇḍra*:
one should wear four *puṇḍras* on the forehead, the heart, and the two arms.
Two [lines] are prescribed for the forehead and the heart, while one is prescribed for the brow.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead is prescribed as the foremost for all.
The wearing [of the marks] is prescribed precisely in the sequence beginning with the forehead. || 2 ||
One should wear the forms of Vāsudeva and the others upon the four *puṇḍra* marks.
And one should wear two [marks] known as Govinda and Kṛṣṇa, and one [mark] of Nārāyaṇa.
O Girijā, this procedure for the tilaka mark has been declared by me for all people.
6. Now, regarding the shape and other characteristics of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*:
it should be like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, or likewise shaped like a bamboo leaf.
Resembling a lotus bud, this triad is known as the Enchanter (Mohana). || 1 ||
The pure and great devotee of the Lord constantly [perceives] the form of Hari's feet.
In the Vaideha country, however, one should wear the ūrdhvapuṇḍra in the shape of a staff.
(In the *Saccaritrarakṣā*):
One should arrange it with an interval of either two or three finger-breadths.
The characteristic of the site for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) should be two finger-breadths wide at its sides. || 1 ||
(In the *Bhāradvāja-saṃhitā*):
One should always wear the discus and other [emblems] within the space between the vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*).
For they have been cast out, filled with rage, and they drive us away from our sin.
Keśava is present at dawn, midday, and evening through the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
Or rather, he gratifies [the ancestors] with those various deeds that have been well-performed, even if they were not previously done. || 2 ||
At dawn he is situated in the divine realm, and at midday he is within the sun.
Satisfying Hari, who resides within his own self, with the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) at evening.
7. Now, regarding those who wear the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with turmeric—(in the *Saccaritrarakṣā*):
"Among all vertical marks, one should apply auspicious turmeric."
Furthermore, whatever powder a man always applies to the image of Viṣṇu after it has been consecrated; || 1 ||
He who wears turmeric shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
(Regarding the summary:
He who does not apply turmeric in the space between the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) [is at fault].
A Vaiṣṇava, moreover, removes both Śrī and me from his forehead. || 1 ||
Now, the presiding deities of the turmeric powder used for the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*—(Hārīta):
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Padmā, Padminī, and Kamalālayā.
Rāmā, Vṛṣākapi, Dhanyā, Vṛddhi, Ijyā, and Indirā—thus [are the names]. || 1 ||
The powers of Keśava and the others are fully proclaimed in the supreme state.
(Pāñcarātra) — The first name of the Śrī Devī is Amṛtodbhavā.
The third is proclaimed by Kamalā, and the fourth is Śāntiśobhinī.
The fifth is "Viṣṇupatnī" (the wife of Viṣṇu), and the sixth is indeed "Vaiṣṇavī" (belonging to Viṣṇu).
The seventh, however, was Varārohā, and the eighth was Harivallabhā.
The ninth is said to be Śārṅgiṇī, and the tenth has Devadevatā as its deity.
The eleventh was Lakṣmī, and the twelfth was Surasundarī.
(In the Āgama):
"The first [Ājñā] is to be known as Śrīdevī, while the second arises from nectar."
The third is proclaimed as Kamalā, and the fourth is Lokasundarī. || 1 ||
The fifth is Viṣṇupatnī, and the sixth is Śrīvaiṣṇavī.
The seventh, however, is Varārohā, while the eighth is Harivallabhā.
The ninth is declared to be Śārṅgiṇī, and the tenth has the God as its presiding deity.
Ekādaśī is Mahālakṣmī, and Dvādaśī is Surasundarī.
These twelve auspicious goddesses are the supreme presiding deities of the Śrīcūrṇa. || 4 || 12 ||
8. Now, regarding the vessel for the turmeric powder suitable for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*:
one should fill it with auspicious powder from any fruit except for the *bilva*.
One who is not a Vaiṣṇava is to be known as such; Hari’s beloved becomes angry with him.

9. Now, regarding the drawing of the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, the invocation of the earth (*mṛd-dharṣaṇa*), the ritual installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*), and its wearing (*dhāraṇa*), [the following are] the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), deities (*devatā*), and so forth:

Oṃ. Regarding the mantra for rubbing the clay for the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*): Varāha is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Anuṣṭup is the meter (*chanda*); Śrī-Bhūmi is the deity (*devatā*); the letter *A* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); the letter *Ya* is the power (*śakti*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of rubbing the clay for the vertical mark, and for the purpose of the consecration of breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) upon the vertical mark during recitation. Likewise, regarding the mantra for wearing the vertical mark: Rāṇāyaṇīya, Sātyamugri, Dūrvāsas, Bhāguri, Gaurguṇḍī, Gaurgulavi, Upamanyu, Gārgya, Sopakarṣa, Kaṇva, Kuthi, and Viśālihotra are the seers. The meters (*chandāṃsi*) are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Jagatī, Paṅkti, Vyāhṛti, Śakvarī, Bṛhat, Rathantara, Virāj, Atijagatī, and Viṣṭārapaṅkti.

The thirteen forms, beginning with Keśava and ending with Vāsudeva, are the deities. *Oṃ* & *aṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Oṃ* & *uṃ* is the pinning-syllable (*kīlaka*). *Oṃ* & *maṃ* is the power (*śakti*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the wearing of the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*). *Oṃ* & *kruddholkāya svāhā*. *lkāya svāhā*. *matkāya svāhā*. *pṛtkolkāya svāhā*. Meditation (*dhyāna*): [One should meditate upon Him] who is endowed with a crown radiant as the sun, adorned with shimmering makara-earrings, blazing armlets, and the Vaijayantī garland which possesses a brilliance variegated by the luster of the Kaustubha gem.

I bow to Mukunda, who is worshipped by the entire universe; whose sides are embraced by Śrīdhara; who is endowed with hundreds of ornaments radiant with the rays of various jewels; and who shines with the lotus and discus resting upon his arms. || 1 ||

This is the depiction of the five weapons, endowed with these characteristics.

endowed with a drop of curd shimmering at the tip of the lower disc.

He is tall, resembling a sapphire, and adorned with a forest garland.
His face has the shape of a goad and is endowed with the wheel of Dharma. || 2 || 1 ||
(The form of Pradyumna)—
resembling a hibiscus flower and adorned with a forest garland.
They know Pradyumna, who holds a bow, arrows, and a lotus, as the bestower of desired boons. || 1 ||
(Aniruddhamūrti)—
[He who is] endowed with the characteristics of Pradyumna, whose face shines with the subtle wheel.
The wise know Aniruddha to be enriched with lines of gold and silver. || 1 ||
(The Form of Hayagrīva):
With a face shaped like a goad, blazing with a long, circular dot.
They call this Hayagrīva, who has the appearance of a ripe jambū fruit. || 1 ||
(Śrīdharamūrti):
[He is] resembling a thick expanse of green grass and adorned with a forest garland.
They know Śrīdhara, who is endowed with a slightly uneven discus, to be the bestower of prosperity. || 1 ||
(Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Mūrti) — The head-disk is of the form described below, perfectly circular and cool in appearance.
There are four wheels at the two doorways, either on the left or on the right.
They know Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa as being enriched with the Śrīvatsa mark, the conch, and the discus. || 1 ||
(The form of Padmanābha):
With a lotus shining from his navel-cakra, possessing a luster like that of a rose-apple fruit.
The wise know him as Padmanābha, renowned as the giver of heaven.
(Govindamūrti):
Dark as a fresh blade of dūrvā grass, adorned with a forest garland.

Thus ends the sixth treasury, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Viṣṇu-Sites, Vaiṣṇava-Symbols, Śālagrāmas, and so forth," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja Mahārāja, the sovereign lord of the preeminent city of Śrī Mahīśūra; he who is the ornament of the entire circle of the earth, the crest-jewel of all lands, the abode of the prosperity of the Karṇāṭaka country; who shines resplendently in the midst of the great seat of Śrī Mahīśūra; who has ascended the divine jeweled throne experienced by the circle of universal emperors, the foremost among his own kings and protectors of the realm, descended through an unbroken lineage of royal dynasties; who is adorned with numerous titles such as: the King of Kings of Kings, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of Unrivaled Prowess, the Peerless Heroic Monarch, the Ornament of the Sky at the End of His Epithets, the Sole Hero of the World, the Moon in the Ocean of the Yadu Dynasty, the Conch, the Discus, the Goad, the Axe, the Makara, the Fish, the Sarabha, the Sālva, the Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, the Boar of the Earth, Hanumān, Garuḍa, the Lion, and others.

Thus ends the sixth treasury, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Viṣṇu’s Sacred Sites, Vaiṣṇava Shrines, Śāligrāma Stones, and so forth," in the treatise known as the *Śrītattvanidhi*. 6.

3. Now, the lingas representing the five elements beginning with earth, etc. (in that same work):
Ekāmbarēśvara is the earth-linga (at Kāñcīpura), [and] Śiva [is the water-linga].

5. Now, the classification of the liṅgas, the sequence of their worship, and their fruits—(from the Śivarahasya):
"Alternatively, I shall describe in detail the various types of liṅgas."

Īśvara said: Sand, rice, food, river-clay, and likewise cow-dung—these are [the materials for the rite].

Flower-garlands, sugar-candy, flour-paste, and fourteen momentary [offerings].

That which is produced from dūrvā grass and guḍūcī prevents untimely death.

The sages have heard that the fruit of being very gentle is crystal-like clarity.
A linga made of silver is to be worshipped for the liberation of one's ancestors.
A person who worships [this] shall attain the heavenly realm made of gold.
One who desires prosperity should constantly worship that linga made of copper.

One who desires to slay an enemy should always [worship] a linga made of iron.
A man desiring long life should worship a liṅga made of red sandalwood.
For the pacification of fever, one should worship an excellent liṅga made of sandalwood.

The Liṅga produced from black agallochum grants all desires to everyone.
The Liṅga produced from Yakṣakardama increases one's joy.

A liṅga made from the flour derived from chickpeas is supremely efficacious for attaining siddhi.
One who desires fame should constantly worship a linga made of rice.

In this world and in the world beyond, that person becomes happy. || 21 ||

Having worshipped with devotion, the wise one rejoices together with Śiva. || 23 ||
In the winter season, one who worships the Liṅga with flowers produced from all [seasons]...
Having quickly shaken off all evil, he rejoices together with Brahmā.

By whatever means, and of whatever object whatsoever.

Gods, asuras, and humans, as well as siddhas, gandharvas, and yakṣas; || 10 ||

9. Now, regarding the necessity of the *pañcasūtrī* for the mobile and immobile lingas of earth:
one should not deliberate upon the ritual procedure of the *pañcasūtrī* in the case of a linga made of earth.

A linga made of gems, one made of diamonds, as well as one of mercury or crystal;
One should cause an unbroken sacrificial offering to be made, consisting of clay, flour, or flowers.
The stationary liṅga is unfragmented, while the moving one is indeed twofold.
Those deluded men who perform [this] do not partake in the fruit of worship. || 4 ||

In accordance with the injunctions declared in the Vedas, for the sake of the complete attainment of the full fruit. || 1 ||
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) according to the ritual injunctions.

On a riverbank, by a pond, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a house.

Having effortlessly brought earth produced from a pure location, |||

Hara, Maheśvara, Śambhu, Śūlapāṇi, and Maheśvara.

The fetching of the clay, its kneading, the consecration, and likewise its carrying;

Salutations to you, whose self is the *nāda*; salutations to you, whose self is the *bindu* and the *kalā*.
Salutations to you, who possess the form of both the unmanifest and the manifest, yet transcend all form.
You are the mother of all worlds; you alone are the father of the entire universe.
You are my brother, you are my well-wisher and friend; you are my father and my great-grandfather.
Whatever worship of this earthen linga has been performed by me, [let that be for the sake of my liberation]. || 3 ||
Therefore, may the illustrious Lord Rudra grant the desired object.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world.
