11. Now, the characteristics of the Bāṇaliṅga:
O believers, that which has been weighed on a scale [to determine its density] in three, five, or seven ways—
That [liṅga] does not suffer any deficiency; it is therefore called the Bāṇaliṅga. || 1 || 1 ||
Now, regarding prohibited lingas in worship: A man should never, under any circumstances, worship a linga that is smaller than an Aksha in size.
One should make it shorter than the thumb; one should never act otherwise.
(From the *Amarakośa*: "Eighty *guñjās* make one *akṣa*; five *guñjās* and so on make one *māṣaka*; sixteen of those make one *akṣa*"). 12.
Now, the characteristics of the nine types of mobile *liṅgas*:
A *liṅga* measuring nine, eight, or six *aṅgulas* is said here to be the best.
The middle [measurement] is traditionally known to be of three kinds: six, five, and four mānas. || 1 ||
That which has a linga of two, three, or one finger-breadth is the threefold Kaniṣṭha.
Thus, the ninefold mobile liṅga has been described in due order. || 2 || 9 ||
13. Now, the determination of the five sūtras—(according to the Siddhāntaśekhara and the Śaiva Āgama): "The width at the top of the liṅga is considered equal to the height of the liṅga."
The enclosure is three times that, and the pedestal is likewise established.
In the same way, there should be a conduit; such is the determination regarding the five threads.
(The meaning of this is as follows:)

Having made the width of the top of the liṅga equal to its height, and having made the thickness of the liṅga such that it can be encircled by a cord three times its [height], one should make the pedestal (pīṭha) circular or square, with a width equal to that [thickness] at both the bottom and the top.
The height of the pedestal, however, should be twice the height of the linga.

In the center of the pedestal (pīṭha), having divided a portion twice as thick as the liṅga into thirds according to the height of the pedestal, one should fashion two or three tiers (vapra) above and below it. Having fashioned an outer rim (mekhalā) on top of the pedestal with a width equal to one-sixth of the liṅga’s breadth, one should fashion an excavation (khāta) inside that is attached to it and equal in size. Outside the pedestal, one should construct a channel (praṇālikā) as long as the liṅga, with a width at its base equal to its length and a width at its front half of that, having an excavation in the middle one-third of its width, and provided with rims similar to those of the pedestal.
Now, regarding the superiority of the *rasaliṅga* over all others: "Among those [lingas made of] clay, *bāṇa*, and mercury, the *rasaliṅgas* are in truth the most excellent."
Among the three, the first is the Bāṇa-liṅga, which is excellent; the Rasaliṅga is even superior to that.

45. Now begins the incarnation of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, the Teacher of the World—(as described in the *Śaṅkaradigvijaya*, *Vaidikavijayadhvaja*, *Saṅkaramandārasaurabha*, and other works):
"In the Kali age, Rudra Mahādeva, the Lord and Father of the worlds..."
Śaṅkara, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita), will effect his own incarnation.
For the sake of establishing the Śrauta and Smārta rites, and out of a desire for the welfare of his disciples.
He will impart that knowledge, which is equal to Brahman, to his disciples.
And [he taught] the essence of all the Vedāntas, as well as the duties shown in the Vedas.
46. Now, these are the necessary acts of veneration in worship—(from the *Sadācārasaṃgraha*):
[one should worship] Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara.
A Brāhmaṇa devoted to the five great sacrifices should worship these five.
335) Now, the rules regarding the arrangement of the five deities (*pañcāyatana*) in worship—47.
First, therein, the sequence for the arrangement of the Vedic *pañcāyatana* in worship (from the *Sadācārasaṃgraha*).
Viṣṇu is declared to be the deity of the sacrificial offering for Satyāmbikā, for the Lord of Day (the Sun), for the Father, and for Manuṣya.
Brahmā, Īśvara, Bhūtabali, Gaṇādhipa, and Yajñeśvara shall be the deities to be worshipped in the sacrifice. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu, who performs intense austerity, is the witness of good deeds; she is the nectar of the Vedas, consisting of mantra, and the state beyond mind (manonmanī).
The son of Bhavānī, who removes obstacles to meditation and bestows knowledge, is called Sthāṇu by the wise. || 2 ||

(Śivapañcāyatana)—When Śambhu is in the center, one should place Hari, Naha, Bhū, and Devī; (Viṣṇupañcāyatana)—when Hari is in the center, one should place Śaṅkara, Īśa, Agasutā; (Ādityapañcāyatana)—when Ravi is in the center, one should establish Hara, Gaṇeśa, Ajā, and Ambikā.
(The Fivefold Sanctuary of the Goddess): Viṣṇu, Hara, Bhava, Vaktra, and Ravi [should be placed] in the Goddess.

(The Fivefold Sanctuary of Gaṇeśa): Lambodara, Aja, Īśvara, Nārī, and Āryā [should be placed]. When facing the directions starting from the East (Śaṅkara), they grant auspiciousness; when reversed, they are the source of loss. || 1 ||
The auspicious deities, headed by Īśāna, are situated to the northeast of the central deity. || 5 ||
Now follows the determination of the directions for the gods: one should designate the eastern direction starting from the face of the deity.
The meaning is: "of the deity situated in the center."
Now, the five deities of the Tantric tradition—(as found in the *Kālahastivilāsa* and the *Pañcāyatanakalpa*)—the Five Deities of Śiva alone: Pārvatī, Parameśāna, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Nandin.
(The Sole Pañcāyatana of Viṣṇu): Śrī, Bhū, Mahāviṣṇu, Viṣvaksena, and Khageśvara.
(The Fivefold Abode of the Sole Goddess): Kālī, Durgā, Bhavānī, Viṣṇu, and Manonmanī.
This very [deity] is also called the (Kevalagaurīpañcāyatana).
(The Sole Sūrya-Pañcāyatana): Bhānu, Chāyā, Daṇḍa, as well as Māṭhara and Piṅgala.
(The Fivefold Abode of Gaṇeśa Alone): Gaṇeśa, Vallabha, Yakṣa, Kuṇḍodara, and Mahodara.

Now, the varieties of the Sāligrāma forms of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—47. Among these, first, the varieties of the Rāma-forms: (Elsewhere) "The Rāma-form is of eight kinds, according to the divisions beginning with Vīrarāma. (1–8)
(Sītārāmamūrtiḥ) — Sītārāma, moreover, is proclaimed to be of two kinds even there.
He was bearing a dark-colored bow that resembled a hen's egg.
Accompanied by two lines at the sides of the door is the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa).
A line in the shape of a bow is seen on both sides.
Or he might have behind him the destroyer of the family of the Ten-Necked One (Rāvaṇa).
(Sītārāma)—In each individual face, there may be four wheels with the luster of the sky.
Equipped with a bow, arrows, a goad, an umbrella, a banner, and chowries.
The Lord who wears a forest garland is celebrated as Sītārāma.
It is said to bestow all desired objects and to grant victory everywhere. || 2 || 1 ||
(Sītārāma): At the two doors there are four wheels, and on the left there is one wheel.
Sītā and Rāma, richly endowed with arrows, reeds, and bows, were accompanied by a garland. || 1 ||
He bestows all good fortune and grants victory everywhere.
It is joined with a single bow, circular, and slightly elongated. || 2 || 1 ||
(Vīrarāma): Richly adorned with a bow fashioned from the bark of the *bārataṇī* tree, wearing earrings, and garlanded with lotuses.
Vīrarāma, who is rich with subtle filaments and wheels, brings what is dear.
On the right side there are five lines, and on both sides [of the central figure] are a bow and an arrow.
One who possesses Bālarāma should be known as a giver of sons; of this there is no doubt.
Equipped with divine arrows and provided with a bow and quiver.
(Vijayarāma): Adorned with a terrifying face, joined with a dot, and graced by a discus.
He whose [son] is named Advijayarāma, who has yellowed wings like a bee.
(Rāma, delighted: "With the plow, the bow, the quivers on his sides, and likewise equipped with hooves, he stands upon my head."
He is renowned as Hṛṣṭarāma, the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(Kodaṇḍarāma)—He is enriched with the name Kodaṇḍarāma; he is auspicious and possesses the brilliant luster of a bow.
May he of beautiful countenance and dark complexion, who is most resplendent, hold the discus.
(One whose form is accompanied by a beautiful garden)—he who possesses a beautiful garden is to be known as one who, when worshipped, bestows excellent fruits. || 18 ||
48. Now, regarding the forms of Kṛṣṇa—(elsewhere): (The form of Kṛṣṇa)—the forms of Kṛṣṇa there are also considered to be thirteen in number.
Black, yellow, and white-bodied, he is joined with a discus on the side of the wall.
The navel should be equal to the door, while behind it it should be shaped like a kūrca.
Kṛṣṇa is the personification of the circular form, the direct destroyer of the sins of all.
He is black, exceedingly black, not corpulent, marked with a discus, and endowed with the Kaustubha gem.

Thus ends the seventh treasury, titled "The Description of Śiva-sites, Bilva-leaves, Rudrākṣas, and Other Matters," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign lord of the preeminent city of Mahīśūra. He is the ornament of the entire circle of the earth, the crest-jewel of all lands, the presiding deity of the Karṇāṭaka country; he who sits upon the divine jeweled throne experienced by the entire circle of imperial sovereigns, headed by the royal protectors descended through the lineage of the full moon of unblemished arts shining in the center of the great seat of the illustrious Mahīśūra; he who bears the titles of Illustrious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, Sovereign of Unrivaled Prowess, Peerless Heroic Monarch, Forehead of the Sky, Sole Hero of the World, Moon in the Ocean of the Yadu Lineage, and is marked with numerous titles such as Conch, Discus, Goad, Axe, Makara, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva-gaṇḍa, Bheruṇḍa, Earth-boar, Hanuman, Garuda, and Lion. // 7 //
Thus ends the seventh treasury, titled "The Exposition of the Five Abodes of Śiva and Other Sites," in the treatise known as the *Śrītattvanidhi*. 7.
Thus ends the Śaiva-nidhi, titled "The Description of the Sacred Sites of Śiva and Other Locations," within the work known as the *Śrī-tattva-nirvyākhyā*.
The eighth is the treasure of arrival;

Śrī. Now,
in the Śrītattvanidhi:
The eighth [chapter], the Treasure of the Descent [of the Purāṇas].
Now follows the determination regarding the expounders of the eighteen Purāṇas and their descent to the world of mortals—(from the *Purāṇasāra*):
Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, became Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
He alone is the bestower [of boons] upon all the ancient gods. || 1 ||
The Purāṇa is the illuminator of all subjects and is equal in authority to the Śruti.
Even today, it exists in the world of the gods with an extent of one billion verses.
For that purpose, it is here briefly proclaimed in four hundred thousand [verses].
Then, having divided it eighteenfold, it was proclaimed in this world of mortals. || 3 || 18 ||
Now, the characteristics of the Mahāpurāṇas— (from the Purāṇasāra): First, the characteristic of the Brāhma Purāṇa is that which was previously spoken by Brahmā to Marīci in its entirety.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of ten thousand verses (10,000). || 1 || 1 ||
2. Now, the definition of the Padma Purāṇa:
that which was previously narrated by Brahmā to Marīci in its entirety.
Brahmā indeed proclaimed this Padma [Purāṇa], consisting of five sections, in the world.
That Pādma [Purāṇa] is said to consist of fifty-five thousand verses (55,000 ślokas). || 1 ||
3. Now, the definition of the Varāha Purāṇa:
Parāśara [composed it] based upon the events of the Vārāha Kalpa.
Those who have declared all these dharmas in their entirety, they indeed know as Vaiṣṇava.
The wise know that Purāṇa, consisting of eight thousand verses (8,000 ślokas), as the one called Viṣṇu. || 1 ||
4. Now, as for the characteristic of the Vāyu Purāṇa: in the context of the Śveta Kalpa, Vāyu here proclaimed the dharmas.
This is that which belongs to Vāyu; it is called the greatness of Udrama.
That Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses (24,000). || 1 ||
5. Now, the definition of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa:
That in which, having taken the Gāyatrī as its subject, the expansion of dharma is described.
That which contains the slaying of the asura Vṛtra is called the Bhāgavata. || 1 ||
(Another version:)—
Those who may be humans or gods in the midst of the Sārasvata Kalpa.
That wherein the account of his life arises is called the Bhāgavata. || 1 ||
The Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of eighteen thousand verses (18,000). || 1 ||
6. Now, the characteristics of the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: [It was composed] by the wise disciple of Vyāsa when questioned by Śatānīka.
The solar dharma has been explained by Sumantu in that very place.
It consists of exactly twelve thousand (12,000 verses) and is called the Bhaviṣya. || 1 ||
7. Now, the definition of the Nāradīya Purāṇa: In this [Purāṇa], Nārada expounds the dharmas based upon the Bṛhat Kalpa.
The Nāradīya Purāṇa is said to consist of twenty-four thousand verses (24,000). || 1 || 1 ||
8. Now, the definition of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
That work in which, having taken the bird as its subject, there is an investigation into dharma and adharma.
The Mārkaṇḍeya [Purāṇa] is said here to consist of thirty-seven thousand verses (37,000). || 1 || 1 ||
9. Now, the definition of the Āgneya Purāṇa: that which is this world, both moving and unmoving, originating from Agni; [that is the Āgneya Purāṇa].
The origin of the sacrificial altars (cayanas) and likewise the arrival of Iṣṭikā. || 1 ||
Likewise, that which pertains to the number of sacrifices and so forth, as it has proceeded with reference [to a specific subject].
That which was proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha’s fire is called the Āgneya [Purāṇa].
And the Āgneya [Purāṇa] consists of eight thousand verses (8,000 ślokas) and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices. || 1 ||
10. Now, the characteristic of the *Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa*:
wherein indeed the Vaiṣṇava duties [are taught] by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The creation of Ambarīṣa has indeed been proclaimed, as well as the creation of Brahmā.
The Brahmakaivarta is proclaimed to consist of twelve thousand verses (12,000 ślokas). || 1 ||
11. Now, the definition of the Laiṅgya Purāṇa:
that which treats of the history of the Īśāna-kalpa.
The *Laiṅgya Purāṇa* was spoken by Brahmā himself as a work of his own composition.
O best of sages, that [work] is declared to consist of eleven thousand verses (11,000). || 1 ||
12. Now, O best of sages, regarding the characteristics of the Varāha incarnation, [I shall speak] in connection with the Vāmana Kalpa.
And furthermore, concerning the majesty of Mahāvarāha.
That which was spoken by Viṣṇu to the Earth is here called the Vārāha-saṃhitā.
That Purāṇa is said here to consist of twenty-four thousand verses (24,000). || 2 || 1 ||
13. Now, the definition of the Skanda Purāṇa:
that which deals with the duties pertaining to Maheśvara as taught by the six-faced one (Kārttikeya).
In that *kalpa*, it was augmented by the deeds and conduct performed by those who were its *tatpuruṣas*.
He composed that thirteenth Purāṇa, known as the Skānda.
It is proclaimed among mortals that its extent is one hundred thousand verses (100,000 ślokas). || 2 || 1 ||
14. Now, the definition of the Vāmana Purāṇa:
it concerns the majesty of Trivikrama, as expounded by the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
It is proclaimed as the Vāmana [Avatāra], which pertains to the three goals of life (trivarga) and the three deities (tridaivatyam). || 1 ||
It consists of fourteen thousand verses (14,000 ślokas), is known as the Śiva[-purāṇa], and follows the Kalpa [named] Kṣāra. || 1 ||
15. Now, the characteristic of the Kūrma Purāṇa:
wherein, in the subterranean realm (rasātala), [the means] for dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation [are taught].
Janārdana, in the form of a tortoise, recounted his own majesty.
In connection with Indradyumna, [he spoke] to the sages in the presence of the Discus.
That *Kaurma* [Purāṇa] consists of six thousand verses (6,000 ślokas) and is an ancillary to the *Lakṣmī-kalpa*. || 2 || 1 ||
16. Now, the definition of the Matsya Purāṇa:
wherein Janārdana, for the sake of setting the Vedas in motion at the beginning of the Kalpa—
The Narasimha incarnation was described by Manu in the form of a fish. || 1 ||
O you of excellent vows, he spoke concerning this, as well as the events of the seven kalpas.
Know that to be the Mātsya [Purāṇa], consisting of fourteen thousand verses (14,000). || 2 || 1 ||
17. Now, the definition of the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
When, in the Gāruḍa Kalpa, the universal egg was produced from Garuḍa...
Having taken that as his subject, Viṣṇu spoke; therefore, it is called the Gāruḍa here.
That Purāṇa is recited as consisting of sixteen thousand verses (16,000 ślokas). || 1 ||
18. Now, the definition of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Brahmā spoke again, taking as his subject matter the majesty of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
That Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa consists of twelve thousand verses, with an additional two hundred.
19. Now, the total number of verses in the Mahāpurāṇas, wherein the detailed accounts of future kalpas are heard, [is as follows]:
This [work] consisting of four hundred thousand verses was proclaimed by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds. (1)
This has been composed in brief by the Supreme Sage for the benefit of the world.
20. Now, the number of chapters and verses in the Śrī Mahābhārata—(from the chapter on the table of contents as stated in the Mahābhārata):

The number of chapters and verses in the Mahābhārata is calculated as follows: in the Ādiparvan, they are measured by mountains, two eyes, oceans, the god of love, the world, and elephants; then correctly by serpents and mountains.
In the Rudra [scale], the notes are said to be five, four, three, two, one, four, six, and six; in the Vairāṭa [scale], they are seven, six, zero, five, nine, zero, and two arms (two). || 1 ||

In the *Audyo*, *Gerī*, *Bhacaṃdra*, *Āga*, *Janavara*, *Ṣaṭ*, *Bhīṣma*, and *Parvaṇya* [years], the lords of the months are respectively: 4, 2, 8, 5, 7, 1, 9, 10, 0, 7, 8, 1, 2, 0, 7, 8. In the *Drauṇaka* [year], they are: 1, 1, 0, 8, 6, 1, 7, 8.
In the Śalyaparvan, there are 94 verses; then in the Sauptika, 56 verses; and then in the Strīparvan, 57 verses. || 2 ||
In the Strīparvan, there are sixty-seven; in the Śāntiparvan, thirty-three; and in the Anuśāsana, it is declared that there are one hundred and sixty-four.

Rava (6), abhra (0), abhra (0), aṣṭa (8), aśvamedha (17), sura (33), bhuj (2), nakha (20), asura (14), āśrama (5), avāsa (8), parva (21), akṣi (2), abdhi (4)—these are the names [of the chapters]; they are six, zero, two, one, thirty-three, two, twenty, fourteen, five, eight, twenty-one, two, four, sixty, two, one, and four. || 3 ||

In the *Māhāprasthānika*, three [steps] are prescribed here for each of the three sky-digits (the three days); however, for the ascent to heaven (*svargāroha*), nine, nine, and eight [steps] are declared for the parvan days according to their respective numbers.

A thousand verses on the lineages of the sages, a thousand verses on the dynasty of Hari, and thus these verses concerning Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Mountain-Dweller (Arjuna)—the sage Vyāsa counted these as the lotus-chapters of the Mahābhārata.

21. Now, the number of chapters and verses in each book (*skandha*) of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam—those chapters and verses narrated by Śuka in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam: in the first [book], known as Nanda-kusa, there are eight chapters and eighty verses; in the second, ten.
Six, six, fire (three), fire (two), fire (one), twenty-five, manun (fourteen), fourth (four), fire (three), sky (zero), six, ocean (four), earth (one), fifth (five), six, and two. (1)
In the sixth [chapter], the mountains are stated as two by two; in the seventh, the number is sixty-four, six oceans, and six serpents; and the verses are fifteen.

And in the eighth [period], they are reckoned as one hundred and eight; in the ninth, as one thousand, nine hundred, and eighty-one; and in the tenth, as one million, two hundred and fifty thousand, seven hundred and twenty-eight, according to the sequence.

In the eleventh [chapter], there are one hundred and twenty-six verses; in the twelfth, one hundred and sixty-three; in the thirteenth, one hundred and thirty-seven; and likewise in the fourteenth, one hundred and seventy-one. In the fifteenth, there are one hundred and eighty-nine; and in the sixteenth, one hundred and ninety-five. In the seventeenth, there are two hundred and twenty-two; in the eighteenth, two hundred and forty-three; and in the nineteenth, two hundred and fifty-eight. In the twentieth, there are two hundred and seventy-four; in the twenty-first, two hundred and ninety-five; and in the twenty-second, three hundred and twelve. In the twenty-third, there are three hundred and thirty-one; and in the twenty-fourth, three hundred and fifty-eight. In the twenty-fifth, there are three hundred and seventy-nine; and in the twenty-sixth, three hundred and ninety-five. In the twenty-seventh, there are four hundred and twenty-six; and in the twenty-eighth, four hundred and forty-seven. In the twenty-ninth, there are four hundred and sixty-three; and in the thirtieth, four hundred and eighty-four. And in the thirty-first, there are five hundred and thirteen verses. Thus ends the section on the number of verses.
In this [work], there are thirteen chapters in the final Skandha, and the number of verses is calculated as one hundred and seventy-four; furthermore, there are twelve Skandhas. || 3 ||
22. Now, the number of books, cantos, and verses in the Rāmāyaṇa:
in the Bālakāṇḍa, the cantos are indeed numbered as seventy-four by the sages.
The verses are proclaimed to be the sky, the arrows, and the swords, as well as the arms. || 1 ||
In the Ayodhyākāṇḍa, there are ninety-one chapters.
The verses are proclaimed to be in number equal to the Vasus, Nāgas, eyes, and Vedas. || 2 ||
In the Araṇyakāṇḍa, there are as many chapters as there are arrows on Mount Parvata;
the verses spoken therein are said to be [twenty-five thousand] equal to the sky, the arrows, and the fires. (3)
The chapters of the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa are considered to be thirty-six in number.
The lotus-eyed one, whose splendor is immeasurable, is perceived by the wise as beyond calculation.
Likewise, in the Sundarakāṇḍa, there are as many cantos as there are houses in a village.
In that regard, the verses number [one] hundred and sixty-three.
In the Yuddhakāṇḍa, however, the cantos are enumerated as beginning with Vyoma and ending with Candira.
The verses spoken therein consist of six, eight, five, and four syllables respectively.
And likewise, in the Uttarakāṇḍa, there are chapters known as Rudra and Indu.
The verses recited there consist of [the numbers] zero, sky, space, and ocean.

The supreme guru has been described as fivefold by those who perceive the Self as Brahman.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant. || 1 ||

Commentary: Regarding the doctrine stated in the *Tantrasāra*, as it is said in the chapter on instruction (*upadeśapaṭala*) by those who know Brahman: "The student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the ascetic (*yati*)"—[1].
Among those who have transcended the castes and stages of life, the wise recognize these as superior in successive order.
For those who are not the best, the preceptors are proclaimed to be the best among the Hari-adepts. || 2 || 5 ||

Commentary: These two individuals—the one who has transcended the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), namely Nāda, and the Avadhūta yogi—are the most excellent among those worthy of being gurus. Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent among those worthy of worship, so too these two, being the most excellent, shall proceed through the lineage of gurus in succession. To explain that further: || 2 ||
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and also the ascetic.
One becomes a guru solely by the power of the excellence of one's knowledge, and not otherwise.

Commentary: For one belonging to the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), the student (*brahmacārin*) or the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) may indeed be considered a teacher by virtue of the excellence of their knowledge; however, there is no other way for this to occur. || 3 ||
O lotus-eyed one, this applies even to the householder, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic.
Only by the power of the excellence of knowledge does one become a guru, and not otherwise.
Commentary (Ṭīkā):

Here, the householder is the teacher for the forest-dweller; the forest-dweller is the teacher for the ascetic. Previously, Kamalākṣa had said that he was superior because of his excellence in learning (*vidyotkarṣa*) among those belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*). There is no doubt regarding this meaning. (4)
O Hari, even those established in the stage of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha) and likewise those who have renounced the world (saṃnyāsins).
One becomes a guru solely through the power of excellence in knowledge, and not otherwise.

Commentary: Here, the forest-dweller and the renunciants have the word of the Guru as their authority. However, in the case of the Avadhūta yogis who transcend the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), even if they lack the power of spiritual knowledge (vidyā), they do not require the word of a Guru. || 5 ||
The Guru who has transcended the castes and stages of life is declared to be the most supreme of all.
O Puruṣottama, there shall not even be a disciple of Naka such as I am.

Commentary: Even among those who have transcended the duties of their caste and stage of life, the yogi who has attained Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all. Yet, he does not possess any disciples whatsoever. || 6 ||
60. Now, regarding the specific rule concerning women and Śūdras—(in another passage of that same work):
"For Śūdras and likewise for women, no such status of being a Guru exists."
The husband alone is the guru of women, but the father is even greater than he.
Alternatively, a wise knower of Brahman is superior to these two in the absence of a [suitable] recipient. || 1 ||

Commentary: It is not the case that women and Śūdras lack the qualification for the status of a Guru to provide instruction; rather, for a woman, her husband is the primary Guru. Since he is her Guru, it is understood that she possesses the fitness to receive instruction in the mantras from him. Furthermore, when one who knows Brahman is present, he is considered the supreme Guru for all of them. || 1 ||
For Śūdras, the higher caste is progressively more excellent, reaching the highest of the high.
In the recitation of the Purāṇas, in mantras, and in the exposition of the path of knowledge; || 2 ||

Commentary: For a Śūdra, one who performs the recitation of Purāṇas, the instruction of mantras, or the instruction of knowledge is superior; beyond that, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas—in this order—are each progressively more excellent as gurus. || 2 ||
The authority of women over mantras exists solely by virtue of their husband's command.
Otherwise, the vow, the mantra, and the fast would become fruitless.

Commentary: For a woman, [the attainment of] the authority for the Tantric path—beginning with mantras, fasts, and so forth—is to be understood as occurring solely through the husband's permission; without her husband’s permission, all religious practices will become fruitless. || 3 ||
Having honored the command of her husband, she may take refuge with another teacher.
In the absence of a progenitor, ignorance would result in the independence of the woman. || 4 ||

Commentary: Since the husband is the primary guru for a woman, if he is deemed unfit for the instruction of mantras, she must take refuge in another guru by his command. She must follow the instructions of whichever teacher he appoints; a woman possesses no independence. || 4 ||
61. Now follows the prohibition against women bathing their heads:
(From the *Sūtasaṃhitā* in the *Śaivaratnākara*)—In sacred fields, at holy pilgrimage sites, during eclipses, and on auspicious days;
During periods of impurity due to birth, impurity due to death, and during the occurrence of menstrual flow; || 1 ||
Indeed, for the husband alone, there is initiation as part of the marriage ceremony of his daughter or son.
A woman whose husband is living shall never perform a head-bath without an oil massage.

Commentary (*Ṭīkā*): As stated in the *Sūta-saṃhitā* within the *Śaiva-ratnākara*: "A woman (*suvāsinī*) should perform a head-bath (*śiraḥ-snāna*) in holy places (*puṇya-kṣetra*) and sacred bathing sites (*puṇya-tīrtha*), during auspicious times such as eclipses (*grahaṇa*), during periods of ritual impurity (*jātāśauca*) and the like, when she is menstruating (*rajasvalā*), after childbirth (*prasava*), on the occasion of the marriage of a daughter or son, and during the initiations (*dīkṣā*) such as sacrifices (*yāga*) performed by her husband. Apart from these specific occasions, an oil massage (*abhyaṅga*) is forbidden; however, a head-bath is entirely appropriate. (2)
62. Now, the rules for women—(in the Śaivaratnākara): "For women, service to the husband is the eternal dharma; there is no other."
For the worship of me, O auspicious lady, is indeed the yoga of the Lord, if it exists.
Having abandoned the service due to her husband, she became intent upon religious vows.
She goes to the Sānāriniraya hell; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 2 ||

Beginning with the mounting of the stone, the supreme worship of Gaurī by women is more excellent than the recitation of the Vedas and other such practices; the reading of the Purāṇas is superior. (3)

Commentary (*Ṭīkā*): As stated in the *Śaivaratnākara*: "For a woman, the supreme and eternal duty is the service of her husband; there is nothing greater than this. Therefore, with the husband's permission, O Pārvatī, she should worship each and every deity. Any woman who performs vows and other rites without her husband’s consent will surely go to hell; of this there is no doubt. (p. 358)

Regarding women, as long as the observances such as vows and fasts continue, the performance of the *gaurī-pūjā*—beginning with the *aśmārohaṇa* (the stepping upon the stone) and ending with the *saptapadī* (the seven steps)—at the time of marriage is considered superior because it is prescribed by the injunctions. From that point forward, it is stated that the study of the Vedas, the recitation and listening to the Purāṇas, and so forth, are conducive to spiritual welfare (*śreyaskara*). Consequently, a woman must practice her vows and other duties only according to the command of her husband.
63. Now, the mantra for the worship of Gaurī, the foremost among women—(from the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa and elsewhere):
"The daily worship of Āryā-Gaurī must be performed with the five-syllabled mantra."
Whether it be Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Śaiva, or dedicated to another deity, [the mantra] should indeed end with "namaḥ."
Mantra is praised for women, but this [mantra] is neither female nor neuter.
This six-syllabled mantra is a forest fire for the great sins. || 2 ||
This five-syllabled mantra is remembered as being inseparable from the Praṇava.

Commentary: One should perform the worship of Gaurī by means of the five-syllabled mantra (Gaurī-pañcākṣarī) of Nitya. It is stated that for women, this mantra should be taught excluding the Praṇava (Oṃ). For this very reason, it is stated that Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, and Śaiva mantras should be taught ending with "namas. Because this mantra ends with "namas," one must consider it a "klība-mantra" (neuter mantra). Therefore, following this sequence, it should be taught to women. As stated in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa: "This six-syllabled mantra, when joined with the Praṇava, is like a forest fire to great sins; however, if this mantra is devoid of the Praṇava, it should be considered a five-syllabled mantra. || 17 ||
64. Now, the mantra for women, Śūdras, and those of mixed caste who seek liberation:
it should be meditated upon by women, Śūdras, and those of mixed caste who desire liberation.
There is no ritual adornment, no fire sacrifice, no purificatory rite, and no libation.
There is no instruction regarding the proper times; this Manu is always impure.
By this very method, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is performed; by that same method, sipping water (ācamana) is best. || 2 ||

Commentary: For those seeking liberation, even women, Śūdras, mixed castes, and the sick are entitled to this five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī-mantra). Regarding this five-syllabled mantra, there is no need for the extensive daily rites (āhnika) such as the purification of the site and the deity, nor for rituals like fire-oblations (homa) and libations (tarpaṇa); since it is a mantra that is inherently pure at all times, why should there be restrictions regarding the time of its instruction, such as the days of planetary conjunctions (grahaṇa) or auspicious festivals (parva)? Women and the sick may perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and so forth using this very mantra.
65. Now, regarding these specific images and so forth for the worship to be performed by women with mantras:
one should worship the God or the Goddess, the Mother of the World, with that very [mantra].
Every month, one should worship Viṣṇu and the goddess Vāg-Āryakanyakā.
One should worship the Lord in his image-form (arcā), likewise in the liṅga, and other deities within the maṇḍala.
The invocation by name of a deity is not the ritual procedure for the installation of a woman.

Commentary: Women may perform the worship of Śiva or the worship of Gaurī using these mantras. Whichever form they wish to worship—whether it be Viṣṇu, Gaurī, or Śiva—they may do so. If they wish to worship Īśvara, they may worship him by taking the form of a Śivaliṅga. They may also worship other deities within the maṇḍala. However, for women, there is no requirement for the invocation (*āvāhana*) or the ritual of the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) regarding the deity. Therefore, men should worship the installed Liṅgas and images according to the previously mentioned method. (The *maṇḍala* refers to the colorful designs and decorations. || 2 ||
66. Now, the number of syllables in the names beginning with Saṃvatsara and ending with Graha: two in the first [group], three in the second, four in the third, and sixteen indeed in the fourth.
In the fifth [chapter], however, the wise have declared two things: the description of the years and the description of the letters. || 1 ||
The two wings, numbering two, are known as the Pāṇḍavas in the solstice.
Of the seasons, three are in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise three in the month of Caitra.
Six months [are assigned] to the number of fires (three), and four [months] to the number two.
I have described to you the number of the ages (yugas) and the two [types] of months according to their colors.
The number nine is declared to be the triple enumeration, while the number four is the enumeration of the ages (yugas).
Regarding the number two, three [categories] have been proclaimed; thus the lunar days (tithis) have been described by the wise.
The pairs are said to be two in number, and likewise the triads are two.
Indeed, one among the [seven] days is said by people to be the measure of a yuga.
The number of arrows is said to be two, as are the number of ages (yugas) and the sages (ṛṣis).
Eight are recorded in the pair, and eleven are remembered in the triad.
The number of colors of the constellations has been declared by the sages for the Kali age.
In the case of the number two, as well as in the three [groups] of fifteen, ten are traditionally taught.
The number of Vedas is declared by people to be two according to the classification of yogas.
In the Aṣṭaka, however, there should be three varṇas, two of which are equal to the number of eyes (two).
And they are remembered as being one in number among the instruments of the Vedas.
In the number two, the flavors (rasas) are declared; likewise, in the number three, there is the pentad (pañcaka).
And thus, one [sign] has been declared among the number of signs in the calculation of the yugas.
The number of Vedas is said to be two, and likewise, the number of sages is two.
The colors of the nine planets have been described by the wise for the sake of understanding.
In the Śaka year [measured by] the four, five, sages (seven), and moon (one) [i.e., 1574].
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kharajyeṣṭha, on a Thursday.
It was spoken by the illustrious King Kṛṣṇa through the compassionate glance of Śrīmat Caṇḍī.
The number of syllables, beginning with the year and ending with the planets, is for the delight of the virtuous. 13.

Thus ends the eighth treasury, titled "The Exposition of the Āgamas and Other Systems," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign of the preeminent city of Mahīśūra; who is adorned by the entire circle of the earth; who is the crest-jewel of all lands; who is the presiding authority over the Karṇāṭaka country; who shines resplendently in the midst of the great seat of the illustrious Mahīśūra; who has ascended the divine jeweled throne experienced by the entire circle of his own sovereign emperors, headed by the royal protectors descended through a lineage of unimpaired treasuries of arts; who bears the titles of Illustrious Emperor of Emperors, Supreme Lord, King of Kings, Possessor of Majestic Prowess, Matchless Heroic Monarch, Ornament of the Sky among Titles, Sole Hero of the World, Ocean of the Milk-Waters of the Yadu Lineage, Treasure-Trove of the Moon, and Bearer of the Conch, Discus, Goad, Axe, Makara, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva-Gaṇḍa, Bheruṇḍa, Earth-Boar, Hanuman, Garuḍa, Kaṇṭhīrava, and many other such titles. 8.
Thus, in the work titled *Śrītattvanidhi*, the eighth [chapter], the *Āgamanidhi*, is complete. 8.

**The Thirty-Two Emblems (Vaṭṭu 320)** Since the Cakravartins [Universal Monarchs] have been born in the city of Yigaṃjīphīna, one must abandon attachment to these worldly emblems. **The Sequence of the Thirty-Two Emblems:** King, Queen, Chariot, Vajīra, Infantry, Banner, and Cāmuṇḍeśvarī as the sole emblem for the position of the Queen, with the Lion as her vehicle—these are the thirty-two emblems. Having enumerated the signs starting from Aries (Meṣa) up to Pisces (Mīna), and having stated the lords of the bodies of those emblems, there are twelve emblems to be adorned. Thus, having joined these sixteen emblems in this manner, they are to be arrayed.

(p. 366) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics based on objects that do not exist, just as one perceives a snake in a rope. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various forms arising from the causal conditions of ignorance, karma, and the habitual tendencies of false discrimination; it is like a dream or a magical illusion. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state where the dependent nature is seen as free from the imagined nature, and where the non-dual reality is realized through the wisdom of the noble ones. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization of the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, the absence of the three self-natures, and the entry into the stage of the Tathāgata through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Mahāmati, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands these four kinds of self-nature, they will quickly attain the stage of a Buddha and liberate all sentient beings."

(Commentary) — In this *Daśāvatāra* game of dice, there are ten dice (*bāju*) with eighteen pips each, totaling one hundred and eighty pips. Having gathered these together, they play; in that game, the night of the battle belongs to Cāmuṇḍeśvarī. Whoever plays the elephant among the dice, whoever plays the fish, and whoever plays the horse—having seized their respective winnings through skillful play, Cāmuṇḍeśvarī sweeps away the winnings of those who have lost. An intelligent person should observe this and play.

There are 16 *yalegals* for the *cakravarti*s (universal emperors). At 160 *vaṭṭu* [of gold]—(1) for one *bāju* of Cāmuṇḍeśvarī, 18 *yalegals* of the color of vermilion (*cinnadabaṇṇa*); (2) for one *bāju* of Īśvara, 18 *yalegals* of the color of coral (*īṅgalīkadabaṇṇa*); (3) for one *bāju* of Viṣṇu, 18 *yalegals* of the color of turmeric (*haladībaṇṇa*); (4) for one *bāju* of Brahmā, 18 *yalegals* of the color of saffron (*piṣṭāpaccebaṇṇa*); (5) for one *bāju* of Indra, 18 *yalegals* of the color of camphor (*kappubaṇṇa*); (6) for one *bāju* of Sūrya, 18 *yalegals* of the color of copper (*vartībaṇṇa*); (7) for one *bāju* of Candra, 18 *yalegals* of the color of lac (*jaṅgālubaṇṇa*); (8) for one *bāju* of Manmatha, 18 *yalegals* of the color of the moon (*candrabaṇṇa*). Thus, for these eight *bāju*s, there are 144 *yalegals*. There are 16 *yalegals* of the color of musk (*bellibaṇṇa*) for the *cakravarti*s. In this *gañjīphiṅga* containing two such sets, for four people, at one *dara* [of gold], there are 40 *yalegals*. Taking one *haṃci* [of gold], in the eighth *ākhai* (section), in the *bāju* of Manmatha, in the *ākhai* of the fish (*mīna*), whoever says "Hukuṃ" [shall receive it]. Having determined which color belongs to whom among those who have come to claim it, and having made the final decision, whatever remains as the remainder, that shall be the share of Cāmuṇḍeśvarī. A wise person should observe this *gañjīphiṅga* of the *merige* [set].

(p. 375) [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna-svabhāva). "Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and characteristics based on the dependent self-nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of various forms arising from the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination; it is like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection. This is called the dependent self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is seen as being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; it is the realization of suchness (tathatā) through non-discriminative wisdom. This is called the perfected self-nature. "Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the Great Vehicle? It is the realization that all phenomena are devoid of self-nature, that they are unborn and unceasing, and that they are equal to space; it is the entry into the stage of the Tathāgata by means of the ten stages (daśabhūmi). This is called the self-nature of the Great Vehicle. "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate the practice of the Great Vehicle by relying upon the perfected self-nature and abandoning the imagined and dependent self-natures. [End of page 375]

When they have thus assembled, during the day or night, Kṛṣṇa shall perform the *ghora* [military formation]. As for the two *akhairu* (elephant-riders) and the fish-bannered (*mīnuyale*) Kṛṣṇa-bāju—whoever performs the *huku* (the signal/attack)—those who follow behind him must act with such skillful intelligence as to leave no trace of their passage. If one were to calculate the total number of *varahā* (horses) required for this array: for the four *ghora*s, there are forty-eight *varahā*s; for ten *rāṇiga*s, there are forty *varahā*s; for four *vajīra*s, there are twenty *varahā*s; for four *padāti* (infantry), there are sixteen *varahā*s; and for four *patāka*s, there are four *varahā*s. Thus, the total number of *varahā* horses is one hundred and twenty-eight. Starting from the *ghora*s and ending with the *patāka*s, for each day of the four *yalegalu* units, those who are to remain behind shall stay, while the others shall advance; having thus determined the conclusion, those who advance must proceed with the *tiladukkolla* (the scattering of sesame seeds as a mark of departure).

(Commentary) — 16. Regarding the *āṭakka* with sixteen *mukhacārīs*, the details for the four *cārīs* are as follows: In one *cārī*, there are three *bīdigalu* (lines). In the center of this *īcārī* (game board) is a lotus; the rest are squares of eight [squares] each. In these [squares], there is one *gaṇḍumanē* (die) for each. (Commentary) — Regarding the six-faced dice game (*ṣaṇmukhada paguḍe*): the arrangement of the four dice (*cārī*) is as follows: In one die, there are two dots (*vīdi*) and one dot; in another, three dots and two dots; in another, six dots and four dots. In total, there are 144 dots across the six dice. In the center of this formation is a lotus; the others are the surrounding petals. Within each of these, one should place a distinct number of dots. On these dots, one should arrange the figures of the various animals, placing them one after another. For this formation, assign a specific number of dots to each animal and move them accordingly. The list of animals for these dice is as follows: - Six *haladī* animals - Six *hasaru* animals - Six *keṃpu* animals - Six *karī* animals - Six *bilī* animals - Six *gulābīraṅgina* animals Thus, there are thirty-six animals in total. Regarding the six cloth strips (*paṭṭa*) on the dice: - For every two dice, there is one strip. - For every one strip, there is one [unit]. - For every one strip, there are three [units]. - For every one strip, there are four [units]. - For every one strip, there are six [units]. - For every one strip, there are eight [units]. - For every one strip, there are ten [units]. According to this rule, one strip is used. From among the other two dice, one must join and calculate the total value: two, three, five, eight, seventeen, and sixty-two. When the calculation is thus completed, the elder players should take their respective stakes, and six people should sit in a circle and begin the game. Three people should sit in a circle and begin by taking the first stake. One should play according to the rules of the dice game, employing the wisdom of the ancient *akṣakrīḍā* (dice-play).

(Commentary) — In the *burajina* (fortress-like structure), four squares (*cārī*) are placed within each square; there are three such squares [per side]. In one square, there are ten houses (*mane*) in the middle square; in two squares on the sides, nine houses each, totaling eighteen; in three squares at the corners (*vaṭṭu*), for every four squares, there are twenty-eight houses, and for four squares, there are one hundred and twelve corner houses. In the center of the squares is a lotus (*kamala*). There are four crossroads (*guṇḍu-mane*). For every four squares, four gates (*saṃdīva*) are added, and four towers (*buruju*). In one tower, there are five houses; thus, in four towers, there are twenty houses. This makes a total of one hundred and thirty-two houses. Within the towers, there is one crossroad house, which is not counted for the scribe.

(p. 383) [The text continues: ...the Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor a sentient being, nor a living soul, nor a person. He does not perceive form, nor feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nor the nose, nor the tongue, nor the body, nor the mind. He does not perceive forms, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental objects. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the eye-base, nor the form-base, nor the eye-consciousness-base; nor the ear-base, nor the sound-base, nor the ear-consciousness-base; nor the nose-base, nor the odor-base, nor the nose-consciousness-base; nor the tongue-base, nor the taste-base, nor the tongue-consciousness-base; nor the body-base, nor the tangible-base, nor the body-consciousness-base; nor the mind-base, nor the mental-object-base, nor the mind-consciousness-base. He does not perceive the aggregate of form, nor the aggregate of feeling, nor the aggregate of perception, nor the aggregate of formations, nor the aggregate of consciousness. He does not perceive the element of desire, nor the element of form, nor the element of formlessness. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena, nor unconditioned phenomena. He does not perceive ignorance, nor volitional formations, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense bases, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor becoming, nor birth, nor aging-and-death. He does not perceive suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruit of a Once-returner, nor the fruit of a Non-returner, nor Arhatship, nor Pratyekabuddhahood, nor even Buddhahood. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive these things that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. [End of passage]

In this [game], one must capture one by one. For this player, the "lotus-sleepers" (kamalada suttalu) are those who, having been placed in the "flower-garden" (guṃdumaneyalli), have reached eighty bodies; these must be captured. In this game, one must join the pair of pieces (burujugalalli) and place them on the edge. To join them in the middle, they must come together. Having separated the pair in the middle, they must be placed in the corner (tirigī) and joined within the buruji. For this player, having given three sets of men (manegalannu), one must move one by one according to the dice roll. This is the description of the bodies for this player: the details for twenty bodies are as follows—five bodies for the die showing one, five for the yellow die (halladī), five for the red die (hasaru), five for the black die (keṃpu), and five for the white die (kappu). On each day, one must fashion the various distinct bodies according to these five types of dice. This player has two "fortresses" (ḍālagalu): in the fortress of the six-sided die (paṭṭina bājugalannuḍālagala), the inscription on the pieces (paṭṭagala) is as follows: 2 per piece (paṭṭu 1 kke 2), 4 per piece, 6 per piece, 8 per piece, 10 per piece, and 1 blank piece (khālī paṭṭu 1). In the first fortress, 12 per piece, 16 per piece, 18 per piece, 20 per piece, 24 per piece, and 1 blank piece. From these two fortresses, one must calculate the value of the pieces (joḍu dāya). One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 2 is called a *phalaya*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 4 is called a *yugava*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 6 is called a *rasaviṃba*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 8 is called a *vargava*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 10 is called a *dikkuya*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 12 is called a *bhānuva*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 16 is called a *kala*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 18 is called a *smṛti*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 20 is called a *kṛti*. One blank piece plus one piece with an inscription of 24 is called a *ghana*. In the other fortress, if a blank piece is used, it is called a *pūjya*. There is no need to play with the bodies. When a piece with an inscription of 2 is used, there is no "juice-value" (*jauḍudāya*). One must play the *vaṃṭikāyi* (the "bunch-body") after completing the sequence of the previous dice throws. Those who possess intelligence should observe the order of the game and proceed.

(Commentary) — Regarding the details for the nine planets in the diagram: In one square (*cārī*), there are twelve threads (*suttalu*) across the middle; there are twelve threads in each thread-line (*dala*). For every one thread-line, there are twelve squares (*manegalu*); thus, for twelve thread-lines, there are 144 squares. This is the sequence for the twelfth parts (*dvādaśāṃśaka*). If one constructs the squares by placing nine squares per thread-line, it becomes the sequence for the ninth parts (*navāṃśa*). If one constructs them by placing thirty squares per thread-line, it becomes the sequence for the thirtieth parts (*triṃśāṃśaka*). Regarding this diagram, the figures should be drawn in the form of the nine planets. The description of their colors is as follows: the Sun is copper-colored; the Moon is white; Mars is red; Mercury is yellow; Jupiter is turmeric-colored; Venus is white; Saturn is black; Rāhu is smoke-colored; and Ketu is variegated. One should color the squares according to these hues. Alternatively: the seven planets beginning with the Sun move in a clockwise direction (*savyagati*); Rāhu and Ketu move counter-clockwise (*apasavya*). One should perform the calculations according to the rules of *Jyotiṣaśāstra*, including their fast motion (*aticāra*), retrogression (*vakragati*), stationary state (*staṃbha*), and direct motion (*ṛjugati*). The sequence for placing these figures is as follows: 1. When the number two is present, place the Sun in the sign of Leo (*siṃharāśi*). 2. When three is present, place the Moon in Cancer (*karkaṭakarāśi*). 3. When five is present, place Mars in Aries (*meṣarāśi*). 4. When four is present, place Mercury in Virgo (*kanyārāśi*). 5. When six is present, place Jupiter in Pisces (*mīnarāśi*). 6. When seven is present, place Venus in Libra (*tulārāśi*). 7. When eight is present, place Saturn in Capricorn (*makararāśi*). 8. When nine is present, place Rāhu in Taurus (*vṛṣabharāśi*). 9. When ten is present, place Ketu in Scorpio (*vṛścikarāśi*). Whichever planet is assigned to whichever number, one should place that planet in its corresponding sign according to the respective number. Whether moving directly or retrogressively, if the figures must be placed again after having been removed, the method of the initial convention is to place them according to the numbers present in the squares. In this diagram, there are sixteen squares; the details for two of these squares are: in one square, there is one row of empty spaces consisting of 2, 3, and 5; in another square, there is one row of empty spaces consisting of 1, 3, and 4. Having constructed the squares in this manner, one should proceed from the bottom upwards according to the sequence of the figures and the presence of the numbers. If the empty spaces in the squares are not filled correctly, there will be no stability (*staṃbha*) in the movement. Thus, the wise person should examine this diagram, extracting its essential meaning.

(Commentary) — Regarding the layout of the four streets (*cārī*) within this circular city plan (*bhūcakradapagaḍe*): having constructed the four streets in the form of a wheel (*cakrākāra*) within this circular city plan, one should construct the following number of houses (*mane*) for each street: in the first street, 64 houses; in the second street, 48 houses; in the third street, 40 houses; in the fourth street, 36 houses; and in the fifth street, 32 houses. Having constructed these houses in such a manner, one should build 29 houses along the perimeter wall outside that [first] street, and then a gateway (*koṭeya*). Within that gateway’s street, one should construct 24 houses, and then a wall outside that. Within that [second] wall, one should build 28 houses, and then outside of that, on the site known as *sāyujya* (union), which is shaped like a large mountain, one Śiva-liṅga should be installed. In this manner, for each of the four directions, one should construct the houses for each street, and having built the perimeter walls for the five streets according to the layout, one should build six houses at the corner where the wall meets the street, and then proceed to construct the remaining houses. *** **Note:** The original text contains archaic Kannada administrative terminology related to urban planning and temple architecture. The terms *sālu guṃḍa* refer to the outer boundary walls or enclosures, while *horagina* refers to the specific layout or arrangement. The term *sāyujya* here likely refers to a sacred space intended for spiritual liberation. The numbers provided correspond to the decreasing number of residential units (*mane*) as one moves outward from the center of the circular plan. The mention of a *Śivaliṅga* at the periphery indicates the religious character of this urban design. The instruction regarding the "four directions" implies a symmetrical radial layout centered around a core area. The final section describes the construction sequence for the outer precincts and the placement of ancillary structures.

Regarding the *ḍālagalu* (the "branch-people") of the first branch (*ḍāla*): for every four *paṭṭu*, there is one *paṭṭu*; for every one *paṭṭu*, there is one [person]; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are three; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are five; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are six. Thus, for these four *ḍālagalu*, for every one [unit], there are twenty-eight [persons]. For those who possess the number of constellations (*nakṣatra*) corresponding to that, they shall certainly obtain the *bīlu* (inheritance/portion). Now, in this manner, for the first branch: for every four *paṭṭu*, there is one *paṭṭu*; for every one *paṭṭu*, there is one; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are three; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are five; for every one *paṭṭu*, there are six. Having thus made these four *ḍālagalu*, for every one [unit], there are twenty-eight [persons]. For those who possess the number of constellations corresponding to that, they shall obtain the *bīlu* by making the elders (*gurutu*). Whichever among these two classes of *ḍālagalu* obtains how much, let them take it according to their respective branches. In each of the four colors—red, yellow, black, and white—there are twenty-four bodies (*kāyi*) for each color. Having made these twenty-four bodies, they shall proceed according to the established order, starting from the eastern direction, then the southern, western, and northern directions, following the sequence of the quarters. In this way, having reached the house of the *sāyujya* station, which is the Śiva-liṅga, and having entered the house where the bodies reside, the *haṇṇu* (gold/wealth) of the bodies shall be distributed. Those who are intelligent shall carry out the final settlement (*niṣkarṣeya*) exactly as it is in their respective quarters.

(Commentary) — Regarding the construction of the *Śrīcakra* with ten petals: **The Description of the Eight-Petaled [Cakra] within the Śrīcakra:** In the eight-petaled [cakra] within the *Śrīcakra*, one should construct four squares (*catur-asra*) in the form of a lotus. Within those, one should fashion nine squares in the shape of *Vṛndāvana*. Beyond that, there must be ten petals. For this octagon, there are 286 squares (*maṇega*). **The Description of Vṛndāvana:** Within the tenth square, which is shaped like a *kalaśa* (vase) for *Vṛndāvana*, one should construct a large square. Inside that, place *Cāmuṇḍeśvarī Ammanavar*. Within that, in one square, there are 13 squares; in another, 6 squares; in another, 15 squares; and in another, 2 squares. Beyond that, in one square, there are 17 squares. Beyond these, in the middle of the lotus petals, there are 21 squares. Following that, on both sides of the central petal—on the left and right—one should place 6 *keṃpu-kāyi* (small figures), 6 *karī-kāyi* (elephant figures), and 6 *hasaru-kāyi* (lion figures). Together, these amount to 12 squares. In the next petal, along with 6 *haladī-kāyi* (tortoise figures) and 6 *hasaru-kāyi*, totaling 12 squares, one should place 115 squares derived from the eight petals. Thus, 286 squares are obtained. Since the squares for the effect (*kārya*) here are 101 and the squares for the cause (*kāraṇa*) are also 101, and since the squares for the figures (*kāyi*) are 24, the squares for the resting places (*viśrama-sthāna*) are 59, and the square for the place of union (*sāyujya-sthāna*) is 1, the total is 286 squares. To proceed with the figures, one must fashion four petals. For each petal: 4 squares, 1 square, 3 squares, 5 squares, and 6 squares. Having calculated these proportions, one must arrange the squares according to the sequence of the figures within the petals. Alternatively, one may construct the petals in another manner: 4 squares, 1 square, 3 squares, 5 squares, and 6 squares. Or yet another way: 1 square, 2 squares, 4 squares, and 6 squares. Or: 1 square, 4 squares, 6 squares, and 8 squares. These are the four types of petals. Thus, by joining the 14 squares of the four petals, they become a single unit. Whichever of these four types of petals one prefers, one should adopt that specific arrangement. ***Note on Terminology:*** * **Maṇega**: A square unit of measurement. * **Kāyi**: A small figure or deity representation. * **Keṃpu-kāyi**: Small figures. * **Karī-kāyi**: Elephant figures. * **Hasaru-kāyi**: Lion figures. * **Haladī-kāyi**: Tortoise figures. * **Dāla**: Petal. * **Paṭṭu**: A specific measure or sub-unit of a square. * **Gurutuga**: Proportions or weights of measurement. * **Sarpa-gati**: Moving like a serpent (a winding path). * **Viśrama-sthāna**: Place of rest. * **Sāyujya-sthāna**: Place of union (with the divine). * **Ishrīcakrada**: Of the Śrīcakra. * **Āṭakke**: In the octagon. * **Māḍikkoṇḍu**: Having made/constructed. * **Melē**: Within/inside. * **Baradu irabeku**: Must exist/be present. * **Doḍḍadāgi**: Large/extended. * **Ammanavar**: Goddess. * **Merige**: Proportion/measure. * **Tāviniṃda**: By means of the sequence. * **Naḍasuttā baruvadu**: It should proceed/move. * **Abhiruci**: Preference/desire. * **Āḍālahalī**: In the respective petals. * **Āḍabahudu**: One should adopt/place.I hope this translation is helpful. He restored the dilapidated temples of Duśivana, Bujīrṇa, Vāgīru, Tirala, and Duddhāra at Hadimūraneya Sālinallinūreṃbhattara, and [established] many shrines for the Lord Īśāna.
In the world of Indra, which abounds in various sacrifices, offerings, and other rites, there was a man named Anūre Bhaṭṭa.
Out of joy at the sight of the Lord of the Mountain, he performed the hospitality due to a guest, and many people from the world of Agni arrived. || 38 ||
By means of many gifts of tawny cows (*kapila-godāna*) and other such acts, she attained the worlds of the sun, the moon, the fire, the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
O Lord of the temple of virtuous deeds, whose mind is dedicated to the feet of the noble Bhaṭṭanēraḷi, you who possess the true nature of the inner soul, protect me like a god.
In the city of Hadineidane, which is adorned with three palaces and surrounded by a beautiful grove, there are many true people who are exceedingly truthful. || 39 ||
On the day of the star Śravaṇa, the noble Vīraśaiva Nāga entered the pure world of Kailāsa.

(Commentary) — For the construction of the square-shaped stone slabs (paṭṭavaṇṇu) according to the *īrīti* style, there are one hundred and seventy-six square-shaped slabs. Including the *kelagaṇa-śūla*, the *naraka-bandhana*, the *sālu-moda-lāgi*, the *hadi-naidana*, the *sālu-varige*, and the *sālu-vandakke*, there are fifteen *sālu* stones and two hundred and twenty-five *manega* stones. Together with the sixteen *devīsāyujya* stones and the one *aṅkita-damana* stone, the total is eleven. Including the sixteen circular (*vaṭṭu*) *sālu* stones, there are two hundred and thirty-six *manega* stones.

In the case of the square-shaped *paṭhakkas* numbered by the count of *ḍālas*, *galas*, *lekkhas*, and *nakhās*: for the *merige* (central unit) of 20, there is no entry for 1 *ḍāla* and 4 *paṭṭus*, nor for 1 *paṭṭu*. For the *kaḍama* (corner unit), there is no entry for 3 *paṭṭus* and 1 *ralli* and 1 *paṭṭu*; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 2; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 3. For 1 *ḍāla* and 1 *paṭṭu*, there is no entry. For the *kaḍama*, there is no entry for 3 *paṭṭus* and 1 *ralli* and 4 *paṭṭus*; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 5; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 6. For 1 *ḍāla* and 1 *paṭṭu*, there is no entry. For the *kaḍama*, there is no entry for 3 *paṭṭus* and 1 *ralli* and 7 *paṭṭus*; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 8; nor for 1 *paṭṭu* and 11. For the three *īḍālas*, one *riṃda*, and one *riṃdahiḍidu*, there is no entry for 100 *varigus*. For the square-shaped *devīsāyujya-dāṭakas*, there are *īḍālas*.

404) This is the inscription on the left side at the junction of the serpent-like path leading toward the square enclosure of the temple of the Goddess, which is the cause of liberation through union with the Goddess (ī-devīsāyujya-mukti), [and] which is adorned with the letters of the Akṣara-mātṛkā;
this alone is the sole cause for reaching the state of Damane-galu.
For one who harms a preceptor, there is the attainment of the Śūla hell; for one who utters falsehood,
there is the attainment of becoming a worm in hell.
One who reviles a virtuous person attains the hell of downward fall;
one who betrays his master attains the Mahāraurava hell;
and one who betrays his mother or father attains the Raurava hell.
Betraying a friend leads to rebirth in the Patana hell;
pride in one's learning leads to birth as a Brahmarākṣasa;
and excessive pride leads to birth as a Rākṣasa.
By showing disrespect to one who possesses the *tāmasa* ego, one incurs birth as a *rākṣasa*;
by insulting a king, one attains the *kuṃbhīpāka* hell;
and by committing an offense against a royal treasury, one attains the *kālasūtra* hell.
For one who reviles the king, there is the attainment of the Asipatravana hell;
for one who aids a traitor to the king, there is the attainment of the Saṃghāta hell;
and for one who covets the king’s wife, there is the attainment of the Andhatamas hell.
If one born of the highest caste drinks liquor, one attains the Vaitaraṇī hell;
if one lacks compassion for living beings, one receives a birth as a donkey;
and if one causes the interruption of another's sleep, one receives three births [as a donkey].
If one's life is spent in vain talk, that is a birth as a deity;
if one merely sings without remembering the Divine, that is a birth as a ghost;
and if one mocks the unconditioned Light, that is a birth as a dog.
If one steals the lamp of a temple, one takes birth as a moth;
if one commits the theft of grain, one takes birth as a *heggaṇa* (a type of rat);
and if one acts as a thorn to the world, one takes birth as a scorpion.
If one steals the garments of others, one will take birth as a lizard;
if one aids those who commit treason against their master, one will take birth as a cricket;
if one administers poison to one's husband, one will take birth as a bat.
O bee, you have attained birth as a human, which is difficult to achieve; you have acquired wealth and established a virtuous household—this is the birth of one who has truly fulfilled his purpose.
405) What other birth could be more meaningful than this?
The birth of one who disregards the thorns of food is like the birth of a worm in a cesspool; the birth of one who disregards the thorns of charity is the birth of a lotus on dry land.
If one disregards the heart of poison, one takes birth as a snake;
if one disregards the forest of discernment, one takes birth as a frog in a pond;
and if one lives with utter contempt for the Lord, one takes birth as a fish.
Birth as a thorn-tree in a marriage grove,
birth as a crow that is excessively deceitful,
birth as a human devoid of intelligence, and birth as a dog who lives for a very long time— these are [the fruits of such actions].
One born under Jñānigalaṃkaṇḍu will have crooked teeth; one born under Naḍadara will have birth as a tree; one who lives by eating the food of others will have birth as a crow;
and one who lives by stealing food will have birth as a donkey.
If one steals the wealth of others, one takes birth as a rat;
if one kills living beings, one takes birth as a snake;
if one censures those who have performed a pilgrimage to a holy site, one takes birth as a tortoise.
From neglecting the performance of virtuous deeds comes birth as a dull-witted person; from excessive regard for one's lineage comes birth as a python;
and from constant longing comes birth as a crow.
If one studies the scriptures without discernment, there is the birth of a donkey;
if one practices hypocritical meditation, there is the birth of a crane;
and if one possesses excessive detachment, there is the birth of a rhinoceros.
If one eats meat from a wild animal during the time of an eclipse, one will take birth as a boar;
if one eats human flesh, one will take birth as a monkey;
and if one forcibly takes a woman, one will take birth as a dog.
If one indulges in sexual union with women during the day, one will take birth as a pigeon; if one practices base conduct, one will take birth as a monkey;
and if one speaks harsh words, one will take birth as a rogue.
If one lives by deceiving those born of the highest caste, one will take birth as a dog;
if one kills them, one will take birth as a pig;
and if one punishes them through force while they are weak, one will take birth as a donkey.
Having been born as a servant to the deceitful King Hiranyaroda,
he died at Kaṇḍavaramaneya; having performed penance there, he was born as Gījavaja.
If one is always devoted to the arts of love and the gestures of passion, one will attain birth as a cuckoo;
if one displays anger toward virtuous people, one will attain birth as a jackal.
If one reviles the supreme Indra out of pride, one takes birth as a crow;
if one is always devoted to the punishment of living beings, one takes birth as a cat;
if one has fallen away from the practice of Śaiva mantras, one takes birth as a śarabha.
If one performs this recollection of the Name for the sake of others, one attains birth as Garuḍa;
if one performs the service of the Vaiṣṇava mantra for the sake of others, one attains birth as Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa;
and if one performs this pilgrimage to sacred sites for the sake of others, one attains birth as a Haṃsa.

If one is constantly devoted to a passion for hunting, there will be birth as a serpent or a wild beast; if one is distressed by the path [of worldly existence], there will be birth as a low-born person; and if there is fickleness even in the performance of virtuous deeds, there will be birth as a human being.
If one is cruel and disrespectful, there is birth as a tiger;
if one lives by the intellect of others without possessing one's own intelligence, there is birth as a parrot;
and if one is arrogant and full of pride, there is birth as an elephant.
If one eats food from a group (gaṇa), one receives birth as a Māli;
if one is devoid of proper conduct, birth as a Śūdra;
and if one desires another man after having given herself to her husband, birth as a widow.

If one is negligent in the worship of the Goddess's mantra, one is born as a lion; if one is envious of others' prosperity, one is born as a dog; if one does not offer food at the sacred site, one is born as a crow; and if one steals the offerings, one is born as a prostitute.

If one enjoys sensual pleasures without having performed the *vāve* rite, one attains birth as a neuter; if one commits theft out of greed, one attains birth as a dog; if one acts righteously but lacks knowledge, one attains birth as a Vaiśya; and if one acts virtuously but lacks knowledge, one attains birth as a cow.
If one performs that [meritorious act] with a mind whose roots of merit have been exhausted, there is birth as a human;
if performed with a mind characterized by pure (sāttvika) egoism, there is birth as a Brahmin;
if performed with desire, there is birth as a king.
By performing the construction of wells, tanks, and so forth, one attains the world of Vāyu; by performing the worship of low deities, one attains the world of Varuṇa;
and by performing the worship of Nīcadevatās, one attains the world of Nirṛti.
By giving gifts of various jewel ornaments, one attains the world of the Nāgas;
by studying the Vedas together with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga-veda*), one obtains birth as a virtuous Brahmin;
and by giving gifts of much gold, one attains the world of Kubera.
For a devoted wife who has practiced devotion to her husband, there is the attainment of the same world as her husband (*pati-sālokya*);
by performing auspicious rites such as the *aṣṭakā* and *anvaṣṭakā*, she attains the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ-loka*).
By understanding the subtleties of the Dharma, one attains the world of Yama;
by dying on the battlefield while engaged in combat, one attains the heaven of heroes;
and by being indifferent to worldly existence, one attains the birth of a detached person.
By restoring a dilapidated temple of Śiva, one attains the world of Īśāna;
by performing numerous sacrifices, offerings, and the like, one attains the world of Indra;
and by always honoring guests, one attains the world of Agni.
The gift of many tawny cows, the attainment of Goloka,
the propitiation of the Lord, the performance of virtuous deeds, knowledge, the path of reality, and the grace of the true guru.
One who has ascended to yoga through the true knowledge of the Āgamas and the Vedic knowledge of Brahman.
If one is negligent regarding the path of reality— namely,
mantra-yoga and jñāna-yoga— there is a fall from yoga.
Upon abandoning the three cravings, one attains Satyaloka;
upon honoring Vīraśaiva, one attains Kailāsaloka;
and upon honoring Vīravaiṣṇava, one attains Vaikuṇṭhaloka.
The recollection of the Name, the contemplation of the primordial sound (nāda), and worship.
Hearing of the state of servitude and the yoga of kingship.
reflection, meditative absorption, and direct realization
O Damana, O Doḍḍa, you who are marked by the experience of bliss and liberation from saṃsāra!
Service at the feet and surrender lead to sālokya and sāmīpya.

Sārūpya (attainment of similarity), Devīsāyujya (union with the Goddess), and Muktīśvara— these are the stages that arise in succession within the state of *anaktita-damana* (the unmanifested subduing).

408) In this [work], there are 106 chapters on the liberation through union with the Goddess (ī-devīsāyujyamukti), 106 chapters on the causes (kāraṇagaḷu), and 24 chapters on the marks such as the grace of the True Guru (sadgurukaṭākṣādi). Thus, there are 236 chapters in total. In this [work] of four thousand [verses], there are three hundred and twenty-four chapters; in these chapters, there are one hundred and fifty verses each, which, when multiplied by the number of nails (twenty), amount to three thousand. One should understand that this is the extent of the Guru-tantra.
28. Now, the explanation of the play with the dice for liberation through union (sāyujya) with the Goddess in the form of the *liṅga*:
Separately, by means of three lines, there are nineteen squares from the top.
Then, above the seventeen [verses] of the two methods, there are fifteen. || 1 ||
In the middle row, there are thirteen pleasant upper chambers.
In the eleventh [day], one should pierce the uppermost of the two cavities.
In the upper portion, there should be thirteen squares in two rows.
Separately above those two, in the two [channels] Vidyā and [the other], there are eleven [deities] in sequence.
Separately, in the vertical row above that, there should be thirteen cells.
Above that, one should draw seventeen squares in the row.
In the sequence of the progressively higher paths, there are sixteen and twelve respectively.
It is recorded by those skilled in games that the remaining [dice] are to be assigned to the compartments in this manner.
This play has been described by the wise as being like the previously mentioned game of dice.
And here, three dice are to be known, with one side marked with a single dot.
On the three sides, however, there are respectively two, three, and one flower, each separately.
Likewise, the Ekokṣaṇya [Yoga] is to be known as having ten, seven, and four [syllables] respectively. || 7 ||
Thirteen, as well as fifteen, and likewise fourteen.
Elsewhere, however, they are easily understood by those who are experts in policy and discerning in their vision.
Then, when five hundred sixty-seven years of the Śālivāha era had passed, in the year named Vijaya, during the fierce summer season;
On the eleventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, joined with a Friday, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the earth, manifested this form of the venerable Liṅga here.

O Mother, in the *Yaṃbāṭa* [temple], there is a painted cloth-scroll (paṭala) depicting the form of a Śiva-liṅga, which grants liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) with the Goddess. || 1 ||
The sage Alas, who spoke of everything from the grace of the true guru to liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti).

From the state of a Piśāca up to that of a human being, there exists the human condition within the petals of the lotus of the heart.
