(Commentary) — Regarding the method of composing this *īpaṭhava* (stone-slab inscription) depicting the form of Śiva-liṅga: there are 236 units (*maṇe*) for the slab representing the shape of the Śiva-liṅga. For the sixteen slabs marked with various symbols—beginning with the trident of Kailāsa and the hellish tortures up to the liberation through union with the Goddess (*devīsāyujyamukti*)—there are 16 slabs. The details for these 16 slabs are as follows: For the first [symbol], 19 *maṇe* on one slab; For the second, 19 *maṇe* on one slab; For the third, 19 *maṇe* on one slab; For the fourth, 17 *maṇe* on one slab; For the fifth, 17 *maṇe* on one slab; For the sixth, 15 *maṇe* on one slab; For the seventh, 13 *maṇe* on one slab; For the eighth, 11 *maṇe* on one slab; For the ninth, 13 *maṇe* on one slab; For the tenth, 13 *maṇe* on one slab; For the eleventh, 11 *maṇe* on one slab; For the twelfth, 11 *maṇe* on one slab; For the thirteenth, 13 *maṇe* on one slab; For the fourteenth, 17 *maṇe* on one slab; For the fifteenth, 16 *maṇe* on one slab; For the sixteenth, which is the slab marked with the liberation through union with the Goddess (*devīsāyujyamukti*), 12 *maṇe* are to be inscribed. Thus, for the 16 slabs, there are 236 *maṇe* to be inscribed. In composing this *īpaṭhava* depicting the form of the Śiva-liṅga, one should draw two large circles on both sides of the liṅga. On the left circle, the goddesses Śīcāmuṇḍeśvarī and Ammanavaru should be depicted, and on the right circle, the verses that follow must be inscribed.

In this Ī-āṭakke division, among the twenty-eight constellations (*nakṣatras*) including those with *lekhās* (lines) and those with *abhijit*, there is one *paṭṭu* (unit) in the first *ḍāla* (section) out of four *paṭṭus*. Among the three *paṭṭus* that have *lekhās*, there is one *paṭṭu* for every one [of the others]: one *paṭṭu* for two, and one *paṭṭu* for three. In the first *ḍāla*, there is one *paṭṭu* without *lekhās*; among the three with *lekhās*, there is one *paṭṭu* for every one [of the others]: one *paṭṭu* for four, one *paṭṭu* for seven, and one *paṭṭu* for ten. In the first *ḍāla*, there is one *paṭṭu* without *lekhās*; among the three with *lekhās*, there is one *paṭṭu* for every one [of the others]: one *paṭṭu* for thirteen, one *paṭṭu* for fourteen, and one *paṭṭu* for fifteen. By adding these three divisions together, the total number of *paṭṭus* with *lekhās* is twenty-eight. Those who possess wisdom should observe this arrangement and construct the *devīsāyujya-paṭhadāṭava* (the sacred forest of union with the Goddess) in a square shape, beginning from the lower part. Thus it should be done by the wise.

(Commentary): Regarding the sequence of houses constructed by Īpaṭhavaṇṇu, there are 236 houses situated on the serpent-shaped layout for the reciter (*paṭhaka*). Starting from the first house of the Kelaginaśūla hell, for each of the thirteen houses, there are 1 house and 15 houses; thus, including the 225 houses, there is 1 marked house within the 16th house of divine union (*devīsāyujya*), totaling 11. Adding these to the 16 houses, there are 236 houses in total.

Along with the three *ḍālagalu* (small measures) and the inscriptions therein, for every four *ḍālagalu*, one *ḍāla* [is calculated] as one empty *paṭṭu*. For the remaining three *paṭṭus*, they are 1, 2, and 3; for one *ḍāla*, one empty *paṭṭu*; for the remaining three *paṭṭus*, they are 4, 5, and 6; for one *ḍāla*, one empty *paṭṭu*; for the remaining three *paṭṭus*, they are 7, 8, and 9. By means of these three sets of *ḍālagalu*, starting from the bottom, there are eighteen units. Having had the wise ones calculate this according to the number of *purāṇas* in the sequence, and having fashioned the *kaḍame* (the vessel/base), those who are intelligent should examine it so that it attains the status of a *paṭa* (cloth/panel) for union (*sāyujya*) with the Goddess in the form of a square (*caturaśrākṛti*).

In the Śālivāhana Śaka year measured by six, five, seven, and one (1756).
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Saturday.
By the illustrious King Kṛṣṇarāja, who is filled with compassion for Śrī Cāmuṇḍā.
For the sake of attaining liberation through union with the Goddess, he assumed a form possessing the universal aspect.
And for the satisfaction of those who play, by means of the wise one's playing.

Having composed the text for the recitation regarding the liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) with the Goddess in her square form, he then composed the sequence of verses for the recitation of the hymn describing her in her cosmic form (*viśvarūpa*). This was inscribed on a stone slab (*lekhya-śilā*) as follows: "In the midst of the cosmic form of the Mother of the World, who dwells upon the peak of the Great Mountain of Mahābala—within which there exist two hundred and thirty-six temples containing the creation of both sentient and insentient beings. (Verse 1)
They say that the universe is but a single atom; [they claim] liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti) is merely the movement of a serpent upon a pillar.
O Rucisiddha Śrī Kṛṣṇa Mahārāja, you who protect the entirety of the excellent path! || 2 ||
The ninth day of the latter fortnight of Śrāvaṇa in the year of victory marked by the digits of taste (six), arrows (five), sages (seven), and kuraṅgas (deer, i.e., one).
The poets, trembling on the swing of their verses, describe him as being like the moon and the stars. || 3 ||

(Commentary) — Regarding the sequence for composing this [work]: there are 236 verses in total on the *Śrīdevīviśvarūpākṛti-paṭala*. The details for each verse are as follows: In the first verse, there are 7 verses; in the second verse, 11 verses; in the third verse, 13 verses; in the fourth verse, 15 verses; in the fifth verse, 17 verses; in the sixth verse, 19 verses; in the seventh verse, 19 verses; in the eighth verse, 19 verses; in the ninth verse, 19 verses; in the tenth verse, 19 verses; in the eleventh verse, 17 verses; in the twelfth verse, 15 verses; in the thirteenth verse, 14 verses; in the fourteenth verse, 13 verses; in the fifteenth verse, 11 verses; and in the sixteenth verse, 7 verses. Thus, there are 236 verses in total.

(Verse)—

(Commentary) — Regarding the sequence for composing the *Īpapaṭṭu*: for one who possesses the form of Vṛndāvana, there are 236 units (*maṇe*) in the sixteen *sālū* [units] up to the first *sālū* of the *kelagina śūlanaraka*, which bestows liberation through union with the Goddess (*devīsāyujyamukti*). For those who possess the *meliṇa-sālū*, there are sixteen *sālū*. The details are as follows: For the first *sālū*: 19 *maṇe*. For the second *sālū*: 19 *maṇe*. For the third *sālū*: 19 *maṇe*. For the fourth *sālū*: 17 *maṇe*. For the fifth *sālū*: 15 *maṇe*. For the sixth *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the seventh *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the eighth *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the ninth *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the tenth *sālū*: 15 *maṇe*. For the eleventh *sālū*: 15 *maṇe*. For the twelfth *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the thirteenth *sālū*: 13 *maṇe*. For the fourteenth *sālū*: 11 *maṇe*. For the fifteenth *sālū*: 17 *maṇe*. For the sixteenth *sālū*: excluding the central *maṇe* marked within the *meliṇa-sālū*, those who possess it receive 11 *maṇe* for liberation through union with the Goddess (*devīsāyujyamukti*). Thus, in the sixteen *vaṭṭu-sālū*, there are 236 *maṇe*.

In this *āṭakke* (multiplication table), there are twenty-eight squares (*ḍālagalu*) corresponding to the number of constellations (*nakṣatras*). For the sake of calculation, the squares are numbered from one to twenty-eight. In the first square (*ḍāla*), there is one row (*paṭṭu*) and it is empty (*khālī*). In the remaining three rows, the numbers are 1-2-3. In the second square, there is no row; in the remaining three rows, the numbers are 4-7-10. In the third square, there is one row with no written numbers; in the remaining three rows, the numbers are 13-14-15. By following this method through three squares, one arrives at the number twenty-eight. Therefore, those who possess intelligence should observe that the subsequent sequence forms a square shape (*caturaśrākṛti*). One should look for it thus.

By the illustrious King Kṛṣṇarāja, who was filled with compassion for Śrī Cāmuṇḍā.
In that fourfold army, he was stationed within an impenetrable array in the form of Garuḍa.
The minister who was a lion to the great king Śrī Kṛṣṇarāja, who composed the *Śiruvai* [poem] titled *Caturaṅgabhedya-vāda-gāruḍavyūha*, and who,

(Commentary)—For each of these eight divisions (*aṣṭaka*), there are 48 units (*kāyi*): 2 kings (*arasu*), 2 chief ministers (*pradhāni*), 4 foot-soldiers (*vaṃṭe*), 4 chariots (*ratha*), 4 banners (*patāke*), 4 elephants (*kuṭure*), 4 horses (*āne*), and 24 infantry (*ālu*). Thus, there are 48 units per division. For these eight divisions, there are 12 houses (*mane*) for each king, totaling 144 houses for the twelve kings. The manner in which these units are to be deployed is as follows: the king, the chief minister, the foot-soldiers, the elephants, the horses, and the infantry shall march together as a fourfold army (*caturaṅga-danta*). When the chariots advance, they shall march behind the four divisions; that is, two houses behind each of those [four] divisions. The banners shall be placed in the middle, two houses behind the [chariots], and shall march behind the [preceding] division.
33. This is the sequence of the distinctions in the movement of the four limbs:
one who possesses abundant lines that are slightly curved, whose acquisition of wealth is stable, and who is dear to his elders.
Intense with the flavor of desire, sung to by the sounds of the lute-like fingers of passion. || 1 ||
With weapons firmly grasped by enemies who were like thick, dark-colored bulls upon the stage of the battlefield.
His mind was uplifted by the stories of various groves that shone with the splendor of the jewels within his home.
Bakhanī was described as having a neck marked by lines like a conch shell, with hands as dark as Rādhā.
In the assembly of the fourfold army of the black-king horse.
34. Now, the sequence for the extraction of the Śrīcakra (from the Vāmakeśvaratantra):
[It consists of] a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, a pair of ten-cornered figures, a fourteen-cornered figure, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and a sixteen-cornered figure.
The three circles and the earth, along with the three abodes—this is declared to be the Śrīcakra of the Supreme Deity. || 1 ||
Another description of the characteristics of the Śrīcakra (from the *Saubhāgyalaharī* composed by Śrī Śaṅkarācārya):
[The Cakra is formed] by four Śrīkaṇṭhas, by five youthful wives of Śiva who are distinct from one another, and by the nine primordial natures (*mūlaprakṛtis*) of Śambhu.
Together with the forty-four petals of the earth, the digits, the three circles, and the three lines, the corners of your feet have been transformed. || 1 ||
35. Now, the names of the deities of the Śrīcakra—(from the *Lalitārcanamañjarī*, within the eighth chapter of the thirteenth section, and from the *Jñānārṇava*):
The Earth-mansion, the lotus with sixteen petals, the eight-petaled [lotus], and the nine-cornered [figure]. || 1 ||
It consists of two sets of ten spokes, eight spokes, and a triangle in the center, according to their divisions.
The wheel that deludes the three worlds and fulfills all desires. || 2 ||
The wheel that agitates all and bestows all good fortune.
The supreme wheel that accomplishes all aims and provides all protection.
The wheel that removes all diseases and bestows all accomplishments.
The ninth, consisting of all-bliss, is the central leader of the wheels.
He who understands the ninefold convention of the wheels is a true worshiper.
They are manifest, as well as concealed, and further, most highly concealed. || 5 ||
The Sampradāyas, the Kulās, the Kaulās, the Nigarbhas, and the Rahasyakas.
These eight are the secrets of the higher and the lower, and they are the most ancient of secrets.
The ninefold convention of names for the yoginīs is prescribed.
She is Tripurā, the Mistress of the Three Cities, the Beautiful One dwelling within the City.
Śrī, Mālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī.
This, known as the convention of consciousness (vijñāna-saṃketa), is indeed the ultimate resort in times of extreme distress.
That group of nine, having its tradition purified, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Here, because of the statement "the one preceded by Ati-rahasya," and because of the statement of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, "O Yoginī named Parāpararahasya, you are preceded by Ati," these are the names of the nine Cakra-yoginīs: Parā, Aparā, Atirahasya, and Yoginī. May there be auspiciousness. 9.

Thus ends the ninth treasure, titled "The Description of Great Delights such as the Game of Dice and Cards," in the work named *Śrītattvanidhi*, composed by the illustrious Mahārāja Kṛṣṇarāja, the sovereign of the preeminent city of Śrī-Mahīśūra; he who is the ornament of the entire circle of the earth, the crest-jewel of all lands, the presiding deity of the Karṇāṭaka country; who shines resplendently in the midst of the great seat of the glorious Mahīśūra; who has ascended the divine jeweled throne experienced by the entire circle of his own sovereign emperors and great kings, beginning with the hereditary royal protectors descended from a lineage of full moons of arts; who is adorned with numerous titles such as: the Illustrious Sovereign of Kings, Supreme Lord, King of Kings, Possessor of Majestic Valor, Incomparable Heroic Monarch, Forehead of the Sky among Birudas, Sole Hero of the World, Moon in the Ocean of the Yadu Clan, Conch, Discus, Goad, Axe, Crocodile, Fish, Śarabha, Sālva, Gaṇḍabheruṇḍa, Earth-Boar, Hanuman, Garuḍa, Lion, and so forth. 9.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Treasury of Curiosities, in the treatise known as the *Śrītattvanidhi*. 9.
